div.head: PRAEFATIO EDITORIS.

p.s: Nearly all of the speeches of August Boeckh contained in this volume were delivered to celebrate the same solemn occasion, the most joyful birthday of the most august King of Prussia.
to these are added two special speeches:
the one that was delivered at the dedication of the University of Berlin, and the funeral oration in praise of Frederick William III.
The author would not have wished these speeches to be published again in a single collection now, had not many people, who had once heard one or two of them, requested it.
However, he would not have seen to their publication on his own initiative, because there are things in them that seem to him to require excuse.
First, because what the author said in each year was adapted to the events and conditions of that year, then, when the speeches were delivered, it was easily understood what each point referred to:
now, after many years have elapsed, statements may seem to have been made in general which were directed at the state of affairs at that time.

Secondly, the author observed that, even against his own intention, the mention of certain matters was repeated in these speeches, because similarity of time or subject had prompted similar statements.
The author excused repetitions of this kind here and there, as on pp. 217 and 296, and considers that he did not say entirely the same things about the same matters.
In the third place, the author confesses that during more turbulent times and events he spoke not without anger and passion;
which the condition of the times excuses.

This matter relates especially to the second speech, in which statements made somewhat more harshly, even if they were acceptable to the listeners then, the author would now have omitted or retracted, had this alteration not seemed both to erase the memory of that time and the picture expressed in that speech, and to be, as it were, a sort of censure of those feelings and struggles by which all Prussia was then agitated.

The orator himself freely confesses on p. 241
that in these speeches he not infrequently indulged a somewhat irritated mind and complied with hatreds that the nature of the times dictated;
and in the same place he took care to warn that enmities ought to be laid aside as soon as an opportunity for reconciliation was offered.

Therefore the author hopes that no one will judge from what was then said with greater bitterness how he himself is disposed in this most happy reconciliation of princes and highly civilized nations which we now enjoy.
As for the style of speaking, the author did not strive to make it similar to the Ciceronian, but set other models before himself as well.
Thus he did not hesitate to follow the usage of the Silver Age, nor did he observe all those rules of the grammarians that rely primarily on Cicero.
Indeed, at times he deliberately departed from them and sought out some rarer expression or word.
In a few places, however, the choice of words, the structure, and a few other things were changed upon second thought, which it will suffice to have noted in general.

Furthermore, it will easily be recognized that the style of speech is not the same in all the speeches, but over the long series of years during which the author delivered these Latin speeches in the discharge of his official duty, it gradually changed to some extent.
I have added the principal arguments of the speeches summarized in a brief overview, a practice, I believe, by no means useless.
Written at Berlin on the Nones of January in the year

div.head: I. Oratio nataliciis Friderici Guilelmi III. celebrandis d. III. Aug. a. MDCCCXII. habita.
On Sparta and Athens, the most famous republics among the Greeks

p.s: When the Senate of this literary community invited some of you and summoned others to hear the speech with which we have resolved to celebrate the birthday of the best of kings, not according to custom but from the heart, most distinguished, most noble, most learned gentlemen, and most beloved fellow soldiers:
We think that none of you was unaware of what was to be expected in this token of public joy.
For Frederick William, the most modest and most civil of kings, does not demand to be praised by word of mouth and in speech;
rather than because he gives laws to the state, but, as he seems to wise Greeks a king ought to be, he himself serves as a living law:

he wants the memory of his virtue to be inscribed on the hearts of citizens, as on tablets, so that, following his example, they may approve, praise, cultivate, and practice moderation, justice, piety, constancy, and finally all the good arts that pertain to the public safety.
Therefore all panegyric praise will be absent, the more so because this entire genre, partly from its praisers, partly from those who were praised, has drawn some slight stigma.

For from the time when the republic of the Athenians, by an excellent policy, established that citizens who, fighting bravely against the enemy, had met a glorious death for their country should be publicly praised:

Although the subject was excellent and magnificent, nevertheless even in treating this subject the greatest orators could not escape the appearance of flattery, because they preferred to wander off into praises of the living rather than to dwell on the virtues of the dead in extolling them.
Although the fault was less in this praise of living men, because not one or another, but the whole state was being praised:
But when the supreme power was transferred from many to one, the praise that had begun from a most noble origin fell back into base and servile flattery.

For to pass over the Greeks, who, when their liberty was extinguished, when that incredible ardor of mind by which they were borne to every most excellent deed was extinguished, and finally when their ancient virtue was extinguished, seemed foolish even to the admirers of the Greek name:
Who would approve the Panegyric of Pliny in every part, although it was spoken before that emperor than whom the earth bore no better?
Who, indeed, a little more liberal, would be delighted with Eumenius, Nazarius, Latinus Pacatus, both Mamertini, and others of this school?
You may excuse their adulatory disgrace by the misfortune of the times;
But who is there among us that would not proclaim us blessed, because we obey this King, whom it is both permitted to praise without flattery and not to praise without offense?
But if I had thought that you, listeners, would wait for the King to be praised worthily by my proclamation, whose accumulated benefits to the fatherland are proclaimed by the voice of all;
truly, conscious of my own weakness, I would never have undertaken to ascend here:
but since I know that something lighter is demanded of me, I console myself in some measure with your indulgence for the scantiness of my talent.
Nevertheless, to grant that that which is by far the most difficult both is and is considered to be, has been remitted;
How great it is to speak on this day, before this assembly, from this place, on any subject whatsoever, everyone understands who wishes to measure the dignity of the matter with a just standard.
But I, myself called into the crisis, feel it so strongly that it almost overwhelms my mind.

For, as Cicero made Licinius Crassus say, it is a great burden and duty to undertake and profess that one, while all are silent, is to be heard alone on the greatest matters in a large assembly of men.
But what an assembly this is, and how great!
What a province, and how great, has been entrusted to me!
It seems so great to me, listeners, that when I consider each detail, my hope already fails that I can respond adequately to it.

For first I must speak not in a mediocre town, but in a foremost city, which has for a long time been most full of urbanity and learning, and in a certain sense in the very royal court, celebrated not a little with the praises of learning.

Then I see here seated the most noble and most distinguished men of the state, and among them, both the overseers and presidents of sacred affairs and of the disciplines of studies throughout the Prussian land, and also of our literary republic, most grave men, who know how to set aside an uncivil and imprudent saying with a witty and wise one most skillfully.
That my speech is approved by them, as I ought to desire greatly, so I scarcely, and not even scarcely, dare to hope.
Moreover, I see gathered here both the fathers of this university and other men distinguished by the fame of their learning and talent.
The more learned each of them is, and the more equipped with sharpness of mind and sense of elegance, the more keenly they must notice faults in the speaker.

Finally, you, fellow soldiers, are present in great number, for whom, that I may narrate something useful for learning, the reason of our affairs seems to demand, but the popularity of the oratorical genre scarcely tolerates it.
Finally, I am not playing my own role, which is indeed a light one.
I am playing the part of the Senate, which is by far the most important, since it has appointed me as the public interpreter of its feelings.
It did this because of the favorable opinion it has conceived of me, not because of my modesty.
When I consider these things, how do you think I am disposed?

Why should I bring forward something worthy in some measure of the celebration of this very day, of the grandeur of this place, of the most crowded assembly of these most distinguished men, and finally of the authority of the most renowned college, which chose me as its speaker?
Listen to what I have devised.

Since I despaired that it could be brought about that I should render any argument so adorned by my diligence that not only the matter but also the talent of the speaker would be approved by you, and since the allurements of oratory and words as if branded with curling irons seemed no less alien to your dignity, to these times of the republic, and especially to the singular gravity of our King, to whom this day is consecrated:
I have chosen a subject that is connected both with our affairs and with my studies, one that would recommend itself by its own weight rather than require any art or eloquence of mine.
I will, however, present to you the images of two cities, which were the most famous among the Greek cities, sketched with first lines:
of which the one was tempered by wise institutions and laws, but was separated by a very long interval from letters and more elegant learning;
The one, by means of all the best arts, not only flourished itself, but imbued, illuminated, and made gentle and tame the whole world:
When these are compared and contrasted with each other, no one will be found who hesitates in casting up the reckoning, which of the two was more effective in forming humanity.

When I mention these, who is there that does not understand that I mean Sparta and Athens, the one established divinely by the Apolline laws of Lycurgus, the other ordered by the liberal institutions of Solon:
Was not each of these states ennobled both by its own splendor and greatness, and by the brilliant talents of the ancient writers, who would not allow the deeds performed by them to remain obscure?
As I adorn this Sparta, as they say, in order to discuss briefly something about these states, grant me this, listeners, that the course of my speech may be aided by the breeze of your favor.
Indeed, when I consider Sparta, I see no commonwealth ever more firmly established, or more distinguished by the virtue of its citizens, so domestic as well as military, at home and abroad.

This they owed partly to the benefit of nature, which had equipped them with those arts so that they seemed born and made for pure and strict morals, and partly to the wisdom of the legislator, by which it was provided that they should never deviate from the simplicity of their ancient way of life.
Since he understood that nothing contributes so much to the happiness of mortals as if they used laws that best suited the character of each people,

For the Dorians, a rustic and hardy nation, accustomed to cultivating mountains, hunting, and waging war, he so described their way of life, as it were, to a rule, that he directed their ancient pursuits to good fruit, confirmed their constant and firm character, preserved the frugality of the old age, tempered their innate ferocity with institutions both sacred and profane, and turned them especially from internal discords, by which they were previously troubled, against their enemies.

He also perceived very wisely that men could not be restrained from continually attempting new things unless the law, which they would fear to harm or diminish, were sanctioned by the majesty of the divine power, so that it might always remain.
And therefore he referred those ordinances to Pythian Apollo, by which the precepts of public discipline were contained.

And whereas in other states laws were given for a time, so that they could be repealed as soon as it pleased the people, at Sparta he proposed them on such a condition that they should never be invalid, and never be rescinded.
Thus it came about that the ancient form of the republic lasted for a very long time, and nowhere were the minds of citizens bound by law more religiously than at Sparta.
But not all had the full rights of citizenship, but the nobles, or Spartans, especially of Dorian stock, who had fixed their abode in the city of Sparta, and excelled in prudence and courage:
The rest of the Laconians lived in towns and fields, free in appearance, but in reality subject.
They say that at a certain time the Laconian land was so divided that nine thousand lots were assigned to the Spartans, thirty thousand to the Laconians, one to each individual:
And it was established that no one should ever become richer than another, so that it was not permitted to buy or sell, to give or bequeath, or to divide the land.
The inheritance passed intact to the eldest son;
It was forbidden to give a dowry to daughters;
Hence two or more portions could not in ancient times come to one person.
The power of the kings was circumscribed by the narrowest limits:
The authority of the ephors, guardians of the people, was at first small, but increased with the ruin of the times:
The senate of twenty-eight men, which before the domination of the Ephors had held the highest power, was chosen from the nobles, being at least sixty years old and distinguished by singular probity;
Nor was dignity extinguished except with life.
And no one is ignorant of what power this equal division of goods and the rule of the best men had.

For since it is established that in the states of the ancients very many disturbances and changes of the republic arose from the excessive inequality of wealth, which Phaleas of Chalcedon, Philolaus of Thebes, and Plato in his ideal state, which he founded in his work on laws, diligently strove to remove;
and since it is equally established that popular dominion, as the license of the common people grows, easily declines into the most arrogant tyranny either of the mob or of one man:
So strong were the Dorian institutions of the Spartans that the state, though disturbed by very rare innovations, never experienced the violence of any tyrant before Machanidas and Nabis.

But the fact that the Spartans obeyed their elders, and those holding the magistracy for life, gave occasion to Aristotle's criticism, who said that this was to be endured where the citizens are upright and well trained:
Yet he says that the same men were not regarded as such by the lawgiver himself;
And just as there is a certain old age of the body, so he reminds us that there is one of the mind.
However that may be, I would certainly contend that the stability of the republic could not have been better provided for than by this honor paid to old age.
For who is more tenacious of the old state of affairs than a composed and moderate old age?
Who is more eager for new things than the sharp and hot temperaments of young men just flying into public life?
And how great is the wisdom of old men?
How great their knowledge of affairs!
What counsels!
What gravity!
What constancy!

Therefore the Spartans, since they thought that boldness belongs to the flourishing age and prudence to the aging one, wanted the young men to excel in bodily strength, in battle and with the sword, and they judged that the things which are administered by reason, judgment, and spirit should be done by the old:
And therefore the highest council of the state, which the Athenians called the Council, at Sparta was both the Senate and was called so.
And just as in a family the highest honor is given to the father of the family, so at Sparta, which the lawgiver strove to make one and undivided family, the greatest reverence was for the elders.

But how they arranged their domestic affairs and marriages, and by what arts they trained their boys and adolescents to temperance, prudence, fortitude, piety, and obedience to the laws, I do not wish to relate to those who know.
But what shall I say, how the legislator kept them from trade, from maritime business, from agriculture and other illiberal occupations?
And indeed, trading was not permitted even to a Senator at Rome.
And at Thebes, those who wished to enter public life had to abstain from all profit-making for ten years.

But for the Spartans, trade was all the more to be disapproved, because it brought both that fatal inequality of wealth and base greed for gain to ancient states, and imported very many things that were by no means necessary for passing life, and not only these, but also foreign arts and customs, which they wished to be guarded against ever approving by those laws by which natives were forbidden to go abroad before old age, and foreigners to stay in the city without any suitable reason.
But you may rightly wonder that the pursuit of cultivating fields did not hold strong and most patient men.

In this matter they held that the Romans, who were equally warlike, disagreed greatly, and that as long as the old discipline flourished, they so wonderfully delighted in agricultural affairs that nothing seemed more honorable to them than a rustic life;
so that in this the Senators were occupied, and those old men;
as in Cicero, M.

To Cato, the pleasures of farmers, among whom he himself lived, seemed to come closest to the life of a wise man, not only because of the fruit that came from it, but because of the wonderful power and nature of the earth itself.

But why do I linger on these matters, which ought to be touched upon and mentioned here, not unfolded and explained, and why do I not hasten more quickly to that for the sake of which these things have been undertaken by me?

For the mention of foreign arts has reminded me to speak about the education of the Spartans, provided that you grant me this indulgence, that I may call by the word 'education' whatever Lacedaemon either produced or endured similar to this.

And so, when the legislator wanted the citizens' way of life to be very simple, he partly expelled, partly restrained, and held as if bound in custody, along with all the instruments of luxury, also literature and the arts, in the manner of the Egyptians, among whom the Greeks relate that the modes of song handed down ten thousand years before have neither become obsolete through the decay of antiquity nor have ever been changed:

Indeed, when comparing the condition of the arts among the Lacedaemonians with that among the Athenians, you may see there statues of crude workmanship with compressed feet, but here statues of the most perfect kind, fashioned with Daedalian, that is, Attic skill, so that they seem to live and walk freely.
The Spartans did not allow any art to be practiced among them that was less approved by the kings, senators, and ephors, the arbiters of morals.
To them nothing newfangled was greatly approved.
At Rome the censors, Gnaeus...

Domitius Ahenobarbus and Lucius Licinius Crassus, when the Latin rhetoricians had opened a school, and there the young men were spending whole days, in an edict by which they were showing their opinion, that these things did not please them, placed these words:

Domitius Ahenobarbus and Lucius Licinius Crassus, when the Latin rhetoricians had opened a school, and there the young men were spending whole days, in an edict by which they were showing their opinion, that these things did not please them, placed these words:
Our ancestors established what their children should learn and to what schools they should go.
These new things, which are done contrary to custom and the practice of our ancestors, neither please nor seem right. This was done at Rome more than once in a free republic:
At Sparta in its best times it was never not observed.

Therefore, content with a brevity full of prudence and strength, which was not peculiar to the Laconians but to the Dorian stock, and which they shared especially with the Argives, they scorned those adorned and, as it were, anointed with ointments incantations of artificial speech:
Therefore, among them there was no zeal for hidden and sublime wisdom, no zeal for handing down to the memory of posterity, in elegant discourse, the deeds of the past:

Therefore they listened to the sophist Hippias discoursing not about the position and motions of the stars, nor about geometry, or numbers, or letters, or harmonies, or rhythms, but about the deeds of heroes, about cities founded long ago, about prudent institutions and laws.
Nevertheless, sculpture had honor and esteem, because of the images of the gods and the reverence for temples.
And the names of Doryclidas, Dontas, and Callicrates, Spartan craftsmen, are not obscure.
Nor were music and poetry, combined with dance, despised.

But because they believed that nothing could be instilled more quickly or more deeply into young minds, and nothing could contribute more to correcting or corrupting morals, than either modest or wanton movements of the body, and rhythms and measures either severe and grave, or light and frivolous;
They carefully took care that no ancient discipline of morals should suffer harm from these arts.

Therefore, they wanted boys to be trained from the fifth year of age only in the gymnopaedic dance, the most calm and moderate of all, and in the pyrrhic dance, invented by themselves with Aristoxenus as authority, in which they practiced warlike affairs.
But those soft Ionic bends, made famous by their wantonness, they ordered to be exiled forever.
In music, however, they embraced the ancient modes of Terpander, by which the precepts of public discipline are thought to have been described.
And not without reason did they boast that they, of all people, had longest resisted the corruption of ancient music that had been introduced throughout Greece.

A public document of this matter is reported to be a decree, by which they punished Timotheus of Miletus, the most famous artist of his age, who, when he had come to Sparta, and having despised the seven strings of the ancient Muse, singing with eleven sounds, and having introduced various and effeminate modes of the chromatic scale instead of the simple harmony, and, as it is in the decree, had corrupted the ears of the young men, and also, in the games of Ceres Eleusinia, having adorned a play with too little decorum, had taught the boys the sorrows of Semele:

He is said to have been publicly reproved by the Kings and the Ephors and forced to cut down from eleven strings, which were more than seven, so that anyone, having observed the severity of the republic, might revere Sparta and not bring anything dishonorable into it, nor ever diminish the glory of musical contests.

If you say that the Lacedaemonians were wrong in this, at least you should hold this: that the most skilled in music among the ancients, and among them Dionysius of Halicarnassus and Plutarch, judged that music was corrupted by Timotheus and those like him.

What about the fact that even Homer was not dismissed without reproach by the Spartans, because he imitated not the Doric life, that is, frugal and self-controlled, but the Ionian life full of luxury and wickedness?

With the support of men both upright and wise, even in this censure of the highest genius—Pythagoras of Samos, Xenophanes of Colophon, Heraclitus of Ephesus, and Plato, the philosopher of divine mind:
so that not unjustly the Lacedaemonians seem to some to be regarded as the authors and teachers of the most ancient wisdom.
Moreover, they used the poems of Tyrtaeus, the incentives of martial valor, not only as marching songs when advancing to battle, but also in camp after dinner each one sang them in competition.

But let us call ourselves back from the affairs of the Spartans, in which I see that I have lingered too long, and let us wander into the more joyful and more delightful fields of Attic learning, where we see the liberal arts born, nurtured, and perfected.
When I think of entering them, and of walking about in them with you as in carefully planted gardens;

I am not unaware that if I wished to pursue so great and so noble a subject more fully in my own manner and style, the deeds could not be matched by my words, and I clearly understand that not only would the abundance of material render me lacking in counsel, and that the day would sooner fail than I should have done the work's worth, but also that it would have to be feared lest the unfruitful recollection of things most well known should create weariness for you.
And for this reason it seems to me both fitting and safer to deal briefly with a matter of this kind, in which, even if you were to be more lengthy, you would nevertheless not accomplish much.

Therefore, when I say that the character of Athens is opposed to that of Sparta with a contrary front, whether I look at the form and institutions of the state, or at the condition of the citizens, their way of life and culture as a whole, I think I do not stray far from the truth.

For the Ionian race, which, after having once inhabited the northern shores of the Peloponnese, was received by the kindred inhabitants of the Attic coast and later occupied the maritime regions of Asia Minor and very many islands, declared by the very choice of its abodes, most suitable for the landing of ships and for commerce, that wonderful agility of mind, a disposition more mobile than firm, and a love of a freer life, which, according to Aristotle's judgment, is generally connected with maritime pursuits:

So far is it from being the case that it has endured the rule of the best men for a long time, or that it has considered the strict discipline of morals, in which the Spartans delighted, tolerable, that it has even judged a life of this kind more suitable for slaves than for free men, and scarcely worth living.
And so, to pass over Theseus, whom they proclaim not only to have vindicated the liberty of the citizens, but also to venerate as a kind and present god even to the slaves themselves:

You know that in the time of Solon, after many disasters of factions, the affairs of Athens had come to this point: that, after debts and the bond by which the poor were bound to the nobles had been shaken off, after that troublesome institution of the peoples of the East had been removed—which had assigned to each tribe its own proper way of life, separated by place, customs, and intermarriage—after the power of the Eupatridae had finally been abolished and shared with all citizens except the proletarians, all enjoyed nearly equal rights, and yet the rule of the common people was not unbridled; for Solon had provided, both by the supreme authority of the Areopagus, that most sacred senate and court, and by the most salutary laws, that such a thing should never arise—laws not passed with the intention that they could never be changed, but with the power given to the people to propose new ones.

In the following time, however, by what means through Clisthenes, and then, together with the growth of the Athenian naval forces, through the efforts of Themistocles, but especially through that famous tyranny of Pericles, the power of the people increased to such a degree that in the age of the Peloponnesian War the furious assembly could be held by no laws, governed by no counsel, deterred by no religion from the most savage and most unrestrained undertakings.
There is no reason why I should explain it more fully.

What of the fact that the slaves themselves, having observed the examples of their masters, and with a law having been passed that no free person should be allowed to beat a slave, became more free and more arrogant than the citizens of Sparta?
Whence Plato wittily declares that in Athens the insolence even of dogs and donkeys is more shameless than in the other lands of Greece.

And yet this freedom or rather license of the Attic people, after the ancient constitution of the republic and the salutary laws had been utterly overthrown, although it proved fatal to very many citizens who had deserved excellently of their country;
although it inflicted a serious wound upon sound morals, and nourished depraved desires in such a way that, like watered grass, they grew up most abundantly;
finally, although it brought the very liberty of Athens into the greatest danger:
Yet it had such force that nowhere did a more joyful and more abundant harvest of all the liberal arts flourish.
No one is unaware that they are nourished and strengthened by nothing more than by liberty, but are cast down and uprooted by illiberal servitude as if by some calamity of a storm.

I maintain that it could not have happened that Athens should rise to the highest summit of universal learning, and should become the parents, nurses, and teachers of nearly all disciplines and arts, unless the laws of the state had granted to its citizens a freer manner of life and a more elegant and more refined mode of living, and had not only not deterred them from cultivating the arts by the example of the Lacedaemonians, but had also bestowed much praise upon literature and learning.
I shall offer as proof of this matter, if I see anything at all, an argument that is by no means weak.

For when Thespis had begun to produce tragedy at Athens, and the common people were greatly delighted by it because of the novelty of the thing, and yet such plays were not yet performed among the public contests;
Solon, naturally teachable and eager to learn even in old age, is said to have watched Thespis performing his plays.
After the spectacle, however, he is said to have asked Thespis whether he was not ashamed to tell such lies and fabrications before so large an assembly.
But when the poet answered that it was not unworthy to say and do things of that kind for the sake of jest, they report that Solon alone, striking him with his staff, cried out:

"But truly it will not be long before we find this mockery, once it has been praised and approved, in the commerce of men." They say that this was said by a lover of ancient and simple wisdom, who nevertheless was himself so excellent a poet that Critias not unjustly declared of him that, had he not devoted these studies to civil affairs and the management of the state, he would have equaled the glory of Homer with his poems:
And others add that he forbade Thespis from performing his plays.
Now even if we grant that these things are false and fabricated, as learned men have abundantly demonstrated by reasoning,

Do you think that, if anything of this sort had happened in Athens, so that the noblest poetry of tragedy had been ordered into exile by Solon's law, it would have emerged so greatly in the following times that it would have roused those three men of divine spirit to practice that art, so that it was established by Aeschylus' sublimity and magnificence, perfected by Sophocles' perfection, and illustrated by Euripides' wisdom, and that it could do so much for forming honesty and the sense of the beautiful and right?
But because at Athens, not only by strength of body and swiftness, as in other Greek states, was glory next to immortality obtained, but also in musical contests a palm was set before them;
because there tragic and comic plays, in the solemn games celebrated for Bacchus, were publicly entrusted at great expense;
Attracted by no small prizes, men of outstanding talent applied themselves to this musical pursuit with the greatest exertion;
Nor did the dramatic art fall before the resources of the state were exhausted and the fortunes of the citizens, weakened, were no longer equal to those immense expenditures once made on the stage.
But what shall I say of oratory, which is almost peculiar to Athens?
Would it ever have reached the summit from its ancient simplicity, if it had not been cultivated in courts and assemblies?
What of philosophy?

Would Socrates have investigated with such subtlety the limits of goods and evils, virtues and vices, duties, and the governance of the state, and would he have brought the study of wisdom from the investigation of things hidden in the darkness of nature down to common life and, as it were, into the society of men?

Would Plato, a disciple equal to his master, have embraced with his lofty mind the knowledge of things divine and human, and would he have handed it down with those allurements of words by which, the more refined each person is, the more he is captivated and held fast?
Would Aristotle's vast and keen mind have traversed the entire universe of learning?

Would these triumvirs have held bound by their authority not only the gentiles, both Greek and Roman, but also men of the Christian faith through all ages, even the most obscure, and would they still hold them today, if such a decree had stood at Athens as the decree by which the Spartans are said to have branded Timotheus of Miletus?
When Sophocles of Sunium had attempted this, a law was passed that philosophers should not open schools, unless it had pleased the Senate and People of Athens.

Whoever had done otherwise would have been liable to capital punishment; so badly did it turn out for him that in the following year the Athenians, having repealed the law, fined him five talents and decreed the return of the philosophers.

And so, since even in the times of lost liberty it seemed unworthy of this people that any art should be either proscribed or restrained by laws, provided only that the ancestral religion were not violated:
which was charged against many, justly against some, as Protagoras of Abdera, unjustly against others, as Anaxagoras and Socrates:

What wonder is it that the city of the Athenians was the workshop of speaking and letters and the emporium of all praiseworthy arts, and that it so excelled among the other Greeks in the glory of learning, especially from the age of Pericles, that it was both called and was the eye of Greece and the Hellas of Hellas?

Now, therefore, when you ask which of the two states lived more happily under these laws, these institutions and customs, I answer that both were equally happy, as long as they obeyed the will and plans of the lawgiver, partly because I follow those great founders of laws with the reverence that is due, and partly because I greatly desire the praise of a fair judge, if there is any, since the way of life prescribed by the laws suited the pursuits of each, to which nature itself had led them.
Sparta stood most firmly for a very long time, living well with little;
Nor is Tacitus's most weighty saying more fittingly applied to the Germans than to Sparta:
"No one there laughs at vices, nor is corrupting and being corrupted called the fashion of the age"; moreover, it was ignorant of very many vices with which other states were afflicted:

From this it came about that Socrates, Xenophon, Plato, and every most prudent one of the ancients approved the Spartan state with their votes, to such an extent that they called it most just and most equitable, and judged that it came closest to perfection.
What of the fact that Plato's two famous models of the perfect republic are not more similar to any of the Greek states than to the Laconian?

What of the fact that Solon, when he declared that his laws were not the best, but such as could have been enacted, and boasted that he knew better ones, seems to have meant none other than the Dorian laws of Pythian Apollo?
What of the fact that in Italy the Pythagoreans, the most divine of the wise, in order to make the people truly blessed, established a form of state not unlike this to a great degree?

But from the time when the Spartans departed from their ancient simplicity, from the time when, after very many of the noblest families had been destroyed in war, the lots of the suburban lands came back to about a thousand wealthy men, from the time when this iron race began to gape after gold, and all the coins from all Greece and from the barbarian world flowed together into Sparta, whence, like beasts from the lairs of a lion, they would never have gone forth:
From that time onward, corrupted and defiled by luxury, ambition, avarice, and all sorts of evil arts, they degenerated the more shamefully, the less nature had made them prone to vices of that kind.

But that Athens, splendid and illustrious, the glory and pillar of Greece, as the Theban bard declared, was blessed in its laws before they left it — why should I undertake to persuade those already persuaded?

For now the sails must be furled, and many things must be omitted, which I cannot include in the course of a single hour, so that at least I may mention one thing, which does not seem to me foreign either to this place or to these times.
Indeed, Sparta benefited few citizens:
Athens propagated the most abundant fruits of talents throughout the world.
That one, great in strength, virtue, and deeds, [was] not [great] in benefits to outsiders:
These have worked not for themselves alone, but for the human race.
Sparta fell:

The learning of Athens, like runners passing on a torch, generations have handed down to generations, and will hand down henceforth into the everlasting memory of every age, so that from it, as from the sacred flame of the prytaneum, the lights of the mind may be kindled:
And they will never perish, as long as humanity, as long as wisdom, as long as literature and the arts are dear to mortals.

But no one will doubt that for our age, not so much that Spartan discipline as the liberality of Athens is to be followed, since even our most holy religion wished that we should be not as slaves, but as free men, and that we should think freely.
Certainly, what the divine Chrysostom not absurdly pronounced, that by the cross of Christ all rustics were made philosophers:
this indeed seems to tend to this, that slavery of minds, of whatever kind, should be judged by Christian men as most alien.

And indeed, if you were to attempt today to confine the immensity of the immortal mind by drawing boundaries, it would be in vain, since the brightest lights of literature have been so widely spread and disseminated throughout all lands that, if anyone, using that force, should have tried to extinguish them and to cover and wrap them in darkness, whether for any nation or any part of learning, nothing would appear sooner than the great misery suffered by those from whom the light of the mind is, as it were, dug out.

And indeed in our state, it is well known that literature flourishes not only through the talents of the citizens, but especially through the liberal counsels of the princes, so that few can contend with us for the palm of learning.
For when we review the memory of times, even in that age in which refined learning was quite rare in these lands, we find several of our princes not moderately learned:
Frederick the Great surpassed them as much in greatness of mind and civil prudence, as in the glory of their deeds, as in the extent of their empire, so in the pursuit of literature.
And under that king it came about—which had it not come about, Plato said the human race could not be happy—that a philosopher ruled and a king philosophized.
But the philosopher, since he wishes to make as many as possible like himself, that Frederick thought nothing more to be promoted than the good arts and the freedom of feeling and speaking:
Where that was oppressed, there you will find even the most wholesome teachings of scholars often condemned because of a vain suspicion of impiety or of any other harm.
Nevertheless, under his rule, this lamentable event occurred: that the sanctity of religion was then for the first time in Germany begun to be undermined by an impious attempt.
From which source how many and how great evils have invaded the fatherland, now at last the imprudent equally with the prudent perceive.
A matter most worthy indeed of the anxious care of wise princes:
And it has not been neglected in these lands;
but you would with difficulty remedy an evil, whose beginnings it was necessary to resist;
Nor can you easily keep a limit in restraining a thing that is most impatient of a limit.

But in our age, so many dangers and ruins of public and private fortune are already beginning to call back the minds of mortals from lowly pursuits to the contemplation of heavenly things, and to teach them to look aloft.

But Frederick William, just as he fulfills all the duties of a good prince, so he combines both praises: that of letters established with the greatest liberality and munificence, and that of exceptional piety, which he conspicuously displays as a kind of example of ancient religion, faith, and integrity.

Indeed, to confine myself now to what seems most relevant to us, when I consider in what times, at what expense, in how short a space, with what incredible ardor for advancing studies, and finally with what successes this school of learning was founded, increased, and perfected:

I cannot help being moved, partly by the noble institutions and plans of a most wise king, by which he has most fruitfully provided not only for us alone, but for all Germany, and not only for this age, but for future centuries, and partly by the prudence, goodness, and singular industry of the most eminent men to whom the guardianship of letters among us has been entrusted.
And at this point I must address you, my dearest fellow soldiers.

See how much this city values you, which has opened a gymnasium of this kind for your studies, which has gathered together so many teachers of the arts from all sides for your sake, which has provided so great an equipment of all learning for your sake:
see that the hope of the fatherland is placed in you, and lest it fall in vain, the state deigns to care for your education with such great concern:
see the examples of your ancestors, the expectation of your parents, the precepts of your teachers, the reverence for the laws;
Consider these things again and again, and take courage in your hearts, so that you may prove yourselves worthy of such great gifts, worthy of such great hope, worthy of your place and rank.
But, I think, I am cheering on those who are running, so that they may run:
I certainly think I know that very many of you are burning with a praiseworthy zeal for learning, and are distinguished by modesty of character and by honorableness.

Is it now surprising that, with this king, with these ministers of the royal will, and—if I may say so—with these teachers and students, our affairs have grown most happily, and are being increased and adorned with new increments day by day, and have not yet suffered any loss?
But when I say 'anything,' I except that which could not be avoided by human means.
Who among you does not understand that I am lamenting that funeral, listeners, which we recently conducted not without groaning?
O bitter remembrance of that grief, by which would that the cheerfulness of this day had not been saddened!
when he was snatched away by an untimely death, he than whom no one could be dearer to us;

Whenever I remember him, whenever I recall his singular candor of mind and his exceptional courtesy joined with such great gifts of talent, so often am I seized with grief, even against my will, and I, who was not a close friend, form a conjecture about you from these things, you who had come to know his virtue through long experience.
Farewell, noble soul.
Your memory lives and will live, which you hold stored in our hearts, in the monuments of your genius, and in the esteem of all good men.
In three words I have expressed our feelings:
We must not indulge in lamentations today.
Let us turn our step away from the funeral and turn to offering prayers for the perpetual safety of our excellent Prince.

And so we worship God, the Best and Greatest, with a pious mind, so that, since He wishes mortals to be as upright and as happy as possible, He may preserve for us Frederick William, the wisest, most just, most merciful King, born to rouse the virtue of citizens and to aid their interests;

may He favor the most prosperous counsels of the state itself, and may He imbue the minds of the citizens with that reverence for the laws and love of the fatherland and of the Father of the fatherland, which can either lighten the most burdensome toils of empire themselves or even render them pleasant:
Then, that he may form the august Prince, heir of the realm, the hope and delight of the people, after the most noble example of his father, and may one day make him excel in his father's arts:
Finally, that he may sustain and preserve the whole Augustan house for all time.

div.head: II. Oratio nataliciis Friderici Guilelmi III. celebrandis d. III. m. Aug. a. MDCCCXIV. habita.
On the prosperity of Prussia established by the virtues of Frederick William III

p.s: If I should say that no happier day has so far dawned for this literary republic, most exalted Princes, most distinguished men, illustrious and most renowned, beloved fellow soldiers, than the one which today has shone forth not only to the joy of our countrymen, but to the common joy of the Germans, indeed of all Europe;
I do not fear that anyone will think that this was said more in an oratorical manner than from the magnitude and dignity of the matter.

For since the birthday of Frederick William is considered most auspicious every year both by all citizens throughout the empire and especially by this school, which was most generously founded by him;

Although this is the fourth year in which we publicly honor the prince, born from this place for blessing mortals, in the previous three years we were not able to approach with equal piety, yet not with this uplifted and cheerful spirit, this sweet and grateful affection, and finally with this great confidence and security in our affairs:

But the fear of a calamity that had long been imminent, which seemed able to utterly overthrow the weakened state, if it did not disturb the joy of the first solemnities, certainly mingled it with the anxieties of the troubled.

At that time, when the most just of kings, lest the public safety should be endangered, was compelled to serve the most unjust cause without his own knowledge and will, to enter into an alliance with the enemy of all, to hand over our fields, cities, and citadels to a treacherous ally, and to send chosen troops against a prince united with him in sincere friendship into northern lands:
At that time, how great grief afflicted the royal mind, no one is unaware:

Finally, when the third day was returning, the liberty of Prussia, begun indeed in the name of the King, was due to the virtue of Frederick William, but not yet completed, and indeed the omens of a glorious outcome were being shown, but the fierce enemy was five miles from the City.
But today, when I have to speak, how greatly do you think I am moved, if I compare the former poverty, miseries, and contempt with the present greatness of our affairs?

If I should embrace in one, as it were, view the wisdom of the King and his generous counsels, by which so great a change of affairs has been effected; if the loyalty of the people, their obedience, their most ardent zeal for advancing the state; if the valor of the armies, the prudence of the generals, so many and so great victories; finally, the outcome of a most severe and most cruel war, so prosperous and so glorious—

For now it seems that we must rejoice and exult immortally, now with bended knee, with hands stretched to heaven, the divine power must be adored, by whose benefit such great, new, and now already unaccustomed happiness has come to mortals.
And not otherwise, as I think, are you affected.
And so, since I think that no one has come here with that expectation, that he would be taught any subject whatsoever, but that he would learn our feelings and mingle them with his own;

I have nothing more foreign to this day and to the minds of the citizens, which are uniquely intent on the merits of the great King, than an argument drawn, as is customary, from some topic of learning.

I see that this is demanded of me, which is by far the most difficult thing: that, having recalled the memory of the deeds performed under the auspices of Frederick William with courage and success, I should set forth in weighty and brilliant words how great he showed himself, how great gratitude, how great reverence, how great piety is due to him from us.

But by Hercules, I do not know whether anyone may seem more unequal to sustaining this most honorable office than I, who have been appointed not by my own counsel but by yours, Fathers, as the herald of royal virtue.
But if it is rightly considered difficult to celebrate great matters eloquently, what shall I say about those things which seem to be the greatest in the memory of mankind?

When you would scarcely think that the eloquence of some Demosthenes or Cicero could suffice for these things, do you think that a man brought forth from the shade of literature into this most brilliant light of the assembly can match the magnitude of deeds with words?

Therefore, since I understand that this indulgence cannot be granted to me, that I should undertake a most serious matter, and yet I clearly see that if I wished to embrace the whole material of praises, my strength would fail me;
In order that my speech may be in some measure adapted to these solemnities, I shall keep a certain middle course:

Concerning the happiness of our state, established by the virtues of Frederick William, I shall speak briefly in such a way that I neither enumerate all the good things which the fatherland enjoys, nor omit those through which, recently emerging from the greatest calamity, it has attained immortal glory.

Nevertheless, even so, I see that I must beg your indulgence, so that, if I have not fully met the requirements, you may forgive my intention, and you may judge what I have said more by your goodwill than by the importance of the subject.

But as I look around to see where I should turn first, just as those who once praised the Athenian state used to place its chief prosperity in popular government, so the sum of our advantages seems to be contained in this, that we obey a king.
But when I say this, if you think that I am speaking of the common advantage of nearly all the nations of Europe, as they are now constituted, and not of our own particular advantage,
and although I grant that you judge rightly, yet I maintain that in our state the excellence of royal government has shone forth most clearly and has stood out most eminently.

For when, against the enemy of the human race, who, not content with our money and fortunes, also wanted to take away the freedom of our minds and sought our blood and life, the state being besieged by hostile forces, its resources being diminished, an army had to be raised not of moderate size, but as great as Prussia had even in its most flourishing age, and this could not be done gradually and at leisure, but had to be hastened with the utmost speed:

Then who is there who would think that such great undertakings could have been accomplished so vigorously, in so short a time, so peacefully, unless everything had been done by the authority of a beloved king?
What empire is more prompt for action than a royal one?
When do the forces of the whole and the resources for protecting liberty agree more than when one person is in charge, who, holding the reins with a strong hand, governs everything?
But where does discord more frequently rage and more fatally break the strength of the republic, than in those states which are governed by the domination of a few or by popular rule?

But if the most noble nation of the Spaniards, which could not be deterred from the undertaking of liberating their fatherland by any labor, by no disaster, by no miseries, by no tortures, by no cruelty and savagery of enemies, had had such a king as we revere, truly you would have seen increased strength, increased concord, increased sinews of conducting affairs.
What of the Helvetians?
what of the Batavians?
of whom the former, harassed by internal evils, did nothing worthy of ancestral glory;

These men, since they showed their minds very much inclined to recover liberty, would have prepared their forces sooner without doubt, had they not been left destitute of a leader who had long been in exile.

Add that by loyalty to a kind king, the minds of men are so stirred and inflamed that they fight for his preservation no less than for altar and hearth, and think that nothing by which his name could be diminished, or honor detracted, or power weakened, is to be tolerated as long as they live and breathe.

And indeed, although many disagree, I do not hesitate to affirm that among the greatest benefits with which God has showered mortals from the very beginnings of the Christian faith, this is by no means the least: that whereas formerly the peoples distinguished by refined learning had for the most part established a popular form of government, while monarchy, or rather tyranny, held in its grip nations that were very rude and covered with the rust of barbarism, gradually He has recalled every most civilized people to the primitive simplicity of royal dominion, which, as being nearest to the authority of a father of a family, is known to have been the original form, and was afterwards overthrown partly by the pride of kings, partly by the impotence of the nobles, partly by the unbridled license of the common people.

I am not the sort of person who would attempt to play the detractor of the ancients, especially the Greeks, to reproach that noble ardor by which they were driven to dare the greatest deeds, their most vehement love of country and liberty, their implacable hatred of tyrants, or to take up the cause of tyrants.

But I see that the eyesight of some is dazzled by the splendor of their deeds, which ought to be and have been an example to us, and by the lights of arts and disciplines, with which they have illuminated the world and, I pray, will illuminate the farthest posterity, so that they think that whatever Greece has produced should be extolled by their own proclamation, and, deceived by a false appearance, they exaggerate its happiness more than is fitting.

For surely the countless disturbances by which their states were struck, surely the slaughters, exiles, proscriptions, and confiscations of property that were almost daily, are not to be regarded as a state of happiness?
Most things were administered by the desires of individuals:
rare was justice among citizens, no moderation among the common people.
Those Athenians, the most excellent of all Greeks, lent their ears to reason daily;
but their minds did not obey.
They squander wealth unjustly acquired since Pericles through fickleness, they waste it with largesses.
But who was allowed to help the same state remarkably with impunity?
Did they not punish the leading men, Themistocles, Aristides, Cimon, Alcibiades, with exile for reasons either trivial or none?
For because the common people pursued all excellence of virtue with envy, it was enough to drive out an exceptional man, if he had deserved well of the republic;

This the Ephesians openly confessed, when they expelled Hermodorus, an excellent citizen and a friend of the natural philosopher Heraclitus, to whom, because he was said to have assisted the decemvirs in writing the laws, a statue was publicly dedicated in the comitium at Rome, with these words:
Let none of us be the best;
but if anyone shall have appeared, let him be in another place and among other people: for this reason Heraclitus judged with his own right that all Ephesians deserved to be punished with death.

These and other things, which the narrowness of this hour excludes, lead me to believe that that singular freedom of Athens and of many Greek states was rather a harsh servitude under a greedy and ungrateful master, and that the domination of the people, a monstrous and changeable beast, is not far from extreme tyranny:
That this very thing arises from that, neither did the ancient philosophers fail to see, and to those who recently admired the French freedom at first, the saddest outcome showed.

But with a royal government established by salutary laws, there is nothing more calm, nothing more just, nor more inclined to doing good, finally nothing more liberal and more suited to promoting the arts and letters.
Perhaps I have lingered too long in the introduction, having made mention of the ancients:
but you will grant this to our studies, in which we all most gladly linger.

Now to return to my point: I understand by 'king' the kind of king we see in Frederick William, given to this people by divine providence, not the one commonly called king, who often differs little from a tyrant.
Yet these, if you look at the truth, are found to be separated by a very long interval and completely different.
For the tyrant is unrestrained in spirit, greedy, proud:
He refers everything to his own advantage;
He neglects the interests of the people, whom he hates; indeed he thinks they are harmful to him.
And so it destroys the fairness of law, drains the fortunes of citizens, and suppresses, as much as it can, the freedom of feeling and speaking:
it prefers to act by force rather than by kindness:
he seeks pleasures for himself from the miseries and labors of others.
Whoever devotes himself to such practices must necessarily also suffer the evils with which he has afflicted others.
But all the king's plans are directed to this end, that the people may be as happy as possible, and this does not conflict with that, but is in harmony with it:
He complies with their harmless wishes and pursuits, because he knows the divine voice of the people:
As God's vicar on earth, glowing with heavenly love of the human race, he is a father to all, fair, benevolent, gentle, courteous:
As a model of all virtues, he strives to form everyone according to his own example.
But is this not an image of Frederick William?

If anyone should decide to praise him, he could not say anything more excellent than his harmony with his people and their society joined by mutual love, in which all the other virtues of a prince who is perfect in every respect are contained.
And nothing is more useful than this common bond of king and people, neither for the glory of either nor for their happiness.

For glory, because the king, deprived of the strength of the people, is weak, and the people, without the king's wisdom and command, is discordant, but when both are joined, each one glorifies the other's name with great deeds;

For happiness, because one fosters the prosperity of another, and the greatest goods of the people are placed in a kind king, but the royal spirit, amid the most troublesome cares and in the very crisis of the republic, is raised and strengthened by nothing more than by the zeal of the people, whom he had won over by his kindness.
By this most auspicious union, therefore, whatever has been done by us in the recent time, it is evident that it has been accomplished in part to the greatest degree.
But this is owed to the noble, merciful, and wise mind of Frederick William.

He, first yielding to the injustice of fortune, bore adversity most steadfastly, and meanwhile held nothing more important or more weighty than to bind the minds of the citizens, whom the enemy wished to be as estranged as possible from him, to himself by his virtues, and to ensure by wise institutions that they would not become slothful and cowardly:

Soon, when the opportunity for action presented itself, a most fierce avenger of liberty, divinely roused, called forth the people, who had been hiding in the countryside and in the cities, having urged on his own men who had long been impatiently waiting, into the sun and the dust;
From farmers, laborers, merchants, scholars, and freeborn youths, he suddenly prepared an army that not only despised enemies, but was eager for victory and prodigal of life.
Behold a spectacle worthy for later posterity to look back upon!

The best prince, unharmed by the ruin of the republic, and the flower of the whole nation, having contended with the tyrant and his forces, which were at first far more numerous but were especially gathered by force!

Then for the first time we saw the virtue of the Germans, as if awakened from a deep sleep, when the sacred cohorts of the most noble youth followed the voice of Frederick William voluntarily, along with a varied multitude:
You would say that grandfathers and great-grandfathers had returned from the underworld, whose examples our men were emulating.
O great good of the people, which is placed in the memory of deeds clearly performed by our ancestors!
The greatness of Frederick the Second, the ancient dignity of the Prussian empire, the bravery of former armies were present in the minds of all:
When they had all decided that that glory was to be recovered, just as the Spartans once, so the Prussian youths, equal to them, promised that they would surpass the virtue of their ancestors:
and they stood by their promises.
There were, listeners, those who placed the glory of the Germans in this, that they excelled in the arts and in letters, who sought in these a sweet rest and a consolation for lost freedom:

Indeed, there were those who even told foreign nations that the Germans were little suited for action, but that they were uniquely born for meditation, for philosophizing, for acquiring knowledge of various things, and who praised them especially for this reason.
O crafty or foolish praisers of German virtue!
O vain little glory of literature, if freedom is lacking!
Did the Germans hold those plans, did they admit that disgrace, so that they found contentment in literature, forgetful of fatherland and freedom?
It is not so, listeners, it is not:

but the learned equally with the unlearned, or even those more, felt the cruel necessity of obeying the harshest and most atrocious master, and yet they did not see how they could shake off the yoke and be freed from their bonds:

But when the opportunity was given, those who were devoting themselves to literature, especially the young men of this university, and even some professors, whom we congratulate ourselves on having restored to us by a happy fortune, spurned the French soldiery that held this city and were among the first to take up arms, and by their example they showed how greatly the minds imbued with the liberal arts burned with love of liberty and fatherland, and how great was the valor of the Germans, and especially of the Prussians, who, by nature inclined to the cultivation of learning and distinguished by the most brilliant lights of intellect, were no less prepared for battles and the perils of life, altogether like those admirable warriors at Marathon and Salamis, who, when under the Persian tyrant they could have devoted themselves to learning, in which they surpassed all mortals, in idle leisure, preferred to go to meet an uncertain death rather than endure certain slavery.
Away, then, with that ambiguous praise of learning!
Let arms be handled just as books are.
For what do letters avail in slavery?
Unless perhaps, like the Greeks, you, a learned slave, render services to a generous conqueror.
Take away the fatherland, take away liberty:
you will have cut the sinews of letters.
For in liberty letters arouse the noblest feelings:
they teach us to postpone these good earthly and perishable things to eternal and never-perishing ones;
they call back the immortal soul from sordid cares:
which is the source of great crimes:
When the same [liberties] are oppressed and enslaved, you may see them creep humbly, which God gave to men so that they might raise them up;
Having fallen into the base flattery of tyrants, they are numb as if they had seen the Gorgon.
And both kings and tyrants know this.
For who has fostered the freedom of studies, from which the most joyful flower of literature has sprung, more than that model of royal dignity and wisdom, Frederick William?

Who has done more harm to the liberal arts, who has confined the cultivation of intellect within a narrower limit, who has been more hostile to the light of learning, than that most unbridled of tyrants, whose name I do not wish to diminish the joy of this day by mentioning?
But I return to the path, so that I may pause a while in the contemplation of our greatness and happiness.
Where then shall I first begin, listeners, or what shall I first celebrate?
The zeal of the Prussian people?
The valor of the armies?
The prudence of the leaders?
All were vying with one another, so that each might surpass the other.
Indeed, my speech would have to become grander and more sublime than itself, if all things were to be told as they were done.
But I console myself with this thought, that I speak before those who were not only witnesses and spectators of the events, but also their directors and actors.
so that it is enough to have touched upon individual points and to have recalled them to memory.
For from that most glorious harmony between the people and the king there arose so great a strife among the citizens, that I know not whether any age has seen its like.

Thus all men of every rank conspired together, so that each one offered to the King and his country whatever was dearest to him: some offered money, gold, silver, which was but a small remnant of their great wealth; others offered their own bodies and those of their children; others consecrated both to the common good.

And although in other places and at another time tribute was paid with difficulty, and military service was even more reluctantly performed, first among us, with the order of things reversed, much more was contributed than was demanded;
Young boys leaving their schools, sons leaving their parents, young men leaving their betrothed, husbands leaving their wives, were demanding military service:

If anyone was hindered by ill health, by public duties, or by private misfortunes from giving in his name, he bore it with no little resentment, because he saw himself deprived of the highest honor, which he thought was placed in defending his country.
Yet those who remained were not sluggish.
Even the domestic multitude had taken up arms, with no distinction of ages or ranks:
The same people diligently devoted their labor to providing supplies and tending the wounded:
Noble women, while tending the sick, found death, which, in the presence of the enemy, it was not permitted to meet except to individuals, because of the weakness of their sex.
No one longed for peace, in order to be relieved of so many and such great burdens, unless peace restored liberty and the dignity, firmness, and security of the empire.
And what shall I say about the armies and the generals?
Whose merits no praises can equal, no rewards can sufficiently recompense.
How extraordinary, how great were the plans of the generals:
What constancy of the soldiers in enduring hardships!
What courage of those fighting!
What confidence before the battle, what moderation among the victors!
What a death in battles!
They breathed out their soul joyfully, when with the proclamation of the divine will they honored the best King.
But to such great efforts, both ours and those of the allies, success responded.
How many and how great were the defeats of the enemy forces, how many thousands of captives, how many leaders among them, how many captured engines of war, how many citadels!
What allies were estranged, how many lands were brought under control!
The city of the Parisii was stormed, which had rashly boasted itself, proud, as the princess and mistress of Europe and the whole world; hereafter, if I see anything, it will no longer boast.
The tyrant of Europe was cast down and sent into exile.
The peace that followed, salutary for France, gave us a king;
Whatever Germany had lost through the chances of war in these twenty-two years, it restored;
And after such great slaughters, the Gauls could have been afflicted more severely, if we had wished to inflict on them the same things that we had suffered from them.

But such was our generous lenity, that with those who had set out from their homes so far away, as once to Rome and Delphi, to harass and plunder all lands, and who had used fortune immoderately, we dealt most temperately within their own borders.
We would spare those who had raged so fiercely against us and had threatened even more atrocious things, once they were defeated.
Finally, to those who had had no faith and no religion, we would show in actual fact that native integrity of the German nation, which is most remote from all pretense and deceit.
But those who accomplished those things now return to their homes, so that they may be citizens as good as they were soldiers.
Not laden with booty, which a mercenary covets, but content with their own poverty and with the glory of the Prussian name increased to an immense degree and with the admiration of the whole world.
But of such great and so manifold happiness, founded not in wealth but in virtue and the goods of the mind, the sole author was Frederick William.

He raised the Prussian people to that height of distinction that it served as an example to all other nations of Germany and of all Europe, just as he himself stands forth as the most perfect model of a king, adorned, of course, with all those gifts with which a prince who is complete in every respect ought to be equipped.
For it befits a king to be brave, so that he may protect the state unharmed from external force;
He should be frugal, lest he waste the resources of the state on unnecessary expenditure and magnificence, yet not sordid or avaricious, but generous and munificent;
Moreover, he should be just, and gentle and merciful along with severity;
The same person should be religious, pious, wise, energetic, and popular with gravity;
a founder of literature and the arts;

Finally, in private life he was upright and pure, and a good father of a family, because it is impossible that a man who does not embrace even his wife and children with sincere love should love those subject to him.
But who was braver than Frederick William?
Who was more frugal and at the same time more generous?
Who was more just and more gentle?
Who was more religious?
But why do I recall individual things?
For there is no one who does not know that all the things I have said are present in Frederick William in a remarkable way.
I will say one thing, which pertains most closely to our own person, what [he] was for good letters.

For although the merits of the earlier kings concerning learning of every kind are not small, nevertheless Frederick William surpassed them all both in the number of his benefactions and in their magnitude.

He who, even at that time when the state, afflicted by misfortunes, lay prostrate, did not found one or two abodes of learning, but reformed and restored the entire system of studies, using the counsel of those wise men who preside over public education and sacred matters, especially of that most excellent man to whom, on account of his distinguished virtue, the care of all internal affairs was very recently entrusted amid universal rejoicing, because he well understood that the weakened forces of the state could not be better aided than by the light of the arts and the cultivation of talents.
He founded our seat of learning with such munificence as no one among his predecessors ever displayed.
In it, the young men, trained to excel not only in letters but in every virtue, have returned greater thanks to the most august King by their deeds than I can express in words.

But since he has done these things amid public dangers and calamities, it is permissible to take from this a conjecture as to what the studies of the arts may expect from Frederick William now that the strength of the state has been restored and its resources increased.
For will he indeed allow to decay in favorable fortune those things which were prepared through adversity with many labors?

Will that most steadfast Frederick William now abandon the institutions which he had set before himself, because he foresaw that they would be most beneficial to the state, after the matter itself has shown how correctly his penetrating mind had divined?
But I do not wish to waste effort in praising the King:
For the deeds done by him do not speak, but they shout;
Nor does he need proclamation or statues and columns, since in the hearts of citizens so many altars rise for him, on which the feelings of a grateful mind are offered, not incense is burned.
This one thing it will be permitted to add.

The divine investigator of human nature, Plato, when he teaches that the various forms of governing a state arise not from an oak and a rock, as the proverb says, but from the characters of the men who constitute it, judges that the minds of some are kingly, of others tyrannical, and likewise that others are shaped to the likeness of popular rule or the domination of a few; and he declares so ingeniously what condition of mind corresponds to each state, that I grieve that these things can be only hinted at by me, not set forth more fully in this place.
But what mind does he call royal, and what tyrannical?
For when he distributes the mind among three provinces, namely reason, spirit, and desire, and accurately defines what they are like;
he teaches that it is characteristic of a tyrannical disposition that desire, together with base lust, violently subdues the nobler faculties of the mind and carries them headlong:
from which arises internal discord, intemperance, madness, a restless and inconstant mind, prone to any crimes whatsoever.

We see that such is the nature of that man who, of all tyrants that ever existed, even in himself exercised this dreadful tyranny of desires, being in the greatest power the most powerless in mind and the most wretched.
But in the royal mind reason governs the other parts;
the desires obey anger:
from this come wisdom, equity, moderation;
from this comes the greatest harmony under the gentle rule of reason;
finally, a truly divine serenity and tranquility even in adverse circumstances.
Thus, was not the most blessed soul of Frederick William formed, managing all things with reason, without anger and partiality, and ruling not only his subjects but also himself and his own desires?
God, best and greatest, with pious veneration we call upon you, to whom we owe such great happiness.
You not only gave us Frederick William, but you shaped him such as he showed himself to his own and to the world.
You destroyed those fierce and monstrous hordes, which had set out to crush Russia, by cold, hunger, and the sword:
You, by so great a punishment, called back piety into the hearts of mortals, roused and confirmed the noblest feelings, especially love of country:
You won for us allies so great and so distinguished, and bent the minds of princes to concord:
You yourself, through these instruments of your clemency, accomplished such great deeds.
Then hail to you, laureate King, under whose auspices this war was undertaken and brought to an end;
hail, and live among us safe and happy to extreme old age.
Hail to you, most brave soldiers and leaders, by whose labors and blood the good things have been bought back for us with the peace-bringing olive;
hail, fellow soldiers, who, sent out from this wrestling-school of studies into the broader fields of battles, have now returned adorned with victorious glory.
And those who have breathed their last are blessed.
Let no one honor them with tears:
their bodies rest in peace;
Their spirits live, their name lives and will live through the mouths of men.
Their late descendants will cherish their sacred memory.

Finally, I pray that God may preserve the King, most wise, most just, most merciful, and the magnanimous Prince, heir of the kingdom, together with the whole August house; may He preserve the strength, glory, and virtues of the Prussian people;
may He preserve peace, the kindly nurse of all good things, and also of the arts and letters.
May the supreme deity make these vows so binding, as they have been piously made by us.

div.head: III. Oratio nataliciis Friderici Guilelmi III. celebrandis d. III. m. Aug. a. MDCCCXVI. habita.
On Albert, Margrave of Brandenburg, first Duke of Prussia, founder of the University of Königsberg

p.s: Wisely and piously, most excellent men, distinguished, most renowned, most learned, most honorable fellow students, from the very beginning of this school it has been established that a gathering should be held every year in our buildings to celebrate the birthday of the best King, because we not only, like other citizens, venerate him as the common founder, prince, and lord of the state, but as the sole author and founder of our affairs:

So that on the day on which Frederick William was born, to the most auspicious fortune of that day this wrestling-school of studies, this joyful abundance of every kind of literature, may rightly seem to be owed.

But what is more fitting for these most sacred solemnities, what is more suited to our feelings, than that a prince be praised in a public speech, to whose zeal for advancing the arts we owe what we teach, to whose generosity we owe that we flourish, and finally to whose virtue we owe that we live?

And indeed, although I understand that I cannot equal the deeds of this king with my words, although I feel that this is by far the most serious of the duties entrusted to me, because I must speak not once or twice, but every year from this place and on this very day:
nevertheless, I judge absolutely that I have undertaken a task that is arduous rather than difficult or full of risk;

Since on the one hand such a great and so blessed abundance of praises is at hand and, as it were, overflows, that I must look around more for what I should not say than for what I should say, and on the other hand, with this king, it is permitted to speak the truth without danger of offense:

Hence it happens that, before I come to speak, I am wont to be struck with the greatness of the matter when I behold it, and soon after, having collected my courage, although I am neither born nor made for flattering kings, nothing seems to me more pleasant, nothing more excellent, than openly to interpret your feelings, Fathers, and the vows undertaken for the best Prince, before so great, so ample, so splendid, so learned an assembly, and to discourse copiously on the royal merits.
