But if we wish to recall the deeds of the past year, we shall find Frederick William not only distinguished in war, but also in the arts of peace:
I can, if it pleases, recount not a few things done excellently by him:

so many discharges and dismissals of soldiers, by which he restored to the fields their cultivators, to the workshops their laborers, to the schools and letters their students, to wives and children their husbands and fathers of families, to parents their sons;
That most sacred treaty, which he made with the Caesars most like himself for firmly pacifying the whole world;
taxes lightened for the subjects;
provinces most recently wisely established;
the church adorned and embellished with magnificent honors;
splendid works of artists procured at great expense for the public benefit;
many other benefits, partly completed, partly begun, partly most kindly promised to their peoples from time to time.
But nevertheless, why I should think that the most abundant material should now be left untouched, there were especially two reasons, listeners.
For first, the modesty of our King is to be observed:
he spurns being praised every year deliberately and being exalted beyond other mortals:

And clearly, what Caecilius says about his Trajan, 'he considers himself one of us, and he excels and stands out all the more because he considers himself one of us.' Then, the things that are vigorously done abroad and in arms, because they reach the ears and minds of all, can rightly and in proportion to the greatness of the deeds be celebrated even by those who were not present:

What happens at home in peace, what happens in the court, in the senate-houses, either by kings or under royal auspices, can rightly proclaim only one who is either a participant in the counsels or an administrator of the state to be governed, thoroughly trained by experience in affairs.
Hence whatever comes into our knowledge, that certainly is of such a kind that I would not say it is as well known to you as to me, but it is known to the public.

There was a time, listeners, when from the oratorical platform the civic virtue of good princes could be recognized openly and worthily, when Pliny, when Fronto, when other upright and eloquent men who had been involved in public affairs, would soothe Trajan, Hadrian, Marcus Aurelius—to whose most sacred company it is right that our King be added—with speeches of thanks;
But those were great consuls who had learned by experience to examine and evaluate public affairs.
We have often heard that we scholars understand these matters too little.
They were active in the light of the forum and the senate.
Our eloquence is forced to hide in the shade and narrow confines of the schools.
Therefore restrain your emotions somewhat, which this day justly claims for itself, just as I restrain myself against my own will in praising the King.

May I be allowed to recall the memory of earlier times, and to summon from the ancestors of the royal line one prince, who in his age deserved well of literary studies just as our Frederick William did in ours;
so that from the comparison of a most noble example, if it can be done through my insignificance, I may seek some addition, of whatever sort, to the glory of our founder and parent.
I mean Albert, Margrave of Brandenburg, the first Duke of Prussia, who by founding the Königsberg academy secured for himself the eternity of his name.

He, the son of Frederick, Margrave of Onolzbach, and grandson of Albert Achilles, who was also called Ulysses, the bravest and strongest of all his peers, after he had received the dignity of Canon of Cologne, at which time he had followed his father in the retinue of Emperor Maximilian, who was then subduing Italy, chiefly at the urging and authority of Joachim Nestor, Elector of Brandenburg, at the age of twenty, was created Master of the Teutonic Knights of the Hospital of Blessed Mary of Jerusalem.
A man who, through the envy and favor of authors, experienced the desire for fame, because his deeds were either composed with implacable hatred by some, or celebrated with excessive zeal by others.
Albertus excelled in courage, piety, humanity, and clemency:
vigorous, upright, prudent, modest:
a faithful friend, steadfast in marriage:

Having respected the dignity of the orders of the state, he exacted contributions and taxes only when they had been granted by those orders, and at the beginning, as Master of the Horse, he shared with the nobility and the towns the rights of war and peace, of treaties, and of embassies.
Moreover, in administering the state and in his counsels he was inconsistent, and he allowed himself to be guided by his intimates, to whom he attributed more influence than a prince ought.
Being more eager to seize the principate and to increase his power, he burdened his subjects, already pressed down by the weight of wars, with tributes.

Amid civil disturbances and the dissensions of factions, especially of the nobles and the farmers, he preserved equity too little, favoring the aristocrats more, so that they would more willingly grant taxes;
He allowed the tranquility of his mind to be disturbed by suspicions and fear:
Finally, religion turned into superstition entangled the weak old man with magical frauds, to be deluded by the tricks of wicked men, especially foreigners.
Indeed, this misfortune of princes is no light one, that if they err ever so little, the more conspicuous they are, the greater it is considered.
And from what they have done well, honor is taken away, because they are thought to have done it not for the common good but for their own sake.
And Albert's condition indeed was so uncertain and doubtful that he had to do many things for his own sake, which a long and sufficiently established power can scorn with impunity.

He, after having waged war with the Poles for thirteen years as Master of the Horse, and after peace was made and the equestrian order was suppressed, became Duke of Prussia; he was compelled to provide resources by which he might protect his rule, which had been acquired neither by force nor by the finest arts, to win renown for himself, to bind the nobility to himself, to retain the loyalty of the common people, to court the favor of the Roman Emperor and the King of Poland, and to defend himself from the hatred of the order, by concealing from time to time his religion, concerning which he voluntarily offered himself for a colloquy, and to assume various forms, as circumstances demanded.
Yet he did not so serve the times as to dare nothing, but he exposed himself to not a few dangers:

Indeed, when he was summoned by Caesar through a herald to give an account of his usurped rule and of his abandoned former religion, and to satisfy his creditors, and after an edict was published in the very senate-house at Königsberg, finally in the assemblies at Augsburg, when the Prussian land was assigned to Walter von Cronberg, Master of the Order, he was ordered either to withdraw from the principality or to plead his case in the supreme court of the Empire, with threats of proscription added; and at last, as had been foretold, being proscribed, he was brought into the utmost peril, had not the loyalty of his subjects prevailed more than Caesar's anger, and had fortune not aided Albert by keeping the imperial forces occupied with more serious wars.

But although he did not adopt religion as a pretext in order to gain power, since he embraced Luther's salutary doctrine, which at that time was being spread throughout Germany and the neighboring lands, with a sincere mind,
Nevertheless, he was not unaware how much it contributed to establishing a new principate.

And Luther, who, when he was seeking aid against the Poles at the Diet of Nuremberg, was even then being reconciled through Andreas Osiander to the Master of the Horse, had urged Albert to lay aside the dress of his order, abrogate the laws, take the principality for himself, and marry a wife;
Philip had also advised the same thing:
Albert smiled, but said nothing.

Therefore, since Albert's rule was supported by new faith, but this could not be sustained and preserved together with a sounder discipline unless schools of the arts were founded in Prussia, in which men suitable for teaching the people would be educated;

Moreover, since he was also pleasing Sigismund Augustus, then king of Poland and his own patron, whose help he needed against the Emperor and the knights who were especially preparing arms in Livonia, by fostering his studies, because these things were especially dear to him;
finally, since he made the citizens' own inclinations more favorable to himself by this matter:
it is understood that the advantages of literature were not alien to the advantage of the Duke.
I do not say this in order to diminish his glory by disparaging it:
For letters, since they make the people happier by cultivating their talents and improving their morals, greatly help every best prince.
They are an obstacle to tyrannical domination.
That one is finally to be considered a good prince, who has learned that letters strengthen his power, not that it must be protected by military aid.

It was added that Albert, who was at that time devoted to learning and accustomed to cultivate learned and pious men and to follow their advice, ardently desired that the light of literature and religion should be spread most widely on account of their own excellence.
He was not only skilled in the Latin language, but he also delighted in it:
In eloquence he is compared with Cicero and Demosthenes by an equal writer with a certainly more generous praise.

But if he advised the senate of the Königsberg academy by letter to use the German language in those things that were to be written to him, he did this not for his own sake, but because, while he was teaching, some of the councilors with whom he deliberated about these matters were so unskilled in the Roman language that time was spent in interpreting documents for their benefit.
A memorable example of a prince far more learned than his band of friends, yet by no means unique in the Brandenburg line:
And in that age solid learning drawn from the sources of antiquity was more common in courts, since French charms and witticisms had not yet subdued them and made them, as it were, tributary.

The Prussian tables, compiled by Erasmus Reinhold, testify that he cherished the same mathematics; and because Albert provided the expenses, just as the Alphonsine tables once did from the king of Castile, they took their name from him.
Moreover, the discipline of theology was so beloved by the pious prince that he not only attended public disputations, but also the lectures of the professors together with the students.
Nor is his double library, one Latin, the other German, to be passed over, partly acquired for his own use, partly for common use.

Finally, his wife Anna Dorothea, daughter of Frederick, king of the Danes, kindled a most beautiful ardor; that her husband was impelled by her to dedicate halls to the Muses, and that the pious work was diligently aided, besides John Brissmannus, George Sabinus, the first rector of the university, testifies in an elegiac poem:

She herself built a part of the house of the academy from its own revenues, provided stipends for noble youths, and if she saw any of the studious young men in worn-out clothing and attire, she ordered them to be called to her and gave them clothes.
Now indeed how wisely, how piously, how liberally Albertus conducted himself in founding the seat of the arts, he himself best indicates in the letter published before the dedication.

For when peace was restored to Prussia, although many civic ornaments had been destroyed or shaken by war, he says that he brought back and fortified the courts, laws, discipline, and censorship of morals, and that he embraced the care of divine matters and of literature, in which God willed that the doctrine of the true religion be included.
After weighing the matter with learned and pious men, he placed over the churches men well instructed in the knowledge of the Gospel and endowed with upright morals.

And because posterity could not have teachers of religion unless literature were cultivated, and without these most civil rights and duties could not be retained, they established schools for boys throughout the towns, where the elements of the Latin language and the Christian faith would be taught, and finally at Königsberg an academy, in which all honorable arts would be explained in order and completely, and the languages, whose knowledge is necessary for the church, would be learned.
There will be many who, lightly regarding the divine service, or thinking that empires are to be governed only by force and arms, not by religion, laws, and discipline, may censure their counsel:
yet to himself the reason of his plan stands excellently firm, who knows that the first care of all in governing the state ought to be that the right knowledge of God be widely propagated;

and that, for those who had shown outstanding courage and loyalty in his own dangers, this gratitude should have been shown, that he should adorn their homeland, as much as he could, with genuine goods.
"Let it be great praise of Athens and Sparta," he says, "that they had honorable laws:"

Nevertheless, this is greater and serves eternal life, because in this region the true knowledge of God shines, and, as we hope, will shine for a long time. Therefore, for the public benefit of both Prussia and the neighboring nations, learned and distinguished men, who were to teach partly Latin grammar and accustom the youth, as far as possible, to the pure and native form of the Roman language in writing, partly to expound the authors of the Greek and Hebrew languages, partly to teach the elements of philosophy and mathematics, civil law, and the medical art, were attracted by salaries more generous than those which were customary throughout Germany.
He even promised additions to those whom he had observed to be more useful to the academy.
He promised the customary immunities and privileges to be obtained, which, however, were granted not by the Emperor nor by the Roman Pontiff, but by the King of Poland alone.

Finally, he recommends the governance of morals, and declares that he himself will undertake this province, so that those who are unwilling to be bent to virtue may be removed, since in almost all academies examples of this kind are seen, which seem worthy not only of Christian schools, but not even of any civil society.
The dedication of the academy, performed according to custom:
Prudent and humane laws were given;
The authority of jurisdiction, not inconsiderable, was conferred:
To those who had completed their studies at Königsberg, not-to-be-despised privileges were granted:
An annual allowance of four thousand marks was supplied, quite generously in that cheapness of commodities;

From this, a fourth part was provided for the students' messes, a praiseworthy institution especially in a city renowned for its throng of people, where although there is opportunity for clever young men to earn their living, nevertheless because the grain supply is not infrequently set on fire, certainly one does not live well on little:
As the price of grain rose, moved by the complaints of the academy, he increased their income, and decided to give them estates, which, however, fearing lawsuits, she allowed to be taken from him:

Moreover, he gave dwellings to the teachers, and adorned them with honors in such a way that he would have aroused the envy of the other parts of the state, if the candor and simplicity of that age could have envied learning.
For in his edicts he placed the Rector and the professors of the University of Königsberg in the first position, after these the lords, the nobility, the knights, the clergy, the towns, and the rest:

Privately he so favored the doctors that, when he heard of the death of Stanislaus Rapagellanus, a leading theologian and one of the few eloquent, although he was outside the city, he returned to attend the funeral, and gave him a place next to his own monument;
He imitated the example, as Sabinus says, of Scipio Africanus, who had honored Ennius with similar distinction.
But how dear Sabinus was to him, one may see from many documents;
and indeed he had earned the friendship of the prince by his distinguished learning:
who, being a Marchian by nation, formed by the discipline of Melanchthon, soon his father-in-law, and refined in Italy, excelled in the knowledge of the liberal arts and of law:

At Venice, he was honored with the laurel by Alexander, archbishop of Oretanum and Brundisium, and was raised to equestrian rank and named a count of the Lateran court; by the Elector Joachim, in the thirtieth year of his age, he was called to the University of Frankfurt as professor of eloquence.
Soon afterward, at Königsberg, he assisted Albert with his advice in founding the academy.
The Duke also sought to lure Joachim Camerarius, a most learned and famous man, into Prussia.
But he rejected the offered condition.
Nor did the prince's efforts and hope of success fail:
a moderate number of students had flocked together just at the birth of the school, although there were only eleven professors;
the discord among the teachers, which had arisen at the very beginning in the manner of those times, was happily settled before the senate.
But how much Albertus contributed to Prussia is evident even without my mentioning it.

For at the time when he invited the inhabitants of the Baltic coast to embrace literature, although Vinricus Kniprodius, Master of the Knights, had established in the town of Culm, at the end of the fourteenth century, a school modeled on the University of Bologna, confirmed by Urban VI, nevertheless because it was extinguished early, teachers of the church and instructors had to be summoned either from Poland or from Germany:
There was such a great scarcity of them even during Albert's reign that Luther could not satisfy the people of Riga and Albert himself when they asked.
Those who were suitable refused;
those who were willing would not be sufficient:
Moreover, the natives in Germany could not devote themselves to literature unless they were either wealthy in family property or supported by more generous stipends.

What of the fact that Sabinus, in a letter to Cardinal Pietro Bembo, by which he attempts to obtain for the newly founded academy the papal privilege, complains of the great savagery of the Scythian people, and that scarcely in neighboring regions can a civilized way of life be maintained by laws, discipline, and authority, judging worthy of the highest praise anyone who should try to lead these peoples, even moderately, to the knowledge of God and the understanding of virtue?

That in these lands the arts and sciences now flourish, that they have produced men distinguished in every kind of learning, poets, philosophers, and the greatest scholars, is owed at least in some part to Albert.
He gradually drove out the former savagery, rubbed off the rust of barbarism, and illuminated minds with the lights of purer learning:
And because he accomplished this in a more difficult time, by so much the more he earned the favor of the people.

Nor do I think it should be omitted that he wished the home of the arts to be especially in that city which he himself inhabited, so that teachers and learners might be before his eyes and ears, and he himself might enjoy their instruction and friendship:
By which indeed he most clearly testified his zeal.

Indeed, those princes seem to cultivate letters but little, who either wish them to be removed as far as possible from their sight, or lend an ear to those who wish it, because in moderate towns both teachers and students live more comfortably, because liberty—I know not whether youthful license—does not suit a palace and the seat of princely power, because young men may be corrupted by bad morals:
Although these arguments are plausible, nevertheless our literary university teaches how little should be attributed to them.
For we have seen academic life improved, license diminished, and true freedom strengthened:
Other disadvantages can be healed by prudent and benevolent remedies.

And so it was very well done that the plan of Georg Friedrich, Margrave of Onolzbach, who was administering Prussia in place of Albert's son, to transfer the Albertine school to Velavia, on account of the dissensions that had arisen between the studious youth and the merchants, a truly trivial cause, was afterwards abandoned.
But for that wonderful favor toward literature, one would wish that Albert had received a better return than we find was then the case.
For the pious prince was troubled by the quarrels of the theologians, especially those of Osiander, Johann Funck, Friedrich Staphylus, and Joachim Mörlin:

when the one party, certainly clever and not unlearned men, reproaching Luther and Melanchthon with Aristotelian theology, painted over the genuine faith with the doctrines of Bonaventure and Pico della Mirandola and other mystical opinions;
the other party, slavishly devoted to Luther's formulas, would pronounce anyone a heretic who had deviated from him even a finger's breadth;

Both were quarrelsome and irascible, so far removed from Christian gentleness and from humanity that they not only fought most fiercely with words, but also it was not far from being the case that they would have fought with weapons.

And they thought that, having completely fallen into madness, the divine power could not be appeased by anything, nor could it be rendered favorable to themselves, nor could the purity of religion be better preserved, than by quarreling about words, by pursuing subtle questions, by inventing accusations, by condemning adversaries, and by persecuting them with more than pontifical hatred.
And so some of the learned were driven out, others left of their own accord;
The leader himself, insolently despised, afflicted with insults, was called into suspicion both among his own people and among foreigners:

Finally, the disagreements of opinions passed into civil discords, not without the fault of the prince, who, while he mixed himself in the tumults of the theologians, while he now strove to reconcile the parties and settle the controversies, now punished the refractory, more inflamed and exasperated the excited minds, which were impatient of kindness as well as of severity.

But if the piety of that age, especially when compared with our own sluggishness, seems to deserve the highest reverence, because it placed divine worship above all other things, and dared to uphold it with the greatest effort even against the authority of those in power:

nevertheless, there is reason for us to congratulate our age, because such troublesome disputes have been removed from sacred literature, minds have been freed from that anxiety and sadness, and the state has been liberated from the evils flowing from them.

But I recall myself from the contemplation of the man who, as my opinion holds, having obtained the principate by divine will, began and completed a most excellent work with such skill, such piety, with a mind so simple, so sincere, that he should never cease to be adorned with the praise and commendation of all good men.
Today indeed almost nothing remains of the old and pure custom, which delights and holds one who considers that age:
Time has changed the form and appearance of almost all things.
Religion yielded to avarice, stern severity to elegant frivolity, fidelity to cunning and flattery and trifling arts.
Nevertheless, the pursuit of literature remained and even increased.
There remained good men, wise, ready, bold for every most beautiful deed, who could restore a better state of affairs.
Our princes remained, exceptionally favoring the honorable arts.
And amid so many ruins and calamities, nevertheless seeds have been sown that will one day yield more joyful fruits.
Indeed, a providence that foresees and is kind governs and guides human affairs;
because it brings good things out of evils, happiness out of destruction, freedom out of slavery:
so that we see the Prussian kingdom, which had been compelled to serve a foreign tyranny, restored to its former power by the truly divine counsels of Frederick William.

Indeed, he not only desires the recovery of the strength of the empire and the glory of arms, but also — which is much greater — he strives to build the happiness of the citizens upon firm foundations, when he intends to grant to the people, whose loyalty he found in his dangers no less than Albert did, whose interests he sees are not separated from his own, the rights to be established by laws, when he undertakes the care of divine matters, when he fosters the arts and sciences with the greatest generosity, not equaling but surpassing his ancestors in emulation.

For to stop with Albert alone, whose humanity, modesty, piety, courage, and other virtues he displays with dignity and majesty, who does not understand how far he left him behind, when in this city and in these buildings he established our school much more magnificently, and furnished it with the most abundant equipment and furniture, not when affairs were flourishing and his power established, but when it was tottering, broken, and diminished?

Let us give thanks to the most merciful King for this benefit, fellow soldiers, not with artificially crafted words, but with the innocence and sanctity which we venerate in him, but with concord and obedience to be shown to the laws and with diligently aiding the public interests:

Let us give thanks to God, the Best and Greatest, because He has entrusted the reins of empire to this king, who can both defend the state with arms and temper it with salutary institutions, who is privately an example of uprightness to the citizens, and publicly the best father of the fatherland.

Finally, we direct pious prayers to the supreme deity, that he may keep Frederick William safe together with the entire August house, and since nothing can be rightly done without divine help, that he may guide all his cares and thoughts, and finally that he may confirm the peace restored to the world and preserve it for our welfare as long as possible.

div.head: IV. Oratio in dedicatione universitatis litterariae Bero- linensis d. XXVI. m. April. a. MDCCCXVII. habita.
On the purpose and character of academic learning and discipline, especially of the University of Berlin, founded with a definite plan by Frederick William III

p.s: What we had sought with the most burning prayers for a long time and had awaited with the greatest longing, most excellent sir, distinguished and renowned gentlemen, most honored fellow students,
That thing is now being done before our eyes by most distinguished men; I pray to God Almighty that it may turn out favorably, happily, and prosperously for our school and the whole republic.

For so great is the seriousness of this act, so great the force and power of the law handed down to us, that if that one has been well and with divine help completed, if this one is never not religiously observed and retained, our literary university will be firmly established, and will remain unharmed for as long as the fleeting and fragile condition of all human affairs permits.
But if the memory of this day should fade, or the most sacred law be neglected, broken, and overthrown, then at last the safety of our affairs would be in peril.
But if this law was established in the presence of God, it cannot be annulled without God.
Today a seat is dedicated to literature, which, having protected its place through seven years amid various vicissitudes, has given proof of itself:

On the day on which I was summoned here to discuss briefly what seemed to me appropriate, and at the same time to give thanks to the august King for the benefit conferred upon us, although a very short time has been granted to me and I must speak almost as if by the water-clock, striving to approach the dignity of the solemn occasion by some excellence of argument, I consider it a matter of religious scruple to speak on any subject other than the very nature of this most weighty institution: what is the purpose, what is the character of academic learning and discipline, what the most wise King seems to have had chiefly in view in founding this school of arts, and finally what has been done by us and what must be done hereafter so that we may best respond to the character of literary study and to the royal will.

And first, I shall not set forth by what beginnings and causes, after the decay of times and the ruin of states, while a deadly tyranny gradually encroached, by which not only bodies but even minds themselves were held bound and constrained, and soon by the incursions of barbarous peoples the most flourishing flower of literature among the ancients was extinguished, the universities of scholars—to omit the Britons—arose in Gaul and Italy and then in Germany, and with letters reborn took growth, dispelled the darkness from minds, opened the purer springs of religion, and spread abroad the light, and finally diligently cultivated very many branches of learning:

I think no one will be my opponent, if I say that in our age universities are either the most important schools or ought to be so, in which, just as parents transmit life to their children, so teachers, perfect in their own kind, transmit solid learning and knowledge, as complete as possible according to the character of each age, to the growing offspring.

But the knowledge I mean, I think, is not to be placed in experience sought from without and in varied acquaintance with things visible or subject to the senses, not in the transmitted knowledge of deeds done and opinions held, not in the powers of memory or in any arts of acuteness and skill whatsoever;

But although the human race can do nothing without the support and service of the senses, nevertheless knowledge is concerned with reason, which holds the purest notions of all things, and which, being simple and immortal and eternal, uses this perishable dwelling of the body until, with its bonds loosened and its prison broken, it is carried back to that most holy fountain of wisdom from which it came.

There is certainly, there is something divine in the minds of men, which, obscured by the mists of corporeal nature and lulled to sleep by inactivity, must be roused and unfolded, so that it may shine with its innate beauty and illuminate the dark parts of the soul.
This divine power can place mortals on the highest step of wisdom:
this is the leader of virtue, this is the guide of life:
to this must be directed whatever we do.
Therefore, rightly, every most liberal-minded person has set no other end of knowledge than knowledge itself, than which you could find nothing greater or more divine.

But that [philosophy] is separated and set apart from the crafts and the gainful arts by this very thing to an immense degree, because it has its highest end placed within itself, because it traces back each individual thing whatsoever from a common origin and gathers it from the first beginnings, and finally because, not deceived by the judgment of the senses nor by opinions, it scrutinizes the most remote causes of things with the keenness of mind and intellect.

Therefore we rightly despise those people and do not judge them to be truly learned, who either estimate the dignity of the disciplines solely from the use of everyday life, or devote themselves to literature for the sake of bread and preparing a livelihood, or, neglecting deeper knowledge, hand over common things, which you may behold with your eyes or touch with your fingers, as it were from hand to hand, and not only deem every higher and somewhat more recondite investigation of nature, whether divine or human, to be vain, but even try to render it suspect.
Since these things are so, it is sufficiently clear what, in my opinion, the method of academic instruction ought to be.
For all genuine culture of the mind must begin with the hearing of philosophers, who teach the method of philosophizing, moral and natural doctrine, mathematics, the humanities, and history:

By dealing with these things, the minds of young men are both best drawn away from that illiberal manner of beginning their studies, which not a few pursue, and are imbued with those notions by which all other things are founded and held together.

Furthermore, no discipline should be so taught or learned that students receive from the teacher and commit to memory a raw and undigested material, neither arranged in proper order nor illuminated by the lights of thought, nor with precepts drawn from a single source.

Nor should one rest content with common matters, which you may perceive with no or very slight mental effort, but minds must be kindled and exercised, so that, desiring to quench the most burning thirst for knowledge, they may plunge deeply into profound cognition, and soon dare to approach the sanctuaries of literature untrodden by anyone before, and to be wise with no guide.

Moreover, since this nature is implanted in men, that they gladly abuse their talent, and turn learning itself into profit, twist their opinions for private advantage or in favor of the powerful, and turn them this way and that, and finally, through base ambition, love to make the worse argument the better:

For a religious teacher, nothing must be provided for before this: that by example and words he sharpen and strengthen the sense of truth and goodness in tender minds, and turn them far away from pretense, arrogance, greed, and profit.

But now I see that I have been brought to that point, listeners, which I was most eager to avoid, that I have fallen into a subject so broad, so rich, that if I wished to pursue it properly, I would have to say many things that would be trite and stale to you, most distinguished teachers, and even if I said the most numerous and weighty things, I would still seem to have omitted no fewer or less important matters.
Therefore, lest I strike against this rock, I draw myself back from my course and shorten sail.
But someone will say:
you indeed remove literature as far as possible from all communion with life and business, and relegate it to idle leisure:
although you may have set them forth as good, as becoming;
so you point out no utility, especially no public one:
this certainly, in this place and on this very day, neither cautiously enough nor appropriately.

But I, indeed, to say nothing of the sweetness of the Muses, which countless people have sung and still sing, first maintain that genuine learning is the teacher of virtue and the most powerful producer of tranquility of mind, being separated by an immense interval from that pernicious opinion which separates honesty from knowledge.
For letters, when properly cultivated, rout out and eradicate the empty images of things and the errors to which vices owe their origin:
They place those who have been drawn away from sordid cares in the contemplation of the best and immutable things.

They lead those who are removed from anxieties to the most limpid springs of divine rites, from which alone you may most fully draw what is beautiful, what is honorable, what is worthy of an immortal human being.
From here are prepared resources which can neither be snatched away by theft, nor destroyed by fire, nor consumed by any misfortunes.
From here come faith, justice, temperance.

Hence grave and steadfast men, who, because they have learned to despise fortune, remain unshaken in adversity, undaunted by the commands of their masters, are not subdued by any force or even by the fear of death, so that they depart from their purpose.

If in our age a scant supply of such men has been found, if we have seen not a few humble, timid, ambitious flatterers of tyrants, I think that they have not derived the best fruit from the study of literature, but have plucked certain dry and sterile little flowers of learning.

For to say in one word what I feel, this seems to me the most excellent praise and the greatest utility of literature, that they bring freedom of mind, in which the highest goods of the human race are contained.

But it is the task of the learned academics to rouse in well-born youths, so that the most unworthy servitude by which minds have been captured may be shaken off, so that human life may be improved, so that superstition may flee away, and religion be strengthened:
That this is not peculiar to philosophy, but can and ought to be done equally by theologians, jurists, and physicians, I need not explain.
But just as letters procure the greatest freedom, so if you take away freedom from them and bind teachers to fixed formulas, you will have cut out the eye of the human race:
The Muses, impatient of servitude, will be silent;
great talents will cease;
but flattery will burst forth;
in place of wisdom, folly, and finally crime in place of virtue, will hold sway.

And indeed the flower and freedom of letters is aided by nothing more than by this union of the disciplines, which is set before us in our universities, where, rejoicing in the fruit of one another, all are illuminated by the common light of philosophy, and they flourish through the bond and kinship that exists among all:
But if the spirit of letters is one, they are best held together in one body.

Therefore the enemy of the human race, in order to suppress literature and the freedom of minds, which was dangerous to him, not only restrained teachers with strict discipline, but also, in order to rule by dividing, wanted philosophy, theology, the study of law, and the medical art to be separated, just as the weaver's craft is divided from the cobbler's and the smith's.
Hence he divided the literary university into individual schools in separate places, and separated the arts as if into islands:
who now himself grows old on the rock of Ocean.
Moreover, since the minds of young men emerge to freedom with greater difficulty if everything that must be learned and done is commanded, and the whole of life is restrained by fear of a teacher;

in Germany we see that in the universities the freedom of schools, and even a certain freedom of living, which they are accustomed to call academic and interpret variously and sometimes worse, has been granted:
Each person chooses for himself to which branch of learning he will devote himself, with what he will nourish his mind, and what way of life he will adopt.
Instead of the military obedience that that same tyrant Corsus had imposed on studious young men, they are governed by paternal advice and by authority strengthened by the power of jurisdiction.
Finally, we are in the place of parents.
You, dearest comrades, are not so much disciples as household members and children, who, just as they have derived their name from liberty, so ought to be treated liberally.
But license must be curbed:
if it can be done, by admonition and exhortation;
but if not, swollen joints or limbs affected with incurable disease must be cut off with the knife.

Now, when you have been thus trained and refined and have come to the exercise of public affairs and the honorable arts, the fruits of learning must be scattered through you and brought forth for the blessedness both of the state itself and of individuals:
The freedom of minds, which a good state values most highly, because without it not even civil life can be maintained, must be disseminated.
The genuine worship of the divine must be promoted.
The gifts of the mind, to which the strength of the body is subject, must be developed.
Justice, equity, and all virtue must be propagated.
The misery of the human race, ignorance, poverty, weakness of bodies, the force of diseases, must be either repelled or alleviated.
From you, recently distinguished even by military glory, the ornaments of peace will now be sought.
In these most useful pursuits, may you never, fellow soldiers, deviate from the straight path, on which, unless everything deceives me, you have deeply resolved to strive;
May ambition, greed, and evil arts never lead anyone astray, forgetful of our exhortation.

Do not forget that a man who was not educated in a life of seclusion, not inexperienced in the conduct of affairs, but experienced in public life and the vicissitudes of fortune, that Tully, having traversed a life spent in activity and devoted to occupations, says:
He says: One day spent well and according to the precepts of philosophy is to be preferred to an eternity of sinning.

But we have learned that the wisest king, when he was founding munificently the seat of the arts, which is dedicated today, and was furnishing it with a sufficiently ample equipment, had no other purpose than that, with the strength of arms broken and shattered, with the boundaries of the empire narrowed by half, with the state subjected to a most cruel enemy and harassed and afflicted by countless evils, he might rouse, strengthen, and fortify the powers of the mind, by which all things are overcome:
What could be thought of more prudent, more liberal, or more worthy of a king than this?
Since we were aiming at this goal, we directed our efforts almost to the point which I explained a little earlier should be the direction.
that the young men entrusted to our care should not regard the liberal arts as a place for practicing trades for the sake of profit;
that they might be raised to sublime knowledge;
that they might conceive and nurture noble plans;
that they might be imbued with piety, love of country, and respect for the laws;
so that they might be both modest, and, where there was need, brave;
finally, that in his own kind each one should be such as I have indicated he ought to be.
And fortune favored our undertakings;
our discipline attracted a large number of young men even in their earliest years:
those who were soon called away to war proved their valor by distinguished deeds.
The greatest part of them now enjoys renown;

Up to forty men met an honorable death in battles or through the force of hardships and wounds, for whom you annually bring funeral offerings with the highest honor, and we will at last at some time erect a monument, by which a distinguished example may be handed down to posterity.
Nor do we mourn only those men:
They do not see this most auspicious day: Willdenow, Fichte, Reil, Klaproth.
These lights of literature, whose name flies through the mouths of men, have been sealed in our hearts; fortune has begrudged us this day, or rather the very days themselves.
But as long as the republic depended on the will of another, we led a precarious life among enemies.
When the freedom of the Germans was begun, then at last our affairs have obtained security.

Therefore, after the wars were finished, they flourished more joyfully, and there is no need to fear that they will fall, as long as we rejoice in this king, the most constant defender and preserver of good literature, freedom, and honesty.
While you preside over us, most excellent minister of the king's counsels, who with such kind and prudent care protect and guard our school;
while we ourselves and you, fellow soldiers, will be at our duty.
I know that certain things stand in our way, which, if I wished, I could mention:
Nor do I fear giving offense, since I speak among ourselves, and I think that all pretense is far from the dignity of an orator:
But I do not wish to say anything more serious or sadder on this day.
Our learning, indeed, harms no one;
And in the royal city, for literature to dwell is advantageous both to the city and to literature:
to the city, lest those who are unlearned be considered learned;
to literature, lest it lie hidden.
But surely the powers of the mind are not less effective in peaceful times than in troubled ones?
Should they, once the empire has been restored, be lulled to sleep as useless?
On the contrary, they themselves must be sharpened and exercised more keenly.
Why indeed?
Do we not know that very many states have grown sluggish in peaceful idleness and have been weakened by sloth?
To prevent this from happening, states must take the greatest care.

Therefore, in order that we may satisfy the most merciful counsels of our Lord, which I think I interpret most correctly, we must diligently pursue the path we have entered upon, and with those arts by which Prussia has always excelled, and by which, setting before its eyes the illustrious example of Frederick the Great, who remarkably protected freedom of thought, it will excel hereafter, we must illuminate the fatherland with their light and promote the happiness of the citizens.
But you, fellow soldiers, continue to show the obedience to the laws and the diligence in literature that you have shown up to now.
If we make these promises most religiously today, I think that a most pleasing expression of thanks has been made to the best King.
But as for the most precious pledge of the king's goodwill that we have received handed over through the hands of an outstanding man, it remains for us to see how it was handed over.

In undertaking this matter, it will not be irrelevant to set forth the memory of times, so that it may be understood with what ceremonies our ancestors inaugurated schools as temples, as cities, as colonies, and so that things placed side by side in opposition may shine forth more brightly.

And so, that I may not pursue foreign examples, from the now royal family, Frederick the Third, the Elector, who soon became the first king of Prussia, the great-grandfather of our King, is the last of the princes who founded a university:

Its dedication was recorded in writing four years later by Christoph Cellarius at the command of the Prince, so that it might be known to posterity with what cares and how great zeal the University of Halle was begun and completed.
While I read these things, I was astonished;
nor can I refrain from drawing some things from it:
But if I should wish to set forth all things according to the magnificence of the matter, I should consume the day in speaking.

For after the Elector, although everything resounded with war, having summoned several teachers, established the academy that had once been agitated in the mind of Cardinal Albert, from the equestrian school which his father had founded at Halle:

When, returning from the waters of Karlsbad to Berlin, he had arrived at the city of Halle, amazed at the number of young men who came to meet him out of respect, and having matured his plan and obtained the imperial privileges, since nothing now seemed to be lacking for the new work except the solemn rite and the religious consecration, he ordered preparations to be made for his splendid inauguration.

It was announced by an edict published in both languages, on the Calends of July, on the very birthday of the Prince, that the Frederick Academy would be dedicated in the ancient manner, with the reasons added which had impelled the Prince to establish a new seat for the arts, and with the suitability of the location commended.
The Magdeburg estates, whose extraordinary generosity was afterwards shown both in founding and in preserving the school, having been admonished by special letters:
The other universities of Brandenburg, invited by the council of professors to send someone to thank the founder, wished well to the newly founded school.
A triumphal gate was built by the students, with elegant ornament, with statues, insignia, tablets, and inscriptions.

As the day approached, with spectators and witnesses of the solemnities flowing together from all sides, especially from the neighboring academies, some were sent ahead from the court to prepare the apparatus and the military pomp.

Then the Elector, together with the most distinguished of his ministers—among whom I name Paul Fuchs, the prince's orator, Ludolph and Everard Dankelmann, and that distinguished ornament of letters, Ezekiel Spanheim—and with the provincial estates, amid the sounds of the bronze trumpet and the thunder of cannons brought from Magdeburg and musical harmonies, was met on his entry into the city with a splendid procession by a cavalry of about one hundred and fifty noble youths, with drawn swords, so that, as Cellarius's words are, they might prove themselves equally prepared in the discipline of Mars as in that of Apollo, and by the professors with the city senate and the priests.
After the day was spent in rejoicing and the night was given to festivity and to reverence for the Prince, with symphonic concerts performed for the Elector and his brother Philipp Wilhelm.
The first of July was a Sunday:
early in the morning sacred rites were performed in the temples;
afterwards all were intent on the spectacle.
And at the ninth hour the Elector, having been conveyed from the palace to the college of the academy, was received there by the professors:

Then the immense procession, distributed into ten divisions, was led into the temple of the citadel in the space of two hours, with the same number of heralds going before, and was magnificently and most splendidly equipped.
A cohort of soldiers at the front:
Another closed the column.

There the dedication was completed, with the Elector sitting on a most ornate tribunal with his brother and the chief ministers of the court, and with the counts who were to carry the insignia and the professors dressed becomingly and their leaders:

After the sacred rites were performed by Benjamin Ursinus, the Prince's preacher, Paul Fuchsius, with eloquent speech amid the various ceremonies, while the attendants brought the insignia as each had requested, inaugurated the academy.
He called the Prorector to the chair, clothed him in purple, and adorned him with scepters, after the privileges, keys, album, and seals were handed over, and each insignia was suitably explained.
Then the oath was taken:
The Prorector gave thanks:
The sound of bells and the roar of cannons filled the sky.

In the forum, coins were scattered, struck in three forms in memory of the dedication, and wine was poured out from a double spring for the common people, while they venerated the divine power in the temple.

After these things, one thousand two hundred were dining in the palace: the regular professors with the Elector and his brother and the imperial legate, others with the counts and courtiers, and the Magdeburg Orders in their own dining rooms;
But in total, up to three thousand men were received on that day by the generosity of the Elector.
On the following day, in the church of Mary, fifty-three doctors and masters were created;
And after the Prince had later departed, in the publication of the privileges Christophorus Cellarius again gave thanks.
I say nothing about congratulatory booklets, letters, poems.
For what reason, then, have I mentioned these things?
Is it so that by comparison with the most solemn ceremonies I may belittle these of ours?
Or so that literature may now seem to be despised and looked down upon because of the poverty of these men?
Not at all, indeed:
For indeed, nothing of that sort can be said without the greatest injustice.

But those things, then done in accordance with the character of that age and the customs of those men, are not to be deemed foolish, since they are pious and seemly, nor are they to be admired as uniquely right, which were done by a prince who was good and most devoted to literature, but undoubtedly too extravagant in expenditures and shows.
We indeed have seen the most splendid displays quickly pass away.
Adversity taught moderation, and to judge the truth of things as more powerful than empty appearance.
And if any appearance is even today put forward:
although not even a court produces such great gifts:
certainly from a school you would prefer any kind of ostentation of learning to be absent.
Therefore, if the pure simplicity of these solemnities needs any excuse,

It has something in the dignity of letters and wisdom, something in the singular modesty of our Lord, which is entirely free from all pretense, something in the character of the most excellent man who manages our affairs, which is most similar to a royal mind.
May God preserve for them this correct estimation of things:

May God preserve Frederick William, the Father of his country, the founder of our university, together with the entire Augustan house, and may He grant to us and to the state a perpetual author and preserver of all good things.

div.head: V. Oratio nataliciis Friderici Guilelmi III. celebrandis d. III. m. Aug. a. MDCCCXVII. habita.
An explanation of how the liberal arts profited the purification of the Christian church, and what the reformed church provided to the arts

p.s: Whenever I must speak before you on the birthday of Frederick William, the Father of his Country, most excellent men, distinguished, noble, colleagues and most beloved fellow soldiers,
so often do anxieties so great distract my mind, that I rightly think that no one can appreciate the magnitude of this office, unless his situation has been the same as mine.
Although indeed it is easy and pleasant to celebrate the virtues of the King and of the Prussian state, for which matter material never fails;

Nevertheless, necessity, which the religious observance of this most auspicious day imposes, if your feelings and the vows undertaken for the best King are to be explained each year by one and the same interpreter, can easily confuse the speaker, because he is compelled either to omit what has long seemed to him most important, or to repeat more than once what has already been said, and to lose all that charm of speech which is gained by novelty.
When I profess this, no one will take it as said in such a way that I deny that in Frederick William there exists a most abundant supply of many and varied praises.

But we are so constituted by nature that generally different people are more delighted and captivated by different arts, and each one indeed directs his mind more keenly to those things that especially please him, considers and admires them more diligently, and proposes them to his audience as things to be looked at and revered.

Hence it happens that among the leading men, who are worthy of manifold praise, the same men return to the same subjects in different years, while different men, each according to his own talent, taking a different part for themselves, at the same time bring forth entirely dissimilar things.

But as for me, to whom the highest honor has fallen, that I should be publicly appointed as the Senate's orator on this platform, if today, for the fourth time, having girded myself for celebrating these most sacred solemnities with my voice, I should depart somewhat from the King, who is far superior to our proclamations, in order to avoid that which I have indicated, whether it be a fault or a disadvantage, this one excuse will sufficiently protect me: that Pliny praised Trajan only once.

What of the fact that it seems not inappropriate to this very day and to the Prince, the author both of the divine service and of the happy establishment of letters, to take possession now of the memory of that greatest deed, notably aided by the most glorious ancestors of our Lord, whose third centennial we are about to celebrate duly in its own time this year:

I mean the restoration and reformation of Christian doctrine, faith, and religion, by which, before these three hundred years, a new light shone upon the whole world and especially upon Germany, so great that mortals have not seen such a light since the birth of Christ, and I think that all or most will judge that it can never be obscured or extinguished.

In this truly excellent subject, although I perceive that nothing can be said by me either more refined or more recondite, since the industry and skill of so many diligent writers has exhausted it, nevertheless I engage in it the more willingly, because I understand that it is most closely connected not only with my studies, but also with literature itself and with the system of public education, and I hope that it will be not at all unwelcome to all of you, even to those who are not devoted to Luther's doctrine.
For I will not stir up this Camarina, so as to descend into the field of controversies and to agitate subtle and thorny disputations;
but, leaving aside the heads of doctrine which are proper and peculiar to theologians, I shall rather endeavor to treat those things which have the least envy in them:

Relying on your kindness, which I have experienced quite often, I will briefly explain what the good arts have contributed to purifying the church, and what the church, once improved, has accomplished for the arts; I will add only as much about the rest as seems sufficient for evaluating the matters.

Therefore, to state my opinion briefly and clearly at the very outset, I maintain, listeners, that the teachings of the Gospel could not have been brought forth day by day without literature, nor could the disciplines and arts have been cultivated as they later were without the correction of sacred institutions.

For when you review with me the earlier times, you will not deny that that age, which I neither despise and which I seem to myself to measure with a just measure, did not lack great virtues and men as distinguished in other respects as they were notable for their exceptional piety;
so you will concede that the ruin and calamity of the church was brought about by nothing more than the encroaching ignorance and barbarism of the best things;

When those who were supposed to be the upholders and preservers of the learning handed down from antiquity, the priests and guardians of the sacred rites, fell into such great ignorance that they had no sound judgment either about divine or human affairs, that they gradually unlearned the Latin language, which was the native tongue of many of them, and some were not even imbued with the first rudiments of letters, which six-year-old boys know, nor did they understand the formulas and prayers which they recited:

Not without the fault of the Pontiffs, some of whom not only scorned and despised literature, but, thinking that sanctity agrees better with ignorance than with wisdom, condemned whatever smacked of learning as a crime of impiety and deemed it dangerous and pernicious to religion, just as unlearned princes are wont to fear for the security of their kingdoms from the learned.
And indeed, if religion differs in no way from superstition, it does considerable harm to that cultivation of the mind which dispels and overthrows superstition:
but if genuine piety cannot be separated from a correct knowledge of divine and human nature, religion will not refuse the light of learning.

But if the ministers of the church had diligently cultivated the liberal arts, had formed, nourished, and exercised their talents with the most excellent studies, then indeed neither would the divine institutions have been adorned with so many human opinions, smeared and burdened with so many tricks, and finally enclosed and constrained by such troublesome formulas, nor would mortals, who were born for liberty and moreover freed from the bonds of superstition by the discipline of Christ himself, have undergone a new and intolerable servitude of minds, from which neither the schools already restored by Charlemagne nor the scholastic philosophers, for the most part captured by received opinions, were able to free them.

More than is owed to those very enemies of the Christian name, the Turks, who, after Greece was captured and Constantinople was stormed, drove the learned men into Italy, for whom the way had been opened by certain men who had gone there earlier as scouts, as it were.
Then the study of languages, especially Greek, spread widely.

And learned Italians dared to speak what they felt, from which Petrarch, Boccaccio, Lorenzo Valla, Leonardo Bruni of Arezzo, Poggio of Florence, Niccolò Perotti, Francesco Filelfo, Angelo Poliziano, and other industrious and talented men partly opened up the sources of antiquity, and partly, by restoring the purity of language, displayed elegance of style and eloquence.

But the Aristotelian theology, to which the scholastic art adhered, was first broken by the sect of the Platonists, through George Gemistius, Bessarion, Marcus Musurus, John Pico della Mirandola, Marsilio Ficino, and the Platonic Academy, so strengthened and increased that it drew to its side the most brilliant and noble ornaments of Italy.

The recently invented art of printing was added, by whose aid every best book was widely disseminated, having been devised more quickly than the voice, which nevertheless, being called winged, was carried even to remote lands.

Nor was the institution of universities, whose number not small emerged in the fifteenth century, although obscured by the darkness of the scholastics, entirely useless then, because young men gathered in great numbers, if any more distinguished teacher had arisen, scattered the seeds of better discipline among their own people.

How much these things contributed to the correction of sacred doctrine, and how much they prepared favorable outcomes for so great an undertaking, is partly testified by Luther himself, and partly can be gathered from certain arguments and indications.
For he indeed asserts that languages were formerly not cultivated in monasteries and universities, lest the demonic empire should suffer a loss of such a kind that could not easily be repaired;
Whence it came about that they could neither write in Latin nor in German, and with their language and gospel corrupted and with reason itself almost stripped away, they were not far from beasts:

But by divine providence Greece was reduced into the power of the barbarians, so that the Greeks, fugitive and scattered, might spread their native language to foreign nations, so that other languages also might be learned, and finally so that the gospel might be revealed:
For not everything was accomplished by divine inspiration and breath, as some thought.
Certainly, unless he had been equipped with the aid of languages, it would have been permitted to him to be pious and to harangue before a few, but not to subdue the Pontiff and the sophists.
The same man, by refuting Aristotle, sufficiently shows that no small advantage is gained for the church.
But those very restorers of literature had elevated the authority of the pontiff and the priest by chastising the perversity of morals.
He shows the popes' masks of those paying the penalties for their crimes, the church filthy with squalor, buried under the weight of shameful deeds, in the underworld:

That gentle Petrarch first signifies the papal court by the name of Babylon, which afterwards stuck, as a reproach, and says that he left Rome, the seat of misery and nursery of error, never to return:
Others with not unrefined verses used to satirize the vices of the priests.

And that the art of printing books was seen as harmful by the Pontiffs themselves, especially in that much greater license of writers than now, you may see from the edicts by which they attempted to restrain the freedom of speech and thought in Germany itself, on account of certain writings published among the Magdeburgers, the Cologne people, the Treveri, and the Mainz people, already at the end of the fifteenth century, more cunningly than rightly.

But among our countrymen, the scholarship which had once been established by men of culture in Italy, and especially by Rudolph Agricola, was adapted to the understanding of the sacred sources by Reuchlin and Erasmus. Of these two, the one taught Hebrew, the other not only rendered the greatest service to the books of the New Testament, considering the character of that age, but also gradually and step by step removed the scholastic trifles that had long been hated by many, and rubbed away the folly of the times with his wit. He himself would undoubtedly have been a great reformer of both learning and sacred matters, had he not preferred to jest rather than to act seriously, and, out of ambition and timidity, to court the favor of the powerful and to adapt his own plans to those of others, rather than to speak with a simple and brave spirit what seemed right to him.
Hence it happened that it pleased neither side.

Now, since the idleness, luxury, avarice, and lust of the priests and monks lay open to the sight of all, being vividly described in the very Lateran Council in the speech of Giovanni Francesco Pico; and since, moreover, the German princes bore with the greatest indignation the tributes exacted by the Pope, and it was established by abundant testimonies that the Christians did not hold God to be more powerful than Jupiter, Christ than Apollo and Aesculapius, and the Virgin Mother than Diana:

For the successful undertaking of new enterprises, almost nothing was lacking except a favorable opportunity, which the quaestors of Leo and Cardinal Albert provided by establishing treasuries throughout all provinces and by most shameless harangues, and a bold man, divinely roused, who did not fear to expose himself to this crisis.

That man was Luther, a man not brought up in luxury, but one who experienced a hard boyhood and a disciplined youth, who, content with little, free from ambition, wonderfully steadfast, likewise diligent, energetic, ready, because he coveted neither honors nor wealth, could not be moved from his undertaken work by any allurements, any threats, or any danger:
In holiness and justice similar to Socrates and Aristides, a friend of so many princes, he died poor, he who had been born poor.
But his power of speaking, combined with richness and charm, equaled his piety;

His oratory, especially in his native tongue, was sharp, vehement, unrestrained, full of spirit and terror; the enervated and delicate elegance and modesty of our age can scarcely contain it, and you should not be surprised that there are those today who criticize it.
And there was as much learning in him as seemed sufficient:
And he learned something every day, and whatever was lacking Philip supplied;
When someone had reproached him with grammar, Luther openly declared that he would not be reluctant to depart from his opinion if that grammarian had judged otherwise.

It is remarkable how much he differs from Gregory the Great, the establisher of ceremonies, who charges Desiderius, bishop of Gaul, with this abominable crime, because he, a priest, had taught some people grammar.

By these arts, one man, a master of philosophy and theology, trusting in divine aid, not only resisted the unbridled desire of Emperor Charles, in whose domains the sun never set, whom Francis, king of the French, then the most powerful of princes, had been unable to oppose in arms, but also broke the power of the Pope, who seemed to himself to be the vicar of God himself, and first inspired, as it were, his own soul into a great part of Germany, and soon into Europe, and changed the face of all things.
He set before all who would undertake a difficult task with the powers of their mind an admirable example of persistent virtue;

But if one has looked at it, who would not be moved by such greatness, and who would think that no statue, no column could be erected for him that would correspond to the magnitude and fruits of the deeds accomplished by him?

Who, I ask, is there that does not understand that for a brave spirit nothing is impassable, and that its onslaught is not checked or broken by outworn terrors, but is rather strengthened and increased by the very obstacles?

For from the time when Luther began to be exposed to dangers and was condemned, he had a more certain protection in his friends, since several princes, more nobles, and almost the whole people understood that the matter concerned not one man, but the Germans, for whom he most rightly proclaimed that he was born for their advantage;
since he had undertaken the struggle for liberty against papal domination, if not greater, certainly more fruitful, than that which in our century freed Germany from the dominion of the Gauls:
Nor is there any doubt that the new doctrine would have taken possession of the whole fatherland, had not punishment been inflicted in many places upon pious men by sword and flame.
Yet in this respect that age excelled, that if anyone had been afflicted in one state, refuge lay open in another:
by which just liberty was strengthened and this was brought about, that princes dared less than the kings of Asia, who exercise their power carelessly among slaves.
No one fails to see how much this matter benefited Luther.
For if, as my opinion holds, such a great revolution could not be accomplished by a man who was lowly and humble, or who timidly looked upon the nods of the powerful;

If a certain fierceness was needed, which is known to have been so great in Luther that, thinking he owed more to God than to mortals, he would not spare even kings, and would not obey even Frederick the Wise himself, a prince who claimed very little for himself in sacred matters, but referred almost everything to learned theologians, both others and those of the University of Wittenberg, in all things:
Indeed, he would have been crushed before he had accomplished anything, if any word spoken too harshly or too freely had been maliciously twisted into an offense against the majesty.
And there were indeed, and there are even today, those who have attributed something seditious to Luther and his teaching.
I see clearly what displeases them.

Surely it stings them that he admonished the masters with a somewhat harsher pen, lest they harass their subjects, that he undertook to protect the rights of the people, that he undertook to shake off the servitude of souls.

But how much he urged the people to obey the magistrates, how he rebuked the turbulent movements and the license of the plowmen, and how he criticized the popular government, I need not explain to those who have read his writings.
Now when you ask, listeners, what it is that I have judged that great utility was brought to the cultivation of talents by the reformation of the church;

To say nothing of the vernacular language, which was admirably shaped by Luther, I think I will have satisfied with this one response, if I say that with the purity of religion restored, superstition was driven out and free inquiry into the most important matters was given back to the human race.
For what is more hostile to literature than superstition?

What retards the eagerness of study more, what dulls the keenness of the mind more, than an imperious authority, in which if you have become accustomed to acquiesce, then there is no need for you to inquire for yourself?
Superstition killed Socrates, whom none of the ancients had come closer to the true knowledge of God, by poison after he had been accused of impiety;

It drove Anaxagoras, who was among the first to philosophize about the mind that governs the world, into exile because he had held a different opinion about the sun than the Athenians, having been ensnared by the same charge.
It condemned the order of the celestial spheres discovered by Copernicus by decree of the Roman curia.
It condemned Galileo Galilei, who had deeply explored the secrets of nature, to prison and relegated him to a remote retreat.
Finally, it handed over so many wise and innocent men of every kind to tortures and punishments.
But what about the authority of men?
Do we not see that those who allow themselves to be bound and held by it are either frivolous and weak-minded, or unskilled and ignorant, or pretenders?

Since these things are so, that constitution of the church must necessarily be conducive to literature, in which it is permitted to escape the authority of men with impunity, to approach and examine the sacred sources, and finally to think freely about the nature of divine and human things.

How much more intense the care for educating the youth is connected with this kind of discipline is evident not only from the matter itself, but is also confirmed by the experience of the time that followed.
Therefore Luther considered nothing more important than to urge princes and cities to found schools:

For he thought that the strength and safety of the state lay not so much in accumulating wealth, in elegant buildings, in roads, bridges, and embankments constructed at great expense, in forts and walls, in arsenals filled with weapons, artillery, and breastplates — resources which, if evil or foolish men should use them, would bring greater destruction than benefit — but much more in the honesty, prudence, and learning of well-educated citizens, by whom wealth could be acquired and properly invested.

When the Romans understood this, they took care that the boys should be educated in Greek and Latin letters and liberal arts in such a way that a great crop of most skillful men, equipped with varied learning, would spring up, and that in a single soldier more learning would be found than in all the monks, priests, and bishops of Germany gathered together.

And so, that which is in no way to be endured, that the state should obey logs and blocks of wood, especially in that felicity of the age, in which it has already been brought about that eighteen-year-old youths can turn out more learned than those who once spent twenty or forty years in the discipline of monasteries or universities with the greatest detriment to their morals:
He wisely recommends liberal studies, the reading of poets, the knowledge of history and of languages, Latin, Greek, and Hebrew.
If these are neglected, not only can the Gospel be lost and ruined, but it can come to such a point that no ability to speak and write either Latin or German remains.

The judgment of these most prudent men seems to us the more necessary to be recalled to the memory of our contemporaries, the more numerous are those in our age who either neglect or despise ancient literature, and think that nothing is more foolish than if anyone should speak or write in Latin.
Indeed, when Luther, a truly German man, declares plainly that those who think that one should devote one's labor to only one language are not at all approved by him:

In this age I fear that those most weighty words of the same man will soon fall, since the Latin language is already now so much becoming obsolete in these lands that the age seems to be inclining almost to barbarism.

But to return to the point from which I digressed: since it had happened through the correction of sacred matters that the immense wealth of the monasteries, abandoned by those who had lurked there, was without a master, lest such great resources, once bequeathed by the kindness of pious men, should be squandered by the princes and nobles who coveted them, and should be assigned to those to whom they least pertained:

Luther wished that they should be restored partly to the needy heirs of those who had donated them, partly be destined for relieving the poverty of the citizens, and partly for administering sacred rites and especially for founding and equipping schools.
Nothing more just or more useful could have been done.
If this plan had been religiously obeyed in all places and at all times, not so many schools would suffer from such great poverty.
Indeed, I recall with no small joy that Frederick William, a most just prince, did this very recently.
But lest I seem to be playing the eulogist too much, I will not conceal what evils, after Luther, invaded our common fatherland from that movement.
I shall speak truthfully, my listeners.
The division of opinions was the cause of the most atrocious wars, by which all of Germany was laid waste, and the newly born literature itself was severely afflicted.
Feuds and enmities arose among the citizens of one republic, one city, one town:
Irreparable damage was inflicted on the German empire, for from that time they almost never coalesced in unity with solid faith:
To foreign nations, whether enemies or under the pretext of friendship, our land was given as prey.
But when you have weighed the matter without anger and partiality, you will not cast the blame upon the followers of Luther, who had no advantage in the civil discord:
but upon the obstinacy of the Popes and Emperors, who with a wicked endeavor were striving to root out the new doctrine utterly with sword and fire.
They were fighting for their hearths and homes:
for these it was superfluous to fight for excessive power.
They were demanding equal liberty for all:
They were not yielding anything regarding the most unjust conditions.

And indeed, although at the beginning of the disturbances Leo himself, with his characteristic gentleness, had even praised Luther, afterwards they all proscribed the followers of this sect and cursed them with the most bitter imprecations:

And without considering what should be granted to the times, what the new character of talents demanded, but despising the Germans, whom the Italians then, as recently the Gauls, regarded as beasts, they resolved to resist the course of the human mind and to overthrow by force those who opposed them.
But those are greatly mistaken who think that the onset of new things is to be eluded by punishments or by throwing obstacles in the way.
It is better retained by gentle measures.
History teaches this, the best teacher of political wisdom and a truthful prophetess, provided that the lust and desire of men do not take away trust from her, as Apollo did from Cassandra.

But these things, which were then so done, it is now vain to deplore with womanish lamentation, and that does not befit those who obey the Brandenburg house, of which a not small part from the beginning greatly favored Luther's undertakings.
For although that very man, who had roused the reformer of religions by the selling of indulgences through Tetzel, was from this same family;
although Elector Joachim the First opposed Luther's doctrine so bitterly, that his wife, devoted to the evangelical discipline, was forced to avoid danger to her life by exile:

nevertheless, those who ruled in Franconia, the Brandenburgers, together with Albert, Master of the Knights, chose this sect for themselves early, whose example Elector Joachim the Second later followed:
And it seems to have happened not by human means, but by divine counsel, that the Brandenburg dominion was greatly increased by the reformation of the church.
I will say something a bit more blunt, but perhaps not far from the truth:

The name of Brandenburg owes no less to Luther and the fall of the papal power in Germany than to its armies and most valiant leaders, since a great part of the lands that obeyed it had formerly been under the power of bishops and other lords connected with the church;

Since Prussia itself, not long after the beginning of the restoration of sacred affairs, passed to the Brandenburg prince, since Halberstadt, Magdeburg, and many other territories were early transferred from the priests to the Elector:
not to mention those lands which have been acquired in our age.
Finally, as if by some fate of the place, almost all those whom Luther's life made famous are now ours:
Islebia, where he was born, Erfordia, where he was educated, and Viteberga itself, where he taught, from which he illuminated the whole world with the brightest lights.
