But in this century, after those most bitter quarrels have now cooled down, and the suspicions have been removed by which the different sects persecuted each other, under the most gentle rule of Frederick William the peoples of both religions are held together united in brotherly spirits.

Since he, after the republic was restored by the strength of arms, embraces sacred matters with the greatest care, and is himself an outstanding example and model of piety, this is not, as with many, sluggishness, but fairness and reason, because he loves neither side more, thinks that neither side has greater trustworthiness, and does not bind the feelings of minds with any bonds.

What of the fact that he has earned the favor of the Pontiff himself, who has not obscurely testified how much he attributed to Frederick William by restoring the Palatine troops to their former seat?

Nor, however, does our King allow the advantages gained by the improvement of the church to be lost or diminished, who adds this to his other virtues, that he promotes and strengthens the study of letters by cultivating arts and disciplines, and by founding schools of every kind partly and partly by increasing them with more lavish equipment.
To whom, I ask, have the greater fruits of this liberality flowed, than to our seat of learning?
Therefore, although the birthday of Frederick William is common to the whole fatherland, nevertheless it ought to seem in some way proper to this university;

And it will never cease to recall with grateful mind the merits of its parent and to proclaim its praises, but every year on this most joyful day it will most religiously bind itself to the words of the most clement Prince and to the laws most recently and kindly given by him, and it will implore the supreme deity with the most earnest prayer that it may add perpetuity to the safety of the best King, of the royal house, and of the Prussian empire.
I have spoken.

div.head: VI. Oratio nataliciis Friderici Guilelmi III. celebrandis d. III. m. Aug. a. MDCCCXVIII. habita.

An inquiry into what is foremost among the benefits that literary studies bring to the public interest, and for what reason they seem to be nourished and cherished with earnest care chiefly by wise rulers of states

p.s: As this day, so greatly desired by me and by all of you, most excellent men, illustrious, noble, most weighty colleagues, and especially dear fellow students, returns, it cannot happen to any city of this kingdom more pleasantly than to our school of learning, that this whole day is accustomed to be given and dedicated to the solemnities, by which we celebrate with the greatest joy the most powerful King given to us by divine providence, proclaim the benefits conferred by him upon the state, and finally offer pious vows for his health and future reign:

Because our university of letters, founded eight years ago by the wisest counsels of that prince, has experienced, as often before, so especially in this year, the greatest proofs of royal kindness, munificence, and clemency.

And indeed, not to mention lesser matters, although in these too there is no doubtful indication of goodwill, will anyone doubt that this was a distinguished favor of the King, because several teachers have very recently been added to our university, and these partly summoned here from other academies, so that they might occupy positions not without detriment to our affairs?
because our institutions, especially the medical ones, have been enlarged and strengthened in this very year?

Because the most wise King, by the laws promulgated in the previous year, has added these scepters, which are now seen for the first time, the most ample and most splendid insignia of our power, with the greatest liberality?

Now, since this year has been memorable for the state, both in general and especially in literary affairs, because of the change of royal ministers who are placed in charge of the highest matters, who does not understand that the King has taken the best care of this university? For when he who had managed our affairs well, diligently, strenuously, and uprightly for so many years was taken from us—he to whom we already owed many splendid things, and to whom we would undoubtedly have owed more; with whom, through long association, we had formed a kind of intimacy; and who, at the very moment of his resignation, candidly declared how dear we were to him—a man has been set over us than whom the consensus of men could not point out one more worthy, nor learning approve one more skilled, nor could those taught by experience desire and seek one more ready, generous, or humane.

A man, I say, distinguished by exceptional accomplishments and by equal fame publicly, in short, excelling in all the endowments of mind and talent, which you would not demand as necessary in a prince of letters, but would wish that each excellent quality might rarely occur.

For what greater advantage can there be for the flourishing of learning than a prefect of such a kind, who seems to direct all his strength and all his care so that the studies of letters, traced back to their origins, may be nourished and spread more widely, and may enjoy that dignity and honor which they deserve?
I say these things at the very beginning of my speech, not because I would praise such an excellent man as he deserves:
for neither does this place admit of this argument:
But so that I may proclaim and extol the judgment of the most merciful King.
Another matter remains, which, even at the risk of giving offense, if not to be explained, certainly seems to need touching upon.

For from a most honorable beginning, from the memory of the church restored by Martin Luther, celebrated at the beginning of this academic year by the alumni of the German universities, because in those solemnities certain things had happened which would incur blame, a great envy of the schools was stirred up against the universities, and among us indeed it was increased by a certain disturbance, which had turned the keen mind of the King himself to attention.

Then indeed those who in this royal city either considered the license of some young men, which could be restrained by the easiest remedies, a greater evil than literature was a good, or thought that this palaestra of learning, still unfamiliar to many, was not to be endured for some reasons or other, most eagerly spread the rumor about transferring or abolishing our school, not even observing the reverence which is owed to the Prince, when they falsely accused the most steadfast King of manifest inconstancy, while they pretended that he was thinking about rescinding what he had decreed the year before.

But in this matter, about which I have begun to speak, the best of princes not only approved of his customary fairness and leniency, but also showed most clearly how skilled an evaluator of young men he was, since he thought that they should not be punished as conspirators, but that some allowance should be made and indulgence granted to the youthful ardor of their talents.
But someone may think that I, in praising the King, use these matters rather inappropriately, since greater things, and things free from every suspicion of envy, could be brought forward.

For my part, I do not consider it a small matter if a leader, especially one educated and trained in military command, amid such great agitations of minds as now exist or are thought to exist, acts gently and prefers to settle and calm minds by milder counsels rather than to subdue them by force and at the same time exasperate them.

Nor do I think that a discussion of those matters which pertain not to the schools of literature but to the whole republic is sufficiently safe, because concerning the greatest affairs, since they are generally conducted in secret, not everyone has a settled judgment, and whatever you may say, you will have given occasion for the charge of either flattery or detraction.
Therefore I keep myself away from this most spacious field, and I prefer not to attain what is highest rather than to risk myself in that which I feel I am unequal to.
Today I stand in literature.
It is incredible with what zeal and with what cares, after the wars have been ended, they are nourished and aided in our fatherland;
which, as it is seen in the other schools being corrected and adorned, so it is most clearly observed in the arrangements of the universities.

For do we not see, to omit now the academies of Breslau, Königsberg, and our own, the academy of Halle, which had been twice destroyed by hostile hatred, restored munificently, strengthened by union with Wittenberg, and enriched with resources?
Is not the academy of Greifswald, for which many had feared the worst, preserved and brought into a better state?

What of the fact that to the Rhine, the river of our fatherland, recently recovered, among the citadels and military garrisons with which we repel the attacks of the enemy, a most powerful bulwark of letters is also being added, which we predict will be no weaker a fortification for the liberty of the Germans than Mainz and the fortresses of Koblenz?

Therefore, in such a great struggle to establish the good arts, it is helpful to understand what it is especially that the study of literature brings to the utility of the state, and why they seem to be nourished and fostered with more intense care by the wise governors of states, among whom Frederick William holds a particularly distinguished place.

For although I do not greatly disagree with those who say that in literature one should not consider utility at all, but that it should be cultivated and practiced for its own sake, like everything that is best and virtue itself;
Nevertheless, if I consider that true utility cannot be separated from those things that are truly good, I readily concede that literature also ought to be useful.

Nor indeed do I call that usefulness by which learning is commonly recommended to some, namely that it provides the state with servants fit for rightly carrying out commands and for managing public affairs like slaves without reason or any feeling, and that it increases the crafts by which the fortunes of citizens are aided, by supplying inventions.
although not even this is to be despised:
but I judge quite the opposite: that literature can neither provide that nor ought to be directed to this.

And indeed, that literature is not subservient to that thing which I placed first, is understood even from this: that each person cannot learn knowledge from outside, but can only draw it from his own mind and, as it were, unfold it with a skilled teacher as guide, and that the force and power of knowledge and literature is not placed in the memory and tradition of everyday things, nor in a certain ability to act according to prescribed laws, but in a liberal, inner, and from the very principles to be derived cognition of divine and human things.
And certainly, if the disciplines had been born and prepared for that use of rulers which I mentioned, they could not and should not be brought to greater perfection day by day;
And for the theologian it sufficed to learn doctrines sanctioned by age, for the jurist the received laws, for the physician precepts approved by the common people;
But philosophy, which by no means allows itself to be reduced to these narrow limits, had to be driven out and banished.
What if there are those who demand this?
Indeed, we know that throughout nearly the whole East, the boundaries of all learning have been enclosed by such limits and, as it were, Chinese walls.
and not without success:
namely, by the unbroken continuity of their discipline, their minds have been lulled to sleep, and at last buried in a torpor more like death than life.

Nor was it far from happening that the peoples of Europe would rush into the same servitude under priestly domination, had not the more vigorous force and virtue of the West broken those bonds in time.

But to return to the point from which I fear I may seem to have digressed a little: since letters, when properly cultivated, not only reject this state of affairs, but endeavor to overthrow it, inasmuch as they approve not what is commonly received, but what the nature of things and right reason seem to demand;
it is clear that the arts and disciplines are suited to nothing less than to forming those servants whom I have mentioned.

Therefore, since those who prefer that the state be administered in that manner rather than wisely corrected according to circumstances do not ignore this, they accuse the learned and wise teachers, as corrupters of talents and of the state, who, although they themselves are inexperienced in conducting affairs, nevertheless dare to criticize the method of practical men with haughty censure, and strive to turn young men away from the right and customary path of business by the subtlety of argument and empty declamations.
The Athenian republic provides a splendid example of this matter, which was not begun now for the first time, but has been propagated from the most ancient times.
When it was being driven headlong by the license and unbridledness of popular rule, which is known to have been equally innate in that age, as the opposite vice is in ours;

Socrates the philosopher, although he was estranged from public affairs and indeed so ignorant of them that he would provoke laughter from the citizens whom he wanted to send to vote, yet by his teaching and admonition he strove that the form of the state might be changed for the better and be established and governed according to the precepts of wisdom; he was accused of impiety and punished by Anytus and his followers, servants of the common people, to whom that condition of affairs seemed best.

When repentance came too late, after it was understood that Socrates alone of all men had had the ruin of the state most clearly in view, and that he had not so much been eager for revolutionary changes as, out of love for his country, had wished to remedy the public evil.

And indeed it is no more for the training of such ministers as I have mentioned that literature ought to be proposed as a goal, so that the resources of citizens and of the state itself may be increased by cleverly devised arts.
For I need not mention that these advantages can be expected only from the mathematical and physical sciences;

Whoever has judged the excellence of learning from this common use in daily life, let him take care lest he place the highest good in acquiring resources, in amassing money, in the elegance and pleasantness of food and culture, and finally in luxury and delights, when he directs the utmost mental exertion, which is applied to the pursuit of studies, to that end.

But I know well that all those things, which make life easier and more pleasant, seem to be sought by me and by you all, not for their own sake, but so that the mind, freed from the cares which the necessity of nature imposes, may more freely follow its divine nature, that is, to cultivate virtue and to acquire for itself the highest knowledge and learning:
Since this learning is very far removed from profit and gain, earlier men thought that it should be included under the name of the liberal arts.
But if anything of utility from literature overflows into the conveniences of life:
and it overflows indeed very much:
let us enjoy this as a by-product, not demand it as a debt;
much less, however, let us prescribe to the learned the duty of directing their studies deliberately to that end:

Whoever would wish this to happen would not even be consulting the common good, because the nature of every great discovery is so constituted that what and how great its fruits will be cannot be perceived at the outset, and is found out only after long use and experience, often even by chance.
But if the common people measure the excellence of literature by that standard:

This is said to have happened to Thales, the founder of philosophy, whose study of wisdom was reproached as fruitless, until, by renting oil presses, he proved with a truly brilliant argument how much profit could be derived from the knowledge of nature.
This indeed we will bear easily, and we will not demand what is unfair, that unskilled men should judge accurately about a matter foreign to them.

But what shall we say, if some who usurp the name of learned men, if the presidents and governors of republics, who ought to have surveyed the universal powers of human nature and the limits of almost all things, judge so basely of literature?
To whom nothing more fitting, as it seems to me, can be proposed than that very well-known, but by no means more contemptible, example of the mathematician Archimedes.
For when Eudoxus and Archytas, the Pythagoreans, had entered upon the path of mechanics for demonstrating mathematical truths, and had laid the foundations of mechanics itself,

after Plato, indignant, reproached them because they diverted geometry from the pure notions of the intellect to the considerations of corporeal nature and to illiberal handicraft, the mechanical art was separated from geometry and philosophy, and was added to the military disciplines:
Nor did anyone who wished to be regarded as a mathematician think that he could excel by mechanical inventions, even the most useful and most admirable ones.

Therefore Archimedes, who excelled so greatly in that art that he said he could move the earth if another earth were given to him on which to stand, and not only boasted such things, but in the siege of Syracuse defeated Marcellus and the very strong forces with the power of machines and engines, like the hundred-handed Briareus or Typhoeus, and prevailing beyond human strength;

Nevertheless, he did not attribute much to his instruments, but he did these things almost playfully, intending to gratify King Hiero, who had asked him to bring forth demonstrations of his knowledge adapted to the comprehension of the common people.

And he was of such liberality and greatness of mind that, although he had gained the reputation of a wisdom not mortal but truly divine through these very things, he did not think them worthy to be committed to writing, but sought his chief praise and remembrance among posterity in the clear and elegant exposition of theorems.
Therefore he ordered that not a wolf, not a crane, not a scorpion, not any engine or torment, but a sphere with a cylinder be carved on the tomb.

But after I have briefly explained, in a few words, in what things that usefulness of learning, on account of which they ought especially to be cultivated by states, may, in my judgment, be placed, hearers,

so that, as far as can be done by speech, by which only certain heads can be plucked, and nothing can be explained copiously and subtly and confirmed by its own arguments, we may rightly consider what connection exists between the state and literature, it seems necessary to go back a little higher.

For among the most ancient peoples of the East, who invented the first rudiments of letters, whatever learning there was, together with the care of divine things, is known to have been in the hands of the priests.
As a weighty proof, the divine origin of learning seemed to be established.

At that time learning was not so much received and cherished by the state, as it was placed in the very prytaneum of the state, like the sacred flame of Vesta and the vital breath of the republic, with the greatest reverence and religious awe.

This the most cultivated nation of the Greeks afterwards brought forth from that sanctuary into the light and sight of men, from which, when the material had been transferred from the priests to the poets, the first philosophers and writers of history received it, who, having divided the stories among themselves, the one drew from them the beginnings of natural philosophy, the other of history.

Thus it came about that the sciences, which once by the seeds of the priests' colleges had governed the state itself, after the priestly authority was diminished, being separated from the ministries of the gods, wandered about as if free, and since the whole institution of divine matters was occupied with ceremonies, partly entrusted to the care of sacrificers and partly to that of families, while the public discipline embraced only music and bodily exercise, they were not aided by public expenditures.
Indeed, because they attacked publicly sanctioned superstitions, they were from time to time ensnared on a charge of impiety.

Therefore, if neither the states nor literature suffered any loss, the most important reason is that the good arts, by their own excellence, had so attracted every most distinguished and most famous man, and whoever had the greatest influence among his own people, that he not only favored learned men exceptionally and spared no expense in rewarding them, but was himself most learned; and because the liberality of that age was such that those who wished to excel in public affairs thought that they ought to surpass others in the elegance and richness of their learning.
When I say this, I am not referring to Pericles, Alcibiades, Critias, or Demosthenes, who in the Athenian state, the parent of every kind of literature, achieved the highest distinction:

But among the Romans themselves, a warlike people, from whom the more refined learning began to be disseminated, who does not know that there was almost no one who, in the conduct of affairs, sought to attain immortality of name without being distinguished by an abundance of learning?
What of the fact that even the emperors sought praise in literature?
For who was more learned than Julius Caesar?
who was more lettered than Octavian Augustus?
And not to mention the studies of Tiberius, or the truly foolish erudition of Claudius, who does not know the contests of Hadrian with poets and men of letters, exceeding the measure of a prince?
Who does not admire the wisdom of Marcus Antoninus and Julian?
Therefore, in this state of affairs, there was no need for the care of the state for liberal studies.
Therefore, in this state of affairs, there was no need for the care of the state for liberal studies.
Although under the Emperor Vespasian, teachers of eloquence began to be supported by salaries when their art was declining,

Thus it then seemed to have been observed that, although letters were separated from the divine stock, human affairs could not be well governed except by those who brought a mind subdued by learning and knowledge, and who had learned to bring forth into common use by their faculty of speech what they had conceived in a mind imbued with the precepts of wisdom.

Soon, when fierce barbarism was pressing upon them, and the powerful sought glory in arms alone and pleasure in luxury, letters returned to the place from which they had set out, and rested in the union of the Christian priesthood:

Nor were the schools of learning, together with the church, for any other more important reason publicly and privately increased in resources and enriched, than because they seemed to arouse, nourish, and cherish the divine nature of the mind, and to bring it about that as many as possible should think rightly about divine and human matters, and pursue virtue more keenly.

And these things indeed I have discussed to this end, that from the memory of earlier times it might be evident that letters, when they were connected with sacred matters, were not nourished from some illiberal and sordid cause, nor, when they were separated from the state and entrusted to themselves, were they neglected by the leaders of states, but were especially cultivated by them.

But to those who consider either of those conditions, this immediately presents itself: that a certain greater utility of learning was present to the earlier men, who understood that in knowledge there lies the vital force of the republic and, as it were, its soul and mind, which penetrates and moves the body that is by itself inert;

And just as, according to the doctrine of the Pythagoreans, the soul of the world is stretched out and extended from the middle fire, which holds the place of Vesta and the hearth, through the whole nature of things, and is surrounded externally by the sky, so from the schools of literature reason is diffused through the state, containing all things and illuminating and rousing them with its light.
But to minds, as the natural philosopher Heraclitus says, nothing is more hostile than rest.
And so knowledge, not all knowledge, but that which is worthy of this name, by its own impulse strives toward perfection:
Hence it happens that it, having thoroughly insinuated itself into the state, spontaneously carries it along and advances it to a better condition.
Now what greater advantage, I ask, can be procured for the state?
For unless it is advanced, while it stands still, it is corrupted by idleness and sluggishness.
Yet those kingdoms which are more firmly supported by their own mass can do without literature, if not with impunity, at least with greater security.
Those states which, like Prussia, like almost all of Germany, are unequal in strength to their neighbors, must make up for what is lacking in resources by the vigor of their intellects.

With the matter thus settled, I could now make an end of speaking about the usefulness of literature, were I not to see many of my contemporaries declaiming into philosophy in quite a different manner and for quite different reasons:
From whom I am so far from thinking that I should yield, that I judge that no part of knowledge is more useful to the state than philosophy.

For although philosophy alone cannot govern states, since much practical experience and accurate knowledge of both the peoples and all the institutions in the state are needed, which history supplies:

nevertheless philosophy not only sharpens and exercises the mind excellently, corrects morals, explains the reasons of the most important matters, frees minds from superstition and from preconceived opinions;

But indeed, what is most important, it shows to those who approach public affairs the limits of good and evil, and it indicates not obscurely in what direction states should be guided, if anyone is willing to listen to it.

For my part, although perhaps I shall be considered an insufficiently skilled judge of these matters, no one seems to me to have written more divinely about the best kind of state than the founder of the Academic philosophy.

The fact that both Dionysii summoned him, as it seems, for the sake of strengthening their rule, against the opposition of a crowd of courtiers and flatterers, can serve as evidence that he was judged fit even for conducting affairs of state.
What if there are examples of states that were administered by philosophers with the most favorable success?
For who does not know that Magna Graecia was most happy while it was ruled by the Pythagoreans, and that after they were driven out it was terribly disturbed by continuous sedition?
Would that the rulers of states preferred the admonitions of philosophy to following I know not what arts!
Certainly we would not see states oppressed by such great avarice, envy, ambition, and luxury.

Now, with the connection of literature and civil affairs, such as I have conceived it, having been demonstrated, it remains for me to say what seems to be inferred from this about the status of literature itself in the state.
For if the end of learning were that which is asserted by some, and which I have explained above cannot exist, literature would have to serve the state:
but if that seriousness and dignity of learning which we ourselves have set forth is the true one, they must be free.

But it is agreed that liberty is twofold: one of lesser value, which is concerned with external things, and another far greater, which when you have called it inner, you will have named it by its own proper name.

Nor, however, do I seek in him that kind of liberty, that the schools of the liberal arts, exempt from all authority of the prince and his magistrates, should govern themselves, and even elect and appoint public teachers by their own votes:
which thing, as it can sometimes be useful, if those who have the power of choosing are far from anger and partiality, and do not regard private advantages more than public ones;

Thus it seems to me that the welfare of literature is better provided for where schools are subject to the gentle governance of the state, which takes care with prudent and attentive concern that laws are not violated, that well-established institutions do not become obsolete through negligence, and that the literary enterprise suffers no other harm, and whatever benefits the pursuit of learning, it recommends, advises, and commands with greater authority.

I say, to such a governance as we rejoice has fallen to our literary university, a governance that combines prudence in planning, diligence in acting, and speed in completing with courtesy, affability, and goodwill.

But I consider this to be the chief sign of external liberty, without which even that greater and inner liberty cannot be preserved, namely that each university be administered in the manner of a college or of a common and public body, and that, exempt from the will, caprice, and envy of the most powerful, it have security and sanctity through the force of laws and privileges.

In this regard, observe the wisdom of our ancestors, who founded schools of learning in the very likeness of municipalities, and granted them two most important things on which they could most firmly rely: jurisdiction over their own members and ownership of lands and revenues.

Of these, the latter has persisted in almost all the academies of Germany, certainly in those that are in Protestant lands, through all the vicissitudes of civil affairs, in various ways, although limited, because the rulers of the states perceived that judgments must be exercised in one way among young students, in another among other men.
except that in a few places the domination of the French had, for some years, driven out the old institution.

The other [part] indeed involved the teachers of the universities founded long ago in various affairs, perhaps not very compatible with the more diligent cultivation of the arts and disciplines and with more recondite knowledge.

But just as it kept the church, so it kept the schools connected to it, for the most part safe from avarice and desire, and it secured for them that stability which could attract both teachers and students, whereas unstable and tottering things deter them.
Moreover, the possession of lands assigned to the literary colleges, among the ambassadors who protect the rights of the people, a place honorable and worthy of learning.
And because the public schools, supported by their own resources, seemed inviolable, the private generosity of pious and learned men was also stirred to enrich them with gifts and benefits.
until the powerful showed that neither shame nor faith nor religion stood in their way, so that they dared to commit sacrilege.
Which things when I candidly profess:
For true history proves that it is not fitting for this place or my person to put on a painted and deceitful appearance on things.

I am not afraid that I may seem to anyone to slander our state, which in such great evils and difficulties has acted most temperately, and while it especially does this, that the flower and honor of the church and of letters may be preserved and grow, it is so far from filth and avarice that it is deservedly considered most kind and most generous.

Nor did I begin to speak about lands and fields in order to reproach anyone with what would be the height of shamelessness, namely that our school of letters does not enjoy this, as it were, pledge of permanence;
But where the course of my speech has carried me, that I did not want to anxiously avoid.
On the contrary, in a plainly different condition, such as ours is, I see no small advantages.

Among these there is this: that schools which are so fortified on every side that they seem unable to be attacked or destroyed by any chance, by any moderate force, by any cause either legitimate or at least plausible, easily languish in inactivity.

While in those matters which depend entirely on the judgment of the state, and which vary according to the plans and institutions of the powerful, all the powers of intellect must be exercised more keenly, and all must advance as if intent and prepared, so that nothing anywhere appears loose or remiss:
Moreover, because these very things can be more easily corrected, adapted to the genius and needs of the age, and finally brought to greater perfection;
And since their safety depends more on the state or on the prince, they are generally cultivated, aided, and cherished by them more than those which are endowed with greater freedom.
And there are indeed two excellent pledges in which academies may trust, one placed in the virtue of the state, the other in their own virtue.
But if that virtue should perish, to which the preservation and advancement of learning are especially devoted, then let literature fall along with the state, as it fell among the Greeks and Romans.

But if the schools of the arts cannot now maintain their dignity and win esteem for themselves by their own merit, it is better for their decrepit bodies to die than to lead a precarious and wretched life, and one most harmful to the states themselves.

For nothing, in my judgment, infects the state with a more pestilential corruption than a depraved and corrupted body of schools, which, instead of learned, wise, and upright men, sends forth ignorant, stupid, and morally perverted individuals.
For this evil, when it has been fixed deeply, as they say, in the very marrow of the schools, you would cure with difficulty by correction, but most certainly by eradication.

Finally, for those who prudently weigh the importance of things, the other kind of freedom in literature will seem much more serious, which I have called inner freedom, and I think it should be placed in the method of teaching and writing, unconstrained and unimpeded by any illiberal laws.

Since this school too has been confirmed by the most sacred statutes, and since, beyond the other advantages, all things seem to have been provided for, so that our teaching may not deviate from the correct goal of knowledge, nor fail to render to the state the benefits I have mentioned:

The wisdom of Frederick William can never be sufficiently praised, who established the seat of learning in this city, the capital of the empire, where the scattered seeds of letters might bear more abundant fruit than in a less distinguished place.

We pray today, with all our heart and with the deepest feeling of gratitude and of the devotion owed to the best of kings, that the Best and Greatest God may add to his life many years that are favorable, happy, and prosperous for us and for the whole state.
I have spoken.

div.head: VII. Oratio nataliciis Friderici Guilelmi III. celebrandis d. III. m. Aug. a. MDCCCXIX. habita.
On shaping man toward complete humanity

p.s: In these most sacred solemnities, dedicated to the name of Frederick William, the founder of letters, about whom I shall speak, nothing is offered, auditors, that is at once more fitting for this day and for my and your person and for these times, than an argument, of whatever kind, drawn from letters themselves.

For while I look around to see what I should most appropriately narrate, I understand that our speech will have very great favor and delight, when I have spoken about the state, which has been brought from a ruined condition into this moderate flower of happiness by the cares and occupations of a most powerful prince, and about those matters especially which have been publicly done and instituted in this year;
But if I have set forth the nature of our academy, such as it has been in these recent times, I see that this lecture will be a most honorable discussion.
But what things have happened to the university each year, whether prosperous or adverse, those must be left to the Rector when he speaks at the abdication of his office.

But although I do not avoid public affairs even now for the first time, nevertheless, because envy burns more fiercely day by day, it now dissuades me more sharply than before from treating that subject.

Therefore, having set aside the greatest matters, which might draw us into the fields of public life, and having removed the brilliant lights that shine from afar, by which you could distinguish and illuminate words, you will hear a slender discussion, not sufficiently oratorical for listening, and, because this place excludes a more subtle doctrine, a little less accurate for reading.
I am about to speak about shaping a person to perfect humanity, and indeed in such a way that, leaving aside present circumstances from time to time, I take refuge in more remote antiquity:

In this matter, if I have departed somewhat from the praises of the King, this can be some consolation to me, because not only, since I must deal with the same material every year, is the inconvenience compensated by the variety of the subject, but also the matter which I am about to treat ought to seem altogether most worthy of being considered on the birthday festival of the King, who excellently aids the humane culture and education of his citizens.
Therefore, when you ask to what cultivation men are to be formed and educated, I answer that it is twofold:
one is peculiar and proper to each individual, by which each person is made fit for the art or trade by which he seeks to earn his living;

The other kind, which is common to all those whom nature has equipped with the talents necessary for it, and whom fortune has placed in a position that allows them, through their private means, to aspire to a more refined education, is not pursued for profit or for the sake of sustaining life, but, having its end placed within itself, it neither accomplishes nor attempts to accomplish anything other than that the entire powers of each individual be unfolded and exercised as perfectly as possible.
Whom they are accustomed to call either liberal for that very reason which we have mentioned, or humane because he regards nothing beyond humanity.
For if we say human learning, we do not intend by the meaning of this word to separate the human from the animal or from the divine nature:

Indeed, since it is understood that it is placed between the two and partakes of both, the principle of human culture is so constituted that it cultivates, by sowing the seeds of religion, and by awakening the knowledge of the divine nature, insofar as we can attain it by thought, and altogether by shaping and strengthening the powers of the mind and intellect, that which in men is akin to the divine;

Then, the part that we share with the beasts, I mean the bodily nature, should be so formed that it is as little troublesome as possible to the mind and obeys and serves the mind's plans as well as possible.
Since these things are so, neither is the cultivation of the mind to be regarded as entirely liberal, nor that of the body as illiberal.
But although the pursuit of shaping the mind and intellect is, for the most part, liberal and truly humane, yet it is well known that this too can be turned to profit:
so that those who profess arts and doctrines are accustomed both to derive and to seek gain from these very things:

And indeed, on the other hand, no one will doubt that he who seeks nothing but the perfection of the body itself, removed from all the sordidness of handicraft, in exercising the body's strength, renders liberal service.

But if the liberal arts have profit attached to them, they are not practiced by those who treat them correctly for the sake of the profit itself, but because they are held and delighted by their charm and excellence, because they greatly desire to spread more widely what seems pleasing and useful to themselves, and finally because they have persuaded themselves that no greater benefit can be brought to mortals by anything than by the cultivation of minds and universal human learning:

But whatever profit comes to them from that, they accept with this intention, not that they have resolved to gather wealth from the pursuit of the arts, with which once acquired they might be released from those occupations, but that, having provided for what they themselves need with their families, they may lead a freer and more secure life in letters.

But to focus now on what I have set myself to treat, setting aside those arts and disciplines, or rather occupations, which individuals have taken up for themselves to practice for the sake of a livelihood:

The Greeks, the teachers of all learning and of humanity itself, embraced humane and liberal culture in two things, music and gymnastics, of which no one is ignorant that the one comprehends the exercise of the body, the other of the mind, since by the name of music they were accustomed to call not only the faculty of singing with strings or flute or voice, but every culture that proceeds from the Muses.

Because this kind of learning ought to be common to all who are properly educated, just as Aristotle judged concerning the study of music, so it must be determined concerning almost all parts of liberal education, that a liberally educated person, unless he has decided to practice an art professionally, should not be required to excel in any one of them and surpass others to the extent that one who professes that discipline does, but rather, imbued with a certain even measure of all things and formed to a certain joyful and beautiful harmony of the mind and of all the powers of the body, he should be so constituted.

Whoever has attained this, whatever path of life or doctrine he is later to enter, in which he will fix his seat, he will pursue it with greater profit, and will not, like craftsmen their sedentary trades, or servants their commanded duties, refer it to the common use of life, but in all things he will regard a more sublime and humane reason:

And because he has embraced not just one discipline, but a certain cycle of knowledge, when he has devoted himself to literature, he will not, as many do to the great detriment of sound learning, neglect or despise all other arts in comparison with his own, but, performing the duty of a fair judge, he will assign to each thing its own praise.

Now indeed, to descend to particulars, musical education included partly music itself and partly the instruction in letters, from the very first rudiments all the way to poetry, oratory, and philosophy:

And music itself, especially that ancient and severe music, which was not only publicly established and guarded at Sparta but also in other places, shaped the tender feelings of the soul to the lawful sounds of rhythm and harmony, and by teaching magnificent modes accustomed the young offspring to seriousness of character;
With the movement of the body agreeing with these, it produced a pleasing and at the same time honorable grace of bearing and of the face:

Indeed, literature, and especially poetry, provided refined and polished judges of all works of genius, and together with the study of wisdom and eloquence enriched the abundance of words and thoughts, and finally set before the mind great precepts of virtue and knowledge, and great counsels.

We know that not only assemblies and courts of law were openly exercised for this purpose, but even the theaters themselves served it, in which, at least in the earlier age, not as is now largely the case, were heard the unpolished jests of rude and unmusical and foolish writers, attracting the uncultivated populace, or were witnessed frivolous dances, but poems of the most excellent poets, elaborated with the highest art.
But just as by musical education, once savagery, cruelty, and ignorance were banished, the principal virtues—I mean temperance, prudence, and indeed justice—were remarkably cultivated;
so bodily exercise called forth courage and steadfastness, and drove out softness and cowardice:

Hence it came about that liberty, which you could hardly defend without boldness, was remarkably strengthened, and that the Greeks were wonderfully far removed from the barbarians' priestly tricks or from the utterly inhuman worship of savage masters who obeyed slavishly, and that the huge assaults of the Persian mass were checked by the most noble deeds.

What of the fact that no kind of learning is more suited to rousing the feelings of liberty, and, since without these upright men cannot exist, to developing virtue as a whole, than that liberal one which had been adopted by usage among the Greeks?

For in the first place, if literature is cultivated not for liberal studies, but with the end that we may derive profit from the ability to teach or act thus acquired, that we may attain to public offices, that we may be increased in honors, it serves rather base desire and insane ambition, which cast men down into the condition of slaves.

Indeed, we have seen that those for whom the highest happiness is placed in wealth, as very many seem to determine today, are altogether careless of liberty, and either love or endure even the harshest domination, and do not even bear the change of masters with difficulty, if only some little profit can flow from it to them;

But that nothing is more pernicious to states than ambition, and that it is so far from being the case that it should be nourished and increased by devising and granting various kinds of honors, as some advise, that even by these the morals of citizens are thoroughly corrupted and infected with an incurable disease, the memory of deeds done, if anyone is willing to listen to history, declares plainly enough.

Finally, nothing was so closely connected with liberty, which the ancients judged to be the highest good, as bodily exercise, which they had forbidden to slaves much more than literature, lest they should ever be able to attain to the honor and virtue of citizens:
And such was the gymnastic art of the Greeks, that it was entirely liberal and was not directed to any use of life or to some definite end beyond the cultivation of humanity.

For although young men were made more fit for the labors of war and for handling arms by exercising the strength of the body, nevertheless that training differed greatly from military exercise, being adapted to a certain particular kind of utility:
This itself, however necessary it is, since in military command there is need of severity of discipline and obedience, is considered by no means suitable for attaining a liberal education.
Therefore, to return to what I said above, those republics of the Greeks which most regarded the liberty of their citizens especially cultivated that humane education of youth:
on the other hand, states opposed to liberty, such as the empires of the East, if they were not so from the beginning, certainly became so in the course of time, neglected it.
Nor is this unjustly:
for no people bears an unjust tyranny more easily than the brutish, barbarous, effeminate.
Thus far I have spoken about the ancients.

But in our age, although we can scarcely equal antiquity, let alone surpass it, since it has produced the most perfect image of human learning, nevertheless because our entire culture is supported partly by the Christian faith and partly by the study of ancient literature, a different world of arts and sciences embraces the parts of human learning.

For just as in this matter both ages agree, because the highest goal of a liberal education is placed in this, that youth is formed to that virtue which is peculiar to the human race, which is most closely connected with knowledge and science of things, nevertheless that is our own special feature, that we have the beginning of cultivating the intellect from the correct understanding of divine things under Christ as leader.

Now, since the Christian religion, as well as philosophy, demands freedom of minds, which is bound by the closest ties to civil liberty, and is so hostile to every kind of servitude that, with this faith spread more widely and fixed in the depths of hearts, the yoke of slavery, under which among the ancient Greeks and Romans a great part of mortals had lain oppressed to the disgrace of human nature, has been shaken off, although the unworthy condition has been retained, if not entirely, at least in some measure, by certain barbarous nations, and indeed in the new world has been restored through the greatest impiety and avarice:
This very thing is contained in the most sacred precepts of our religion, that, whatever government we obey, men may be trained for just freedom.
With this word, although ambiguous, it will be permissible to use it with impunity.

But the study of literature, which has already grown to such great extent, in our age, after we have been strengthened by so many aids for learning and teaching, pertains more variously and multifariously even to liberal education.
In these matters, the native language must be placed first.
For although in the most ancient times our nation produced poems not to be despised, which were brought to more celebrated notice recently by the labor of some learned and patriotic men;

although before these three hundred years, through that teacher not only of Germany but of Europe, Luther, the vernacular speech was so cultivated that it lacked neither clarity nor wit nor vigor and strength:

Nevertheless, since the flower of German learning, just beginning, was soon extinguished by the atrocity of wars, and afterwards learned men used either an uncultivated and barbarous style or the diction of foreigners in writing, and courtiers and more refined men, with French literature introduced, had infected the native simplicity of the Germans with a foreign poison:
The manly speech of the Germans was long neglected and was brought into the light of literature only late.
And so in earlier centuries it scarcely, and not even scarcely, pertained to human culture:
now, however, it shines so brightly that in almost any genre, and especially in poetry, not a few examples of excellent diction are found:

except that we are deficient in history and eloquence, of which the former demands a freer state of affairs than can be achieved among us, while the latter, if you set aside sacred orations, has scarcely found any ground granted to it up to this time where it could flourish.

Therefore, in liberal education, the principal poets among the native writers seem especially to be recommended, by whom one may be raised from this low and wretched condition of life to higher and more joyful things, and, filled with noble thoughts, may be kept safe from the contagion of this common depravity.

Moreover, the power that music had among the ancients in education, although I think that music is by no means to be excluded from liberal culture, nevertheless I do not know whether poetry now holds it more, especially since the nature of ancient and modern music is clearly different, and among the duller ears of our people the force and efficacy of musical sounds does not seem so great that they insinuate themselves into our hearts as much as into those of the ancients.
And indeed, although oratory may lie especially neglected among us, I do not judge the faculty of speaking to be entirely subordinate in the studies of humanity.

But since nothing is more worthy of a free man than to be able to speak what he thinks, the less public life contributes to forming eloquent men, the more effort and diligence must be devoted to that matter, lest when one must speak openly, you hear them stammering who have accomplished the greatest things in secret.
Moreover, in this age, this is demanded of a liberally educated man: that he have some knowledge of both mathematical science and history.
For mathematics, whose immense usefulness for the conveniences of life is evident, yields a much more excellent fruit, in that it sharpens the mind and renders it apt for subtle treatment of things.
Whence I seem to myself rightly to wonder, what it is that impelled Socrates in Xenophon to that perverse saying about geometry, that he thought it should not be practiced beyond its common utility.

Unless this should rather be attributed to Xenophon's not sufficiently refined judgment, and Plato came closer to the teacher's opinion, for whom it is well known that the study of mathematical disciplines is considered a meditation on philosophy:
For indeed, when rightly cultivated, it prepares thought for the understanding of pure notions.

But the knowledge of history, besides being absolutely necessary for one who has decided to enter public life or to dwell in any branch of literature, is more closely connected with human culture, because it shows the vicissitudes of the human race and the causes and origins of prosperous and adverse fortune, because it teaches the greatest examples of virtue and vice, because it declares, with experience as guide, the right estimation of things and what is to be judged good or bad, and finally because whatever the philosophy of morals embraces in its precepts, that it presents as if placed before the eyes by opening the broadest field of history.
With these things explained, it remains for me to speak about the study of ancient literature and wisdom.

And concerning the former, although I wish to speak modestly, lest anyone think that I want to heap praises upon my own art, I cannot but say that the study of antiquity can in no way be separated from human learning.

For first, since nearly all the learning of modern peoples has proceeded from Roman, and partly also from Greek, literature, who in our age can be even moderately learned, if he is utterly ignorant of the sources of our learning?

Who, since all learning is held together by this common bond, and since nothing can be rightly handled unless you are learned in Greek and Latin, would have excluded the knowledge of these languages and of these peoples from humane letters, under which name the study of antiquity has especially been celebrated?
Indeed, whatever is not the property of a single art, but is the foundation of all arts, that must be reckoned among the disciplines of humanity.
It is added that, the more remote ancient literature is from common use, the more liberal it is to be considered.
if, however, their excellence is as great as it is thought to be.
But of which discipline, I ask, are the fruits greater for rousing the powers of the mind?

What discipline sets forth more clearly described examples of self-restraint in great matters, of constancy in adversity, then of courage, love of country, equity, dignity, finally of any virtue whatsoever?

The reason why not all who devote themselves to ancient literature are moved by these things as they should be, and shape and conform their characters to them, is to be sought partly in the innate and incurable perversity of certain particular minds, partly in the fact that they do not use a liberal method, but either abuse a most excellent thing for the sake of making money or gaining a reputation for learning and acumen, or because they pluck out certain minute and trivial scraps of this discipline, or, in general, not like human beings but like trained animals, with no emotional involvement, they have acquired for themselves only some skill, and do not consider what they are doing, nor perceive what they have learned.

Moreover, since the Greeks and Romans cultivated especially those arts by which the highest degree of culture is comprehended, and above all taught the most perfect form of oratory by examples that will never perish, anyone will readily grant that by these models, as the poet says, to be turned over by night and by day in hand, a man is exceptionally formed.
I do not say this in the sense that I would recommend a servile imitation of the ancients:

Indeed, in the case of the Greeks, this especially holds me: that in them, with no external aid brought in, an image of culture born from the very character of the people is seen complete in all its parts, which we should not imitate, but, as far as it can be done according to our own reason, we should emulate.

And indeed, since the Germans, whose language is most similar to the speech of the Greeks, began to devote greater attention to Greek literature, we too have made progress by observing their excellence, and we have been recalled especially from the imitation of the Gauls, by which, together with the ancestral culture, love of country could have been overthrown.

For nothing seems to alienate us more from the piety owed to our fatherland, than if we are too devoted to the literature of another nation, not of one that once flourished, but of one that now thrives, and, disgusted with our own goods, we gaze at foreign things.

Moreover, that I do not mean that all should be as versed in the study of antiquity as those who are especially devoted to it, is sufficiently understood from what I said at the beginning about liberal culture:
For I rather demand that no educated person should be ignorant of what it is shameful not to know, than that he should thoroughly know what it is honorable to know in each field.
Finally, that philosophy completes the liberal education, since it has been believed by very many both formerly and certainly among you, there is no need for me to explain at length.

Indeed, what I have just said about ancient literature can be asserted to a large extent with a few words changed, and besides other things no less important, which, excluded by the abundance of the subject, I now omit.
I turn to bodily exercise, that is, to a matter which in this age has been agitated by the fiercest not only contentions but also hatreds.
I, led by no party spirit, will say simply what I feel.

Indeed, I think all will agree on this point: that today no less than among the ancients, bodily strength, agility, swiftness, and finally the flourishing of health must be especially cultivated, because the body itself, without these virtues, will both perform many things less conveniently, and will burden the mind, which even a strong body disturbs with the force of desires arising from it, even more by its weakness, unless someone, which is the case of few men and not altogether commendable, has learned to rule the body so imperiously that he keeps it not so much trained as exhausted.
Moreover, as I indicated above, physical exercise, in such a harmony of both parts of human nature, also arouses, aids, and strengthens those virtues of the mind that pertain to courage.
Therefore, that certain games should be established, by which the body may be best exercised, seems to me hardly doubtful.
Although it can be asked, which arts those games ought to include.

And first, dancing, which produces only grace of movement, although it should not be rejected, nevertheless has absolutely no force of the kind we demand from bodily exercise, but partly approaches more to musical education, partly, if one may apply the words of ancient philosophy to this matter, seems to belong less to gymnastics than to the art of adornment, being an ape of gymnastics.

Then riding and the handling of arms, which I by no means despise, are indeed too military, and they do not so much exercise the body itself as they teach the use of the instruments which the body directs.
There remain those exercises which were especially cultivated by the ancients: running, jumping, which was also remarkably pleasing to our ancestors, likewise wrestling and things similar to these.
By these the skill and strength of the limbs are remarkably increased.
Nor are the gymnastic associations to be blamed, by which, when properly directed, youthful grace and modesty are formed together with manly seriousness of character.
These societies, organized after the manner of guilds, were open very widely throughout the ancient states.

Finally, I do not recall having read among the ancients, what even in our times, with the whole form of things changed, seems rightly to be able to be inferred from the nature of these arts, that gymnastic games support popular government:

But among them, neglect of the gymnasia seemed not only to corrupt morals, but also to bring about the domination of an uncultivated mob, while the perfect cultivation of both body and mind seemed to hand over the reins of the state to the best citizens.

But I also concede that foreign elements, which must be kept away, can be mixed into the gymnastic games, and I do not want all perfect wrestlers and boxers to be liberally educated, nor, if I judge that softness must be expelled, do I recommend the rough way of life of the Cynics or contempt for a more refined culture.
Now I have finished what I had proposed to say about perfecting man.

And since universities serve this purpose, besides the scholastic discipline, except that they embrace not only humanistic learning but also other branches of knowledge, it behooves us to strive with all our might to excite and confirm in the young men committed to our care the love of liberal culture.

By doing this, we will best comply with the counsels of the wisest king, who, it is certain, aims at nothing other than the humanity, virtue, and happiness of his citizens, and wishes to rule not over slaves but over free men.
And that he may forever retain this will with his accustomed constancy, we piously beseech God, the ruler of human minds:

To these we add the greatest prayers, that the supreme deity may direct the counselors of the Prince and all the magistrates of this empire to increase the happiness of the people, to equity, justice, and to bringing aid to the oppressed; may preserve harmony in the state composed of various orders and nations, and tranquility in troubled times; may settle disturbances; may avert evil counsels:
Finally, that he may protect the safety of the Prince and of the whole Augustan house as long as possible.

div.head: VIII. Oratio nataliciis Friderici Guilelmi III. celebrandis d. III. m. Aug. a. MDCCCXX. habita.
What the power of literary universities is, and what the goal of teaching in them; with what intention they were founded, and what relationship exists between them and other schools

p.s: Having been appointed as the orator for the annual birthday celebrations of Frederick William, listeners, I do not think that this task has been assigned to me solely for the purpose of continually and deliberately celebrating the praises of the most beloved King, which I have already set forth more than once, since I see that the glory of princes lies less in the flattery and proclamation of contemporaries than in the memory of deeds handed down to posterity and in the judgment and estimation of the wise after several generations.

But the sum of this most delightful business seems to me to be this: that it should be declared by a public document that we too are notably imbued with the public joy with which the whole Prussian empire resounds today.

Although this ought to be believed even without this testimony of our senses, since it is rightly considered impious not to venerate the founder, especially that founder who established this school of letters in the very seat of the kingdom and, as it were, in a royal dwelling, so that the arts might be closer to him;

Nevertheless, to make this clear, both the duty of gratitude demands it and the custom handed down from antiquity, which it is the less proper to omit, the more the ancient customs in literary universities are already becoming more and more obsolete.

But at the same time, since I must perform the office of an orator, I think that nothing should be avoided more than the appearance of a declaimer, who does not direct his speech to some definite end and to the reason of things, but for the sake of tickling ears composes words and in an argument either fictitious or foreign displays eloquence for the sake of speaking:
for I judge that this is unworthy both of your character and of the solemnity of this day:

Indeed, since it is especially the orator's role to give counsel and to explain what is right, excellent, and useful, we must approach the state of affairs that now exists and choose something in which, if we cannot instruct you, most excellent and distinguished men, who understand such matters much better than I do, at least we may remind you of one or two things about the condition of our affairs.

Therefore on this day, which is sacred to the name of our founder, at this time, in this crisis of the literary states, when not only are very different opinions of men of various kinds about their nature put forward, but also the supreme council of the princes of Germany has zealously turned its mind to the improvement and more careful governance of the universities, and has set over each one its own overseers, who would observe both teachers and learners, and above all would take care that nothing should take root in them that would be contrary to the purpose and character of these schools, as it ought to be:
It seems especially fitting to explain modestly what, in my opinion, is the power of universities, and what the end of teaching in them is.
From my opinion, I say:
Yet since I have learned by long experience and familiarity that yours, dearest colleagues, is the same, if I have set it forth, perhaps I shall have done something not unpleasant to you.

Moreover, that the judgment of the king, who is most wise, and of those ministers and counselors who have been placed over us is not different, is gathered with certainty from this, that they especially chose and summoned you, to whom the education of youth would be entrusted.

But since I cannot treat the whole subject, which is most important and, because nothing concerns us more, I long ago selected certain topics from it, in a manner worthy of the dignity and richness of the argument within the narrow limits of time granted to me, I shall now, passing over the other points, dwell on this one alone, about which there seems to be the least agreement among all: whether, as some contend, universities have been founded or should be founded with the purpose that future magistrates and ministers of the state be formed, and the entire discipline of an academic teacher should be adapted to this end, or whether they have been established and instituted not for this practical use of the state, but on some more liberal principle for the propagation of literary learning.
I do not wonder that there is the greatest dispute about this at the present time, since in our age the most important matters are partly consigned to oblivion and partly called into question.
since even about the condition and power of the state itself, within whose boundaries we are all contained, there is no agreement.

Finally, since only those seem able to understand what the power and nature of universities ought to be, who have been not moderately versed in letters and have learned from the memory of earlier times what sort these schools have been from the beginning.

For my part, indeed, whether I consider the origins of the academies or the present state of learning, it is clear that their purpose is none other than that in them studious young men should thoroughly learn the very doctrine of letters under skilled teachers as guides:

But if by this matter it is at the same time brought about that skillful ministers are provided for the states, this both increases the usefulness of those schools and brings a notable advantage to the state; nevertheless, this is not to be regarded as the highest and primary end of academic education.

For first, if we may go back to the most remote times and consider what among the ancients, the wisest teachers of all human culture, was in some degree similar to the institution of universities, we find that the schools of the philosophers in Greece were not altogether unlike.
This was understood by those who wished that the literary universities and the lower gymnasia of scholastic youth should be called by names derived from there, academies and lyceums.
To the philosophers, who embraced the nature of things and the precepts of morals, were added the rhetoricians, who taught the ability of speaking eloquently on any subject;
Grammarians were added, who together with the philosophers and rhetoricians handed on the complete circle of liberal education:
Soon, with many teachers of the arts established in one city, they provided young men with the opportunity of acquiring varied learning;

And indeed at Athens, Alexandria, Apollonia, and in several other cities, so many men gradually flocked together for the sake of study that those places seem not badly comparable to literary universities.

Although both the study of wisdom and of eloquence made men fit for conducting public affairs, and the sophists, professing either both or one of the two disciplines, promised that they would bring it about that their pupils would be equal to public business;

Yet so far is it from being the case that the highest importance was placed on these studies, that many even called their students away from engaging in public affairs, such as they then were, and those especially who pursued studies for the sake of profit or vain little glory, the sophists, made a pretext of the practical use of public life; in short, the states themselves thought that those literary pursuits had nothing to do with them, except that, captivated by the splendor of learning, they revered philosophers, rhetoricians, and grammarians, and for the most part deemed them worthy of the highest honors; and far more rarely, fearing the lights of learning, they destroyed wise and learned men, beset by slanders, by exile or death, or, when the flower of the state was tottering, as happened at Athens on the motion of Sophocles, they took away the freedom of teaching.

Then, not to mention the not very good times of the Roman Empire, even before the revival of letters in the West, universities were founded at that age in which that order of civil servants, which now flourishes, had not yet been established;
so that from the beginning it may easily appear that academies did not serve for forming those [men];

Since knowledge of Roman law, which shone forth at the University of Bologna, was not at all necessary for the magistrates of the state, although the doctors of law were both frequently consulted and possessed the highest authority;
Nor were those who practiced medicine ministers of the state, in which class they are not counted even now, but just like other artisans they practiced a private art;

And to say nothing of philosophers and teachers of the arts, the theologians and priests of the church would obey the command, which in those times, exempt from civil power, constituted a distinct and peculiar state throughout all Christian lands.

And so, although the universities are found to be far earlier than this widely extending class of civil servants, which arose in the immediately preceding centuries, if you consider the origins of things, in which the true principle of each institution is wont to shine forth most clearly, because it is, as it were, overshadowed by no additions;
you will understand that they err who judge that the highest and original end of academic discipline is placed in educating public servants:
This is no more true than if someone were to say that schools were established with that intention.
When Charlemagne was laying the foundations of these in his kingdom, who would have thought that he was thinking of equipping the state with skillful ministers?

Indeed, it is well known that in earlier centuries both schools and universities were not attributed to that civic advantage, which is by no means to be despised, but, like temples and monasteries, to the piety of a single prince or of states, and to their love of literature, which they wished to be disseminated more widely.

Moreover, if literary universities had been founded for the education of public servants, that institution, which survives from ancient times along with a few others, and which is even now considered peculiar to universities alone—I mean academic honors—would certainly have had to be regulated by far different laws;

For then those who seemed fit to discharge the civic duty would have to be appointed as teachers and instructors, not those who had been so approved in some branch of learning that they could cultivate, advance, and profess it.

Since even those who have been engaged in public affairs with the highest praise and skill cannot in any way aspire to academic honors unless they have acquired a more distinguished proficiency in letters, and on the other hand those who, although unequal to public business, excel in learning are judged uniquely worthy of obtaining those honors, it is clear that the essence of academic discipline is to be placed in the cultivation of arts and sciences, not in shaping men for conducting business.

Nor if the leading men and the state have advanced and honored the teachers and masters created in the academies with certain prerogatives, and have even made them splendid with a certain nobility in former times, did they do this because they saw their servants being trained in the universities;

But because they thought that those who had been cultivated in these schools up to this degree of perfection, so that they had attained academic honor, were equipped with such great learning that a certain distinguished authority of theirs ought to exist among all men and in the state itself.

And that great benefit, indeed, formerly conferred upon the academies, has gradually been so diminished that, apart from empty names, scarcely any trace of their former dignity remains; and this is certainly the more to be lamented, because not those who broke the force of such great privileges are to be accused, but those who, partly treating a matter once regarded as most serious lightly and negligently, and partly led by desire for gain, have raised ignorant and uncultivated men to academic honors.

Finally, where literary universities have most retained their ancient character, it is most clearly seen in Britain that the purpose of those colleges is not to produce skill in public service, but to contain the teaching of the liberal arts and the formation of teachers of religion.

I do not say this in order to prefer the old universities to the new ones, or the English universities, which are perhaps too tenacious of the old system, to the German ones, which are rightly considered much more perfect, but in order that by this argument also it may be understood what the origin of universities was:
Moreover, although I am not unaware that not all were established according to the same standard, I nevertheless know of none that was founded except for the purpose of spreading learning.

Now, since the limits of this speech exclude a more careful treatment of this matter, which would be strengthened by more precise arguments to be drawn from the storehouse of history, I turn to the present state of letters and the condition of public education, in order that I may briefly set forth what place universities occupy, in my judgment, among the other institutions of this kind.

For since the light of learning and religion, especially from the time of the reformation and restoration of the church in Germany, has gradually spread to men of all ranks, various schools and colleges of learned men have arisen down to our own days, which seem to me to be best divided into five classes.

The first kind includes the schools that are called popular, in which the infantile and childish age is imbued with the first elements of letters, which are most necessary for every person for the use of life, and likewise with the precepts of the Christian faith and of morals, and with certain very small particles plucked from the circle of learning, which it is fitting that no one should be ignorant of, and which even tender or uncultivated minds can grasp, and is nourished, as it were, with the milk of common notions:
If these schools had not been established in almost every village, there would hardly be any way to distinguish a man from a beast.
Therefore the zeal of our age and our state is all the more to be praised, because it is directed toward founding and improving those schools.
Nor indeed do I judge those games, which some have called civic, to be very different from these.
except that they ought to include somewhat more subjects, and among them certain arts useful for handling crafts.
The other kind is that of the so-called learned schools, gymnasiums, and lyceums;

In these [schools] both those are cultivated whom parents have wished to pass over to the business of common life, but to be distinguished from the rude multitude by a certain more elegant culture, and especially those who desire to devote themselves to letters and learning with diligence, and among these also those who, because they were born in a higher place, or for the sake of seeking a livelihood, have conceived with immature counsel, not suited to that age, [the intention] to approach public affairs and to perform civic duties.
In these schools, according to the consensus of the wise, the whole course of instruction ought to be directed toward liberal education, by which minds are made fit for undertaking higher studies.

In the third rank come the universities, which, because of the immense abundance of subjects, are divided into four parts; and these are now so constituted that students can pursue the course of learning begun in the gymnasia, and whatever art they have chosen, in it they can, by the instruction of their teachers, arrive at a certain degree of perfection.

For those studies, which are pursued in universities, although they are especially suited for training the ministers of the state, are nevertheless found to be so arranged by the very presidents of the republics that you understand that the purpose of the institution is not even now placed in that matter, but in the transmission of universal learning:

Whence also teachers have been given to those arts which, being very far removed from common use, are wholly engaged in the knowledge of hidden and abstruse things, nor is the explanation of any doctrine confined within very narrow limits of public utility.

Therefore, universities are separated from the lower gymnasia by no distinction, except that they teach a higher science and embrace a wider circle of doctrines, with those arts added which young boys, not yet strengthened, who are educated in those schools, cannot rightly perceive;
In this class are counted not only the inner knowledge of divine things, of law, and of medicine, but also the various parts of philosophy:

All these things must be learned in universities in such a way that not only those things which pertain to the skill of public service are picked out, but whatever in each discipline is true or false, whatever is useful or harmful to the human race, whatever history and right reason teach, and finally whatever opinions, precepts, and doctrines you can hammer out with the strength and effort of your mind, should be set forth according to the capacity of the students, even if those things cannot be adapted to the conduct of public affairs in the prevailing state of affairs.
