Although I would readily concede that no discipline is so useless that some benefit from it could not at some time also flow into the state and common life.

And so these schools, to which the name of universities was once given because they were regarded as bodies of teachers and learners endowed with certain rights and privileges, just as the guilds of artisans were, now deserve that designation even on this account, that they embrace the whole field of learning with the widest compass, bounded by no other limits than those of what is honorable, upright, and true:
Whence in some edicts of princes in earlier centuries they are called general studies.
But if the nature of universities were different, in the order of public instruction, most wisely arranged, the highest grade would be lacking;

If anyone should contend that learned societies, which are also called by the common name of academies along with universities, should occupy this grade, he will certainly not have me as an assenting listener.

For these, being most closely connected to universities by the liberality of their studies, constitute in the fourth place a particular community of learned men, differing from the nature of universities to the extent that it is not the role of those societies to teach less experienced young men;

But associates should share with associates whatever each has discovered, with equal or nearly equal learning and talent, and each should help the other with his own understanding and be helped in turn, and all, with united strength, ought to accomplish in literature those things which cannot be completed by individual scholars, either because more see more, or because a greater apparatus is needed than the industry and resources of one man can provide:

especially when most of the members have been granted that leisure, so that, freed from other occupations and cares, or at least burdened with not so many, they can devote either all their time or the greatest part of it to advancing literature.

Finally, in the most recent times especially, a fifth institution of the discipline has been added, which has been dedicated either wholly or to a large extent to the exercises that are usually called practical, and this is varied according to the nature of the art and of the students and according to the end toward which it tends:

Since some institutions of this kind are intended for ecclesiastical orators and ministers of the divine word, others for teachers of schools, whether elementary or higher, others for future judges, others for physicians or surgeons, especially military ones, others for agriculture, forestry, veterinary science, and other affairs of this kind.
But these things are partly such that they seem necessary for completing higher studies;
This is the point to which a great part of medical, theological, and philological exercise pertains, and to which a place has rightly been given in the universities themselves.

In part, in those schools, the empiricists are trained not for liberal and profound science and genuine erudition, but for a certain skill to be exercised according to precepts as if commanded and experience acquired by use but for the most part destitute of reasons;
This method of instruction is inferior to academic schools.
Partly by the institutions which I have mentioned, young men, after completing their studies at the university in due form, are trained for the proper conduct of business and the discharge of duties;
To this end, to use examples drawn from our own state, candidates are trained in the courts and in the boards placed over the administration of the provinces in a most useful manner;
To this end among us seminaries for schoolmasters have been established, and at Wittenberg the most wise king recently founded a seminary for clergymen with remarkable piety.

Although these things have been explained briefly, even without my pointing it out, I think it is clear that in this fifth class of institutions alone, and not in the whole of it, but in only one or another of those forms which I have described, the public ministers of the state are deliberately trained.

And that these things have been established by me not arbitrarily, but according to the truth of the matter, you may also understand from this, that for the benefit of the universities and other schools all are admitted who wish to apply their mind to letters, but to those parts of the exercises which I mentioned last, access is open almost only to those who have declared that they are seeking public offices.

Indeed, who among you, listeners, would not rejoice that a more correct opinion concerning the system of universities is so firmly implanted in the most wise King and his counselors, that all academies of the Prussian state are exclusively adapted to that form which we demand?

For not to depart now from our own affairs, who would not understand that these magnificent preparations and the most ample and most splendid supports of learning of every kind, which are an ornament not only to this literary university but to the royal city itself, and which by the munificence of the most kind King and by the prudent and liberal care of that most excellent man who presides over public instruction in this empire are daily increased more and more, these, I say, have been provided with no other purpose than that the study of the best things should be pursued not for some sordid reason but on account of its inherent excellence and should be cultivated more widely and more deeply?
Who does not see that the same institutions have been observed and are still observed in the very selection of teachers, whether one considers their talents and learning or their number?

For as soon as that opinion, against which we have been arguing, was given a place, because it seemed that the needs of the state could be satisfied with small resources, and both those things and the greatest part of these men were scattered as superfluous, and with the common bond of learning dissolved, which certainly is least needed for forming only the servants of the state, separate schools of some disciplines were established in place of the universities:
Therefore, in the present state of literature, since the individual disciplines have already been too much separated, nothing would be more pernicious.

Then not only the students, many of whom even now, when another end of academic instruction is held, hastening to public offices, to the great detriment of both literature and the republic itself, are estranged from accurate learning and liberal studies, would also be content with a more slender and meager knowledge of things;

But also to the doctrines themselves, if the universities were to be reshaped into another form, the greatest harm would be done, since besides the learned societies, whose effectiveness cannot be as great as that of universities among all people, given the circumstances, no seat would be left for higher learning.

Nor would men distinguished by learning, but skilled pragmatists, who now, unless endowed with exceptional talent and knowledge, are considered insufficiently suited for this task, be about to occupy the chairs.
Finally, with the freedom of teaching removed, not what is right and true would have to be handed down to learners, but what was acceptable and approved by the powerful, the rulers of states.
What could be found more unworthy than this for learned men?
But indeed there is another reason why every most civilized state, and especially ours, supports the study of literature in universities and spends no small sums on it;
for it is exactly the same reason that brings it about that the church is supported by public expenditure.

For since it is understood that not only the human race, if not illuminated by the light of religion, would go to ruin, but that the sense of the divine is so implanted in human minds that not even any barbarians, unless utterly brutish, lack it:

The state takes care that this natural disposition of the human mind is cultivated and nourished, and it is the state's duty to provide the opportunity for developing and advancing the highest gifts and goods of mortals, not to tolerate or foster them only insofar as they seem useful to rulers for governing their subjects.

And yet, since the system of letters is on a par with these, the state also founded its own temples for them, lest, being left to the judgment of private individuals, they should be neglected by chance or human carelessness.
Among these, universities hold almost the foremost place.
And it has turned out well that these schools have been scattered throughout all the provinces, especially in Germany, so that scarcely any is bereft of literary renown;

But the most wise King has done excellently in adorning the principal cities of the realm with universities, where, to say nothing of other advantages, literature may conveniently exert a most powerful influence on men of various ranks.
Nor should expenses be carefully matched with the number of students who are to be educated.
This is what a certain person recently dared to do, in the manner of money-changers or bankers rather than of learned men.

For these literary associations were not granted revenues so that the wages of instruction might be paid publicly to the teachers, but so that the flower and honor of studies might be firmly established.

Finally, when the state saw that those whose minds had been properly refined by education were governing the city most wisely, and that neither those who had been cultivated by private industry nor those who had been trained in other schools were equipped with such great skill in letters as the students of universities are accustomed to have;

It gradually gained strength, so that almost no one was entrusted with a magistracy or any more serious public office unless he had devoted several years to studies at universities, and those who wished to prepare themselves for civil affairs embraced exclusively the discipline of universities:
Hence some, deceived by the empty appearance of things, think that universities were founded for the purpose of forming public officials.
Moreover, that honorable judgment concerning the discipline of universities was beneficial both to the state and to literature:
For the state, because nothing can be more useful to it than the light of arts and sciences, which, like the life-giving and guiding soul, pervades all the members of the commonwealth;

For literature, because those who have thoroughly learned its power through good education, when they have been placed in charge of the highest affairs, support the pursuits of the arts with greater kindness and generosity:

Since the governors of states, whether unskilled in literature or imbued only with the first rudiments, especially if, as usually happens, arrogance has been added, despise learning or hold it suspect.

And from this it is at the same time understood how much the states must beware, lest they suffer any loss, or lest their dignity be harmed by unworthy words or deeds, or lest it be corrupted by internal vices;
Since it is reasonable that such things should arise from time to time among such a great multitude of young men, care must be taken that they do not grow.
But a skillful hand must be applied, lest the wounds fester.

And wise physicians will so treat present evils, that neither former ones, which although inveterate the opportunity of the times has almost removed by divine rather than human counsel, may return with more violent force, nor new and deadly ones arise.
Which indeed we need not fear at all.
Trusting in the kindness of a most merciful king, we sail in the harbor;
And God, who brings forth the best from the worst beyond expectation, will calm the present disturbances.
We, colleagues, seem to ourselves to know what our duty is;
I urge you, fellow soldiers, never to forget what the end of academic discipline is, which I have shown to be placed in the cultivation of the good arts with the greatest assiduity and diligence;
Therefore, apply your minds to those things, and eagerly seize these immortal blessings, which the kindness of the most wise King offers to you.
Our affairs this year, if not cut down, have certainly been diminished by certain accidental losses:
Death has taken away two most distinguished teachers, most dear to us, and them placed in the flower of age:
But no republic applies a more prudent and more fortunate care to repairing the losses of literature than ours under the auspices of Frederick William.
May God, the Best and Greatest, preserve this king, adorned with the virtues of peace and war, for us and for the whole state, to extreme old age;
may He preserve the royal August house, supported by so many most upright and most brave young men.
These are not our prayers, but the prayers of all citizens;
they are perpetual, not of today;
but on this day they are so much more sacred, as this day is considered more sacred.
I have spoken.

div.head: IX. Oratio nataliciis Friderici Guilelmi III. celebrandis d. III. m. Aug. a. MDCCCXXI. habita.
On Pericles as the most fortunate patron of the arts and letters

p.s: Even after frequent practice, it seems to me a great task, which I undertake, to speak about the King, the delight of the people, on that day on which the whole city rejoices that he was given to it by divine providence, that is, on that day on which, since it is difficult to equal the feelings of the mind with words, however much you may say, you will think that not only the listeners but even yourself have not been satisfied.

I judge it to be greater, where, when ample material has been set before the orator, a manner of speaking must be sought and care must be taken, lest you speak in such a way that the speech seems to conform less to the King's own quite singular modesty;
For we are not unaware that he wishes not so much to be praised as to do praiseworthy things:

It is a very great thing to speak about him before those who, if anything either somewhat unpolished or less appropriately or rather coarsely said should slip out, you know are sharply stung and reproached.
But again, in those matters in which the greatest difficulty is placed, in the same I see consolation and remedy to be present.
For first, because I speak in the presence of those who have come with minds most ready and exceptionally well-disposed to revere the King;

If I have not set forth the virtues of Frederick William according to their abundance, but have run through them as if doing something else, what I have touched upon lightly will be taken up by you in a greater sense and will grow in your minds that cherish them:
so that a tiny spark, as it were, thrown into your hearts, may kindle a most burning flame of love and admiration;
then, by the King's observed modesty, I shall escape the appearance of an importunate praiser;

Finally, among the learned or those eager for learning, it is permissible, from the memory of earlier events, to mix in such things that, even if they seem not to pertain to this matter, they should not reject them as foreign, but rather delight in them, while they consider and compare how distinguished men, in various times and in different states of affairs, have deserved well of the human race.

For this brings almost the greatest pleasure to thoughtful men, not if someone tells them things in which nothing is left to their own intellect, but if you have offered ample material for inquiry, which they can review, weigh, and judge, from which they may draw richer thoughts, opinions, and feelings than those contained in the speaker's words.
Therefore today I have decided to return to more remote times and to say a few words about a man once most great, whose merits and fame, although he was not a king, scarcely any king has equaled:
I shall bring forward Pericles, the founder of arts and letters, so fortunate that no age has produced his equal;
but from the deeds of so great a man I shall especially select those things which seem to me to be suited to the solemnity of this day.

Concerning Pericles, therefore, before I come to those matters for the sake of which I have decided to speak about him, let me first make a few preliminary remarks: it is well known that he did not suddenly creep into the commonwealth as a new man, but that he was born of the most noble parents, who had held no small part in the state.
For he had as his father Xanthippus, under whose command the Greeks had defeated the Persian fleet at Mycale;
His mother was Agariste, an Alcmaeonid, from that family which traced its origin back to Nestor, son of Neleus, and was formerly related to the royal line at Athens.
His maternal grandmother was the daughter of Clisthenes, tyrant of Sicyon.
His mother's uncle was Clisthenes, son of Megacles, the Athenian legislator, under whose leadership especially the state had shaken off the rule of the Pisistratids.
But Pericles, emulating his great ancestors, proved himself even greater than they.

After he had won the favor of the people by defeating the aristocratic party, when he saw that the liberty and power of the Athenians could not be supported except by naval forces, following in the footsteps of Themistocles, who had attributed the greatest importance to the sea, he partly preserved and partly acquired for his country allies and revenues so many and so great that no city was stronger than Athens, and Athens itself was the wealthiest of all.

But when he accomplished this, if he seems to have admitted many things that cannot be approved, one must consider that the state of affairs was such that he had to do many harsher things not of his own accord, but unwillingly, because nearly all of Greece and the individual states were troubled by constant discord, and the power of the Lacedaemonians, who were particularly hostile to the Athenians, had to be restrained, since they, though as desirous of supremacy as the Athenians, were nevertheless unequal to maintaining it.
But even in those matters which you might justly criticize, Pericles did not pursue his own private advantage, nor did he ever do anything base or contemptible:
Whatever he did, they are evidences of a great mind;
Greater were the things which he attempted but did not accomplish:

Indeed, it is not obscure that a common league of all the Greeks in Asia and Europe agitated for this, by which, besides the restoration of the temples destroyed by the barbarians and the celebration of common religious rites, the duration of peace and free and secure navigation would be ensured.
The Lacedaemonians were the greatest obstacle to this league being made.

Nevertheless, the same man, although he omitted nothing that would be magnificent for the fatherland, accurately discerning what could or could not be done according to the state of affairs, preferred to preserve the empire he had acquired with singular moderation rather than to undertake distant and dangerous expeditions.

And although others thought that Egypt, which had already been ruinous to the Athenians before, Sicily, which after Pericles was destruction to the Attic forces, Etruria, and Carthage should be attempted, he was unwilling to put the citizens at risk, but sought glory as a war leader especially in this, that he would undertake nothing too difficult or uncertain, and that the soldiers, as he himself used to say, could, as far as it lay in his power, be immortal.

But although he earned a great name among posterity either by the counsels of the wise alone in governing the state and by deeds bravely done, by which he raised the Athenians above all the other peoples of Greece, nevertheless you might doubt whether he wished to acquire for his fatherland so great power that arts and letters and the whole culture of humanity could be more generously fostered and flourish more joyfully, or whether he strove for these very things more notably, in order to increase the glory and splendor of Athens.
Concerning this I judge thus: that Pericles did not act with the exclusion of the one or the other;

but since he saw that the Attic state could not be chief unless it excelled in commerce, wealth, army, and fleets, he likewise perceived that, even when strengthened by these very resources, unless the glory of the arts and the light of letters were added, it would be a rude and unformed mass:
therefore he thought that not one of the two for the sake of the other, but each for its own sake, was to be procured as a good.

For to confine myself now to literature and the arts, Pericles embraced them neither for the sake of display nor for the sake of the cheap conveniences of common life, but because he understood that nothing is more honorable or more glorious than they are.

Indeed, his intellect was formed and polished not only by boyhood education, but also in his adult years by the instruction and intimacy of the most learned men, and was furnished with the knowledge of the most important studies.

For first, in that one art by which states were then governed, he so possessed eloquence that it was said that the most powerful thunderbolt of that language was in it, and the imperial voice in the forum was compared to the thunderbolts of Olympian Jove:
Whence he alone reigned in the assemblies, and no one easily resisted his prudence and strength, with which he was powerful in speaking.

But that man nourished his full, weighty, magnificent, sharp, and concise oratory with the teaching of the philosophers, which strengthened the greatness of mind implanted in his nature with excellent precepts.
And indeed at that age, when two philosophical schools especially flourished, the Eleatic and the Ionian, he associated familiarly with the leaders of both.
For he heard Zeno of Elea, the disciple and friend of the great Parmenides, when he was staying at Athens, along with other nobles.

His dialectical and abstruse method of philosophizing, although something could even be derived from it for speaking well, yet being chiefly concerned with understanding the nature of things and being very far removed from visible objects, can serve as evidence that Pericles did not seek only those things which he could use on the platform, but was led by a liberal and genuine pursuit of wisdom.
Truly, that age is worthy of the greatest admiration, in which men educated in philosophy commanded great public affairs and armies;

a spectacle worthy of admiration: Pericles, the disciple of Zeno of Elea, fighting with his fleet at Samos against Melissus, the son of Ithagenes, who, having written a book on being and nature at nearly the same time as Zeno, became famous among the leaders of the Eleatic school.

And not being devoted to this one kind of doctrine alone, which you would especially praise in a man placed at the head of a state, whom it behooves to know and tolerate various systems of philosophy, not to despise or exclude one in preference to another, Pericles was especially devoted to Anaxagoras, a wise man of a quite different school, a natural philosopher, a man of great spirit, who, led by a divine impulse of philosophizing, had left his house and fields, and he admired him remarkably.

Plutarch reports that Protagoras the sophist was employed by him, and that he had long discussions with him, and these about arguments of such a kind that, just as it seemed ridiculous to Pericles' son, so it may also seem ridiculous to us.

This he must be thought to have done either for the sake of exercise or of his mind, or because it was in his interest to investigate more carefully, for some reason that is not of this place, things that to one considering them more lightly are thought to be of no use.
Now indeed, to speak of the artists, it is established by reliable authorities that Damon the musician was a companion of Pericles.

Since he was both most skilled in civil affairs and held such great authority in the state that he was banished from his country by the votes of ostracism, and since he practiced music not only with his hand and voice, but also embraced the force and power of numbers and modes with philosophical and mathematical reasoning, it is probable that that Pericles had him as an assistant and friend and counselor both in the affairs of the state and in judging poems, music, and poets.

But whatever pertained to building and adorning edifices and to sculpture and related arts, in that no one is ignorant that Phidias, an immortal man, who did not merely attain but enhanced the majesty of the gods through the statues fashioned by himself, was not only an adviser to Pericles but also a supervisor of the works.
Thus he, as befits a ruler of a state, measured with his mind nearly the whole world of arts and letters:
And just as he himself neglected no part of them, so they all then flowed together to Athens and fixed their abode there:

Not because the state, with Pericles urging, spent money on maintaining everyone, but because the elegant and splendid administration of the city and the remarkable freedom granted to literature and the honor paid to the good arts invited outstanding talents more than other places, and because the minds of the Athenians were so raised to every best pursuit that at their city every most cultivated person wished to be heard, seen, and approved.

Therefore, to begin with poetry, among the epic poets, whose art was then languishing, the one who is thought to have excelled alone, Choerilus of Samos, the most distinguished herald of the Persian wars, he seems to have been especially approved and cultivated at Athens;
But the genre of lyric poetry, which especially survived at that age, the dithyrambic, was especially practiced by the cyclic choruses of the Athenians.
But no part of poetry was flourishing more joyfully at that time than the scenic, which was hardly anywhere formed and perfected except at Athens;

And tragedy indeed, after Aeschylus, Pericles earlier and, because he was a lover of the old discipline, rather alien from him than devoted to him, Sophocles perfected, who, when the play Antigone was produced, was elected colleague of Pericles by the Athenian people in the Samian praetorship;
Euripides followed, and I infer from a certain indication that he too was remarkably devoted to Pericles.
And although enormous sums were spent on lyric and tragic performances, even comedy, though hostile to the leading men of the state, was not neglected:

for such was Pericles, who could easily bear the insults and reproaches of the envious and much more of scurrilous and witty men, and did not think that the freedom of jesting should be restricted by plebiscites:
But if the license of old comedy was once checked under this very law, that law did not remain in force for more than four years.

At that time also a writer of history became famous, whom they are accustomed to call the father of history, Herodotus, who is said to have recited his work or part of his work at Athens, and was undoubtedly connected with Pericles, whether before he became a citizen of Thurii, a colony founded by him, or afterwards;
Nor will anyone who has read his books more carefully deny that many things were written to please the Athenians and especially Pericles.
Thucydides himself, indeed, than whom no age has produced or will produce a more excellent historian, owes to that age the force of his oratory and his political wisdom.
What shall I say of eloquence?

When Gorgias and other sophists, and among the Athenians Antiphon of Rhamnus, were reducing it to the form of an art, Pericles himself, although he left nothing in writing except decrees, perfected that grand style of speaking, of which Thucydides gives examples, together with his contemporaries.

After them, Lysias, although he was of a later generation, would nevertheless not have cultivated the subtle form of oratory at Athens unless Pericles had existed, since his father Cephalus of Syracuse had been persuaded by Pericles to move to Athens.

In philosophy, moreover, besides those schools which I mentioned above, the sophists, tolerated in the Attic state and attracted by the gifts of wealthy men, excited a zeal for arguing about all things on opposite sides.

In these disputations, Socrates, eminent, laid the foundations of Attic philosophy with that dialectical and critical method of inquiry and with the most sacred precepts of morals, whose splendor shines most brightly down to our times.

But when in that age too there were those who, subdued by vain superstition, shunned the light of philosophy like owls shun the sun, or who, with cunning pretense, used religion as a screen for private interests or enmities, Pericles, freed from anxieties of that sort by the physical doctrine of Anaxagoras, protected the philosophers as long as he could;

And after the party of the adversaries had grown strong, so that they themselves might be especially troublesome, they accused Aspasia and Anaxagoras—who nevertheless, thinking most worthily about divine matters, said that mind adorns and governs all things—of impiety; but by the authority and prudence of Pericles it was brought about that, while he himself was alive, no one of the philosophers was punished too severely.
Certainly he rescued Aspasia by his entreaties, and Anaxagoras, sent away secretly, from danger.

But afterwards, through the arts of wicked and fanatical men, not only was Protagoras reduced to such a state that he avoided destruction only by flight and his books were publicly burned, but Socrates himself, the most upright of philosophers, was punished as a despiser of the divine and a corrupter of youth.
But the arts surpassed the flower of literature, which then existed, if that is possible.

For after it had been sufficiently provided for the collection of wealth and the filling of the treasury, Pericles did not want the Athenian people to lie in wait for riches as if greedy, nor that gold and silver should be hidden away in the treasury, but he decided that as much as could be spent without public loss should be expended, so that the city and the temples of the gods might be magnificently adorned, and that part of the common people which would not spurn labor might be supported by an honorable livelihood:

Moreover, since he saw that the Athenians could not live on their own produce and be, as it were, bound to their fields, like the Spartans or Boeotians, but that a state which enjoyed popular government and maritime power ought to excel in the excellence and renown of its manufactures and in the commerce thereby increased.

Therefore he persuaded the people to undertake such works that eternal glory would accrue to the state and all arts and all hands would be set in motion, and almost the whole city would be at once adorned and nourished from itself;

Those who worked marble, bronze, gold, ivory, cypress, and ebony, craftsmen of every kind, stonecutters, sculptors, goldsmiths, painters, embroiderers, dyers, and finally those who brought material by ships or wagons, were so employed by Pericles' plan that at that time there was the greatest industry of workshops and craftsmanship in Athens.

And what you may especially wonder at, in a very short space of time he completed not one or two buildings, but very many and especially lofty works: the Parthenon, the Eleusinium, the receptacle of the initiates, the Odeum, the Long Walls, the Propylaea, and others.
not those destined to fall soon, but such as could withstand, I will not say the injury of time, but the devastations of savage barbarians.

For those who, after the people had gradually degenerated from the virtue of their ancestors through various misfortunes, reduced it to the most unjust slavery, from which may it now be delivered forever through the magnanimous struggles worthy of the fame of their parents, could not entirely destroy the monuments of its former splendor.

But just as all the more refined culture throughout Europe originated from the Greeks, so those works are even now an example to our artists, and in this very city the remains of the statues preserved in the pediments of the Parthenon, reproduced in images by the kindness of our King, are to be seen.

Now indeed, to pass to the other part of the arts, which is especially concerned with music, under Pericles, in the festivals of the gods, scenic performances and choruses of every kind and solemn processions were celebrated with such great splendor, not indeed rude and barbarous, but magnificent and elegant, so that it may be thought that more expense was spent on these things than on military expeditions for freedom and supremacy:
Actors, singers, dancers, flute-players, and lyre-players of the highest distinction arose at Athens.

Although their perfection cannot be perceived today by eyes and ears, yet whoever could have pleased the most cultivated men, whoever could have pleased Pericles or Sophocles, must have been supreme in his own art—only one ignorant of antiquity would deny this.

Thus it happened especially through the merit of Pericles that the Athenians were formed to approve and rightly judge only the most beautiful things, and that excellent learning and elegance of judgment and subtlety were spread among all citizens.
At the same time, since the arts had not yet declined into softness, the minds of men were incited to noble plans and great deeds by the seriousness of the great things that were being viewed.

Yet the same man, who devoted all his effort to adorning the state with the most distinguished honors of every kind, was in his private life modest, frugal, and so far removed from all luxury that he kept his household goods furnished in the simplest manner, and was never invited to dinner except once at the wedding of his relative Euryptolemus, and even then he attended the banquet only up to the beginning of the drinking party.

In this respect too he was utterly unlike the later leaders of the state, who, while the city was occupied with paving streets, building fountains, and covering roofs with tiles, and was undertaking almost no work worthy of its ancestors, built for themselves more spacious houses than the state possessed and abounded in luxury.
But perhaps I have lingered too long in contemplating Pericles, my hearers;
and yet I have not accomplished what someone might have expected me to accomplish:
I cannot match such great matters with meager words, nor is it permitted, confined within these limits, to run out into each one in such a way that I could satisfy by speaking.

Finally, I have not undertaken to delineate the whole image of Pericles, nor to speak about him for his own sake, but I wished to set forth the leading citizen of the state, who had especially supported literature and the arts.
In this I chose him, whom it would not repent to have set forth as a most polished example and one complete in all respects.
If you had tried to adorn him with words, you would have achieved this one thing, that he would seem greater by praise.
But if I had spoken about the princes of the Medici family before him, I could rightly be reproached for neglecting the greatest things and aiming at lesser ones;
although I would by no means deny that these are worthy of the highest praise:
but if I had brought forward Louis, king of the French, whom the flattery of his contemporaries wished to be called Great, I would fear that my speech would be despised;
I understand that Octavianus Augustus, who was certainly well-disposed to literature, follows Pericles at a long interval.

With what face should I have brought the Egyptian kings, the Ptolemies, who were most devoted to learning, but for the most part foul in their depravity of morals or luxury, into this assembly which is being held today?
Yet I readily concede that our times are much more similar to those which I have just mentioned than to the age of Pericles;
And just as those ages, so this age of ours can emulate, but not attain, the Periclean age.
For the culture of each age arises and is completed by the concurrence of many and various causes.

But our age, if any other, is separated by a very long interval from the native simplicity of Pericles' time and from the other virtues by which Greece then excelled, which it would be long to set forth and not suited to this place.
Therefore, whoever today has set before himself to become a Pericles as much as possible, by attempting and by lavishing anything at all, will not accomplish much.

For no one will bring that state of affairs to pass by his own counsels, which has its foundations laid in the whole nature and character of the people, in the course of earlier times, in the condition of the present, and, to embrace everything in one word, in the fate of the nation divinely predetermined.

Nor, however much one might attribute to Pericles, will anyone deny that Pericles did not provoke all those talents, but fostered them and equipped them with resources, and used them liberally and munificently.
In our age, indeed, it is certain that the face of all things is entirely different.
The field of letters is wider than before.
Literature itself is manifold.
Of these, some kinds are liberal, others are either adapted to the use of life or invented for it.
The use of the arts which they call beautiful extends less widely.
Others, indeed, are equally celebrated as in antiquity and, according to the judgment of our men, which is especially held concerning music, more perfect.
Others, in many lands even of more civilized Europe, after glorious beginnings long ago, have become almost obsolete.
Reverence for the divine in minds, ceremonies for the most part without splendid display:
The common people intent on gain, with almost no sense of beauty or reverence;
Nor have they learned to separate learning from usefulness.

Therefore today, whoever has been placed in charge of the state and has decided to look after the arts and letters, given the present character of affairs, will have to follow, at least in part, a course of action far different from that of that Pericles.
And certainly Frederick William, a most wise king, does diligently what can be done.

For first, to speak of those arts which are employed in fashioning statues and images, in engraving and carving, and finally in drawing and painting, their task of assisting, which was once simple, if you set aside the instruction of schools, which I will omit at this point, is now found to be especially twofold.

For after the Greeks, for the most part, and then also those of the more recent artists who, since the revival of letters, have especially distinguished themselves in painting, taught the correct method by their excellent examples, and different schools of artists arose, by which various things were attempted and accomplished;

Since it has been understood that both artists are to be trained and the minds of spectators are to be formed by examples, which are not found everywhere, it is necessary to collect monuments and to set forth the best models, in which the origins, progress, and decline of the arts, and what was excellent and what was to be avoided, might be recognized.

But by heaping up fragments of marble and painted panels, however splendid, the arts are not revived, unless worthy and abundant material is provided for the talents, which are never entirely lacking, in which they may not merely test their strength once or twice, but may attain perfection through continuous use and frequent practice.
Frederick William provides both kinds of support especially from that time when the power and dignity of the empire were restored by his most prudent counsels and the valor of his armies.

After he recovered the most precious treasures of elegant works, which had been magnificently furnished by the generous care of his ancestors, from the spoils of the enemy, he increased them at his own expense with new and distinguished additions, and he will increase them;

And since this apparatus, scattered through the royal houses, cannot serve the conveniences that are desired, he ordered a museum to be founded by the arts, which, when it has been completed and adorned, will offer to students no less delight, and to artists utility, than several leading cities already offer.
But Frederick William does not confine himself to this.
For just as the kings of Prussia long ago wished that even workshops and common trades should be brought to a higher perfection, so that we might emulate foreigners;

so Frederick William, under whose rule the state has obtained distinguished artists, supplies to architects, sculptors, statuaries, and painters abundant material for undertaking most famous works, which seem able to endure for an age:
the pious king adorns temples, builds monuments, places statues, grateful toward the people, the army, the leaders; the emperor [does so].
The theater, consumed by flames, was restored by a civil prince who indulges in the delights of the city.
Nor would I fear to say those things which the morose may have considered trifling, the scenic and musical arts;

To these, so much the more earnest attention must be paid, the more, if they are viewed as charming, the minds of the citizens are daily shaped by hearing; if they are perverse or less decorous, judgment and morals are corrupted.
For who is there who thinks that anything is detracted from the severity of Pericles because he adorned his fatherland with scenic performances?
Who does not understand that it is fitting for the leader of the people to be involved in pleasures?

Who does not know that the Athenians were made more refined by nothing more than by the discipline of the stage, which is almost their own, and that from all Greek literature nothing more serious or more magnificent has come down to us than the stage plays and the songs written for the musical games?
Therefore, it is entirely Periclean that in these matters a splendor worthy of this kingdom should be established.
The more so because the private life and habits of Frederick William are seen to be simpler.
so that you may see that he aims not at ostentation and pomp but at public dignity.

But having dismissed these matters, that I may come to those things which are nearest to us, that literature also must be aided in a different way than in antiquity, there is no need for me to explain at length.

Although these studies once sought almost only security from the state and honorable esteem, since those who taught them either by writings or by voice were themselves sufficiently equipped with domestic means, or demanded a huge fee from their students, it has long been the case that they need the care of princes and states, and they must be increased by founding schools and by salaries for teachers.
In this matter, what Frederick William has shown himself to be, this very university, this very assembly is proof, which, unless we had been summoned by him, would not be taking place in this place.

Nor indeed does he, led by some partiality, as princes are wont, favor one kind of schools or one kind of discipline and disregard the rest, but, which is by far the best, he treats all with a certain equal kindness.
Therefore, to say nothing of the lesser games, throughout the entire Prussian empire, gymnasia and lycea are furnished with suitable teachers quite lavishly;
for those matters that pertain to the common life and the advantages of the state, special schools are established;

but as for the universities, in which a higher knowledge of the sciences is imparted, none of those princes who have existed for a long time has preserved, restored, or founded them more munificently and wisely.

While I run through these things as briefly as possible and do not embellish them with many words, nevertheless I seem to have accomplished this, that the mention of Pericles, thrown in, is not considered entirely empty nor foreign to these solemnities.

Therefore, just as that age brought forth a rich harvest of the best things, with the remnants of which we still delight and are educated, so may the reign of Frederick William, I pray, be more conspicuous day by day in the flower of arts and letters, and may it bring forth such things as to transmit to future ages a similar fame and fruit of learning.
So that he whose name is sufficiently provided for posterity by the integrity of his life, the goodness of his rule, and the greatness of his deeds, may also be honored with that glory.
By these qualities, Frederick William has gained and maintains the love and veneration of his citizens.

And what Pericles is said to have said when dying, while some of those standing around praised one thing and others another in his life, that these things had also happened to others and were common to him with fortune, but that this was by far the greatest and most beautiful thing for him, that no Athenian had put on a black garment because of him, this Frederick William surpasses:
We have seen him wrestling with fortune, through whom not only has no one ever put on a dark garment, but on whose birthday citizens use a festive and joyful garment.

Therefore may God, the Best and Greatest, keep such a king safe together with the Augustan house, and may He lead him and the state, which he wisely governs, on a calm, happy course proceeding toward all good and prosperous things.

div.head: X. Oratio nataliciis Friderici Guilelmi III. celebrandis d. III. m. Aug. a. MDCCCXXII. habita.
On the study of antiquity

p.s: Of all the assemblies that are held in our buildings and especially in this senate house throughout the year, none is more frequented, none more distinguished by the nobility and dignity of those present, none more sacred by the gravity of the matters transacted, than these solemn rites instituted annually and to be instituted hereafter for piously honoring the name of Frederick William, our most beloved King.
The more I understand this, the less I ever satisfy myself not only in speaking, but even in choosing the subject itself.

And although the treatment of almost all things is made easier by use and practice, this one task, the more often I undertake it, the more clearly I see that it is so difficult that it far, far exceeds my strength.

There is added to the other difficulties this not least one, that since those things which are most conspicuous in a king pertain to the state, and the material sought from that source seems most worthy, which we might set forth before such and so great an assembly, I scarcely dare to touch that most abundant matter;
because my mind, estranged from public affairs, is occupied only in literature:
This we know to be especially in accordance with the will of our most wise King.

Therefore, with the greatest things snatched away, what remains, listeners, except that, withdrawing a little longer from the proclamation of the King's praises, which he neither desires nor demands, I take refuge in an argument sought from the school, lest I engage in those things for which I may seem less suitable?

When you have granted me this, since it is probable that each one of those who dwell in these places will speak, if not excellently, at least tolerably, you will at the same time have granted that I speak about the discipline of ancient literature.

But do not fear that by proposing those things which seem to me more than to you, and more suitable to any other day than to the birthday of the most deserving King, I shall be troublesome to you today.

I am not so foolish as to try, by immoderately boasting of those letters, as some do, to detract from others, intending by an illiberal and arrogant discussion to produce nothing but nausea in my hearers;
nor will I wander so far that my speech may not find a way back:
I will confine myself to those things which I think are not entirely foreign to any of you, who are all furnished with this most important part of public education;

And since nothing can be entirely separated from the state's affairs, I will conveniently arrive even at that point, which perhaps you hoped I would reach earlier, namely, to seek praise for the ruling house and the most gracious Prince from those things that have been well established in this empire.
Finally, that you may be fair judges to me, I do not ask, unless you will recognize that I am not an unfair orator.
For, to begin with this, those who have labored longer in some field and have buried their mind deeply in it, I do not judge it unworthy if they attribute the most to it:
For if they did not value it most highly, it would be surprising if they did not abandon it entirely and transfer their zeal and industry to all other things:

But if anyone has not yet understood that, according as each person is carried by his natural talent, different people excel in different things, and that in the whole circle of learning there is no province that rules, none that serves in a somewhat broader capacity, and none that excels alone, so that the inhabitants of the rest are, as it were, counted by their capitation;
let him know that he has made little progress, and that he measures literature not by a just standard, but by the very narrow measure of his own petty mind.

I know that there have been and are theologians, jurists, physicians, philosophers, philologists, physicists, poets, who think that they alone know what is worth the effort, and that others know either nothing or trifles, and that all the remaining arts are to be valued at a penny.
who seem to me by this very pride of judgment to confess that they do not know very many things:

For if they were completely ignorant of everything that lies beyond the boundaries of the discipline they have embraced, or had only lightly touched upon those external matters and tasted them with the tips of their lips, they would have recognized that in the individual arts, when properly handled, there is the deepest knowledge.
But as in those schools in which one or another doctrine is taught separately, let us allow this one to pride itself in its own separate place;

Certainly in a university, where distinguished teachers are appointed for each discipline, if anyone among the teachers should despise the other subjects, he is the less to be tolerated, the more easily he can correct his error from the association of his colleagues, and the more harmful he can be to his students.
For he who lives in solitude, because he rarely compares what is foreign with his own, will more often be led to value his own more highly than is right;
On the contrary, nothing learned can more strongly compel one to modesty than the daily, as it were, sight of the various arts.
And he who, by disparaging others, draws learners away from learning them, takes from them a great part of those things by which they nourish their minds.

Therefore, intending to speak about the study of antiquity, I will especially take care to remove diligently what is falsely accustomed to be proclaimed about it to the detriment of other disciplines, especially since I understand that something is commonly attributed to it which seems rather to be common to all good arts.
For it has become established that the things comprehended in this discipline are called studies of humanity:
From this some, having set out, thought that humanity is proper and peculiar to this kind of literature.
This is so far from being true, that I think no science, which is worthy of this name, can be without humanity.
For first, if you should think that humanity consists in elegance of manners, in courtesy, gentleness, and charm;
everyone understands that letters of any kind contribute something, but only something, to these, because by them all manners are softened and desires are tempered:
Indeed, many have complained that those who are occupied with the study of antiquity are not always found to be the most humane when compared to that power of the voice.
Although I would hardly concede that severity, and in its own place even harshness, conflicts with genuine humanity;
For who would approve of compliance in all matters and toward everyone?
Who would not rather judge that vices, malice, and corrupt morals should be pursued and censured with the greatest force?
For truly, one who shows himself obliging to everyone, I would call him not so much humane as cowardly, or cunning and feigned like a little fox.
And no one would deny that Cicero and Demosthenes, although they rushed against their adversaries with great force, were nevertheless most cultivated men.

But I judge that something greater and more serious is comprehended by humanitas, I mean the faculty of acting rightly and according to the precepts of virtue, of conceiving in the mind universal notions of things, which they call ideas, and finally of explaining aptly what you feel:
Since these things are proper to man, they alone seem to contain the force of humanitas.
But who is so stupid as to think, especially in the present state of learning, that those things are founded solely on ancient literature, or chiefly on it?

For not to mention the shaping of life toward virtue, that the purest notions are innate in every discipline, and that philosophy excels in these very notions unless it is ruined by vain fancies, there is no need for us to demonstrate.
And who would dare to exclude theology from humanity, unless one who has ordered God to be exiled from man?
But the science of law and the medical art, just as they rest on use and experience, so they are based on the most profound notions.

And although we may concede that perfect philology could have seemed to some especially humane, which in the most perfect works of the human mind experiences the immense depth of the human spirit, and comprehends through inner knowledge whatever is magnificent, generous, sweet, and pleasant, whatever moves, strikes, calms, and uplifts the minds of men:
Nevertheless, those written Muses do not alone breathe sweetness;
even the cups and corollas of flowers are inhabited by Venus and Grace:
Those Empedoclean principles, love and strife, by which human beings are driven, also govern the nature of things, gather and separate inanimate matter, unite and disunite them;
and reason, diffused through the whole universe, in the greatest and smallest works of the divine maker, pours over the mind, intent on those things, the forms and images of notions.
Nor, if I wished, could I say by what right the most subtle grammatical questions could be considered more human than the microscopic observations of physicists.
What of the fact that the whole material of ancient studies, if you except the old languages, is contained in the other disciplines themselves?
If they did not pertain to humanity, that study which is composed from them could not be called humane.
Unless perhaps you have sought humanity in this, that in the letters of philologists only the slight beginnings of individual things are handed down, and the more abstruse matters are neglected:
Just as Aristotle did not want the liberal arts to be taught in such a way that they become perfect in them, but that they be imbued with the rudiments,
And although this was well said about liberal education, it should not be transferred to the method of judging doctrines.
For my part, as I have sufficiently indicated, humanity seems to consist especially in the understanding of concepts.
And where these fail, there I think the work of a petty craftsman begins;
By which I see that not a few of those very men who devote themselves to ancient literature are held fast.
I mean all those who, unequal to their predecessors, pile up a rough, unshaped, and gloomy mass of matter and words.
But let us also consider that part of culture which I said consists in this, that you can speak what you feel.

I do not deny that the study of ancient literature can be of exceptional benefit, since it examines and scrutinizes the words, thoughts, style, and speech in the most perfect examples of the most distinguished writers;
Nevertheless, this benefit is not as great as is commonly supposed.
For first, it is established that people become eloquent chiefly by the gift of nature;
But practice must be added, which among students of antiquity is usually very slight.
Then critical and grammatical discipline indeed forms and shapes judgment, but it rather draws back from ready discussion than brings that faculty.

Indeed, we see that very many of those who engage rather diligently in that kind of study (and I do not except myself) are not greatly practiced in speaking, but are brought to such a point by the careful and subtle examination of language that both a supply of thoughts fails them, and their very speech, because they perceive faults more keenly and guard against them more fearfully, as if distrusting itself, flows less freely:

Almost like Aristarchus, the father of grammarians, who, as it seems, when asked why he did not himself compose a poem, since he had the best knowledge of the faults and virtues of poems, is said to have replied that he could not write as he wished, and did not wish to write as he could.

Others, by constantly turning over the best models, have achieved this one thing, that, as is especially charged against Latin orators, they say nothing in many words, or, like the Emperor Claudius, they write elegantly but ineptly.

Finally, if you wish to call by the name of humanity that balanced cultivation of the mind's powers, which the study of ancient literature is said to provide, though it has not provided it to many, that very balanced learning depends more on the goodness of natural talent, and will be the more perfect the more things, properly worked over and arranged, the mind can embrace in thought;

In this, the greatest philosophers will be those who, if any, having traversed the whole circle of learning with the greatness of intellect that we know existed in Aristotle and Leibniz, will have done so.

Since these things are so, I pass over that distinguished title imposed on our literature, and I refer it back to the age from which it was propagated, in which the European nations, emerging from the filth of inveterate barbarism and growing warm in the contemplation of the ancient authors, sought from there the seeds of all better culture, in which the great poet Dante Alighieri looked up to Virgil as a specimen of his art complete in all respects, Francesco Petrarca was thinking about restoring the Latin language to common use, in which in the books of Plato and Aristotle the only sources of sounder philosophy gushed forth;
Finally, with regard to the imitation of the elegance of the ancient writers in the Latin language, to which the best minds were rightly turning their attention:
But now that literature has matured, a different judgment seems to be called for.

Therefore, when you ask what and what kind of philology is in my judgment, I answer in the simplest way, if it is taken not in the broader sense that lies in the word itself, but as it is usually referred to ancient literature, that it is the historical and philosophical knowledge of all antiquity.
Of all antiquity, I say:

In this respect it differs in some degree from history, which chiefly teaches the deeds accomplished in the order of time, whereas philology embraces the whole life of ancient peoples and tries to know it in all its parts.
However, whoever examines the matter more keenly will find no part of philology that cannot become a subject for history.

Therefore, those who restrict the boundaries of this discipline to the arts of the interpreter and the critic seem to me to err greatly, for it is clear that these arts contain not the highest limits of learning, but the instruments for discovering truth:

I say this not in contempt of those arts, but because the matter itself demands it, since I understand that there is in them something more recondite than most people see, provided that they do not think that criticism consists solely in correcting the errors of copyists, while they call it divine, thereby of their own accord ridiculing and prostituting its divinity by that paltry use of theirs.
Nor do I judge it less disgraceful if someone should hawk a crude heap of miscellaneous things as philology.

When I attribute philosophical cognition to it, I mean that the highest notions are to be sought out as innate in the nature of ancient nations and as expressed, as it were, in visible images in the individual parts of ancient culture:
Which notions are not to be established arbitrarily; how they can be found by the right path, I will not now explain.

Now, to avoid lingering too long on this matter, which is indeed great, and which I would call the head of all learning, when you have come to the individual parts, an exposition of each one must be presented not only well arranged and confirmed by suitable witnesses, but also consistent with those highest notions, so that, while each thing is spread before our eyes, we may understand that it has been shaped not by chance but by inner necessity, as much as this can exist in human affairs, and that it has undergone these changes in the course of time.
But I indicate the parts themselves, which are to be divided again into their own subdivisions, in three words:
first, the knowledge of public affairs, with the notice of times and places, and of civil institutions, and also of law;
the second, the demonstration of private affairs, the third, of religions and arts;

the fourth, the history of all doctrines, of philosophy, of moral and natural disciplines, of styles and literary genres, and finally the perfect explanation of the language, to which the primitive knowledge of the nation is innate:
Why I have so composed and separated these parts, which embrace the whole subject matter of philology, demands a more extensive investigation.

But if you have delineated the study of antiquity in this manner, you will concede not only that the deepest and broadest learning is exercised in those studies, but also that, as for many arts, so for this one no single person suffices:

Indeed, it is evident that whoever strives to become perfect in all parts cannot attain the highest in any one, just as Eratosthenes, who first used the name of philologist, was considered not first in any field but second in all.
By dividing the tasks, much will also be gained here, since, as Hesiod says, the half is more than the whole.

But in whatever particular part they place their more distinguished industry, they ought to be equipped with the most important notions of the whole discipline, lest they occupy the place of artisans.

Finally, since it seems certain that, just as the Greeks traced the beginnings of all arts back to Homer as their author, so all the arts that have been cultivated in our times have their roots in antiquity;
It is clear that philology is common to all learned people, not peculiar to those who are called philologists, and that it cannot be completed without the support of the other disciplines.

I seem to myself to have accomplished what I wanted, listeners, namely to show that I do not wish to adorn my studies with words beyond measure, but that I am conducting the common cause of all learned men, as is fitting in such great harmony of the various disciplines among us, of which none is judged by those most distinguished men, whom the Father of the Fatherland wished to be placed over us for our greatest benefit, to be either more excellent or more useful;
At the same time, I think it can be gathered from my discussion that the study of antiquity is not unworthy to be cultivated by the efforts of many scholars.
And yet not even this is perfect, if someone, despising the arts of our age, has known nothing but ancient things.
But since I have spoken thus far about the science of antiquity itself, I now pass on to that which may be referred especially to public utility.
For since it is found that, in ancient literature, by a custom handed down from the previous age, a special place was given in the instruction of the schools;
it was asked whether this institution was rightly retained up to the present or not:
for it had been understood, as I explained above, that even the other disciplines of humanity scatter seeds.

But I will not descend to the arguments with which the two sides have contended, nor will I explain how one who properly learns a language in childhood not only exercises the powers of his mind most keenly, but also, as if unknowingly, imbibes an immense store of notions:

The prerogative that is attributed to ancient literature in the education of youth seems to rest especially on this foundation: that whatever excellent things the recent age has produced, the ancient classical writers have not ceased to be the most important, and the tender minds ought to be imbued with those things that are best, so that they may be filled with the most beautiful forms.
I see indeed that it can be doubted who are the classical writers;
But to cut short a long discussion, I call that classic which, the more you consider it, the more it pleases, not that which, even if it pleased at first, becomes worthless by constant contemplation.
Nor do I speak of the judgment of only one man or of a few:
what is classic grows with the consensus of succeeding ages as it grows old, if indeed what always flourishes grows old;
We measure the charm of other things by their novelty.
Time tests all things;
In time, those ancient writers were approved;
and the judgment of centuries, especially in those things which are publicly established, is not to be made of the least importance, nor is anything to be rashly innovated.
But I conjecture from certain indications that our ancestors, most prudent in handing down the ancient authors to youth, also had something else in view.
For although to scrutinize the nature of things is deservedly considered excellent, yet human affairs are nearest to man;

But among human things, nothing is more common to men, nothing ought to be dearer, than that society established by nature itself, which contains all the goods of man, the city, the fatherland of each one.
And indeed the love of one's fatherland is so diffused through nearly all the ancient writers that I would call it, as it were, the vital breath of antiquity:
Unroll the poets, the philosophers, the orators, the historians;
You will find that the love of liberty, which is essential to a fatherland, is deeply implanted in the innermost hearts of all.

When I consider this, I do not hesitate to affirm that no explanation of the history of the fatherland, in which we altogether limp, because excellent writers of this kind rarely arise among our countrymen for certain reasons, no knowledge of the laws and institutions of the fathers, no public solemnities so foster the love of the fatherland and the sense of just liberty as the reading of the ancient writers, and that boys rightly instructed in that discipline, with the very first rudiments, by reading Nepos himself, by other excellent examples, [are so fostered].
Indeed, since no better teachers of political wisdom can be found than the ancients, not only boys will be trained from them in love of country, but also men in the conduct of affairs.
But about this, although it can be approved by the authority of the greatest men and by the matter itself, I think it better to be silent, lest I exceed what befits my person.
What I have placed in the first position, it is pleasing to illustrate with conspicuous examples.
Let Frederick the Great and the Emperor Napoleon serve as examples.
Of these two, when the latter, with his characteristic shrewdness, understood that the treatment of the ancient writers was hostile to unjust tyranny, that treatment greatly displeased him;

That Frederick the Great, the principal founder of this empire, so that everything that could nourish the mind and free it from servitude, thus especially the Greek and Latin authors pleased him and seemed most suitable for scholastic instruction, is a thing most well known.

He who, on the threshold of old age, with bodily strength worn down but with mind unimpaired, when he had ordered the best Greek authors to be read aloud to him constantly, although he had been educated especially in French literature, which is most alien to the Greek character, and knew those very Greek authors themselves, deprived of their force, only from French translations;

Nevertheless, having been exceedingly delighted with them, and, to dwell on this one point, having admired the excellence of his genius in Demosthenes' speech On the Crown, which is filled with great thoughts and the dearest affection toward his country.

We know that he, led by his own counsels, not by those of his friends, ordered that the principal Greek and Latin writers should be read most diligently in the schools, and that not only the words of the young men should be committed to memory, but also the method of treating subjects and the subjects themselves and the opinions should be explained.
Thus, while Frederick the Great was reigning, in this empire and especially in this city, the foundations of a better discipline were laid more firmly.
These institutions, which Frederick William, our most wise king, not only retained but also strengthened,
The same king, having defeated the common enemy of Europe, warded off that barbarism which threatened from him.
Therefore I cannot but praise that institution of which I have spoken:
For this is the pledge of liberty.
Those who feared it for any reason have taken care that those writers should not be handed over intact to the youth;
so that even minds might be mutilated, lest limbs be able to move:

Although those men rarely attained what they desired, because, to adapt the words of a most distinguished writer to this matter, the memory of a succeeding age cannot be extinguished by present power.

Nor indeed, when the young generation is nourished by those means and is mixed into the conduct of affairs, for which the ancients themselves, with their years set apart for this matter, were not equal;
But, far removed from the contagion of present affairs, it moves in pure air, which the youthful mind ought to draw in with its breath.

Therefore, those who, when they wanted to portray genuine Germans, being for the most part not hostile to the study of ancient literature, thought that those studies should be either banished or confined within very narrow limits, seem to me to have erred greatly.
Let us therefore preserve this common good of the human race, by which all ages have been nourished:

But let us also give thanks to the most merciful Prince, whom we indeed always venerate silently, but today openly, under whose auspices the discipline of the schools is aided with the most favorable success by those most distinguished men who are also placed over us.
From this it is understood that they have a clear view of what things the true salvation of the people is based on.
for I may seem to say something ridiculous;
Nevertheless, I will say that neither armies, nor resources, nor the most illustrious men are as great a protection to the state as good teachers of youth.

Among these, we indeed are the first, but as schoolteachers, of whom not a few are equipped with such an abundance of learning that they would even suffice for greater duties, they seem to me all the more worthy of remuneration, the greater their toil is and the less splendid their position.

In the more ample establishment of universities, the rulers of states do not always seem to have been averse to ostentation, because such great authority was once attributed to them, and is partly still attributed, that a whole kingdom can boast of one university.
Where the institutions of schools, being less conspicuous, are deemed worthy of the same care, it is evident that not vain display, but the very truth of things is exclusively regarded.

But Frederick William was adorned with both kinds of glory: on the one hand, with the greatest munificence towards the universities, which he established and furnished with a most ample equipment, and with a generosity entirely free from all ostentation, which we especially owe to him; and on the other hand, also with the glory of the schools, which were more and more increased.
But for us, besides the other ministers of the state, the scholastic and ecclesiastical teachers must be trained, who can satisfy the needs of the republic and the desires of the most gracious King.
How great this duty is, none of you fails to understand.

My mind is stirred, listeners, when I think how much, especially in these times, when the eyes of all are cast upon us, we must strive to answer the prayers of our founder, who desires the best of everything:
But when he has seen our good will, since nothing perfect can be accomplished by human strength, he will calmly grant pardon for those things that are left unfinished.
My mind is stirred when I see in one view how much we owe him.
My mouth is stopped while I hesitate what to say first, what second, what third.
Therefore, to embrace much in few words, whatever I have said over so many years about our most dear King on this day and from this very platform:
For I have said many things, with you as witnesses, which I do not think have been consigned to oblivion by any of you, whom I know to have always been attentive listeners to me:
Therefore, whatever I have said so often in previous years, know that it all now fills my mind at this critical moment;
Recall it in your mind, and from that make a conjecture how great is what I feel.

Filled with these sentiments, you also pray with me to God, the author and preserver of all good things, that He may preserve that most sacred head for us and for the state into extreme old age, and that He may keep the entire royal house whole, safe, and unharmed forever.

div.head: XI. Oratio nataliciis Friderici Guilelmi III. celebrandis d. III. m. Aug. a. MDCCCXXIII. habita.
On the virtue of the learned

p.s: Since, from that time, listeners, from which our seat of learning was founded under the most auspicious patronage of Frederick William, you have heard, once every year and on this very day, from this place, the praises of the most beloved King set forth;
this year, which we are now passing through, it has happened by a remarkable gift of God, that at today's solemnities we venerate the best Prince not for the first time but for the second:

After we saw that most joyful day, on which the whole state congratulated us with the highest feeling of piety, that the Father of his Country had completed twenty-five years of rule through virtues and benefits.

There had then gathered a truly splendid circle of distinguished men experienced in public affairs, and in the foremost place had taken his seat the King's son, heir to the throne, the hope and delight of the people:

Before them, our highest magistrate, when he understood that a more magnificent and more abundant speech was fitting for the special solemnities, which we pray with all our might may not remain special, and since he himself had once conducted public affairs, and had judged an argument drawn in large part from a more intimate knowledge of affairs to be suitable to his own person and to those who were present;

These things, I say, since they were so, he then spoke in such a way that he would expound at length whatever had been excellently done by Frederick William through so many five-year periods at home and in war, whatever was prudent, pious, civil, generous, and finally would praise the Prince exceedingly through all parts of public and private life, and, with pardon for saying so, would snatch away from himself, or rather from his successors, all material, however ample, before a secondary orator in the presence of mindful ears.

Therefore, what I did in previous years, namely, not to set forth the King's universal merits with deliberate effort, but to treat some matter that was in a way external, and to adapt it to the present state of affairs, and from that to derive the King's singular praise, that one thing I now see is left for me.
Although you will understand that even so the path of speaking is not clear for me, if you consider that today I am delivering the tenth speech in these very solemnities;
If my talent has any power either in celebrating the name of the King or in unfolding the theme that befits this day and you, I have long since exhausted all of it.
Finally, since I judge it unworthy of both you and myself to repeat what has been said before, the material must now be sought from afar.
So that he is unfair who would charge me with a fault for what is an inconvenience of my condition.

But as I reflect on how often I have proclaimed the distinguished services of Frederick William to literature, this thought has occurred to me, that it is especially noble for a prince to come to the aid of literature, particularly in this age, when learning has been brought into suspicion, and the century, raised up to liberal and profound knowledge, is attempted by the obscure contentions of certain men to be reduced back into darkness;

However, it is not an absolute praise of the king that many princes are known to have combined both learning and the pursuit of learning with the utmost depravity of morals and savage and unrestrained domination.
Therefore, not much is to be attributed to that kindness toward the arts, unless it has flowed from a mind alien to all depravity.
When we compare Frederick William to this standard, what in him delights us more than that great harmony of virtues?
For while he fosters literature and the arts, he is also pious and religious without superstition;
while he nourishes the reverence for the divine power both most sacredly in his own heart and spreads it in the minds of his citizens, he is also a vigorous leader of the army;
And, equating the honors of public virtues with private morals, he tempers severity with courtesy.

Therefore, since our excellent king is such not by my opinion but by the consensus of all, what wonder if he demands from the learned, especially from those to whom he himself entrusted public instruction, not only learning and skill, but also integrity?
Hence my plan is to discuss now briefly those things in which the virtue of the learned seems to me to be discerned:
So that I may explain, as far as can be done in this brief time, how we may most rightly satisfy the expectation of the wisest King, in my opinion at least, by our conduct.

Although I scarcely hope, and not even scarcely, that I will be sufficient for this task, I who am fully conscious of my own weakness, nevertheless, in accordance with your indulgence, which I have experienced so often, you will forgive my willingness the more readily, because I have come here not trusting in my strength, but through the duty of my office.
But someone may ask whether I am going to speak about the virtue of the learned man:
Do you think that learned men have a certain and peculiar virtue of their own, removed from the habits of other mortals?
By no means, I reply.
What things are good and beautiful in all men, what are considered the human or civil, private or public duties of each one, these are also the duties of the learned:
indeed, the more they have cultivated their mind, the more they ought to surpass others in the common virtues of all, so that others may be formed according to their example;
