And even the most learned man is to be despised, who, as some people once especially did, denies that he is bound by those precepts of an honorable life which are commonly prescribed.

Nevertheless, since the learned have a certain business by which their occupations differ from other men, one virtue of the human race seems to be contained in the learned, insofar as they are learned, and another among those who are engaged in a different kind of life.
For although knowledge may be useful also for the state, for private and domestic affairs, for trades and lucrative arts, its end is certainly not to be sought anywhere but in knowledge itself.
And since the learned man is occupied in knowledge, his proper virtue is to be regarded only in this.
But since the notion of knowledge cannot be separated from truth;
unless the learned man has attained true knowledge, he will be deprived of his virtue:

Therefore, just as all virtue is comprehended in knowledge according to the opinion of the greatest philosopher of antiquity, so in the virtues of learned men I think wisdom and correct knowledge of things are most important, and that they have departed from their genuine virtue to the extent that they are entangled in more numerous and more serious errors.
When I say this, I do not fear the criticism of those who refer virtue solely to the will.
For since the intellect moves the will, from defects of the notions corrupt plans arise;
And by excusing any errors whatsoever through sincerity of will, you would have removed virtue itself.

But if nevertheless many disagree about the greatest matters, I do not therefore think that either party is to be judged depraved, because very different opinions have not rarely flowed from the same eternal truth, which the weakness implanted in our nature hinders from perceiving pure and undefiled, while one person by mixing in one thing, another another, obscures the divine form, and perfect knowledge follows at a distance.

But whoever does not combine the study of wisdom with self-knowledge will follow it after a very long interval, for only by self-knowledge can one understand how much progress one has made, what one knows, and what one does not know.
so that, being self-controlled, he may keep himself within his own limits, and not meddle with those of others, to which he is unequal.
Opposed to this is the vice of arrogance, by which some are oppressed, even those who seem modest.
I mean those who undertake to teach to others disciplines which they themselves do not sufficiently master.

For this reason the opinion of those who say that the education of youth should be entrusted not to the most learned but to the most upright men seems to me the less to be approved, since one who takes upon himself a task of which he is in no way capable cannot be regarded as most upright.

Now indeed, to pass from those things that pertain more to knowledge to that which is of the will, just as the health of the body seems to consist in the absolute harmony of all its parts and powers, so the concord and agreement of the mind makes a just man, and without this concord there is no virtue of the soul;
But what greater discord can there be, than if someone should think one thing and say another?
But the force of desires that are ill-restrained also drives even the learned to become false, and teaches them, as he says, to keep one thing hidden in the breast and another ready on the tongue.

Among these there are few, but there are nevertheless some, who, especially when they have acquired some reputation for themselves, puffed up with immense pride, despise all others in comparison with themselves, and if anyone else excels, cannot bear it without envy;

who try to persuade others that they know everything best, and although they themselves understand that others have deserved well, nevertheless they disparage them, wish to detract from their praises, and to obstruct their undertakings;
for no other reason, indeed, than that since they wish to be considered the only wise ones, they take another's glory as a diminution of their own eminence.

This wicked desire for glory, just as it cannot arise except from a corrupt mind, so he who is possessed by it no longer seeks the truth in order that it may be understood as true, but, referring everything to his own name, attempts either to attack the truth itself or to shroud it in darkness, whenever he has judged that it serves his cause.

For my part, although I know that many think otherwise, ambition seems to me not only not a great force for virtue, but also, both in public life and in letters, to be a most pernicious evil, and that not a fault residing in the very thing I have just now set forth, but one spreading much more widely still.

For in those disciplines which it is valuable for everyone to know, for those who think that the knowledge of things divine and human is not foreign to them, especially in philosophy and history and the teaching of civil affairs, and finally in the science of theologians, according to the character of the ages, at one time one thing, at another another, pleases both the common people and the powerful;
Seeking to curry favor with these, ambitious learned men adapt their opinions to those by whom they wish to be approved, and thus creep into their minds:
Therefore they bend and twist their opinions this way and that, and first deceive others, then soon themselves.
The same men, according as it has seemed convenient, change what they had previously embraced;
such men as the Greeks used to call cothurni.
Indeed, the divinity of learning does not allow that those (doctrines) be fitted to the opinions of patrons, as dishes to the palates of cooks;
Nor, if we resolve to proceed along the pure path of knowledge, can we look around in every direction to see what will please each person in each period of five years, and what will displease.

But if, according to the varying institutions of rulers, even letters would have to change, then there would be one set of these in a popular government, another under aristocracies, and another in kingdoms.
although their condition is such that they obey only reason, which is one and simple.
Indeed, since reason is also spread and disseminated through all the parts of every best state, rightly pursued learning cannot conflict with a well-constituted republic:
If they disagree with each other, it is necessary that either the letters or the states be corrupt.

But in literature, since not a few manage everything according to their own will, but rather with the combined talents and efforts of many learned men, since one corrects another, corrects errors, teaches truer things, and so many learned men cannot be subjected to the authority and, as it were, tyranny of one man, being accustomed to freedom of thought and solely intent on searching out the truth;
Unless, perhaps, by the fault of the state itself certain fixed resolutions, not the best, are cherished, and better ones are prohibited, the whole republic of letters cannot easily rush into ruin.
When a well-cultivated governor of the state has understood that individuals have erred by misusing letters, scarcely anyone will deny that it is his power to restrain those men.

Only let not the fault of one be transferred to all, and on account of the error of an artisan let the art itself be considered pernicious, and let liberty be taken away from literature, which, when you have removed it, even the most diligent care will not be able to restore.
But he who has reviewed the memory of times will find that ruined states or their guardians have not infrequently been hostile to learning.
For not only on account of confession of faith and religion have pious men experienced iron and fire;
But because philosophy seemed to censure unjust power, it also had those by whom it was harassed;

As once at Rome, when Junius Rusticus had published the praises of Paetus Thrasea and Helvidius Priscus, and had called them most holy men, on the occasion of that crime all philosophers, just as formerly actors and Chaldaeans, were removed by a decree of the senate and were banished from the city and from Italy.
Everyone concedes that the fault at that time was not that of the philosophers, among whom were most upright men and Epictetus himself, but that of the Prince and the Senate.

And indeed, who would not think that those who, being learned, have shaped their teachings to the agreement of such masters, become participants in the impiety of tyrants and are to be regarded as parricides in the republic of letters?

Therefore, to return to the point from which I have digressed, if any apply their learning to this end, that they may flatter either the common people or the powerful, in order to win favor for themselves or procure honors, I call them not truly learned, but sophists:

For it is the mark of a sophist not to devote himself to eternal truth and genuine knowledge, but, by putting on the appearance of a philosopher, to serve the pleasure of those whose approval he is eager to win, and to accustom his mind to their opinions, so that he thinks and says nothing other than what they approve, and judges the same things as they do to be good or bad, beautiful or ugly:
For he does this to gain a little glory, to satisfy his ambition, and finally to make a profit.
You see, listeners, that I in speaking spontaneously arrive at a fault, which among the learned I consider not the least, namely the desire for gain.
For not few seem to be those who, considering learning as a trade, devote mercenary labor to it;
which both the Greek sophists once did and many in our age, especially since payment began to be given to writers:
I do not say this in such a way as to deny that those who devote all their leisure to literature should be rewarded with prizes;
While they are intent on these pursuits, they cannot seek in another way the things that are necessary for maintaining honorably their livelihood and culture;

But the pursuits of learning ought to arise from the impulse of a mind inclined to the practice of the good arts and, as it were, by a divine instinct, and ought to be directed to the propagation of truth; they ought not to proceed from the desire of acquiring wealth, nor to be turned to profit.

And the fruits that are derived from these pursuits, whether they are to be held in the second or in no place, are to be done either nothing or very little for their sake, unless a reward has been set before you, you would not have done them.

But I turn my speech away from the vices, which the rule hostile to justice begets from evil desires, and I refresh myself with the contemplation of that virtue, by which, since no single virtue can be held without the others, the rest are perfected;
I mean courage of the soul.
For courage is not merely a military virtue:
although all mortals, each in his own way, in a certain sense serve as soldiers:
but wherever there are things that frighten a man, those terrors must be overcome by courage.

For first, no one who has been more keenly engaged in these matters fails to understand with what difficulties the path of wisdom is hedged about, how steep, how obstructed it is, and with how many labors and vigils the inner entrance of the sciences is opened.
Therefore, through laziness and torpor no one can become learned;
although there are certain lazy minds, which, spurning solid knowledge and relying on the goodness of the talent they boast of, imagine that the deepest knowledge is revealed to them as if in dreams.
Indeed, if you wish to make progress, there is need of strenuous effort, and impatience of toil, sloth, and distrust of one's own strength must be overcome with a brave spirit.
Then, being learned, in whatever discipline he has undertaken to teach, let him not spare his strength in both thoroughly knowing it and diligently transmitting it.
Let him boldly defend the truth with the weapons of his intellect; finally, when there is need and it is necessary, let him profess it even at the risk of giving offense.
For as I praise compliance and modesty, unless hypocrisy lies beneath,
As I prefer prudent silence to untimely license in speaking, I will not approve of the man who, without any compelling necessity, has thrown himself headlong into danger:
Thus I think that a learned man can be brought to such a point that, unless he prefers to admit wickedness or hypocrisy into himself, he cannot avoid the crisis.
Therefore, if anyone has been reduced to that state, a constant and resolute mind will hold him back, so that he does not timidly abandon his opinion;

And rightly judging what is truly fearful and what should not be feared, he will not so much dread threats and terrors, by which the immortal mind cannot be subdued, as the sharpest stings of conscience, which burn and prick too late.
For, to speak with the poet, the ardor of citizens commanding base things does not shake with firm mind the just man tenacious of his purpose, nor the face of a threatening tyrant;
The same man, since he wishes not to seem good but to be good, will not fear the appearance of wickedness in the midst of the highest justice.
By this greatness of soul Socrates became famous, by this John Huss;
this led Luther through so many crises of dangers unshaken:
by this, if it is permitted to compare a heavenly man with mortals, the most holy author of our faith testified to and sealed the divinity of his teaching;
And those whom the madness of their contemporaries condemned, the judgment of the ages has acquitted and crowns with garlands.
This seems to me to be the highest virtue of the learned, my hearers, and whoever follows it will also hold the other virtues, which it is long and unnecessary to set forth.

For although virtue is one, though divided into its parts, I do not think it necessary to descend to each of the secondary particles, because he who holds the most important ones has possessed all the rest.
And I must also consider your position, my dearest colleagues, that is, of men most distinguished in letters, who seem to have known even better what I can set forth according to my own capacity.

Now indeed, whoever has entered upon the plan which I have set forth will have great influence for living happily in tranquility of mind, in good conscience, and in the awareness of duty, and for him at the threshold of old age no anxious cares about the life already lived will arise, but he will live with good hope in whatever fortune.

But we, whom Frederick William, a most upright prince, has called together for the purpose of educating the youth, ought especially to do this: that we ourselves be upright and honest, and that we make our pupils such by our instruction.

If they have become accustomed in their studies to look exclusively at what is true and right and to admire it, and to restrain their minds from the base desires that drive mortals astray, then even in the other walks of life and in business and in the state itself they will show themselves such as Frederick William demands, and they will excel in purity of morals, obedience to the laws, loyalty, and piety, and they will spread those same arts more and more widely throughout the whole commonwealth.

Nor do I think that in our state letters have anything to fear, since Frederick William demands not servitude of minds but liberal obedience, and we do not live in a corrupt republic, but in one in which the citizens, distinguished by love of country proved by deeds, are united as it were into one family by love of a good king, the strongest bond of concord:

Although they differ in the situation of their lands, the nature of their climate, their customs, and their institutions, yet in loving and choosing their king they are wonderfully united in affection and judgment.
When this feeling of affection has failed, we must fear that the state, however well constituted, may be shattered or fall apart.
Hence the greater is the praise of the king, who by justice, moderation, and clemency attracts and fosters the zeal of the people.
For just as these things are acquired and retained by good arts, so when they have been relaxed, they can hardly be recovered.
And with the mutual trust of the prince and the people removed, suspicions, hatreds, the discord of factions, and finally seditions begin to rage.

Since so many kingdoms have been troubled and torn by these, and are still being torn, it can be understood how much we owe to the wisdom and moderation of Frederick William, who provides a tranquil state to this city and happiness to its citizens.

But returning to the praises of the dearest Prince, as I said at the beginning, I have not undertaken to repeat a well-worn theme and to explain each and every one of his virtues by discoursing at length:
Nevertheless, I will not pass over one thing, to which the argument of my speech leads me of its own accord.
For, as I indicated above, a truly just man is free from every kind of ambition, and ambition itself, since it is to be counted among the desires, harms virtue more than it helps it.
But many princes give much to fame.

Brought up in great affairs, in a court that displays a more splendid appearance than the truth of things, they are accustomed to become used to certain empty images of magnificence, liberality, and glory.
But what of Frederick William?
He, far from empty show, wishes not to seem good but to be good.
He practices virtue for the sake of virtue.
He will indeed have eternity of name, but he does not seek it ambitiously.
And since I have mentioned liberality, everyone agrees with one voice that no one shows himself more munificent to letters and arts than Frederick William.

Of this praise there are so many proofs, so many indeed begun, but because great undertakings cannot be completed in a short time, not yet finished, they will exist in the future, so that even if I should wish to enumerate them, my time would not now suffice.
But are these things boasted of?
Did Frederick William undertake these plans for the sake of his own name?
Indeed, the King's modesty in conducting these matters is so great that I can scarcely dare to praise them myself.
Therefore, Frederick William's kindness toward literature is found to be such as it is fitting that it should be;
Recognizing this with a grateful mind, I also urge you, fellow soldiers, to show yourselves grateful to your excellent Prince:
This will be done most correctly when you satisfy his expectation.
But what does it expect and demand from you?
Nothing indeed else, except that as in the other institutions of life, so in the pursuit of letters you be upright and honest:
that each one in his own kind of knowledge may turn out so perfect, as the weakness of the human mind and the nature of each one may allow;
which cannot happen without diligence and industry;
Finally, so that you may attain that virtue which, unless a learned man possesses it, he must be considered to have lost all the fruit of his labors.
And yet I have taught that continence and temperance are also included, which should admonish us not to meddle with others' affairs.

But nothing seems more alien to the knowledge of learning than the plans of societies forbidden by laws, such as are accustomed to be established in academies, which have recalled not a few not only from the eagerness of studies, but also have entangled them in greater evils, which would have been more serious in the future, had not the king's clemency pardoned those who had lapsed.
Therefore consider with what purpose Frederick William founded this home of letters:
Take care to satisfy this end, and diligently beware of whatever is opposed to his wise counsels:
Consider what gifts he has bestowed upon you and bestows daily, with such great opportunity for learning offered to you, which is increased day by day by gathering resources from all sides;

And you testify to your minds mindful of benefits, our countrymen by piety towards the Father of the fatherland, foreigners by recollection of the discipline, by which you enjoy liberally from his institution, both by reverence for the laws and royal virtue.
But for us, dearest colleagues, what should be done, I would be arrogant if I wanted to say;
We have been taught, we hold sufficiently.
Let us nevertheless confirm in these most sacred solemnities the oath sworn to the best Prince:
Let us pledge that we will propagate the light of literature, love of country, safety of the empire, piety, and virtue by our example and instruction.

Finally, let us all who are present invoke the aid and kindness of the divine power, that it may add many years to the life of Frederick William, that it may protect the good minds of him and of his ministers and of all citizens, and finally that it may preserve forever the ruling house, the harmony of the state, and all the dearest goods that it has bestowed upon us.

div.head: XII. Oratio nataliciis Friderici Guilelmi III. celebrandis d. III. m. Aug. a. MDCCCXXIV. habita.
On vigorous and strong knowledge

p.s: About to celebrate the birthday of Frederick William, the best of kings, this year, listeners, I do not think I can seek a more serious beginning from any matter than from the memory of that day on which the whole state, with the greatest zeal, prayed for a happy, fortunate, and prosperous marriage for the king's son, heir to the empire, and for the august wife, and rendered the entrance of the royal bride distinguished not only by such great splendor, which indeed we had not seen before in this city, but also by that ardor of minds which would provide the surest proof of inner affection.
For whatever was given to the son in honor on that day, by that very fact it is established how greatly the father was loved by the citizens, and at the same time it was proved.
And indeed this is not a small thing.
For the offices of reverence and affection that are offered to princes, you may often scarcely distinguish whether they are true or feigned.

Indeed, such is the unhappiness of those who rule in the highest fortune, that there are found people who, the closer they are to them or wish to be, the less sincere, less simple and open they tend to be; moreover, the more intently they say and do everything by which they either preserve or acquire their favor for themselves, concealing servile obedience under the pretense of goodwill for the sake of private advantage.
Ambition creeps in from every side, and especially in great upheavals, the more hateful those who disparage, the easier the access for the flatterer.

But when the people are numerous, what happens joyfully for the imperial house, they accompany not with their own joy but with exultation, the impulse of faithful devotion bursts forth without hope of rewards;
In public joys each one sets aside his own gains, losses, advantages, adversities.

Now indeed, if we inquire what things excite so great a fervor of the people, although I do not deny that the due offices toward the head of the state claim something for themselves from that source, because the uncorrupted citizens and the very plebs, if they do not perceive, certainly feel that the king sustains the person of the whole state;

nevertheless, by far the greatest part of the virtues that stand out in princes — of justice, kindness, clemency — seems to be attributed to the silent esteem and to the memory of a gloriously administered rule:

Since even those whom the prince has not distinguished by any notable favor are found to be filled with these feelings, it is clear that those popular demonstrations are far removed from private advantage.
Therefore nothing can happen to the prince more desirable than that most beautiful spectacle of public joy.
Since we too have been especially permitted to share in this, a greater opportunity has then been given to testify our goodwill than that which recurs every year on this very day:
On that day you seem to be compelled, not without your own detriment, to use my poor speech repeatedly.
And at that time the courtesy of both the King and the king's son was a great consolation to us;
and it was understood that a youth faithful to its prince is nurtured by us:
What could have been more acceptable to us than this, especially at these times, when literary universities, once held among the ornaments of Germany, are subject to the gravest accusations?

Therefore let us give thanks to the wisest king and to the interpreters of royal counsels, because we seem at the same time to be freed from the blame and suspicion of those evils which have been eradicated among us.
Indeed, it is a great thing, dearest colleagues, to undertake the education of youth, great at any time:
for the discipline of the present age shapes the fortune of the future:
it is greater in a critical state of the republic and in a huge crisis, such as foreign power has stirred up for almost all of Europe a few decades ago;
But it seems to me most important, since the shaken world has not yet settled into complete rest.
For literature lifts up minds, drives away drowsiness:
or at least, when they first begin to shape sleepy pupils, let them be strong.
And so it can happen that they apply minds roused by literature to a bad purpose, those whose nature is prone to worse:
yet it is not the fault of literature, if someone abuses the ability acquired through literature.
Indeed, it seems to me that the supreme deity can scarcely bestow a more excellent gift upon mortals than a vigorous and sound knowledge:
in place of which, when they take up a dead one, the loss in this is so much the greater, as the salvation in that is more effective.
But what do I mean by a vigorous and sound knowledge?
Not that which stirs up tumults, which attempts revolutions:
which is not even knowledge, nor will it be called by that name by anyone:
I mean something conceived in the mind, which, especially before you, I feel myself scarcely equal to explaining eloquently.
I therefore ask pardon from you, if the outcome does not match so great an undertaking.

For just as nature has given to each living being a life separated to some extent from other things, and endowed with its own powers, which our people call organic, and has comprehended it in an inseparable union of body and soul—of soul, I say, which, as it were, penetrates the whole structure of the body, communicates form and motion to the limbs, and unites the dissociated and inert particles of matter into one whole and fills them with vigor—
so also does vigorous knowledge seem to be constituted.
Of course, the beginning of its life lies within itself;

and even if it is nourished from without, especially by the state, and is connected with the principles of other human affairs, nevertheless it does not receive its power from them, nor is it their servant, and therefore, unless you wish to corrupt its excellence and beauty, it cannot be cultivated to such an end that it serves alien uses or the pursuit of livelihood:
But those who devote themselves to literature ought to be warmed and stirred by the divine sparks that are within us.

Therefore the rulers of states, who wish well for literature, ought to take care and see to it that men do not occupy public chairs who practice the good arts without being inspired by any nobler impulse, but treat them like common services, as hirelings do:
For what will more readily deliver students to idleness than the daily sight of a teacher who teaches his doctrines not in accordance with their worth nor with the ardor with which he ought?
Again, only that knowledge will be vital and strong which you yourself have hammered out with the generative force of your own mind.

so that the ability to teach seems to be much less dependent on transmitting doctrines than on stimulating minds, and on rousing them to reproduce, according to the disposition of their nature, what the teacher demonstrates.

But if you should try to compel and drive anyone, as if by laying hold of him, to the knowledge of any matter from which his nature recoils, you will accomplish either nothing or this: that, since nothing can be transferred into anyone against the bent of his nature, he will not grasp the knowledge with his mind, but only a superficial acquaintance with his memory.
as if you had made Apollo's form out of a wooden block;
they cannot be drawn out of a man's mind, whose seeds are not placed in it.
Now, since we see that very few mortals have been given such a favorable vein of talent that, whatever matter they have applied their mind to, they accomplish it with equal success;

The universities of Germany are understood to provide a great advantage to learners, because in them free power of choosing various disciplines has been left to them, and they can themselves find out by experience in which they may place their study, whether Minerva is unwilling or propitious:
On this matter we are so agreed among ourselves that anyone who calls it into doubt is judged to be bound by a heavy stupor.
But I pass over this;
so that I, who think these commonplaces should be run through briefly, may not have your learning disdain my words.
But from that generative power of the mind, the mother of all, notions abound, by which matter is governed:
But just as this is indistinct and confused without those, so those are deprived of their body without this.

Both must be so adapted to each other that the mind rightly arranges the abundance of matter, that the abundance of things fills out the forms of notions, and finally that there is an indissoluble bond between the two: this is what scholars must strive for.
But this is accomplished with more difficulty than very many think.

Since, among those who strive with the greatest force to know pure concepts, some not infrequently fall into this fault, that they both hold and peddle the barren designation of empty places or empty formulas as the science itself, and indeed, puffed up with these very things, consider themselves far the wisest; while others, by excessive dividing and distinguishing, so dissect and cut up the elements of knowledge that neither juice nor blood remains, but a certain thin appearance and shadow of learning, scarcely clinging to the bones.

On the other hand, there have been and still are those who are busy piling up a rough heap, in which, as Anaxagoras said, all things are mixed together, and intelligence has not yet permeated the mass.
These people, too, from time to time seem to themselves to be the only learned ones, and they despise all others before them as illiterate.

Just as everyone will find examples of these faults in his own discipline, so in my studies I see others, endowed with remarkable acumen, but insufficiently aided by adequate learning, err through their very subtlety; others have their mental vision dimmed and hampered by the mass of material, because they have either weak intellectual powers, or they do not cultivate the ones they have.

But even if each of the two methods can bring some benefit to literature, it is nevertheless clear that neither contains the truly vital force of knowledge, but that force is seen only in that harmony of concepts and things.
If you ask where that same thing can best be aroused and unfolded in the minds of learners, I answer that no way accomplishes this more surely than the living voice of the teacher:
For this reason, he who draws knowledge from books must himself, as it were, restore to the things written there the life and motion which they have lost.
The words that flow from the mouth of the teacher, if he is a suitable teacher, insinuate themselves with their own liveliness more easily into the minds of attentive students.
But I would not call that a living voice which, as I am now doing according to the custom received in solemn orations, recites what is written and hands over what is to be written and carried home:

but although in the immense apparatus of literature, which no one alone is sufficient to comprehend, not every smallest detail can be held in mind and memory, so that accordingly some moderation is needed in this matter;

Nevertheless, it would be surprising if even a mediocre teacher, while teaching, were not carried along by a free course of thoughts, and did not express those very things which he had pondered, distinguished by clearer lights, than when he sat in his study.
The very presence of the learners adds a spur to the one discoursing and kindles the sparks of genius;
Indeed, that which has passed into a proverb, that one learns by teaching, this seems to me to be referred especially to this point, not to be interpreted as an excuse for unskilled teachers.

Therefore, not indeed an ornate and copious diction of an orator or declaimer, which is somewhat remote from accurate learning, but an elevated, prompt, and, as I may say, spirited exposition of thoughts is required.
I have set this forth not with the intention, my dearest colleagues, that you should be taught what you had to do:
But I judge that in this respect especially, while nearly all the universities of Germany excel, your schools also excel (for allow me to praise you).
Hence it happens that this discipline forms young men for the most part not slow and sluggish, but inflamed with the most eager desire to spread the good arts.
This very desire, the more it blazes forth, can recall them from adopting foreign things, and things that do not suit this age.
Thus, well-trained young men will hold the learning they have acquired not by memory alone but by understanding.

For just as nothing can be learned without memory, not even philosophy, because one who lacks it will retain neither things nor concepts, but everything will flow out of him as from a perforated vessel;
so that being mindful also brings great importance to a learned person:
Yet that knowledge which is supported only by the powers of memory and recollection is not vital but dead.

From this it is at the same time understood that letters cannot flourish, if a certain and perpetual discipline, which is handed over to memory rather than to the mind, is to be followed, much less if prescribed rules are to be followed:
And just as this discipline itself will grow old more and more day by day, so it will give even fervid minds, unless they resist with innate force, to languor.
Certainly the notions of the human mind are constant and eternal, which, because truth is immortal, are never abolished nor obliterated;
but these too are regenerated by free thought, not according to a prescription:
what must be done, you should command; what must be avoided, you should forbid;

And if any pernicious opinions are spread abroad (although in a state tempered by good morals and institutions these rarely creep further), lest the republic suffer any harm, one must undoubtedly take precautions with milder remedies, or, where necessary, even with harsh ones.
But what is true, what you think, what you are convinced of, cannot be commanded.

Therefore, by prescribing fixed doctrines, you will accomplish nothing, except that both teachers and learners are dulled, indeed become stupid and foolish, or pretend one thing while keeping another hidden in their hearts.
Or should we think that letters, which are constrained by boundaries drawn at will, can grow more than a tree, which has been deprived of light and surrounded by a wall?
Those bonds, indeed, which were once most strongly imposed upon literature, were woven chiefly by superstition, lest, with the darkness dispelled, minds should be set free.

Indeed, the governors of states, the wiser they are, the more they desire that the light of literature be spread abroad, because the more intelligent their subjects become, the more their industry, agility, and even their modesty and entire virtue are strengthened.
Thus the state flourishes, and in the midst of the citizens' happiness the house of the rulers is firmly established.

On the other hand, just as the unskilled common people, so also the peoples held in the servitude of their minds, rush headlong by a chance impulse into new things and into any crimes whatsoever that must be dared.
Sometimes even the states themselves perish together with their literature, wasting away with a long decay.
For although by the hidden counsel of fate established by divine will, at different times different nations are increased or diminished, nevertheless the nations themselves hasten their fates.
And the neglect of literature, which had previously flourished, seems to be a sign of a decrepit state and, as it were, a foreboding of impending ruin.
And indeed that (neglect) has not been brought about in all places or times by the fault of the state;

on the contrary, the idleness and indolence of private individuals can bring greater harm to literature than the wicked laws and decrees of states, especially when corruption of morals and an insane desire for gain, together with illiberality, grows strong.

For indeed in the Greek states especially, in which literature and the arts reached that flower which up to this very day has nowhere yet been restored, learning was born and took its growth not from public institution, but from the innate character of the race and the common pursuits of private individuals;
so that if you should make a conjecture from the Greeks, you would judge public aid to be not at all necessary for literature:
Indeed, by the time money began to be spent by the states on literature, literature had already long been in decline.
Therefore, those whose virtue and talent nourished the disciplines, by their negligence can hasten the destruction of those disciplines.
Nevertheless, for the good arts, it matters very much what the condition of the republic is.

For not to mention how much the savage tyranny of tyrants impedes the investigation of human and divine affairs, how much it disturbs and breaks the mind with anxiety, which was proved at Rome by the rule of the most atrocious men and those hostile to the whole human race;

Therefore, to omit this, is there not a great importance in the cultivation of the arts, in what may be expected or demanded from those who are to handle public affairs, who are to administer the laws, who are to manage sacred rites?

Would the eloquence of Pericles or Demosthenes have stood out in Greece, if the Athenian assembly had tolerated a rough and unpolished speech, and if access to public affairs had been open equally to uncultivated men as to the most elegant and learned?
Would Marcus...
Tullius Cicero, C.

Would Iulius Caesar and Octavianus Augustus have been about to acquire that abundance of varied learning, if the wisest of their contemporaries had judged that anyone could be distinguished in public life who had scarcely been imbued with literature?
What of the fact that the ancient Greeks and Romans excelled especially in those disciplines which seemed to make men most fit for conducting public affairs?
Therefore among them no part of the more liberal education was more cultivated than oratory, in which we are especially deficient, because all things were governed by the power of speaking:

And although we may concede that the Greeks were born for the fashioning of oratory, nevertheless, unless that form of state had come to them which favored the more vigorous exercise of this faculty, they would not have made much progress, as Sparta shows, which never produced any orator.
Nor indeed did philosophy seem alien to the Greeks from the management of public affairs;
for which reason philosophy was the more celebrated among them:
whose place at Rome the skill of law in a certain way occupied.

Since these things were so, we do not wonder that very many who excelled in learning among the ancients were not born in a humble station, nor were they versed in the shadow of schools, but each in his own city was either powerful or illustrious.

Just as among the Romans themselves, although they are not to be compared with the Greeks, if you except some poets especially and rhetoricians and grammarians who were freedmen or plebeians, almost all the best authors were knights, senators, praetorians, and consulars.
And although it may rightly be judged unfair that the path to literature is closed to elevated minds, which lurk in the rustic plebs itself and among the pupils of the shopkeepers,

Nevertheless, I am not sure whether in ancient literature this had great force, that men distinguished by nobility of birth, wealth, and honors were eager to become famous for their learning, which they had retained from a good education, and did not leave it to insignificant men of low condition or to those oppressed by hunger.
Therefore it cannot happen but that they become cheap.
And we see that in our age and in our republic the pursuits of leading men are being revived.

But in the different disposition of our people, who are less inclined to the liberal arts, and in that rust which the greater part of the nobility, no less than the common people, seem to have retained from their former barbarism, since, unless the state had founded and maintained public games of every kind of literature, literature would soon have been about to fall.
This excellent burden of nurturing the good arts had to be undertaken by the state, and it was undertaken.

That she will bear very well, if she will provide not only buildings and equipment for literature, and a living for those who teach, but also will grant to literature its just freedom, so that it can thrive, and indeed she will restrain wantonness, immodesty, and fierceness, but she will allow to think what you wish, and to say what you feel, and moreover she will praise the open profession of one's opinion:

Finally, if he will demand a more distinguished literary skill and a strong and vigorous knowledge from those who have wished to approach the state and to perform its duties, he will indeed reject those mercenaries, who seek nothing from literature except a slight practice, which would scarcely suffice for their duties, and this very practice for the sake of bread.
But if this does not happen, both public and literary affairs will rush to ruin, and in vain will effort be made to prolong a life that is no longer vital to a dead body.

Thus, however many schools were founded by the Roman emperors as the empire was declining, however many salaries were paid to rhetoricians, grammarians, philosophers, physicians, and professors of law, partly much more ample than in our century, however many prerogatives and honors were conferred—

Those benefits could not hold back the impending ruin, because, with spirits broken by servitude and vigor lost, literature had become numb, and those who devoted themselves to it, for the most part, sought not refined and liberal learning but handsome incomes from public offices.
But what did the discipline prescribed through the seven arts profit in the Middle Ages?
With what rudiments did the sad and severe discipline of the monasteries nourish the mind?
Of course, the less exact learning could be imposed on the clergy in barbarous kingdoms, the more it happened that they did not even attain to that which had been commanded.

So that we should be proclaimed blessed, because that age did not destroy all the best monuments of a more refined life, but certainly handed them down to posterity, in which those who, having broken their bonds, dared to think for themselves might grow warm.
But I turn myself away from the contemplation of these things, which perhaps has led me a little too far;
Let us consider the plans of our most dear king.
For the Prussian state has for a long time enjoyed the praise of vigorous science and of understanding diffused through all parts of the commonwealth;
to this, not to its bulk, its force is to be attributed.
This most excellent reputation, as long as we obey these kings, does not seem to be feared lest it perish.
Indeed, whatever has been changed in the form of our affairs in these recent years, it was not done with the intention of detracting anything from literature.
Nor has anything been taken away.
Why should we not also in the future be confident, with the King attempting nothing immoderate, and proven by the most brilliant examples of clemency?
This confidence is increased by the affection with which the whole people embraces him, as Germans are devoted with their whole soul to their princes:
For he feels secure and beloved, no less than a father of a family among good children, and he understands that his own safety and that of the people are the same.
The same man is stern, energetic, modest, averse to luxury and pleasures:
but he tempers private and public frugality with that generosity which is fitting.
But although munificence is also seen in giving and in rewarding merits, yet that which spends its wealth on the liberal arts and letters is far more excellent and useful.
From this, lasting honors are prepared for the state.
How much Frederick William excelled in both, both in arts and in letters, I have proclaimed not only on many other occasions but especially in a certain Periclean oration.
Now let it be permitted to add this one thing, that the education of youth and the literary enterprise did not seem to the King to be that part of the state in which one should spare expenses.
That time is evidence, when this kingdom was fined more than half of its borders, evidence is this very literary university, which was then founded.
And afterwards nothing was relaxed, but we have experienced the King's perpetual kindness.

Finally, how much the public care for this entire class of things has grown can be understood even from this, that it seemed to be separated from the other affairs of the internal state and worthy of a special administration, entrusted to the best and most experienced men, and if one may judge from the distribution of the supreme government, it claimed for itself the same importance that is held for all revenues and taxes and military and foreign affairs.
Therefore, we see that, concerning what I have discussed above, even from those who seek public offices, no ordinary learning is demanded.

Nor do letters alone flourish, but also, whatever disturbances the ruinous clubs have produced, academic morals have been eminently corrected, and the former savagery has certainly been so driven out among us that it seems scarcely likely to return.

Since the course of my speech has turned aside to this point, I must warn you in a word, fellow soldiers, that you should persevere in this moderation, in this liberal obedience, and that you should never forget that, although this is proper for the citizens of all universities, yet to you it ought to seem a more sacred duty, who live not only in the royal city, but in the immediate neighborhood of the royal house, nay, in the very eyes and sight of the King.
Nor is it only that Frederick William is a witness to your character, that he ought to serve you as an incentive to virtue;
but this also, both yours and ours, inflames the love of the best Prince, that we enjoy his very sight.
For whereas princes are commonly said to appear greater to those who behold them from afar, that is true indeed in the case of those judges who wrap their head in the splendor of majesty:
The splendor that strikes unaccustomed eyes more violently, by daily familiarity ceases to be venerable.

But Frederick William, a popular king, since he possesses those virtues which, the closer you approach, the more distinguished they appear, I understand that he is indeed equally dear to all citizens, but I declare that he is so loved by those who are nearest to him that at the same time they deeply feel and most exactly know why they love him.
You therefore, listeners, both feel and know this best, and indeed with my mouth but with your minds you pray for the help of the highest deity for the Father of the Fatherland.
May the propitious God assent to our prayers, and may he add many glorious and prosperous years, both to himself and to the republic, to his pious worshiper.

div.head: XIII. Oratio nataliciis Friderici Guilelmi III. celebrandis d. III. m. Aug. a. MDCCCXXV. habita.
On the University of Berlin, founded with a new plan, enlarged, and adorned by Frederick William III in the chief city of the kingdom

p.s: Since this is the fifteenth year, listeners, since this literary university of our most beloved King, whose birthday we today piously celebrate, was founded by his wise counsels, and the ninth year since it was dedicated by his command with solemn rite;

Although during this period of time, for almost an entire year, the pursuits of the arts have been relaxed because of the turmoil of war, and with arms laid aside our school has been, as it were, begun anew, nevertheless this school, not indeed by our own merits but by the kindnesses of our excellent Prince, has in a short time grown to such a degree of splendor and attendance that, not to say anything too boastful, it yields to no academy of Germany and surpasses very many by far.

For what we proclaim with grateful mind and posterity will remember and recall, the flower of literature and the education of every kind, by which the people might be made more civilized, no one of our ancestors nor of contemporary princes fostered more lavishly than Frederick William.

Nor is it surprising that in this matter he himself accomplished something greater than the most glorious kings who formerly ruled Prussia, greater than Frederick I, truly the splendid founder of the University of Halle, greater than that great Frederick, the eternal star of the Prussians;
and not only greater, but also different in many respects from the earlier institutions.
For all other things are according to the same pattern.
Consider this state of the empire, compare the former one:

You will find not only the borders extended, but the condition of the republic so changed that, just as formerly the Great Elector and soon Frederick the Second were the pillars of the kingdom, so Frederick William seems in a certain way to have restored it.
We owe to him so many excellent institutions, he adorned the city with so many ornaments, he heaped so many benefits upon the people.
Indeed, a few decades ago we saw our fatherland struck and prostrated by a great calamity.
Then the envious exulted;
They mourned, who had learned to appreciate the virtues of this kingdom;
They endured and hoped with their Prince, the best and bravest:

And soon, by the auspicious counsels of Frederick William, the vital force of the empire, which to some already seemed to be languishing, already seemed to be dying out, was restored and overflowed, and, permeating the whole body of the state with most joyful vigor, what fruits of healthful benefit did it not produce?
I am not the one who could precisely point out, by weighing each and every part of the state, how they were gradually changed for the better under King Frederick William.
This cannot be done without the greatest experience of affairs.
What lies in everyone's sight, I mention briefly.
For there is a different arrangement of affairs among the King's highest ministers than there was formerly.
Another division of the provinces and form of government, both sacred and profane;
a different constitution of urban affairs, and most pleasing to the citizens;
the crafts freed from the bonds of the guilds;
the condition of the rural multitude, freed from servile burdens, was alleviated;
the land itself, by division, more cultivated and more fertile;
the system of military service, revenues, taxes, and commerce was changed.
The army, once not cowardly, indeed ennobled by immortal victories;

But a large part was gathered from mercenaries, who guarded no more than they were guarded, or was enrolled from country folk and commoners, who, after being kept for many years at the standards, returned to their own people corrupted and scarcely fit for civil affairs, or grew old in military service;
The wealthier and more educated youth was free from military service and unwarlike:
Hence the soldier was more unskilled and had to be restrained by severe punishments, and was more estranged from the citizens:
Finally, in place of the right of military service, which was considered honorable among the ancients, there is the most burdensome servitude.

Now all are trained in the exercise of arms, but in this city, which nevertheless is accustomed to be called military, they are discharged earlier than in any other, and are returned to their households, fields, trades, and good arts;
Indeed, what especially concerns us, while they serve, they devote themselves to literature in the universities.
How few in the previous generation were there who thought that things which seemed impossible to unite could be joined together?
Hence the cohorts are full of young men liberally educated, whom gentle discipline, if indeed there is need, corrects and composes to modesty;
the soldiers themselves, with pride removed, are most honorable and most temperate:
and the number of soldiers is smaller, but the number of warriors is greater.
Nor is a certain order placed before the rest more in military service than in a peaceful state;
The path to the higher ranks is open, and to every merit its due honors.
Taxes and tributes, if not reduced, at least more fairly distributed and more conveniently arranged:

No longer is internal commerce hindered by any obstacles, whereas formerly individual cities were so fenced and closed that whoever set out from one to another seemed to himself to have reached the borders of another kingdom, and all were daily subject to tax collectors:

Now, with guards removed, cities are open day and night, and the gates of many towns have been demolished so that they cannot be closed, and trade, which was previously very slow, is being accelerated by the paving of roads and other useful institutions.

Nor indeed did the King order these and other things that differ from the previous form out of a desire for novelty, for he, as a ruler of the state ought, especially favors preserving the ancient custom where it is good and useful;
But he understands that a new age must be tempered by new laws and institutions;
that the republic, like all mortal things, being changeable, ought to advance, lest it fail;
and lest it languish through sloth, fresh and vigorous juices must be poured in.
But is it not the case that, although I have selected very few out of very many, these alone are such great benefits as only the best princes could confer upon their peoples over many years of rule?

But if those great upheavals that convulsed the world brought no slight distress, from which the states still suffer; if the changed condition of very many things has entangled one or another class of citizens in various difficulties; if the very fertility and kindness of the soil afflicts the farmers:

let us consider that not even the times of the most praised emperors, not even the age of the Antonines, were free from miseries, and that the calamities themselves are relieved munificently by a most merciful King.

Therefore, chance misfortunes or unavoidable ones, and if anything else of good things seems to be lacking to one or another, will not deter us from proclaiming the fortunate reign of Frederick William, who provides for the state gloriously restored and wisely administered, at home justice, equity, concord, and from foreigners security.

Of this happiness, not the least part is also this, that public and private morals seem to have been corrected, partly because the contemplation of the saddest events has filled the minds of mortals with the religion of the divine deity, and with the more widely disseminated understanding of truth, men are also rendered more upright, partly because the life of the rest is accustomed to be regulated according to the example of the king.

For Frederick William combines with royal arts the virtues of a private citizen, an excellent father of a family, moderate in food and dress, and averse to the delights of the court, finally temperate in all his life and so modest that after so many victories he does not even allow a laurel to be inserted in his hair.
But to the state, what is dearer than good morals?
Take away these:
so that although it abounds in resources, in arms and men, it will fall with a ruin all the more disastrous, the greater its appearance had been.
But I return to the point from which I began my speech.
For just as in other matters we see Frederick William entering upon a new path, so in founding the seats of learning he followed new plans.
For not only has the whole care of public instruction been greatly directed to this end, and the lower schools of every kind been excellently supported, partly even established for the first time;
Not only have the slender revenues of most old universities, as is often the case, been wonderfully increased, but also new ones have been founded, and old ones completely restored.
Nor can the equipment that these had in ancient times be compared in any way with that furniture with which Frederick William equipped them all.
Finally, what I said about the face of nearly all things being changed under this king, that is seen most of all in the universities.
This city is a witness, the seat of the court, of the empire, the camp of many thousands of soldiers;
Although this city was already distinguished by arts and letters before, yet Frederick William adorned it with a new kind of beauty of the same.
Even before Frederick the Great, Berlin had flourished with the praise of learning and arts, and had possessed Leibniz himself and the royal society of science:
And that king, although he was devoted to foreign literature, nevertheless encouraged the studies of the natives:
And there were at that time in this city most refined intellects, whose memory will not perish.
Afterward, even the more sublime philosophy took root here, and Fichte, who was soon given to the university, taught the city dwellers beyond others.
Mixed were the gatherings of men and freeborn women, whom those most learned men used to teach:

Scarcely anyone could conceive in his mind that a rather unrestrained crowd of young men, who are being educated in the universities, could be carried along, flowing together from all sides, into the royal city and into the royal house.
Indeed, the primary cradles of the universities were the cities, Paris of the Parisians and, closer to us, Prague.

But afterwards, with a change in the manner of life, the universities that were established in large cities were generally less famous, if you except the Königsberg one, which for some time was illuminated by the lights of Kant and others.
Therefore it was a new thing that Frederick William resolved to found a literary university in this city.
This matter, although it seemed doubtful at first, the outcome approved.

For although the most beloved King fosters all schools of the arts with equal kindness, nevertheless it would be surprising if the one that is nearest to him were not so regarded as to seem especially worthy of the city, the capital of the nation.
Hence it happens that it is exceptionally augmented in all respects.
Then the city contains most precious equipment of every kind, partly collected by earlier kings, partly procured by Frederick William, by which our studies are eminently aided.
The King opened his royal library to the doctors and students of the university.
Although it is not perfect, it is nevertheless so rich that, apart from Göttingen, no university in Germany is furnished with so great a treasure.
And since the university was founded, it has been increased at great expense every year, better furnished, and adapted to common use.

Indeed, whatever nature produces, whatever mountains hide in darkness, whatever herbs, shrubs, and trees even the most remote regions of the earth nourish, whatever living creatures walk on the ground, crawl, fly, or swim—museums and well-arranged gardens contain all this, set before the eyes with admirable abundance and beauty.
The inner structure even of the human and animal body, the norms and monstrosities of nature, lie open to the observer.
I would not bring these things forward if they were commonplace;
But they are so constituted that they are an ornament not only to the university, but also to the city and the kingdom.
What shall I say of the many and ample medical institutions?
Nor are there lacking seminaries for training theologians and philologists.

Now that is excellent, that although very many universities excel indeed in letters, yet the students can contemplate there either few or no works of the arts, especially of sculpture and painting, while this city also abounds in these.
We already have museums that are not to be despised, but the best things lie hidden.

But the king's magnificent buildings, which are now rising at great expense, are of a kind not attempted by his predecessors; and when they are completed after a few years, the statues, paintings (of which there is a great number and value), engraved gems long celebrated in fame, coins, and other monuments, now scattered through many palaces and houses, will be so arranged that a new splendor will accrue to this city from them, and the minds will be educated by the daily sight of the most beautiful images along with the eyes.

What of the fact that our own artists have given splendid examples of the revived art, by which the buildings and streets of the city are adorned, certainly unlike the vulgar and monstrous fictions of earlier centuries?
Thus young people, looking at more perfect works, become accustomed to nobler feelings, which, in my judgment, magnificent statues form no less than admonitions.
Moreover, the very magnitude of the city and the seriousness and variety of the affairs that are carried on in it accustom the mind to a greater measure;

Hence it comes about that academic teachers are called away from lawsuits and quarrels, which they would otherwise engage in with mutual envy, and students are called away from that arrogance by which, while they are carried away by empty disputes, they seem to themselves to be the first of all men.
Finally, these men, instead of that sordid and fierce dress and manner, put on an elegance of manners without silliness, and draw in a certain silent color of urbanity.
Therefore the academic manners in our state have been eminently corrected;
Hence there were very few censures and marks of blame, and hardly any except against those who had come here already corrupted.
And let no one think that young men attracted by the allurements of a great city devote less effort to their studies:
Even small towns have their own delights and an abundance of wantonness;
and one may enjoy innocent pleasures in the city itself with less expense and loss of leisure than when, as is customary, neighboring cities are sought for their sake:
Finally, in a larger city, academic citizens, the more safely they hide, the less they are subject to the insolent power of associations, which lay snares most pernicious to the severity of studies.

Nor, if suitable discipline fills young minds with the ardor of learning, is it to be feared that the sight of other things, whatever the city's bustle brings, may call them away from the pursuit of literature.

Finally, you yourselves, dearest comrades, if we except very few out of so great a number, have up to this point shown such eagerness for study, that by this success also the judgment of the most wise King has been approved:
And that you will use the same diligence hereafter, former examples promise.

But if nature has granted to this place less fertility of soil, and not the pleasantness of valleys, let us console ourselves with the saying of Socrates, who thought that a man is taught by a man, not by trees:
The soil of Athens itself was barren and rocky;
but necessity itself, the mother of the arts, spurred on their talents:
and our city has been endowed with so many internal goods that external ones are less missed.

Therefore let us celebrate this institution of Frederick William, who founded this school of ours in his own seat, especially suitable for nurturing literature, and equipped it with all the endowments that can increase the flower of learning.

Indeed, since the same has also been granted by the most gracious King to the other universities of this kingdom, and all of them have been adorned both with the most distinguished teachers summoned from everywhere and with whatever resources, ...
so that provision may be made for the renown of these, there is no need to forbid citizens the use of foreign ones:

And this very thing Frederick William established newly and liberally, that whereas formerly our countrymen had to devote themselves to letters in our universities, now all schools of Germany are open indiscriminately to them, unless something particular seems to stand in the way, and each one can choose for himself that one which seems most suitable to him either according to the nature of his studies or of his domestic affairs.

This law is so firm that not even the corporations of those states are excluded, whose citizens are not allowed to approach our [universities], and so that, if any school has been excepted for a particular reason, as soon as the reason has ceased, the exception ceases:
This has been demonstrated in this very year by the restoration of the freedom to approach the University of Jena.
Surely, if someone has freed the commerce of goods from the bonds by which it was constrained, why should he circumscribe the commerce of minds with narrower limits?
Nor does Frederick William wish that the wills of private individuals be so constrained by laws that whatever they undertake, the law should be an obstacle.

But he thinks that these are the duties of the laws: that they restrain the wicked, protect the good, and, as far as can be done without harm to the state, provide to each person as much freedom as possible to manage his own affairs securely, freely, and according to his own judgment.

But to return to our own affairs, although they have long been brought to such a degree of perfection that if nothing new were added, but the most excellent minister of the king and his most prudent counselors, who govern public education with zealous care, were to maintain the former state, the wishes and desires would have been satisfied:

Nevertheless, every year not a few good things are added, which, if our piety can be increased, may bind our hearts more and more entirely to the most clement King, and may testify to the benevolence of the prefects, in whom we have trusted with the greatest confidence.
Many things indeed this year have been established usefully and splendidly;
which I would recount, were they not to be reserved for the speech of the highest magistrate in laying down his office:
Nevertheless, this very day demands that I speak about one example of royal munificence and of the generous care of the prefects.
I mean the prizes which today are for the first time publicly awarded to the academic citizens, and hereafter, as often as these most auspicious solemnities return, will be awarded.

You might say that one who burns with genuine love of literature neither needs the spur of industry nor is led by ambition or gain, but is held by the excellence of the material in which he is engaged, and with some divine impulse, without any additional goads, runs to the goal;
The rest, even if enticed by rewards, will not do the work worth the effort.
Although I think this must by no means be denied, yet it is certain that by emulation literature and the arts reach the highest point:
This is contained in the fact that we strive to attain, not so much to satisfy any desire for glory or anything else, but rather what seems best to the best men.

Therefore among the Greeks from the most ancient times, prizes were set for running, wrestling, boxing, and other bodily exercises, in which they thought virtue resided, partly monetary, partly crowns, of which the greater authority, because besides honor they had no utility:
And in like manner poets of every kind, especially lyric, dithyrambic, and scenic poets, as well as musical artists and even the actors themselves, contended with one another for the palm.
And at Corinth and Delphi a contest in painting was also established.
But in the more recent age, literary contests especially began to be held, and these of various kinds.
There is a certain kind of literary contest, a little more remote from the young men who are engaged in the discipline of universities:

This is what learned societies, or academies, strive to achieve: that the studies and efforts of scholars be directed toward the most difficult questions, for the successful treatment of which either the most ample abundance of knowledge or the greatest power of intellect and a judgment refined by long practice must be brought to bear.

When the arguments for these are selected in such a way that what is most suitable for the present needs of each discipline is presented, if competent authors work on them, it cannot happen but that no small benefit accrues to literature from them.
There is another kind of commissions, which has long been accepted in our university:
Since this is rather slight and not to be compared with the former, I would not mention it, unless we had also experienced its usefulness.
For since almost every year a certain sum of money was handed over to the Senate, by which the neediness of honorable and industrious young men might be relieved;
From it, several orders of the university paid out rewards to those who had presented suitable proofs of their skill.
From this it is understood that these rewards were indeed awarded to the worthy, but not for the sake of honor, but for relieving need.

Since these things are so, these honorary prizes are different and new among us, to be distributed from the gift of the most merciful King to those citizens who have come out superior in the literary contests of the university.

But since the Prorector of this school has explained the reason for these commissions in the transfer of the fasces, I will not say how they are now instituted, but why they were not instituted before, after they were propagated from the University of Göttingen to others.

For as far as I remember having once learned, at the time when this seat of learning was founded by Frederick William, since he wished it to be adorned with every kind of ornament, this institution was therefore omitted, because the strength of young men, not yet confirmed, does not seem sufficient for explaining somewhat more abstruse questions:
whence you may fear, lest by rewards you entice out pamphlets of little use, of which in this age, most fertile in books, the supply is not cheap.
It may be added that the desire of attaining praise can invite one or another to the treatment of a subject, from which if he abstained, he would better consult his own studies:
Another may be puffed up by success itself with the pride of learning, than which nothing is more pernicious to him.
But these disadvantages are easily overcome by advantages:
nor should good things be let go, because he who will not use them rightly will incur loss.

For although from young men one would hardly expect a complete exposition of learned questions, nevertheless they must be encouraged in every way, so that they may make trial of what they themselves can do and learn by the judgment of those more experienced:
nor would you say how much anyone is worth, unless you have tested him:
and it is well known that the first attempts of talented young men, full of vigor, are not seldom superior to a late and aged offspring.
Finally, talents must be known, and those that are outstanding must be brought forth into the light:
which is accomplished best by this institution.
But with a certain moderation applied, suitable material for youthful industry and diligence must be chosen, in which one who has spent several years in academic studies may engage with profit.

Therefore it seems to me especially relevant that, since this age is intermediate between those who are being shaped by the discipline of the gymnasia and those who are approaching the conduct of affairs, we should refrain from arguments of such a kind that they demand not only an abundance of learning but also that experience of affairs which is proper to men of action.

For indeed, when the young men in the gymnasia are so cultivated by a certain general and elementary circle of learning that, whatever part of science they are about to embrace, they approach it prepared and imbued with the necessary preliminary knowledge:

now the schools of the universities open up the very broad fields of the individual disciplines, and they hand down the teachings of each one with a more sublime and more subtle investigation to those who have applied themselves wholly to it.
But it is not beneficial to approach practical exercise unless you have thoroughly formed your mind with knowledge over many years;

indeed, whoever approaches it before he has thoroughly grasped the doctrines through long study, he will neither excel in knowledge, nor will he conduct affairs or practice an art with not only somewhat more than ordinary skill but also experience:

And we do not see anyone except those who, with a sluggish disposition toward studies and without a more sacred impulse, but for the sake of bread, devote themselves to literature, and, having spurned more accurate knowledge, hasten to apply themselves to those things which they themselves or insufficiently qualified advisers may think are suited to the use of life.
Therefore, for the consideration of these contests, only those arguments are suitable which are derived from the very science itself:
Especially since the things that pertain to conducting business and practicing an art cannot be handled correctly except by those who have been engaged in action for a longer time.
Now indeed, since it is clear that no one can expect from the alumni of universities that skill in acting which would suffice for setting forth practical matters more distinctly:

We also understand that, in the view of those who established this literary contest for them, the highest goal that academic citizens can and should attain is seen to lie not in the ability to conduct affairs and handle business, but in the acquisition of knowledge itself.
This we rejoice at greatly.

Therefore, thanks must be given to the most merciful King, both by us, because with such a liberal plan he both enlarged and adorned this seat of the good arts, and by you, fellow soldiers, to whom he gives ample opportunity for showing your talent and gaining praise.

Never forget that Frederick William, if any prince ever did, has earned the name of Father of his Country by the most prosperous constitution of the state, and that he shows himself especially kind and courteous to the young, and omits nothing by which he may look after your interests and your welfare.
Confirm every year on this most auspicious day the covenant of loyalty owed to the best of kings.

Declared by your reverence for the laws, by the integrity of your lives, by the seriousness of your studies, may your minds respond to the plans and expectations of Frederick William, and [may you feel] what he has done and does for you;
May your hearts feel [this];
Finally, join with us in sending most holy prayers to the supreme deity, that he may protect and preserve Frederick William, who is beneficent to the state, to literature, and to the youth.

div.head: XIV. Oratio nataliciis Friderici Guilelmi III. celebrandis d. III. m. Aug. a. MDCCCXXVI. habita.
On the connection of philosophy and history with the other disciplines

p.s: On the birthday of Frederick William, when I am about to speak today, what else, listeners, should be offered first than those truly divine blessings, which the best King has brought about and brings about for us, namely public happiness, peace, and harmony?

Those blessings, I say, which, after many calamities of warlike turmoil, are now especially reviving both all Germany and Prussia, and are bringing forth the most joyful fruits of literature and arts, placed under the protection of an outstanding Prince?

This thought moves me the more strongly, the more I see that some kingdoms, which have been shaken by the same wars, cannot yet return to tranquility, because they are delayed by the immoderate and unrestrained desires of men contending among themselves.
Among us all things are tranquil and moderate:
and these things remain.
And this very moderation in our state, the highest of civil goods, is owed especially to Frederick William, whom nature itself, because of his equal M.
Cicero says that Cato, with regard to honesty, dignity, greatness of soul, justice, and finally all virtues, was a great and lofty man, and he fashioned him as such.

With this same self-control, no doubt, he governs himself, with it he equips the state, he transfers it, as far as possible, into the minds of friends, magistrates, and citizens, and spreads it throughout the whole empire like abundant streams.
It can hardly be said how much this also benefits literature.
For in a state undisturbed by any storms of passions, the mind traverses the straight and pure path of knowledge on a quiet journey.
The zeal and madness of factions disagreeing either in civil or in divine matters, which are not alien to the state, deflect the clouded minds from the truth;
They force knowledge, than which no holier gift has been bestowed on mortals by the supreme deity, to serve the plans and wills of men;
They arm the sophists with captious arts, who may protect the utilities of these very things.

Moreover, although literature both can and ought to contribute much to the conduct of life, nevertheless, whoever rashly adapts it to the present state of affairs and to the often deceptive appearance, it cannot happen but that he is entangled in the gravest errors:
Which, since it is understood in the authors of all disciplines, then especially in historians and philosophers.
For although there is a great abundance of examples, I will dwell on this one, since both parties are accustomed to dispute about the character of the age, as it is called;

they think that the character of the age is generally seen in those things to which each one has directed his mind more, and which part of present affairs has been especially presented to them, or what contentions, what plans they themselves pursue;
so that the wise poet rightly said that they sell their own nature for the nature of the age;

which seems scarcely able to be known, unless, being separated by divine influence from the contagion of the age, you have thoroughly discerned, as from on high, all things that are done, and by what causes, and with what outcome.

Indeed, how uncertain, how subject to the passions of men, especially amid great upheavals, this whole divination concerning the character of the present age is, not unlike the Etruscan art, seems to me to be better demonstrated by no example than by that of the greatest historian among the Germans, who for some time even lived in this city, and was distinguished among few for the elegance of his learning, the immense abundance of his erudition, and the candor of his mind.
