He who was at first the fiercest adversary of the French Emperor, soon reconciled to him by a courteous address, prophesied that he would bring a new and almost golden age, whose power was abolished after another five-year period, not without the common exultation of all mortals, so that scarcely any traces remain.

I recall this matter to memory, not to reproach the shade of that excellent man, but to show that even the best of scholars are deceived and led astray when they are caught up in the storms of political upheaval, and that only in a calm condition of the state can there be a sound judgment on the most important matters.
Now if history and the study of wisdom are subject to those dangers, will it not be permissible to say the same about all knowledge and every discipline?
For all these take root in philosophy and history.
These seek nourishment from those; if those are removed or neglected, these themselves perish.
Although it seems hardly appropriate to set this forth in this assembly of most distinguished and most learned men,

Nevertheless, because I understand that from this more distinguished gathering, which sits nearest to me, what is expected is not those things which might be suited to it either by their novelty or by their weight of eloquence, but rather what it is certainly useful, if not necessary, to remind fellow students of, and what can at the same time be referred to the praise of the undertakings instituted under the auspices of Frederick William, since in explaining this connection of philosophy and history with the other disciplines both advantages are present, I have decided to set forth briefly, not with dialectical subtlety, which is proper to the schools, but in an oratorical manner, and then to return to the point from which I have digressed.

Therefore I maintain that philosophy and history, together with the parts dependent on them, to which not without reason natural science, mathematics, and philology are usually added, contain the whole of human knowledge, which has its highest end placed in itself:

From it, certain branches of learning were early separated like branches and joined into specific disciplines, and they turned the historical and philosophical science to the most beneficial fruit of the human race.

And of these disciplines, indeed, one especially aids and heals the corporeal nature of men, two strive to rule the minds with the precepts of laws and justice, to correct and elevate them with the most holy religions, to unite them with the dearest bonds of the state and the church, and finally to console them with the better hope of dying.

But who would deny that these same disciplines are supported by the historical and philosophical doctrines I have mentioned, and that they themselves are developed partly by philosophizing, partly by historical inquiry?

For indeed, to begin with jurisprudence, just as all its sources, whether domestic or foreign, cannot be opened and explained except by the historical method, even up to the Romans and beyond them, so from the Greeks, the teachers and leaders of all arts, philosophy also undertook the treatment of law and of all civil affairs.
And indeed the principle of legislation itself seems to be this, that it is mixed and composed from historical and philosophical knowledge.
But what about theology?
Is there any discipline that by its very nature stands in greater need of the light of history than that one?
For the things that have been revealed divinely to the human race, we have not experienced ourselves, but we have received them handed down from remote times;
and in these things, which have been handed down, the religious mind finds rest:

except that it strives to strip away the sacred stain that they have contracted from mortal additions and especially from superstition, and to restore it to the pure and genuine form of doctrine, which cannot be done without historical knowledge, and to rub off the rust that has been acquired;
after the most holy ceremonies have been corrupted, with divine providence bringing a remedy and rousing noble men, who dare to oppose inveterate errors:

We have recognized with singular gratitude, both long ago and especially in this year, that our King, distinguished for piety, finds both Christian truth and the consolation and salvation of souls in that faith alone, to which Luther recalled Christian doctrine when he referred it to the authority of the sacred books.

Again, because divine literature has handed down the deepest and most weighty opinions about those matters which are of the greatest importance to mortals, in which even philosophy itself is engaged; nay, because the religions of almost every nation contain its primitive wisdom as it were enclosed in a seed;

Whoever dares to aspire to the innermost sanctuaries of learning, to open and unfold the seeds of the most sacred doctrines, and to unite the scattered elements into one body of discipline, will not accomplish this without the meditation of a philosopher.

What of the fact that a deeper familiarity with sacred and profane literature was both confirmed long ago by the laws for the directors of public education and very recently increased in this republic, since from that time certain parts of theological study have also been recommended to those who embrace the disciplines that serve the education of scholastic youth?

This matter will have a most favorable outcome, if the necessary balance is maintained in it, which one may safely expect in a most temperate state, and piety—which we need not fear, whether true or feigned—will not seem able to supply the lack of thorough learning, nor will those advantages be removed which, from the separation of the two pursuits, have undoubtedly flowed to the schools in this very empire.
Finally, I need not explain that the study of medicine without natural science is nothing.

And this is even proved by practice and authority, so that in many universities, and even among us, several professors of medicine, far removed from the practice of the healing art, are occupied solely in investigating nature, and very recently it was wisely established by the most excellent and most distinguished men, to whom Frederick William entrusted this part of the state, that no one should be admitted to seeking the highest honors in medicine unless he had proved his sufficient knowledge of natural things by undergoing a special examination for this purpose.

But who does not understand that this is most beautifully established by physicians and their students, that they investigate the origins of their art from the most remote age, that they do not deem worthy of their care only those things which were proposed or invented yesterday and the day before, but in the treatment of individual diseases, returning with a truly historical method through the spaces of all ages up to Hippocrates, the father of their art, they diligently repeat from there whatever is either useful or memorable?

Who does not know that these same men, both in former times and especially in our own memory, have followed the doctrines of the philosophers more zealously than any other learned group, in order that they might thoroughly understand the causes of nature and the vital forces by which the inner structure of the body is held together and set in motion?

Therefore, since it is agreed that all disciplines partly draw their material from philosophy and history, and partly use their method and reasoning in discovering, explaining, and confirming their own subjects, let it be permitted to say a few words about the study of antiquity.
From this, because in the age of the rebirth of letters nearly all branches of learning had their beginnings, rightly the first place was given to it in the education of the young:
But with the mature literatures of more recent peoples, the dignity of Greek and Roman antiquity no longer seemed to be such that the beginnings of learning had to be derived from it.

Therefore those who, captivated by their excellence, wished to retain those studies, which had been received into the schools for the reason I mentioned, when they wanted to teach why this ought to be done, after the former use and fruit of them had been abolished;
Looking around keenly, they could not find anything else than that Greek and Roman literature, and especially the languages, should be treated for the sake of what is called formal education.

I am so far from being persuaded of this, especially since I do not see that men who especially hold Greek and Latin grammar far surpass other mortals in a well-formed mind, that although it is suitable material for forming minds, I would think that ancient literature should be expelled from schools, and that the talents of boys and adolescents should be exercised, following the example of the ancients themselves, in other things that are closer to us, unless a more important reason remains for which those [ancient letters] are chosen.
Indeed, that whole line of reasoning is deceptive, and it was devised for this very reason, because it was not correctly assessed how ancient and modern literature were even now connected.
Even now a great part of history must be drawn from the monuments of antiquity;

even now there is no philosopher of somewhat greater distinction who does not consider the doctrines of the ancient philosophers worthy of examination, who does not admire the great geniuses of Pythagoras, Plato, and Aristotle:
Finally, not to mention the most accomplished poets and writers, if you except a few particular parts of natural science especially, the sources of all disciplines flow from antiquity.
Where did the Christian faith take its origin and growth?
Where has law been perfected to some extent?
What physician, unless unlearned, despises the ancient authors of the art?

Finally, what is this wisdom, by which, after we have followed in the footsteps of the ancients and acquired a moderate education, you would order the foundations to be torn down, because you are busy building a roof?

Since these things are so, we are instructed from childhood in Greek and Latin literature, because our own cannot be thoroughly learned without them, and those, as it were, by manifold offshoots, permeate our entire education and are diffused through it:

Since in this state, if anywhere, those who are at the head of public affairs understand this very well, from those who, after completing their academic studies, proceed to the conduct of business, some knowledge of ancient literature is also demanded.
Hence, as I hear, Latin examinations will be established for candidates in law in the future.
Hence for future doctors of medicine a moderate degree of scholastic learning, which is for the most part acquired through ancient literature, has been judged necessary.
From this it is provided that those who have not sufficiently neglected the letters of the schools are not admitted to academic studies unprepared.
For in general in the Prussian state, and especially under King Frederick William, public discipline is tempered by the wisest institutions and laws, by which the flower of letters is aided:
And what seems to me not to be passed over, we are devoted to a liberal education, not a shadowy one;

Nor are we so blind as to form students who are most learned in speaking Latin and Greek, but in almost all other things infants, but we have also introduced other kinds of literature into the schools, and especially we have equipped them with the study of mathematics, whose power is rightly considered not the least in exercising young minds.
So much for this.

You understand, listeners, that while I briefly run through the individual heads of that argument which I had undertaken to treat, I have in almost every one pointed my finger at those things with which our state, governed by the will of the wisest king, has been especially furnished in this very year, so that, according to the measure of my powers, with a speech indeed meager but sincere, I might connect in a certain continuous thread, as it were in a garland, the prudent decrees concerning the direction of literary studies.
Now someone might say:
But these are trivial things;
Why did you not, with the overflowing horn of plenty that is at hand, pour out the very many and greatest merits of the most kind King concerning this empire?
But I, having so often performed the praises of Frederick William from this platform, do not act as one who turns over a barren subject;
I do not think that the same things must be repeated every year:
Just now, as I did in the previous year, I am deliberately setting forth what Frederick William accomplished for the entire commonwealth.

Just now, in accordance with the opportunity of the times, having selected the more important parts for myself, I celebrate his martial valor, or the patronage of arts or letters undertaken by him, in a fuller discussion.

Finally, I am not satisfied with myself, because I have shown the great plans of Frederick William in great matters, unless I also demonstrate that he himself was provident in those things which seem smaller, and that his ministers were provident.
Although I do not know whether those things in which I have taken my stand are not insignificant.

For is this a small matter: to establish institutions, to write laws for shaping the pursuits of those from whose learning, skill, and integrity the honor of letters, the safety of the state, and the goods, bodies, and minds of all citizens will depend?

who will spread the light of knowledge not only throughout the whole state, but will hand down what they received from their predecessors to future generations, just as parents pass on the vital fire to their children?

This most sacred duty ought to be constantly kept before the eyes both of teachers and of learners, so that they never, led by profit or ambition, decide anything in literature contrary to a good conscience, and so that they do not adapt their opinions—to return to the point from which I started—to the changeable spirit of the age, to the passions of men that rage at a certain time, and finally to some passing intemperance, which is observed in the air and sky as well as in human life.
I am speaking of a great and difficult matter:
and it is not approved by all:
but it seems to me that knowledge ought to serve no one, neither to court popular favor nor princely favor nor any other, but to pursue only that which right reason prescribes.
And yet this does not always happen:

Just as philosophy, just as history—which, however, the ancient precept proclaims should not be bound to any sect—so the other disciplines, connected with them, are carried here and there by chance or external impulses.
These are followed, not rarely, by the very precepts of law and sacred matters.

But if, as an ancient writer says from the sound teachings of the Stoics, law is the highest reason, implanted in nature, which commands what must be done and forbids the contrary, and this reason is established and perfected in the human mind;
to that reason all law, both civil and public, ought to be directed:
but we see that it has been diverted from that to other things at every turn.

We have received, under the principate of Octavian Augustus, two ornaments of peace, Antistius Labeo and Ateius Capito, who followed different paths: the one favored the old liberty, the other, by wonderful obsequiousness and by bending his opinions to the nod, so crept into the favor of the masters that, in the judgment of Tacitus, though skilled in human and divine law, he disgraced an excellent public character and good domestic arts.
These things, once begun, recur in almost all ages in those republics which nourish the pursuits of factions.

If among us nothing of this sort is detected, thanks must be given to the moderation of the excellent King, which brings it about that no suitable material for factions is left in this empire, nor must the power of the principate be supported by cunning aids; and how beneficial this is, all citizens learn daily by experience.
But you perhaps wonder, listeners, that in our republic I maintain that no material for factions has been left:

For will not someone say that we have seen those young men, especially the students of universities, rush headlong into the abyss through a deadly conspiracy, almost all of whom, twenty-eight in number, the supreme court of Breslau recently condemned for attempted treason and punished with the severest penalties?
Certainly those offenses, in which, not to dwell on them, the sanctity of this day and the common joy prevent me from lingering, can never be sufficiently lamented;
But that was the impulse and madness of a few, and it was not born from a faction that had spread more widely, but was eager to bring about a faction:
And moreover those wicked contentions have been almost entirely extinguished in this empire:

Indeed, even those who govern our affairs, most excellent and most distinguished men, with their characteristic kindness, wish that it be publicly proclaimed today how grateful and pleasing this is to them, that we all, both teachers and students, abhor those mad attempts of some reckless young men, and that we are devoted with our whole heart to the laws of this state and to our excellent Prince.
These things indeed about public affairs.
But perhaps that is even greater, that greedy and ambitious men abuse divine religion to pursue their own plans.

For after minds, moved as once by prodigies and portents, so in our memory by great changes of affairs and by the enormous mass of public and private evils, understood that rest from earthly cares and a harbor into which you may safely take yourself are provided only by reverence for and piety toward the supreme deity:
There are certainly those who try whether, having cleverly used that inclination, they can bind peoples with new chains of servitude, so that a few may rule more licentiously.
But if that should succeed for them, a most pernicious superstition would be recalled, and the marrow of minds would be infected with corruption.
But from this empire, which for a long time has been fostering the freedom of minds with remarkable protection, that poison is defended;
piety grows, vices are gently opposed:
The best king is an outstanding example of piety, but devoted to no superstition, and finally, in these matters too, which are by far the greatest, as in all others, he is the firmest pillar.
I will not delay you longer, listeners, and the announcement of the literary commission urges me, which compels me to be briefer than I usually am and wish to be:
Therefore I will embrace in few words what remains.

Indeed, wherever I turn (and in the course of years I have traversed in thought almost all parts of the state, occupied with the praise of the best King), wherever, I say, I look around, although nothing human is perfect, nevertheless our state, composed by Frederick William as its guide for tranquility and concord, seems to me to seek solely what is right and good, and to wish to attain it not by a turbulent path nor by a disorderly struggle, but by a slow and quiet progress, which is very far from sluggishness and lethargy.

How we have already attained the good things, when all citizens joyfully acknowledge it, bound together with us in one spirit and most ardent vows to the most beloved Prince, I demonstrated last year on this very day.
This will ripen in the future time and will increase with new growths.
And these things are owed and will be owed first to God, the supreme arbiter of empires, then to Frederick William, whom may the grace of God protect.
I have spoken.

div.head: XV. Oratio nataliciis Friderici Guilelmi III. celebrandis d. III. m. Aug. a. MDCCCXXVII. habita.
On royal virtue.

p.s: Since this duty, both most splendid and most weighty, has been conferred upon me, that I should speak annually in these solemn assemblies before you, hearers,

I have understood that nothing is more to be avoided by me than the noise of empty proclamation and the disgrace of flattery, which that kind of speech would be alien not only from your and my character, but would not suit the virtues of Frederick William:
For flattery applied to a prince is, as it were, a reproach of him:
Indeed, I have even been accustomed to give a concise just praise, since it was too arduous and demanded such an abundance of eloquence and such maturity of judgment as I did not trust to be in me.

Nor, approaching directly at once in a straight course to praise the King, did I treat this or that argument a little more fully, from which I then strove to draw out those things which you desired and which were suited to this day.

But the more often I speak before you, the more confident I become, partly because I judge that you know me well enough, and partly because I know your indulgence, which will grant me pardon if anything falls from me rather imprudently:
And so I now almost dare to pursue the praise of Frederick William with no other argument mixed in from outside, deliberately:

The longer I have been engaged in this matter, the more ardently I have desired, repeatedly reflecting and looking more deeply into the excellent mind of Frederick William, that the best things, the more they are observed and examined, delight and move us all the more, while those things that shine only with a showy brilliance become cheap when considered more frequently.

And I seem to see, although you were always most willingly going to hear me discoursing about the best King alone, nevertheless that you would bear with the greatest difficulty that I should turn aside elsewhere especially in this year.

There is no one, not only in this empire, but also among foreigners, whom the health of Frederick William, impaired by an unfortunate accident, has not made anxious, for whom it has not been a grief that a man, previously tested by great public and great private calamities, as gold by fire, now nearer to old age, should be beset by this additional misfortune, if anything is fortuitous:
What vows were undertaken for his safety, and with what joy did his restoration affect everyone!
Why say more?
The King himself testified by a public edict how greatly the zeal of the people and of all the provinces had pleased him;
Not a few cities have testified, not by a pretense of affection but by heartfelt emotion, by proclaiming festal days on account of the health of their most beloved Prince.
In declaring these sentiments, although perhaps we are the most recent, yet you do not wish us to be the last:
Wherefore today I think we must not depart from the person of Frederick William.
But if you should ask why Frederick William is so intensely loved by all, I do not find the cause in his private virtues, which he possesses in abundance:
for they do not love him as a private person, but as a prince;

Although even domestic customs are observed both by those nearby and by those farther away through reputation, so that generally the people do not only look at those things which the rulers of states publicly say and do, but they also scrutinize private life and habits, friendships, marriages, dwellings, dinners, and amusements along with serious matters:

Nor is it because he is king by birth that this wins such great favor for Frederick William, although princes born to the throne, since they are wont to be more gentle and are held by a lesser necessity of harming their own people, and since a bond of mutual concord has been handed down from their ancestors, are generally dearer to their citizens;
Yet it is not for that reason alone that he is beloved by his people;
For even those, over whom he has recently gained power, love him:
Finally, this does not even seem to me to be the true reason, that we are happy under this king;
For even those less blessed love him equally, and the people's zeal was not at last provoked by favorable circumstances, but was extraordinarily increased by the very adversities.
Therefore, to comprehend everything in three words, Frederick William is most dear to all, because they either feel or understand that all royal virtue resides in him.
I have said something great, listeners, and perhaps more than my own judgment can approve.
For why?
Am I the one who can discern, weigh, and examine royal virtue?
What of the fact that no one but a king can know it thoroughly?
We shall not, I think, tolerate an unlearned man who judges about learned men:
Will it be permitted for anyone to judge kings, even one who has not approached public affairs?

Indeed, I could defend myself against these words of Niccolò Machiavelli, who in the dedication of his Prince, a most ingenious book, written to Lorenzo de' Medici, contends that just as those who are about to map out regions are accustomed to stand on some plain in order to consider the nature of mountains and elevated places, but in order to recognize low and depressed places they are placed on mountains, so, in order that you may better perceive the character of peoples, you ought to be a prince, and in order that you may understand the reasoning of princes, you ought to be a popular man.

But to that excuse of his, which is more ambitious than befits my mediocrity, this somewhat more modest one seems preferable: that I shall not explain, by a profound discussion worthy of a man experienced in public affairs (from which I am rightly absent), what sort of prince one ought to be, but rather in a popular manner, as one who has now decided to set forth why the people are so greatly bound to the best King.
Finally, to speak of the King, since I am bound, I may speak of him even as an inexperienced person, as if I were not inexperienced.

Indeed, intending to define royal virtue, I will not recite to you a list of all the gifts of talent, which, as they ought to be in other good men, so they ought to be in princes, but I say that it is contained in a twofold character of mind: vigorous courage and gentle wisdom, which, even if they can seem contrary to each other, nevertheless in a good man entirely conspire.

And indeed courage is needed, so that a ruler may defend his empire against any enemy, both foreign and internal, not only by the strength of arms, but also by the boldness of plans to be undertaken promptly and at the right time; when these are delayed by fear or by the avoidance of danger, the neglected opportunity often cannot be restored even by the strongest armies:

Then, besides war, in peaceful matters themselves a brave and steadfast spirit is required, so that in difficult affairs that demand keen mental concentration you may persevere diligently, and grow hard against everything by which you could be broken.

If such is the king, and if in addition the other good qualities come to him, about which I shall speak immediately, the people will safely entrust themselves and all their fortunes to him, because they know that he will not neglect anything through softness or weariness of occupations, but will do everything most vigorously.

And the citizens will admire him all the more, the more prone to pleasures kingdoms are, the more difficult it is to maintain perpetually in the abundance of all things the severity necessary for a prince.
He can scarcely avoid the rocks to which the sweetest Sirens lure him, unless he is a man endowed with the best nature and educated and formed with care.
Whoever has stuck fast in these, although he may be received with courtesy, yet soon idleness and sloth will bring him into contempt.
But the duty of a prince is not fulfilled by courage alone;

And easily, unless, as the harmonic theorists temper grave sounds with acute ones and harsh with sweet, the spirited impulse of the breast is tempered with a gentler virtue, it rushes more fiercely into the slaughter of nations, especially when princes have devoted themselves to soldiery alone, to whom that precept of the Etruscan teacher has been too often chanted, that a ruler should have nothing else before his eyes, should practice no other art than the warlike, which alone is princely, and finally should care for nothing else than military discipline and military institutions.

This is so far from being true that he who regards only the army as his concern seems hardly half a prince, and does not understand that the army is maintained and kept for the sake of the state, not the state for the sake of the army.
Not to mention that the authors of that opinion established a tyrant rather than a prince, or, what is even more harmful, confused the one with the other.
But indeed, that tempering which I mentioned is provided to the royal mind by wisdom, which drives away any fierceness, and especially moderates the reins of civil government.
just as we have learned that the most celebrated and most beneficent founders and legislators of their states, of whom it will suffice to have named Solon, were distinguished by the praise of wisdom:
But that, as I think, comprehends almost all the rest, which must be added to courage.
I do not speak of the bookish wisdom of schools and sects, which no one will deny a king can do without with impunity:
Indeed, that an abundance of learning does not shape good princes, Tiberius demonstrated by his own example, along with other most learned Roman emperors;
and the excessive learning of Hadrian, in other respects an excellent prince, although it was useful to many, harmed both himself and not a few others:
as M.

Antoninus, even if Fridericus Magnus had been less of a philosopher, less adorned with the glory of literature, they would not have been destined to rule worse, given the excellent arts implanted in their nature.
Indeed, the beginning and sum of wisdom is the consciousness of the divine power, which holds the world together by reason and governs it by providence;
just as that very Antoninus writes that God is a mind permeating all things and ruling the universe throughout all time according to the ordered cycles of the ages:
He whose mind is filled with that wisdom will religiously examine whatever he is about to do.

He will be pious without superstition, and will strive to direct his actions according to the divine model, since that evil, which in princes is by far the most deadly, has not infrequently raged with madness against peoples, or at least cast unworthy chains upon their minds.

He will not wish to be regarded by the citizens as a minister of God, so that greater authority and servile reverence may accrue to him, but he will be held in his own estimation, who has been set over free men to care for the salvation of men.

Nor does a king necessarily have to be equipped with that prudence in all parts of administering the state which we demand from those who handle each individual part, but just as the orators who once governed the people by the power of their intellect and eloquence were not greatly skilled in law or warfare or the management of revenues and taxes, yet they steered the state not without great cleverness, so the royal art governs the whole community to the extent that it appoints individual administrators for individual matters, whom it uses as instruments, while it itself embraces the sum of all the matters which they have prepared, judges what the overseers of the individual parts have supplied, decides the most important things, and orders and entrusts what must be done.

Thus, to use a very recent example, it is fitting even for a prince to have some knowledge of letters and to value them highly, and he himself ought in some measure to direct the literary institutions of the state, and to understand what their force and character are and how they may best be organized; yet he should not, as Dionysius the tyrant of Sicily strove with poets, Nero with singers, the Emperor Hadrian, Henry VIII and James I kings of England with the learned, with immoderate zeal, aspire to the praise of learning, so that of course in this kind too he may be regarded as a prince.

Finally, not the least part of royal wisdom is self-control, by which the prince himself imposes a limit on himself, and modesty, by which he listens to those whom he has seen to be experienced, and allows himself to be taught by them.
Indeed, in such great power it is difficult to apply the reins to the mind:
and yet he who does not know how to command himself will not rightly rule others;
nor will he whose mind is not composed be able to compose those subject to him.
But many think it is kingly to yield to no one, and they take stubbornness and obstinacy for constancy, and a mind disposed tyrannically for a royal one;
Indeed, the greatest princes erred especially in this, that they trusted themselves too much;
and too late they understood how much it would have been better to have obeyed prudent advisers:
There are also those who resent advisers and fear to acknowledge reason as mistress, because they think that by obeying those who show what is right, their own power is diminished.
Moreover, in the choice of friends and in their use, how cautious the prince ought to be, no one fails to understand.

For not only from those who surround him is a conjecture made as to what sort of person he himself is, but the power of the empire to a great extent depends on this: whether he has chosen good or bad men, and whether he favors the former and restrains the latter, or not.

Whether he allows himself to be deceived by flatterers, who praise even things that are not praiseworthy, or report false things, because they judge those things to be pleasing to him, or whether he can tolerate the honorable freedom of speech, and those who prefer to reveal even unpleasant or sad things rather than conceal them are even more acceptable to him.

For all these things, there is need of keen judgment, which penetrates the minds, plans, and character of men, and especially of a certain simple sense of truth, by which one can choose the best and quickly embrace them.

Therefore, equipped with these arts, and joining courage of mind with wisdom, at the same time benevolent to all men, fair, just, faithful both to his own and to foreigners, he will be a leader, and in all matters he will keep measure;

He will temper severity with gentleness, giving to each its due measure as much as it deserves, neither relaxing justice through lenient policies, nor being inclined to harsher measures by a gloomy disposition, nor being prone to suspicions from a certain melancholy.
He will be sparing by reason and again liberal, because he knows that neither is right except with reason.
In short, he will do nothing without reason and judgment.

And whatever he will undertake, although he will not neglect a good reputation, nevertheless he will not do it in order to make his name famous, but he will exercise royal virtue for the sake of virtue.
Indeed, the insane desire for glory has rendered very many princes of the best character, who seemed to have been born for making peoples happy, most hostile both to themselves and to others.
Finally, a king so constituted will become a partaker of genuine happiness.
Indeed, you may see that the leading houses, although placed at the highest pinnacle, are not rarely lacking in happiness, which more easily falls to the lot of the humble:
But if, according to the old proverb, the wealthy have many things with which to console themselves, nevertheless not a few evils come upon princes, from which the lesser are free.
The greater the place, the greater the burdens and cares;
Scarcely any space for rest is left for him who must look out for all:
The lower classes are refreshed by the familiar companionship of wife and children;

For kings, even if they are not troubled by domestic calamity, or by the disgrace that happened to Octavian Augustus, rarely is there that prosperity of marriage which private individuals are accustomed to enjoy.
Add that whatever troubles and afflicts the whole state, by these the head of the republic is struck more bitterly.
But the royal mind, in having fulfilled all parts of duty and in the consciousness of good, will find the greatest and sweetest reward of its labors;

Nor will he who is subject to fortune compare his lot with the outcome, since fortune is no more enslaved to kings than to those who obey, but being steadfast and least broken by human misfortunes, he will bear whatever adversities have fallen.

In a popular manner, as I promised at the beginning, I have sketched the royal virtue, as far as I could by my own judgment, and not treating everything as fully as perhaps was fitting, because the subject is boundless and the time allotted to me is short;

But turning your attention to those things which I have discussed in summary, you have understood, I believe, even without my reminding you, how greatly Frederick William corresponds to the royal virtue:
Nevertheless, I hope I shall not do an ungrateful thing, if I repeat at least the more important outlines of the description.

And so, to keep the series I have begun, Frederick William, following the custom of his ancestors, took upon himself the care of the army, yet he is not excessive in it, nor does he subordinate civil affairs to it, and he so moderated the soldier that he did not fight with the civilians as once he did, but lived in harmony with them:

The King himself proved himself keen in military service and a brave warrior, brave also as a man in enduring misfortunes, by which he was not overwhelmed, but was strengthened by them, having emerged greater from a calamity that was by no means slight, having gathered the fruit of wisdom from the vicissitudes of fortune, just as bees produce the sweetest honey from thyme, a most bitter and dry herb.

I am not saying anything more than the truth, but I stop reluctantly far below the magnitude of the deeds, far below those zeal of the people, which the most beloved King won for himself by his counsels and deeds, accomplished after divine help by his own virtue and the loyalty of the citizens.
Those who were present then remember and will appreciate them.
But what shall I say about the King's industry and endurance of labors?
Who is more removed from pleasures, to which even strong men sometimes yield, who is more removed from all luxury and softness, who is more frugal?
Indeed, no citizen is unaware how small a part of the revenues is spent on the court, with almost all of them turned to public benefits.

At the same time, Frederick William so tempers severity that, whereas severe princes are usually feared by their subjects, in this prince one cannot even ask what those curious about such matters have often asked: whether it is better to fear the king or to be loved by him.

For those very things which you might think could be accomplished by fear alone, the love of the prince together with the reverence owed to him accomplishes, and the force of the laws through which he rules.
Indeed, stronger supports and bulwarks of the empire than troops and citadels, with which we are especially fortified.
But piety, the foundation of wisdom, Frederick William does not have on his lips, but in his heart;

nor does he wish to lead the people and bind them and, as it were, deceive them by religious rites and ceremonies, as many kings thought they had to do for themselves, but to improve his own people by the true knowledge of God;

And his piety is not placed in the empty knowledge of dogmas, nor is it contaminated by blind and superstitious opinions, but it penetrates into the things that he does, and is illuminated by much thought.
Now who better holds the measure of himself?
Does he not combine the modesty of a private citizen with royal power and dignity?
Of this matter I will bring a great proof, even at the risk of offense.
We do not have the liberty, which they call, written on a charter;
Nor is the authority of the civil orders, as they are called, great in this state:
but through the whole administration of the republic a certain moderation is diffused, which Frederick William leads by his commands and example;
whence nothing is done anywhere eagerly, nothing violently, nothing by faction, and thus we are freer than those who seem the freest.
Consider this system of the universities:

Although these [schools] were, by a common decree of the German Confederation, eight years ago, subjected to the more attentive care of the prefects appointed over them, have they therefore lost the just freedom either of teaching or of learning?
Are they not freer than the British and Gallic [schools], from which these especially seem to be disturbed by illiberal contentions?
I will not speak more particularly about the prudence and diligence of Frederick William in choosing and consulting ministers and friends;
nor is it proper for me to name the living;
The deceased are evidence, who under his own auspices, twelve years ago and before, accomplished the greatest deeds at home and abroad, and remain fresh in the memory and minds of the citizens.
On the contrary, the whole tribe of flatterers is banished from this kingdom and from this court.
But the wisdom of the most beloved Prince is perfected by that keen sense of truth, which I mentioned above, which aims with certain aim at the right, the honorable, the useful in any matter:
Since this excellent character is known to almost everyone, no one doubts that the King will rightly judge whatever things have come to his notice.
Such a man cannot fail to be just, fair, faithful, and kind to all who are worthy of kindness, but at the same time severe toward those who offend.
From this source proceeds the proper measure of punishment or leniency, of generosity or frugality.

Although it has long been established by very many proofs that all these qualities are present in Frederick William in a distinguished manner and in the way in which they ought to be, nevertheless I will mention two things which this year has brought forth: one of justice and equity, the other of munificent liberality.
Of these, the former is of such a kind that thanks were publicly given to Frederick William even by foreigners:

For since for the space of many years no state had been willing to pay what was owed to the creditors of the former kingdom of Westphalia, our King was the first, on his part, to order that they be satisfied under certain conditions.
But the latter matter pertains to our affairs.

For although Frederick William, just as he enriched the other literary universities of this kingdom, so also enriched ours from its foundation with exceptional resources and repeatedly increased them, yet with regard to stipends by which needy young men might be supported, we were certainly less well provided to the extent that, in such a great multitude of academic citizens as we flourish with, a number that no school of arts in Germany has had for a long time, it is fitting that there are very many who must be publicly assisted.
For whom the earlier resources were not sufficient, although they themselves had been gradually increased.

Therefore in this year the most benevolent King made an excellent arrangement, that from the treasury not inconsiderable stipends should be paid out both to others and especially to the sons of deceased clergymen and scholars, who among us should devote themselves to their studies:
and since private individuals very willingly follow the king's example, there is hope that more gifts of this kind will be added in the future:
In the same way, in this same academic year, two merchants of noble mind offered a not inconsiderable gift to the university for the same purpose.

By these arts, Frederick William, although not led by any desire for glory, but because, as Tacitus says most beautifully about Galba, he was neither careless of reputation nor a seller of it, obtained the praise of a good king, and at the same time attained the true happiness of a prince.

He is not outwardly wrapped in the appearance of happiness, surrounded by arms and horses and the display of an army, but within, the voices of desires and the anguish of conscience testify against that empty splendor, and the secret groans of citizens sing an ill-omened accompaniment to the fame of his name:
but the tranquility of the breast is unfolded in the serenity of the brow;
Whatever fortune distributes, he accepts it with moderation, assigns to each thing its proper place, so that his mind is neither excessively contracted by adversity nor exults in prosperity.
Finally, in the affection, loyalty, and zeal of his fellow citizens, and in the love and harmony of the royal family, he rests secure.
I seem to myself to have accomplished what I wanted.

Let us therefore pray to God, the Best and Greatest, that He, who has recently restored to us from illness, may long keep the prince and father happy among us, and that He may graciously look after and provide for this most powerful and flourishing empire, and finally for the Augustan house, which we have congratulated this year as well, having been increased by a most pleasing marriage.

div.head: XVI. Oratio nataliciis Friderici Guilelmi III. celebrandis d. III. m. Aug. a. MDCCCXXVIII. habita.
On the relationship that exists between learning and the state.

p.s: Since there are very many reasons, listeners, why we celebrate the birthday of Frederick William every year with such great festivity, and these reasons are partly common to the whole state, because it is equally the interest of all to venerate the best Prince, to recall with pious mind the benefits conferred by him upon the state, to give thanks to God, the Best and Greatest, for his health, and to make vows again and again; but partly they are proper and peculiar to us, because he not only founded this school, but also fosters it with more distinguished care, and so loves it that he has recently adorned it with his own name;
Then one thing seems to me so singular that, having set aside other places which I have pursued in previous years, I have decided to dwell on this one today.
I speak of a simple matter, not unknown or doubtful to any of you.

For if nothing contributes more to the prosperity of individual peoples, not to say of the human race, than the love of country implanted in the minds of citizens, which in no age has failed to produce the richest fruits and to give birth to the most beautiful deeds;
what should teachers of youth consider more important than to imbue and inflame those whom they have undertaken to form with that very virtue?

Indeed, the feelings which a boy and a young man has imbibed with his first training, having been insinuated into the innermost recesses of the mind and, as it were, clinging to the very marrow and vitals, are retained both most firmly and most durably.

And I do not know whether the ancients, especially the Greeks, nourished that most sacred flame, by which it is certain that they burned uniquely, with anything more than with suitable education and gymnastic and musical instruction, which, with any pretense of foreign color rejected, accustomed their offspring to ancestral customs, ancestral worship, ancestral literature and arts.

But we find the love of country and the love of the prince, who satisfies his duty, so united among the peoples who are ruled, that he who loves his country cannot but love the prince, and since the person of the prince contains in itself the whole state as expressed in a visible image, without that most grateful affection with which we embrace the head of the republic, not even the country could be dear enough to our hearts.

Thus we are bound to the prince and the fatherland by the same law, formula, and faith, not as slaves, who have a master and no fatherland, but as free men, who, just as at home they regard the father as occupying the place of the prince, so in public they regard the king as occupying the place of a parent.

These feelings, with which among us every best person is devoted to Frederick William, these pursuits, scarcely known to that most praised antiquity, intensify, ennoble, and fill with wonderful sweetness the very love of the fatherland;
And it is so far from being the case that the prince seizes what is owed to the fatherland, that whatever he has claimed here for himself of sincere love, that has been claimed for the fatherland.

Therefore, is it not the case that in the schools, both the higher and the lower, the youthful minds are to be directed to reverence and love for the prince, and that together with the teaching of letters, effort must be made that the students be penetrated with those feelings?

Although this is not to be done on this one day alone, but on every occasion that presents itself, whether we must use eloquent words or whether it will suffice to set forth those things from which the learners can of themselves gather right counsels;

nevertheless this day, joyful and festive for the whole people, is at the same time most suitable, on which each literary college may testify that it is by no means unmindful of that most weighty duty.

And indeed I am confident that you, all of you who are present, most pleasant colleagues, are as fully aware as I am myself, how ardently you love and admire Frederick William on account of the virtues divinely implanted in him, on account of his justice and moderation, piety and wisdom, gentleness and courage.
We understand our blessings; we understand who is their author:

And who would ever have thought that we, captured by the excellent arts of Frederick William and heaped with the greatest benefits, would so forget the oath sworn to the Father of the Fatherland as to be able, whether by teaching or by exhorting, to strengthen and spread the love of the citizens toward the most beloved King, which seems scarcely able to be increased?
But here someone may already ask:
What is that, then, which, if you take away the bare admonition, learning and youthful training can contribute to arousing love for the fatherland and the prince?

But what do you, who are placed in the very seat of the empire, who ought to have a thorough knowledge of the excellence of this kingdom through closer acquaintance and, as it were, daily experience, contribute to prove what is said to be your purpose?
And how many of you are there who, shut up within the walls of a museum and bent over aged volumes, deserve well of the state, of the fatherland?
What of the fact that literature is common to the whole human race?
because almost all peoples are held together among themselves by the bond of the same arts?

That the cultivation of letters draws men away from action, and having drawn them away, fixes them, as it were, in a foreign land and in an imaginary realm of pure notions, while agriculture, commerce, and all other business keeps them in the affairs of the state?
Indeed, excessive devotion to one's country harms even literature itself.

When not a few peoples are carried away by this to arrogance and pride, they cut off the flower of their own learning by despising foreign learning, while the Germans have the opposite fault, who, marveling at foreign things, disparage their own people enviously.
But does not philosophy, the mother and nurse of all learning, seem to shrink from the conveniences of common life and of the fatherland?

Thus, to mention Thales at once, from whom this science almost took its beginning, and Anaxagoras and similar men, there were already among the ancients those who would say that they were indeed wise but by no means prudent, and that they had known things difficult, admirable, and altogether divine, but useless, because they did not seek human goods.

And do not say that this is the property of the physicists, for Socrates, who is said to have first brought philosophy down from the sky, placed it in cities, and even introduced it into homes, was far from common utility, and, paying little attention to his native soil, when he was asked where he was from, declared himself a citizen of the world.
The same view pleased the Stoics, who nevertheless were no less alien to moral philosophy than Socrates.
And Plato says that those who from youth are occupied in courts and other public assemblies seem to have been brought up as slaves, if they are compared with the one whom philosophy has imagined.
For this man, he says, does not even know the way to the forum, nor does he know where the senate-house or any other council of the state is.

And in truth, his body alone is placed in the state and lives in the position of a foreigner, but his soul, having scorned all these things, investigates the things that are above the earth and below, and the whole nature of things, by no means lowering itself to what is near.
Nor does Aristotle not prefer the contemplative life to the active:
And you might say that joining both is difficult, because literature demands leisure, and business demands strenuous industry.
Indeed, not only philosophers teach such things:
We have even heard emperors proclaiming that it is not fitting for learned men to cast votes concerning the affairs of the state.

Finally, literature is thought to offer some most welcome refuge and a retreat full of solace, where, tossed by the waves of public life, you may rest secure, where no one may disturb those Archimedean circles, but as if in the cloisters of monasteries you may hide away freed from all contagion of miseries.

If any learned man should approve of these and more things of this kind, which I refrain from setting forth, do you think that he will be sincerely loyal and devoted to the prince and to his country, or that he will be affected in a very different way from the Alexandrian poets and men of letters, who were nourished and well kept for the sake of display by kings of foreign stock, who kept the people in their own land, devoid of a fatherland, by fear and superstition?
Indeed, that condition seems to me to differ from ours by an incredible amount.

And I would think that anything should be conceded sooner than that the learned men of this empire should be so estranged from Frederick William and the Prussian people that their learning should be completely separated from the state's policy, and that our minds should not be bound to both the King and the republic by a deeper bond of piety.
If we were lacking this piety, this very solemnity of this day would not be to be valued beyond the giving of thanks.

Now, since a very close connection between the state and literature seems to exist, which I do not doubt that the most wise King, aiding the studies of learning with such great munificence, has not only perceived himself, but also demands that both teachers and learners keep before their eyes:

Although you perhaps have a better knowledge of these matters than I do, nevertheless, since it is my duty to express your opinions to the best of my ability, I advise that knowledge, by no means estranged from the fatherland, serves the interests of the fatherland in a threefold manner.
For first, what the wise provide for the human race, they provide at the same time for their fellow citizens, and they ought to be citizens at once of the world and of a particular state;
Then, since the fatherland is defined not so much by its soil as by the common character of the people or of the state, education contributes very much to cultivating this character.
Finally, vigorous learning passes into all parts of the republic.

For if Aristotle truly taught that man is a political animal, then human life is perfected and completed in the state, and the state itself seems to be nothing other than the natural condition and state of the human race, formed and composed according to the standard of reason;

Therefore, whoever strives to aid the perfection of mortals and the progress of the human race—which is certainly the mark of an educated person—even if he devotes his efforts to no particular state, whether to enlightening minds, or to correcting morals, or to discovering useful things, by deserving well of all men he at the same time earns the favor of his fellow citizens.

And when the same person, if he has learned to reason correctly, is not unaware that human nature itself demands that the human race be divided into several societies, he will understand that he too, although a citizen of the world, owes a certain particular state as his fatherland, just as each person has a certain nation and family, and that he must especially love it, whether he will have been born a citizen of it or granted that right.
What of the fact that those very men, who first called themselves worldly, did not neglect their fatherland or the republic at all?
Or did Socrates ever leave Athens, except to fight with arms for his fatherland, and once for the sake of seeing the Isthmian games?

Does he not, in that most famous conversation which he held with Crito in prison, although he praises Sparta and Crete, nevertheless declare that he was never desirous of any city other than Athens, nor of any laws other than those of Attica?
Did he decide to live according to these and to perform the duties of a citizen, and to obey them?
Did he not prove these resolutions both by his life, which was devoted, as to philosophy, so to the correction of the morals and institutions of the citizens, and by his very death?
Did not his country afterwards mourn him, unjustly condemned, and honor him with a bronze statue?
But did the Stoics, because they wished to be citizens of the world, live in idleness?
On the contrary, the Epicureans were the adversaries of these.
Or did Marcus?
Did Antoninus, who affirms that for himself as a man the world is his country and his commonwealth, decline the burdens of empire?
Indeed, these examples clearly demonstrate, if I see anything, that the wisdom which makes its followers citizens of the world does not harm one's country.

For just as commerce, which in this matter is most similar to literature, spreading light through all the regions of the world, while it opens the intercourse of nations, does not seem to dissolve the bonds of one's country;

that the most holy Christian faith, which wills that the pious have an invisible and heavenly country, does not diminish the love of this earthly one, but rather binds it with religion and stirs it with divine instinct, so that we devote our life to country and prince, and pour out our blood for altars and hearths.

But mortals, placed at the very lowest stage of human culture, at first confined their fatherland within the nearest and very narrow boundaries of the field or town where each one had been born and grown up, comparing the familiar and the foreign from their seat and soil;

Indeed, they were bound to their fields, streams, and hills by the sweetest familiarity, and they delighted in places known to them from infancy, the sight of which affects no one who is even moderately gentle without a pleasant recollection of past times.
Soon, a person more alert and already capable of conceiving higher things in his mind understands that the state, tempered by laws suited to his character, is his fatherland;

Then, no longer as if bound to the soil, he measures his fatherland by the community of his nation, and first of his own smaller tribe, then of a people embracing several tribes closely related in origin:
Just as the Greeks, who began late to be called by a common name, even later and scarcely ever firmly coalesced into one body, although each one had his own country as a republic exceedingly dear;

Just as the provinces of the kingdoms that now exist gradually and not without disturbances and wars came together in such a way that citizens of different provinces recognized a common fatherland for themselves.
And indeed the republic with liberty, which cannot be separated from it, the Greeks especially judged to be their fatherland, which, as if confined to no place, could even be transferred:
Thus the Phocaeans, besieged by Harpagus and driven to the last extremity, transferred their homeland to Corsica, and soon afterwards to Velia.
Thus Bias of Priene tried to persuade the Ionians to leave Ionia, sail to Sardinia, and establish a city there, in order to preserve their freedom.
Thus Herodotus reports that Themistocles thought about transferring Athens to Italy.
Thus, wherever the Greeks occupied land in the most diverse regions—Asian, Libyan, Italian—that very land seemed to them to be Greece and was called Greece.
And rightly so;
since a state does not consist of lands and buildings, but of laws and institutions.

Of course, when to the communion of language and customs, without which nations can never be rightly united into one state, there was added this civil communication of rights and duties, of government and obedience, of advantages and dangers, and a certain perpetuity of public and private discipline, by which the natural character is strengthened;

To these the zeal of the citizens attaches itself, and the love of one's country, which formerly clung to the soil, that mute and inanimate thing, is now transferred to this form of the republic, this character of the people, this living and immortal society of souls having the same end of action and agreeing in the same counsels, which, although it is composed of all the citizens and can even be preserved to some extent without royal dignity, nevertheless is best and most perfectly contained in one head of the republic, the legitimate prince.
And this love of country grows the more, the more the people's own character is formed, the freer the condition of subjects, the more certain the harmony between citizens and the prince.

Nor do I fear to say that even those peoples which have come to any state through the outcomes of wars and the fortuitous division of lands can be united among themselves by these bonds, if only some agreement of primitive character and disposition, which certainly inheres in all nations of Germanic stock, comes to their aid, and the rulers of the state understand that weaving work which Plato's Statesman imposes on them, namely joining together dissimilar threads.

Does not, although this kingdom has grown together from various peoples as if by a fortuitous concourse of elements, the power of a ruler holding a certain balance, and a certain equality of laws and institutions, to which even the equal pursuits of letters and arts are to be counted, and one who governs all, who is fair to all, the spirit of a most beloved Prince, unite the inhabitants of the Rhine and the Vistula, the Oder, the Elbe, and the Saale, and all the intervening provinces, not by arms, but by the consent of their wills, into this one Prussian name?
And even if there are some (though there are none or very few) who have not yet become sufficiently accustomed to gentle rule, they will soon be charmed by the virtues of this state;
But by the love of Frederick William I judge that even those are already now captivated, who previously were most hostile to Prussia.

That therefore, which I have said, the character of the people and of the state is manifestly formed to a great extent by public education, especially since those who are placed in charge of affairs are almost all educated in public schools.

Therefore, although, with the connection of the most cultivated lands of Europe having been increased immensely, literature cannot retain as much of a peculiar national character as it once did among the Greeks, nevertheless our discipline ought to harmonize with the inner spirit of the people and the state, and to bring it, as far as possible, to perfection.
How this is to be done, I will not explain now:
Nor can this be explained except by examining the institutions of the state, whatever they may be, and the policies which it itself has followed through a long series of years.

But I think no one will deny that the Prussian state is endowed with a certain and indeed excellent character, which, having gained such great strength under its most glorious kings and leaders, has attracted and still attracts very many foreigners, whom it by no means excludes, departing very far from the Spartan rejection of foreigners, and in a certain way transforms them to the nature of the natives.

But if we imagine that pupils have been entrusted to us with a view to that character of the state for which freedom of mind is especially fitting—as all, or at least most, will admit—we shall fulfill our duty both to the fatherland and to Frederick William.
Thirdly, I said that vigorous learning is spread into all parts of the state;
Since this is well known, I will not pursue it except briefly.
Indeed, considering the public utilities of theology, jurisprudence, medicine, natural science, mathematics, and the disciplines of politics and economics, no one will fail to see what I mean.

But philosophy and history are both the foundation of many of these doctrines, and they set forth precepts and examples, by which it is not doubtful that the state's condition and institutions, once heard, can also be corrected.

But above all, those [philosophies] oppose with their own light the worst evils of states, the unbridled domination of tyrants, and the insane superstition by which cunning men are accustomed to seize the weakness of mortals.
This is the chief reason why both wicked princes and priests greedy for power have been hostile to them at all times.

Finally, these so-called studies of humanity themselves also assist the other disciplines, and it has been established by long use and approved by the judgment of our princes as well, that they, when rightly handled and confined within the just limits of liberal education, are most suitable for educating those whom the state employs in conducting its affairs.
I knowingly refrain from other praises, which seem to be a little more remote from the immediate advantage of the state;
Although Cicero, certainly not ignorant of public affairs, did not even in the forum fear to recommend the good arts to these men too.
But he would be unfair who should wish to confine literature within the limits of common usage.

For not only can you not easily foresee what will be useful in the future, but literature has its own value even without utility, and knowledge, divine and human, explores all things, the innermost recesses of nature and the mind, and whatever men have done and thought, driven by the innate impulse of discovering truth, for the sake of knowledge itself.

But if anyone should think that only that part of that manifold apparatus of learning should be retained in the state which seems to suit his own purposes, and should undermine the foundations of literature, those hidden things and not suited to common use, and should act not much differently than the Cynics, who, because they thought that a man suffices for himself for living rightly, are said to have scorned with club and wallet and pot and cup, or even with a hollow hand instead of these, whatever of furniture and utensils adorns life and makes it more pleasant.

I judge that this one thing must be conceded: that there is a certain, as it were, dead learning, or rather a semblance and imitation of learning, which, however much it may boast itself, is utterly illiberal and shadowy, and neither exercises the mind nor sharpens the judgment, nor fills the soul with notions, nor teaches anything or refreshes and delights, but packs empty chaff into its granaries, and dwelling among the volumes of books alone, comprehends nothing with the mind.

Therefore, just as we allow that doctrine to be exiled from the state, so we shall say that lofty and profound learning, although far removed from common use, together with poetry and the other arts of this kind, is the glory and ornament of that state.
Nor should we fear that we, who discharge public duties, may become too estranged from the republic, or that we may become bookworms in this city:

Indeed, that institution of Frederick William, of placing the primary schools especially in the principal cities, besides its other advantages, seems also to have this, that both teachers and learners become accustomed somewhat more easily to a just measure of those things which are outside of learning.

I have briefly run through what I had promised, listeners, because some time has already been cut off for the orator by the public recitation of the opinions that have been delivered concerning the literary commissions;
But although I have not today deliberately proclaimed the praises of the most beloved Prince, yet what need is there for me to show that almost all the things I have said are suited to his person?
Frederick William indeed both wills and understands that literature is useful to the state, but he does not derive its dignity from this use:
For I think no state has prescribed a freer course or granted a wider field to them than ours under the auspices of this king.
He so increased the flower of learning in this empire that he may rightly be called the chief protector of them in Prussia.
He corrected and enlarged everything received from previous kings.
He added so many new honors that he left his predecessors far behind.

Finally, the king unites those three best things, truth, goodness, and beauty, with each other, and the arts of peace and the prosperities of the civil state with military virtue and power, and he teaches piety and moral integrity to the citizens by his example.
Nor are those things of such a kind that they are suitable only for this age:

Just as the things that Frederick the Great did excellently have propagated their fruit to posterity, so Frederick William is going to benefit the state after himself, as long as, although the present necessities, increased by the unfairness of earlier times, may demand a huge expense, he does not stop establishing lasting institutions and scattering the seeds of a future harvest.
And so the safety of this prince, embracing the prayer of all and the conveniences of the whole state, is [our] concern;
Here he is fair and courteous to all good men of every rank, here a refuge for the wretched, here uniquely popular and civic-minded.
In short, the same things are joyful and sad to him as to the citizens.

Would that the supreme deity might grant our prayers, that Frederick William may enjoy perpetually the happiness he most deserves, and that a green and long old age may befall him, seeing the success of his undertakings;

so that the tranquility of the state and lasting peace may correspond to that tranquility of mind by which he has attained the true happiness of the wise man, and that the plans undertaken for the restoration of the state may prosper;
finally, that the whole Augustan house may be preserved and increased, and that this security and glory of the empire, once confirmed, may endure for the longest time.

div.head: XVII. Oratio nataliciis Friderici Guilelmi III. celebrandis d. III. m. Aug. a. MDCCCXXIX. habita.
On the relationship between the martial and military state and the disciplines of the arts

p.s: The Persians, once a most distinguished nation, seem to me to have wisely established, my listeners, that legal action should be taken against a person who, although he could return a favor to one who had deserved well of him, was detected as ungrateful, because they thought that the same person would also neglect the gods, parents, fatherland, and friends, and they judged that an ungrateful person differs in no way from an impious one.
For indeed, to pious, gentle, and tender souls, that most sacred feeling of gratitude is especially sweet.
Nothing stings them more sharply, nothing in the whole nature of things is more atrocious and foul, than a man forgetful of benefits:

And if it is permissible to establish certain grades of harmless pleasures, the sweetest thing seems to me to be doing good, the next sweetest to be grateful for good deeds, the third to be affected by the pleasantness of benefits, and finally to receive less gratitude than is actually due, which indeed no one would demand back, if, as is rightly prescribed, one should immediately forget what one has done well for others.
But from these, the fourth and indeed by far the greatest has been divinely given to the Father of his Country, whom we always venerate, both silently and openly, but today more solemnly;
to us the second and third have been left, these also exceptionally good:
on account of which, lest our piety be missed, deservedly this day is held by us as uniquely joyful, happy, and festive.

For who is more beneficent, who more worthy of the praise of grateful citizens, than Frederick William, a prince both vigorous and gentle, restorer of the republic equally in peace and in war, corrector of morals, establisher of the arts, fair and just to all, generous to the deserving, a comfort to the wretched and afflicted?

But on this solemn day I have not only repeatedly pursued that king with praise, whom you, when praising, sing to such a degree that what Antalcidas the Spartan said, not without wit, about the sophist who recited the praises of Hercules, applies: 'But who criticizes him?' but also I think that what kind of man Frederick William is should be considered not only in his own person:
In the state's condition, situation, institutions, and policies, the king's virtue shines forth most brightly, because he himself shapes the commonwealth and is in turn shaped by it.

Concerning this, although I am about to speak, I will indeed avoid the very appearance of flattery, although among you, who are bound to the best Prince with sincere hearts, it is not even to be feared; yet I will no more depart from setting forth the distinguished virtues of Frederick William than those who were once publicly appointed at Athens to celebrate the memory of citizens slain in war seemed to have deviated from their subject when they recounted the blessings of their country, to which those brave warriors had added glory and advantage, and to which they themselves owed their valor, having been formed and roused to noble deeds by the education and most illustrious examples of their parents.

But when I consider how many and various matters this subject includes, which not even the greatest learning and experience, combined with the richest resources of eloquence, could in any degree exhaust, I am almost deterred from the undertaking:
And certainly it will be permissible to dwell on some small portion taken from this, which may seem neither foreign to literature nor to the times.
But what times do I mean?

Indeed, from the time when the kingdoms of Europe were freed from the powerless rule of one man, if you make an exception of the seditions that arose in some badly constituted states, and the expeditions—more like skirmishes than wars and battles—that sprang from them, this part of the world has enjoyed profound peace, and has begun to revive and flourish.
The West indeed is even now wretchedly disturbed and oppressed;
A war undertaken to abolish the most atrocious slavery is devastating the far-off East.
The middle nations are secure, and beyond light suspicions and, I might say, threats, nothing more serious is dared, while the wisdom of princes maintains peace.

This condition of the times, as I, occupied in letters, contemplate it, has suggested a reflection concerning the relation that exists between the warlike and military state and the disciplines of the arts, both in any republic and especially in our own state.
Help me, listeners, with the breeze of your kindness, as I am about to speak a few and meager things about this.

And first indeed, since the Prussian kingdom is commonly called military (nor did I myself once hesitate to pronounce this with a certain reason), you might wonder that this empire excels so much in the cultivation of the arts, as it excels without doubt.

Although indeed in war the strength and talents of peoples are sometimes roused as if from sleep, and just as storms purify the air and fertilize the soil, so those things heal the diseases of the state, and especially luxury, negligence, and idleness, by which I do not deny that a better cultivation of letters can also be provoked;
Nevertheless, not every war brings these blessings.
For wars that are waged, so to speak, by soldiers alone, with no more vigorous efforts of the people, afflict the people indeed equally with other wars, but do not equally uplift them:

Those wars which neither restore to the republic the liberty in which literature especially thrives, nor bring a broader knowledge of the world, nor augment the native arts with the useful arts of foreigners, or by which lands are excessively devastated — how they could benefit nations, I do not see.
Therefore the Peloponnesian War and the wars that the Macedonians waged against the Greeks were less favorable both to the states and to literature;
nor did the civil wars bring any good to the Romans in literature;
nor did the arms of Louis XIV bring to the French that praise of literature which existed during his reign;
but that thirty-year sacred war utterly eradicated all the literature of Germany;
nor did the Seven Years' War greatly stimulate talents;
But the expeditions of Neapolis did not benefit literature, neither those in Gaul nor those against conquered peoples.
But the Median wars, with liberty increased, helped the learning of the Greeks wonderfully much;

Alexander the Great, while he opened the East, enlarged the knowledge of both human and divine things, and scattered Greek literature on barbarian shores; and similarly the crusades certainly provided some utility to the West;
And in the Second Punic War, when the arts of the Greeks were brought into Rome, the Muse, with winged step, as the old poet says, introduced herself into the wild and warlike race of Romulus.

Finally, in our memory, the war undertaken for freedom not only enriched the Germans with a great abundance of most noble songs, truly worthy of being compared with Tyrtaeus and Alcaeus, but also, having diverted their minds from frivolous things, impelled them to everything that is best and indeed to the pursuit of literary studies with new eagerness.
Indeed, war can also increase the arts in another way, just as it increases the rest of the state's equipment, when it transfers the wealth and tributes of conquered peoples to the conqueror:
By this way Pericles filled Athens with all kinds of literature and most splendid works:
But this is not without reproach, nor without the vengeance of injustice, which followed Athens, as later Rome and recently Gaul;

And you may infer that this cultivation of Athens was not owed to war, but was implanted in the Athenians by nature as a love of the best arts, from the fact that neither Sparta nor Rome, from similar and greater plunders, obtained a comparable fruit.
Now indeed, what we have said about war seems to apply also to the condition of a peaceful state, which has been exclusively prepared for waging war:
except that domestic warfare does not even provide that it adds to the minds of the citizens those incentives which a war undertaken with the consent of the people brings to them.
Finally, just as war stirs up talents, peace ought to mature them;
and the arts of peace are both called and are literature:

This kindly peace not only, as Bacchylides proclaims, dispenses wealth and brings forth the flowers of sweet-sounding songs, and summons young men to gymnasia, to the flute, and to revels, but also nourishes those higher gymnasia of learning and knowledge and the most excellent music of philosophy, and brings it about that leisure and wealth may be devoted to the gentler arts.
