For is it not true, to use the words of the greatest British poet, that just as fields, meadows, and orchards degenerate through wild growth in war, so youth, having unlearned the arts, becomes savage?

But can princes, with all their money turned to the necessities of war, devote as much care to the arts as the best King, after a most joyful peace succeeded the long wars, bestowed on the magnificent institutions of letters and arts throughout the empire, whether founding or equipping them?

Indeed, the Prussian state, which perhaps once could have seemed to rest solely on military power because of its large number of mercenaries, is no more military than any state ought to be, nor to the extent that this is considered a vice.

For since three orders especially constitute each somewhat more perfect state, one that seeks what is necessary, convenient, and pleasant for food and culture, one that educates and teaches the rest, and one that protects what has been acquired by force of arms, and the safety of the republic is placed in the harmony and concord of these;

That state will rightly be considered imperfect and defective in which one of these orders is either less cultivated or lies wholly neglected or oppressed, and one has so prevailed over the rest that all things incline toward it, and it rules over the others.
Thus a state is to be judged mercantile, priestly, or military, according as each part of the commonwealth stands out too much.

Thus, in order that I may seek from ancient republics the most perfect examples of military affairs, such as in our age you will scarcely find except among barbarians, which, although they were so small that they were confined to one city or to the communion of a few, nevertheless offer the clearest images of the various forms which the state has assumed, and for this very reason, because they were simpler, they exhibit the individual elements of the state more distinctly;

Thus, I say, Sparta and Crete were almost uniquely military states, because the powerful army of the aristocrats ruled over the rest as if they were slaves; the clients, for the most part harshly treated, cultivated the fields; and just as the work of agriculture, however useful and delightful, so too trade, crafts, and other pursuits were held in no honor; indeed, letters and arts, except for gymnastics and music and any other things deemed necessary for the worship of the deity, were excessively neglected; and the citizens, as Plato excellently perceived, were trained not for universal virtue, with all of whose parts the state ought to be imbued, but almost solely for courage.
Thus Rome, falling, from the time when the power of empire was in the hands of the Praetorian Guard, presented a miserable spectacle of military monarchy.
But does our state perhaps obey soldiers?
Is a greater part of the revenues spent on the army among us than in other kingdoms?
Does the army harm the other orders of the state either in number or in authority or in prerogative, whether assumed or conceded?
Has not excellent provision been made for agriculture by the best institutions, by improving the condition of the farmers, and especially by the division of the lands?
Are not the trades aided by loosening the bonds of the guilds, by establishing schools, by showing honor to this order as well, and finally by every kind of support?
Have not the taxes and customs been so established, and such agreements made with foreigners, that as far as possible provision is made even for merchants and traders?

What of the fact that this kingdom is so far from striving to protect its position by force of arms alone, that although we have no allies of our own in military matters, but are ourselves enrolled in the confederation of all Germans, we nevertheless have allies in revenues, freely united with us by a common interest?
But what shall I say about the arts and sciences?

Is there any state, not only in Germany but in all Europe, that has made and continues to make such great expenditures for those [purposes], in proportion to the extent of its resources and territories, as ours has?

which, with equal care and generosity, cultivates and fosters every kind of school, both the lower schools, which are intended for the education, to some extent, of the common and plebeian multitude, and the gymnasia or lycea, in which the rudiments of liberal education are imparted, and the literary universities, which initiate learners into higher studies;

It protects the worship of the divine deity not in order that the people may serve more willingly, but in order that they may be imbued with piety, with uprightness, with gentleness of character, in such a way that neither are the things taken away from the priests and ministers of the divine word which it is right and fair to grant, nor is harmful power granted to them;
It collects at great expense whatever is suitable for forming minds, for cultivating the sense of the good and the beautiful, for spreading learning more widely, and offers it for common use;
which now, with Frederick William as its agent, is most richly adorned with the finest works of artists and is daily becoming more adorned.

But since I have on several occasions from this platform deliberately treated these matters at greater length, mindful of my plan, I consider it sufficient to have indicated them today in a few words:

But that is truly admirable, that such a great flower of the good arts has already sprung up among us, that there are those who fear lest we become too learned, lest too much be granted to the liberal letters, and lest the education of boys and youths be directed too little to the use of life.
Indeed, whatever is excessive is rightly said to turn into a vice.
And although the people never seems able to be too learned, nor right knowledge to be spread more widely than is fitting;
Nevertheless, there are things that can be said not without reason against the excessive cultivation of literature, wherever it may have arisen (for in this republic, I think, it has not yet arisen).

For first, just as it is far better that the people be most cultivated, so the order of literary men who practice the art can exceed the just number no less than soldiers, and more than is advantageous for the state can be drawn to the pursuit of literature:

But if too many people will despise the gainful arts and business, the most excellent talents will be delighted solely by literary leisure, and even those who are endowed with moderate or no talent will decide to consume their life in literature and to procure their livelihood from this;
You might say that citizens are too much called away from action, and that, like some priestly race of Indians or Egyptians, they are rendered wholly devoted to contemplation, unwarlike:
Just as we see that bookish scholars are utterly unfit for practical affairs, and are timid, and ready not with their hand, nor even with their tongue, but only with their pen:

Indeed, you might say that even literature itself is turned to base profit, and that the disciplines are corrupted by the trifles of half-learned men who live wretchedly, and by the mass of volumes composed more by fingers than conceived by a deep mind.
Then, although in literature nothing is small, and even the smallest things cannot be neglected without danger of error, nevertheless some things are greater than others;

But if more is attributed to those things which are lesser, which happens not rarely in the handling of literature, in this respect also too much is done, and that in such a way that at the same time little and not worth the effort is accomplished, because the highest matters and universal notions are placed after trifles, and very many, exclusively occupied with certain individual things, no longer strive to comprehend with a great mind that immense orb of their discipline, as far as it can be done through the weakness of mortals:
Indeed, there are those who teach that in literature, as in the workshops of artisans, a great deal is accomplished by the distribution of the work to be done.
Although I may grant that this is most correctly said about the collecting of the material of knowledge, yet I doubt whether it can be applied to knowledge itself.
However it may be, certainly who would deny that learned labors can be divided too much?
Finally, in the scholastic instruction itself, a just measure can be departed from.

Since, in my opinion at least, it (the academic profession) ought to have set before itself the goal of training students not for the practice of some particular kind of business or literature, but of forming them with a liberal education, and of making them fit for taking up with profit that discipline which each one will have chosen in accordance with the bent of his nature; at the same time, to imbue them with those studies which, as Cicero says, accompany youth, delight old age, adorn prosperity, and offer refuge and solace in adversity:

The teacher will err who has decided to open to beginners the inner sanctuaries of some recondite discipline, in which he himself is zealously engaged, which they cannot penetrate unless many other things are set aside, or who burdens them with that apparatus and those so-called instruments of the art, which are not needed for a liberal education, but for practicing and performing the art itself.
But you may easily cut away these excesses, when they have arisen in a body of literature that is, as it were, full of sap.
It is more difficult to come to the aid of those who languish in leanness and torpor.
And lest the people be enervated by an idle life, a prey to every most valiant barbarian, let him exercise them in warfare and not allow them to become slothful.

Therefore, as in ancient republics, it has been most wisely established in this state that the citizen and the soldier be the same person, and that all be thoroughly disciplined by the training of the camp.
so that all may be ready to defend that same fatherland, which is the mother of all,
hence it comes about that this empire is military in the manner in which it ought to be:

at the same time, you may see that those who are placed in command of the troops are so trained by learning that, just as educated young men serve as soldiers, so not a few of the military leaders are found to be most learned, and we are distinguished by a perfect harmony of wisdom and courage.

But if, with Demosthenes, it is permissible to assign to states a certain and peculiar fortune, and I believe the philosophers will not deny it, this seems to me to be the good fortune of this commonwealth above others, that, endowed with moderate resources, free from luxury, it excels in the strength of intellect and arms:

But just as fields sown with different crops in alternate years are more fertile, so that city has at intervals shone more brightly now in arms, now in learning, until it was strengthened by the union of both virtues.

For to pass over the earlier princes of the royal house, Frederick William the Great Elector, although he was also kindly disposed to letters by founding the University of Duisburg, was nevertheless more ennobled by military glory;
Frederick III, the first king thereafter, most splendidly supported the fine arts;
His son was devoted to the army;
But the great Frederick won both laurels:

And Frederick William, whom we today with grateful mind acknowledge was given to us by divine providence, after he overcame the adverse fortune not of this empire but of the whole world, which had also seized this in its due share, both restored the kingdom by war and adorned it excellently with the arts of peace:

He himself, equally skilled in military and civil affairs, brave and gentle, temperate and moderate, and with the same temperance governing the various parts of the state, and at the same time frugal and not given to luxury, seems to me to demonstrate that the fortune of the Prussian empire, which I mentioned, was entirely innate in him.
Nor does he do anything from desire for glory;
And so whatever he excels in through the arts, he does without ostentation, by which not a few princes are led.

When I consider this, I hardly dare to touch upon one point, which nevertheless seems to me to remain for completing the argument, namely whether from wars or from literature greater fame accrues to the state.
And about this matter indeed I do not doubt much.
For compared with deeds and great exploits, I judge both poems and the works of painters and sculptors and the private studies and discoveries of learned men, however excellent, to be lesser.
Nothing is more noble than for a brave man to be ready to redeem victory with his life.
For this opinion I have as a supporter Plutarch, a man among the few learned, and he also in public affairs to some extent distinguished.

For since no city was more distinguished in arts and disciplines than Athens, at the same time those (arts) were so equipped both with frequency of commerce and with military power, that from the three kinds of life, which we mentioned above, they were most suitably mixed;

Nevertheless, the philosopher of Chaeronea thought it should be asked whether the Athenians were more famous for war or for wisdom, and he did not fear to claim the greater praise for the martial valor of the Athenians, not daring to prefer marble statues, painted panels, tragic and comic performances, the frenzy of dithyrambs, the discourses of philosophers, the force and elegance of orators to the expeditions, battles, and toils endured with the greatest boldness and constancy, and to the trophies of Marathon, Plataea, and Salamis.

And not undeservedly, at the end of his little commentary, he seems to scorn the sophistical care applied to trifles by Isocrates, preferring Chabrias and Iphicrates, because while they were winning Greece for their fatherland by victories, he, idle at home, would twist the curls of his oratory, and would spend the ninth part of a very long life—as the philosopher of Chaeronea says, that is, nearly three Olympiads, the number of years in which Pericles built the Hecatompedon and the Propylaea—in revising the words of the Panegyricus, more than a soldier fears the sound of arms, the clash of phalanxes, and wounds, fearing lest he should clash a vowel with a vowel, or utter a member, as they call it, shorter by one syllable.
Yet literature and the arts also shine most widely and endure most long;
By them no less than by arms are peoples captured and, as it were, reduced to subjection;
and the glory of arms is fleeting and not destined to last, unless writers, poets, sculptors, painters have added to it permanence by their own proclamation.
The fame of the ancient generals would not be so great, had not distinguished authors matched their deeds with words;

The city of the Athenians would not be preferred to Sparta and to Rome itself, which accomplished much greater things through its generals and forces, unless you had been the teacher of the whole world.
The Augustan age would not have become so famous, unless the most joyful flower of literature had come to it.
The kingdom of the Ptolemies would not be more celebrated than the equally powerful Seleucids, unless they had favored the learned more.
The arts and literature brought greater praise to the Medici family than did its deeds in war.
And not by arms but by learning, such as it was, the French have conquered Europe since Louis the Fourteenth.

And the Greeks once subdued the world with letters, and spread their language into Italy and the Gauls, beyond the pillars of Hercules and to the Cimmerian Bosporus, into Persia, to the Syrians, into Egypt and Libya and Ethiopia; and long after their republics had perished, the lights of their genius survived, from which the new nations kindled the torch of the best studies.
And to their late descendants, as once by the Romans, so now also by all good men, on account of these services of our ancestors to us ourselves, honor is paid, and we pray for all the best things.
Indeed, in Germany itself a small town, because it fostered with exceptional kindness and friendship the chief ornaments of the fatherland's literature, has gained no small fame:

This house, among other examples, I name with the more ready goodwill, because from it the royal family has been increased by two most noble mothers of families, of whom the one has already borne offspring to the stock, the other, as a new bride, very recently entered this city amid the distinguished zeal of the citizens.

And to the grandfather of these matrons, indeed, it had happened by a rare favor of fortune that into his lifetime fell the crop of sublime talents, which, as young men, were to mature and perfect the literature of the Germans.
Since these qualities were lacking in the young Frederick the Great, it was only in his old age that he prophesied the future virtues of native learning.
But we pray that they may never fail Frederick William, who may be able to satisfy his magnanimous plans at home and in war, and under his auspices may increase the state with the best things.

Since he, although vigorous, does not delight in war, nor uses it except for the protection of his country, may that pleasant peace, most flourishing in arts and disciplines, befall him, so that he may rest from his former hardships, and enjoy the love and prosperity of his citizens, of which he himself is the author, and enjoy domestic happiness, by which we all know he is especially blessed, and recently, when his daughter, returned from the throne of the united West and East to her natal home, was given back for some time to her most beloved father, we saw him not without the common joy of the city.

Finally, may God, the Best and Greatest, grant that all those things happen to Frederick William which correspond most fully to his own will, to the wishes of the citizens, to the prayers of all good men, and lastly to the growth of the republic and to the greatness of the Augustan house.

div.head: XVIII. Oratio nataliciis Friderici Guilelmi III. celebrandis d. III. m. Aug. a. MDCCCXXX. habita.
On the kinship of letters and the arts

p.s: The day that gave to this republic the best king, dear to everyone, most serene Prince, heir to the throne, most distinguished auditors of all ranks, that festive day is observed annually by the whole people with the same feeling of devotion, because Frederick William with the same perpetual affection pursues the citizens, with the same constancy protects and strengthens the welfare of the republic, peace dispensing all good things, public and domestic resources, the strength of the army, the flower of arts and letters, and finally all common advantages of all, and any private advantages of individuals.
Thus the King, with steadfast counsels and a sure hand holding the reins, guides the Prussian state in an even course.

But if nothing of great new increments were to accrue to the state, nothing singular and preeminently excellent would attract our minds, the ordinary tenor of royal goodness itself would suffice for nourishing the zeal of the citizens.
But that evenness, which I mentioned, implanted in the Prince's mind and propagated from the Prince into the state, has nothing indolent:
motion accompanies quiet;

By this moderation it is brought about that, as the seeds gradually grow, everything that is best matures with a tranquil progress, and once matured, by its own excellence draws the eyes of all others to itself, and from this new nourishment for the gratitude owed to the Prince flows into our hearts.
Now in what year the great work was, if not completed, at least advanced, by the care or kindness of Frederick William, what should we consider more than that very thing?
Of course, just as one face appears whole in each of many mirrors placed before it, so the same virtue of the Prince who governs all things is seen undivided in different matters;
and it will be pleasing to observe it especially in that matter which at every time is, as it were, more present.
Indeed, the arts and sciences were already excellently nurtured by the Prussian kings even before that most recent and fatal destruction of the state:

But Frederick William, having undertaken greater things afterwards, when the fatherland had scarcely been restored, brought literature, which had previously been hidden in the academy and gymnasia, into the light of this university in his own city, and placed it in the palace nearest to his own residence.
Soon, with the power of the kingdom restored, he founded a treasury of the arts, that famous Museum, opposite the royal citadel, the seat of the empire.
Behold, literature and the arts are most splendidly placed among the ornaments of the princely court!
And indeed our affairs have long been flourishing;

They have survived the fierce and glorious wars along with the other parts of the state, of which we were participants, as the monument conspicuous in this senate-house testifies, and they have grown beyond expectation into the frequency of citizens:

But as for the arts, although an excellent school was established long ago, and they have already been approved by their splendid works, nevertheless this new institution adds a crowning touch to them by the abundance and variety of its resources.
Nor indeed is it of no importance for literature that the arts flourish;
for both, as if related by birth, proceed to almost the same ultimate end by a path however different, and the one owes much to the other:
so that whichever state favors the one and neglects the other seems to take insufficient thought for both:
only by joining both together will you have perfected human culture.

Since it seems not foreign to the solemnity of this day, as the King fosters both with equal care, nor to this place and our person, to set forth the kinship of both, let it be permitted to me to dwell a little on this matter, not that I may investigate the most splendid subject with a subtle and sufficient philosophical discussion, but that, although unequal to greater things, mindful of my oratorical duty, I may contribute something plausible, not so much exhausting as tasting the sum of things.

For those who are exclusively occupied with exploring and representing the corporeal nature of things, which is subject to the senses, unless you would call these empty pastimes of the human intellect, I see no other ultimate goal than something divine, from which they proceed, which they explain, and to which they return.

But did not these [arts and letters] emerge, like a mother goddess from the sea waves, from that deep fountain of religions, which you could not measure with any plumb line, not only among the nations of the East, which have scarcely ever left the cradle of learning, but also among the Greeks, who were the authors of purer science and more refined art, and also among the Christian peoples themselves, at the time when they began to cultivate letters and arts?
Do not even now individuals, who approach literature and the arts rightly, are they not driven at the first moment by a divine instinct, without which nothing excellent is begun and completed?

This is that wonderful love of the deepest things, which you do not yet know but have divined, to be sought with tireless zeal, the guide and parent of discovering the true and the beautiful, of science and art.
This reason, innate in mortals, strives to comprehend by thought and the bonds of concepts what it first divined not without admiration and a joyful awe of the divine;
And the very particle of the divine breath, since like is known by like, recognizes in universal nature and in human affairs the supreme mind pervading all things, in which alone truth resides.

But into however many parts science is divided and descends, whatever and of whatever kind it treats, whether the hidden principles of the universe, the forms and forces of natural things, the life and constitution of a strong or sick body, or the recesses of the human mind and the laws of thinking and feeling, whether numbers and figures expressed in space, whether the recondite causes of speech and languages, sacred and public affairs, and customs and laws, and whatever things have been done at home and abroad, and whatever other human things there are:

Since universities are accustomed to embrace the very broad circle of all these things, ours especially shows even to the less attentive, by the number of teachers and schools that it has, how manifold and varied the disciplines are:
Finally, whatever work is diligently placed by scholars in the study of visible things, common and trivial, and which do not seem able to be reduced to definite principles;

Nevertheless, we must refer everything to the notions of the mind, and even in those things that fall under the senses, we must search out the traces of divine and human intellect impressed upon them, valuing the greater ones more highly, but not being so disgusted even with the lesser ones, which often bring unexpected light to the greater, to the point that we are unwilling for letters to have their own painters of filth and artisans of detail and fabricators of the tiniest works, such as Myrmecides and Callicrates, sculptors, once were, not without nature as their author, which itself takes pleasure in constructing even the most subtle things with the greatest care.
But to avoid lingering too long over literature, what do the arts attempt to achieve?
By the images, he says, which they fashion, they move our hearts.
But they do not merely move;

They even raise us up and fill us with the noblest sensations, leading us from these sordid concerns of daily life to something that rises above the human, is placed above mortal things, and is adumbrated in those very images, both revealed and concealed, with matter, as it were translucent, affording access to that eternal beauty which lies hidden within, to those whose sight is not blunted by the contemplation of earthly things alone:
What is impenetrable to reason is nevertheless conceived by the imagination of the mind.

Indeed, the perfect artist in every genre, endowed with the poetic power of generating beauty, which both Plato taught to be common to all arts, and Simonides of Ceos had long before indicated, when he declared that painting is silent poetry and poetry is speaking painting, represents in his work the innate vital and immortal form of each thing, which philosophers call the idea, comprehended by that imagination I mentioned, with scarcely any other aid, in which the soul is wonderfully fused with those things that you perceive through the senses.

Whether it uses words and thoughts woven together in verse, or the rhythms and harmony of sounds, or movement through figures and gestures, or the aids of statuary, sculpture, engraving, or of lines and light and shadow and colors, so that it may clothe the soul with a body.
This soul, the governor of nature, nowhere appears more excellently than in the human form and face, both the temple and image of the divine power;
From his face shines forth, gathered together, whatever of the divine mind is diffused through the whole universe.
Therefore, in expressing especially the human form, sculpture and painting, which according to the plan of our discourse we will be able to consider most, achieve that which is proposed for the arts.

But it is not proposed to imitate slavishly natural and common forms, but to show in beautiful forms that which is more beautiful than anything else, the soul and mind, which penetrates the external appearance:
For the mind is beauty itself, dwelling in and illuminating these earthly things, which are called beautiful, just as the soul dwells in our body.

It is, I say, that which Diotima of Mantinea beheld, the beauty of an admirable nature, for the sake of which, whoever has been led by the love of beauty has undertaken all the earlier labors of knowing it, which neither comes to be nor perishes, neither grows nor is wasted away, but is everlasting and eternal, by itself, with itself, uniform and simple, pure and unalloyed, by participation in which all things that appear beautiful are beautiful, but in such a way that, as these are born or perish, it itself remains undefiled by mortal contagion.

And so knowledge and art, though close in origin, although they employ different powers, different action and work, and are occupied with things most diverse in appearance, yet in reality are similar in their own nature; both strive to behold the heavenly and eternal in earthly and perishable examples, to trace these back to that, and to immerse the minds of men in that.

With what zeal they come to the aid of the most burning desires of mortals, and as ministers of blessedness itself they lead to the highest good, which the philosopher seems not without reason to seek in the absolute conjunction of the beautiful and the true and of measure or proportion.
Indeed, not even the forces by which each acts are so opposed to each other that in science there is no place for imagination, or in art for reason;

But that [knowledge] is also necessary for that [person], lest the science be killed by the thinness of formulas; this [knowledge] is necessary for the arts, so that the artist, while he makes the work, may at the same time understand what and how he makes it.
But here someone may object:
You indeed, imbued with Platonic precepts, say that something sublime is set before the arts;

Or has he forgotten how strongly the same wise man, who alone embraced the knowledge of the purest concepts, condemns the talent of the arts, because they are wholly contained in imitation, and that too of things often not the best;
because they render images of images, shadows of shadows:
because poets, ignorant of what they invent, are drawn without reason by an alien force, as if by a Magnesian stone?
Does he not boast of the inveterate and perpetual dissension between philosophy and poetry?

Does he not censure the divine Homer, the teacher of Greece, to whom even Phidias owed the image of Olympian Jupiter, for many reasons, and especially because he instills into men the excessive emotions of the mind, recommended by the most illustrious examples, even of the gods, together with all comedy and tragedy, than which art can produce nothing more magnificent, and drives him out of the perfect state, adorned with crowns and anointed with ointments?
Indeed, a man by no means last in judging the beautiful, on whom Winkelmann himself depends, did not throw out these and similar remarks carelessly;

and I see that Friedrich Schiller, although an excellent poet, once warned to some extent similar things, though arranged differently according to the character of the age, in the essay which he wrote on the necessary limits to be set to the use of beautiful forms.
For if the arts serve only the senses, flattering lust and desire, delighting the eyes, tickling the ears, which they do not infrequently;
they oppress rather than lift up the mind:

Nor would I deny that Homeric poetry, which is engaged in vividly presenting things that fall under the senses and in most truthfully describing the emotions of the mind, contributed much to the result that the minds of the Greeks, which were spontaneously inclined in that direction, were more and more delighted with external appearance, and that the desires to which the mortal race is subject were nourished.
Since Plato was more keenly affected by this inconvenience, being present and in the midst of those men,
Posterity admires the judgment, the causes of which, being very far removed from that age by times and condition, they no longer perceive themselves.

Just as they wonder what it is that he in civil affairs favors the aristocrats, and is hostile to popular rule, since they are no longer oppressed by those evils by which at that time the best men were undoubtedly afflicted.

Nevertheless, I would readily concede that a wise man, wholly occupied with philosophy and turned to contemplate those pure and simple exemplars of things which are comprehended by reason alone, would have shown himself a stricter censor of the arts, since he would not wish them to be seen in other images except those which the father of the universe himself had fashioned.
But that philosopher, who combines the deepest knowledge with the highest piety and incomparable charm, would not have spurned the Jupiter and Minerva of Phidias.
He would not have spurned the sanctity of the Virgin Mother of God, transferred from the mind of Urbinate onto the panel.
Again, so that you may be less unfair than Plato to the arts, you would not deny that in cultivating and esteeming them one can go even to the point of vice.
For he who attributes more to imagination, the mother and offspring of the arts, than to reason, in acting easily deviates from the right path;
Moreover, a slothful veneration of images clings especially to those ceremonies that love to subject knowledge to authority, and the zeal for seeking truth to light credulity.
Thus with the very aids of the arts, superstition spread clouds over minds.
Now reason has scattered these.
Those who have been enlightened by its light, why should they not, being secure, reverence God present in images?
Are the statues to be torn down and broken, because there were those who abused them?
Therefore even wisdom will have to go into exile, because it has turned into sophistry.

Let us rather rejoice that the Prince, distinguished by genuine holiness and piety, scorns that harsh and gloomy sadness, for which religion is to gaze upon a painted picture, and equally the barbarous disdain for knowledge that has seized some who call themselves pious, and has begun to restore their ornaments to the temples as well.
So far I have passed over one topic, which concerns the emotions of the mind.
Why, indeed?

For since all art, like poetry, must above all represent those emotions, because it requires action, and in any action the mind is more or less stirred, in that stirring the whole character of human nature and its innermost recesses are laid open:

If art consists solely in the imitation of desires, and especially of the worse ones, and does not diminish but increases and intensifies them even in the hearts of spectators or listeners, as Plato generally assumed;
That reproach seems to stick and cannot be washed away.
But I do not think even this is true;

Art rather, while it expresses the aroused and agitated passions, partly aims at something greater in them, namely the mind, which acts through their peculiar force and virtue, and partly soothes and calms them in the listener or spectator.

This is, if I am not mistaken, that celebrated purgation of the disturbances of the mind, which Aristotle attributes to poetry and music, meeting, I think, the Platonic doctrines with rather obscure words:

Although fortune has denied us the richer explanation of this matter that he himself promised, nevertheless from his Politics you may understand, according to his opinion, that just as those who are driven by sacred frenzy, having used sacred songs, are calmed and composed, having obtained medicine and purification, so those who are prone to fear or pity, or generally to disturbances of the soul, having tasted these emotions by watching, are relieved with pleasure and purified, being to some extent released from them.
Although this can happen in many ways, and Aristotle seems to have aimed at nothing other than a remedy from homeopathy, which is properly referred to the emotions of the mind:

You will at least concede, listeners, whether in tragedies or in painting or sculpture, which can approach tragedy most closely, as Niobe and her children show, that they arouse pity and fear, and at the same time produce perfect artists, so that the minds of the spectators are not overwhelmed by compassion and horror, but that, while you fear, while you pity, you feel the same thing, that those heroes who have endured misfortunes are superior to this softness of our pity and fear, and that by enduring with lofty and unconquered mind they have escaped the chances of this fleeting life, just as the divine savior of the human race, in portraying whom artists have rightly labored much, overcame the pains of death, and that nothing perished with his desires and through them except that which they had drawn from mortal contagion, the divine breath returning to the place from which it had set out.
Is this, then, a very slight purification of disturbances?
Does not art, rather, in this its moral character also emulate science, which, moderating and restraining desires, teaches what is to be sought or avoided, what is to be borne or pitied?
Finally, the dignity of art and science is the same, because each has its end in itself, and is not valued by common utility.
Since no one does not concede this concerning the works of artisans:
For who has ever demanded or even now demands that a statue by Polyclitus or Lysippus, or a painting by Raphael or Antonio Correggio, should serve any other purpose than to please by its beauty?

Nevertheless, we often hear it reproached to literature, and especially by those who govern states, with the greatest injustice, that it is too much occupied with things that offer no practical use for life.
But I think that what is useful by its own nature for forming and elevating the mind, namely the true and the beautiful, is most useful for the human race.

But if literature and the liberal arts at the same time serve conveniently for procuring the necessities of life more correctly and easily, for aiding the crafts, and for furnishing the state and the household better and more splendidly;
which also no one doubts that they excel in;
I do not think that this is to be demanded from them as a debt, but that it is to be received with a grateful mind as spontaneously born.
Just as learning and the arts have never ceased to strive to return the due favor to the states, princes, and private individuals by whom they have been aided.
Who among us is there who does not greatly rejoice that the most excellent men, whom Frederick William's sound judgment placed over our affairs, think the same way?

Now we rejoice no less in the arts for this reason, either because the resources had to be acquired at great expense and it is fitting that the most beautiful things be arranged most splendidly, and also because aid was given with even more distinguished generosity and splendor by a most munificent king.
When I name him, I do not wish anything to be taken away from the praises of our ancestors.

We know that a not inconsiderable part of the furniture was collected at private expense by the earlier princes of the Brandenburg house, Joachim II, Frederick William the Great Elector, Frederick I and II, and by the most merciful King's father, over nearly three centuries.
These things I do not enumerate individually, because I judge that the orator's duty differs from a mere listing of names.
Certainly we owe very many resources to this King, to whom this day is sacred.

Who, even if he had not added so many and such splendid works, would nevertheless be said to have obtained the palm, because he brought together into one the scattered ornaments of palaces and villas, consulting the common good, making private things public.
While these things were being gathered together, it was understood that a house, however spacious, would not suffice even for a carefully selected complete equipment:

From there, besides the plaster casts, an excellent aid to studies, and other things to be preserved separately, the monuments of Egyptian antiquity have been left in a city garden situated not far away, where we see whatever that clever and industrious people fabricated for the adornment of their domestic and daily worship, as if snatched from the underworld, together with the most ancient images of the gods, not yet having been rendered with the beauty of the human form according to the Greek manner, but hard, stiff, and grim, so that they might be even more significant by their monstrosity.

But on the field, once trampled by military exercises and the crowd of pagans, which is now cultivated with trees planted in the form of a garden, and soon to be irrigated by a spring of water of extraordinary height, where also that great bowl, hewn from native rock and polished, will be placed, a magnificent house of the arts occupies the ground snatched from the river, rising on high with a lofty portico of eighteen huge columns, conspicuous also for its acroteria.

The lower floors will contain the precious ancient and new coinage, which in its little images represents the course and changes of the whole plastic art, a cabinet of gems with casts and descriptions, and one made most famous by the very name of Johann Winkelmann alone;
They will contain a very rich collection of highly elegant painted vases, restored to the light from the darkness of tombs;
I do not speak of the bronze and clay seals of various kinds, lamps, and other manifold utensils of the ancients.

When you have ascended, you will enter the rotunda, whose roof is surmounted by a bold arch, surrounded by twenty columns of artificial stone, between which, however they shine, the marble statues of the gods, although worn by the rust of age, nevertheless gleam with their own splendor;

The remaining rooms adjoin, supported by columns of various colors of the same material, displaying statues of gods and heroes and statues of men, along with herms and breastplates, with reliefs suitably arranged on the walls:

until in the recess you come to the one new work that has been brought in, the laurel-crowned conqueror of Europe, who, had he not fallen by the great counsels of Frederick William and by our arms and those of our allies, this house would not stand, nor would it be filled with the decorations that he had carried off.
Now, with the intolerable power of the great man abolished, he himself is placed among the ancients.

I am not afraid that I may seem to have disparaged the merits of our Princes, if I say in passing that these excellent forces, among which one youthful statue of a worshiper in bronze is to be compared to a great number, cannot be compared with the wealth of Italy:
not to mention that we should ever equal that people of gods, who once inhabited Greece.

We read with wonder that even in the age of Roman domination, when the flower of Greece had long since faded, Athens alone contained three thousand statues, and as many Olympia, Delphi, and Rhodes, which was adorned even with a hundred colossal statues;
Even the fierce Aetolian people had so many statues at Thermus, where they used to assemble, that the Macedonians destroyed two thousand statues there.
And what shall we say of Rome, the capital of the world?
What great quantities did the Marcelli, Quinctii, Fulvii, Aemilii, Mummii, and Sullae amass from conquered foreign nations!
Three thousand statues were brought by Marcus.
Scaurus, when aedile, displayed them in a temporary theater;
Sixty thousand, they report, were returned to Roman soil by those who made modest calculations.

Piety, old-fashioned frugality at home, public munificence, and finally the long-continued practice of workshops enriched Greece above all with so many ornaments; how great this was, you may infer from the fact that Lysippus alone is said to have made fifteen hundred works, and that three hundred and sixty statues, of which many were equestrian or stood on chariots or bigae, were set up by the Athenians for Demetrius of Phalerum, completed in less than three hundred days.

Let us be satisfied if, from the immense shipwreck, some examples have been brought to this northern region, not snatched away, but well acquired, so that we may behold the perfection of the art of the ancient sculptors, which our artists now successfully emulate.
And what we possess, the King's kindness increases, and will increase.

But what lights and how great are spread before the eyes, when you have approached the most ample treasury of paintings, which stores the illustrious documents of revived art, breathing the milder genius of Christian worship!

Here the whole world of the noblest art, from the austere beginnings of the Byzantine and Tuscan brush, with the works of artists of every kind set before one, of Italians, Germans, Belgians, not with the paintings of different ages and schools confused, but with each suitably joined, lies open to the view.
Here majesty dwells together with the Graces and all charms.
Soon these things will find those by whom they may be worthily proclaimed;
There are among you most discerning judges of all elegance:
I fall silent.
Often we hear in the circles of not inelegant men it being reproached to this royal city that it has no antiquity.
Truly great is the glory in the monuments of the virtues of parents;
but that is a greater reproach:
Once there were vigorous Milesians.
There are those for whom nothing is venerable except ruins;
The rust of the Middle Ages, which they long for, does not seem to me to sit well on this republic.
Our antiquity is recent;

This kingdom did not take its growth in the age of papal or imperial power, but with both broken, and only in the last century was it so strengthened by the virtue of Frederick the Great that it could hold its place among the more powerful states by the strength of its intellect and its remaining vigor.

Those who in that century gave new life and form to literature and the arts, for the most part either born or received into this empire—Leibniz, Christian Wolff, Kant, Fichte, and that restorer of the arts, John Winckelmann, full of divine inspiration.
Other nations grow, others diminish, says he;
Have we not been better provided for, in that we live in the dawn of a rising greatness rather than in the twilight of a declining one?
Therefore it is our duty not to be astonished at ancient things.

And if we must use ancient examples (and we certainly must), we will no more confine ourselves to ancient matters than distinguished men in any field are kept out of this state because they were born abroad.
The King judges as ours whoever are intelligent.
He strives to win them over to us, if it can be done.
All antiquity is ours, from which we may draw, which we may enjoy.

This the most wise Prince sets before the students of the arts, that by the sight of excellent works the eyes and minds may be trained, that a stimulus may be added to the artists, not those who imitate earlier works, but those who wish to learn from ancient masters, having been taught to dare new things by their own strength:
In the same way, learning and philosophy itself were not more roused from their slumber and corrected by anything else than by the revival of ancient literature, which had lain neglected.
Thus indeed each later age receives the light transmitted from the earlier one together with life, not to rest idly in what has been handed down, but to draw new fruits from what it has received.
For neither, when I say that we should not be fixed in the old as if in a stupor, do I say with impunity that the excellent things which earlier ages produced are to be despised;

The arts themselves are evidence, which in the previous century, having abandoned the footsteps of their ancestors, had so degenerated that the most cultivated princes lacked talents that could produce what the age could bear.
Now, for those who have entered upon a more correct path, the magnanimous studies of Frederick William come to their aid in a timely manner:
He who, because he wishes Prussia to be deprived of no praise, devotes unwearied care equally to all parts of both the state and of human culture.
May God preserve him, his devout worshiper, safe, and keep him for us as long as possible.

May God favor his undertakings in such a way that both he himself and those who now live may reap the fruit of his plans, and since the best men at the same time look out for posterity, may not only the present outcome prove the excellence of his well-begun works, but also the late success and the judgment of future generations, so that our descendants may one day hold the memory of Frederick William as sacred and dear as we love and venerate him while he survives.
May God hold these prayers as valid, as they have been conceived by us piously and sincerely.

div.head: XIX. Oratio nataliciis Friderici Guilelmi III. celebrandis d. III. m. Aug. a. MDCCCXXXI. habita.
On the mutual affection existing between prince and people

p.s: Last year, my listeners, when on the most joyful birthday of Frederick William I spoke in this assembly, the first news of that enormous upheaval had scarcely reached us, by which, after the fatal error of the Bourbon king, or whatever name one may wish to call that most ruinous undertaking, stirred up the undisciplined mass of the urban multitude against the praetorians and the remaining soldiers, the leading city of the Gauls, polluted with slaughter and blood, and within the space of a few days stripped of the ancestral kingdom, driven from the ancestral soil, that family which a few decades earlier our armies and those of the allies had established and stabilized once and again with most fierce battles and much blood.

On that day, when the state of affairs was still perfectly calm and there was the utmost peace, how few were there who understood in what great matters we were placed at the very threshold and entrance!
But what a change meanwhile invaded nearly all of Europe!
How many misfortunes, discords, seditions, battles, disasters harassed the peace, if this is to be called peace, which daily threatens war!
You would say that the world was shaken and knocked from its hinges, that all the furies of civil war were let loose from the underworld.
For after the Gauls had conquered themselves by a disastrous slaughter, the turbulent populace of the Belgians was inflamed with madness:
By the slaughter at Brussels the forces of the Batavians were broken;
The most populous and wealthiest cities of Belgium, the strongest and best-equipped citadels, into which the allies had expended great sums, fail;

Finally, after the king, who had shown his justice, fairness, and goodness to every good man, was spurned with the utmost audacity, the Belgians were separated from the Batavians, so that they might satisfy their anger and the hatred conceived long ago and nourished with much skill.
Soon the same movement drew in part of Germany, which had been most faithful to its princes for a long time;
The duke of Brunswick was driven out by his citizens, after the citadel itself was burned;
There was disturbance among the Chatti and among the Saxons.
Now indeed, while the Prussian kingdom remains inviolate,
(For who would count the Aachen uprising, subdued by the citizens themselves, or those nocturnal revels in our city?) Discord leapt over toward the East:
With a fierce and immense force the Poles blazed up, already ruined by mutual slaughter;
The rebellion spread widely through Lithuania and to the farthest Sarmatia.
Not even the Swiss cantons remained quiet;
The kingdom of Hanover was also disturbed, which had never been governed more innocently, the origin having arisen from the most celebrated seat of learning, which owes many benefits to kings.
Several provinces of Italy were stirred up and were immediately settled by foreigners.
Britain itself, which seemed secure in its ancient laws and institutions, was driven by tumults and factions to the point that the question of reforming the form of the republic was discussed.
What shall I say about the Spaniards and the Lusitanians, whom domestic discord has not yet ceased to harass?
They have already forgotten Greece, being occupied with nearer and their own troubles.
Among these things, armies of nearly all Europe have been prepared with enormous expenses, not indeed for undertaking war, but for maintaining peace.
And lest the peoples of Europe alone should be afflicted with those calamities of which they themselves are the authors, nature, laboring by divine impulse, presses upon us.
From the foul cradle of Asia burst forth a dreadful plague, spread more widely day by day along the routes of armies and trade, and now it has entered our borders as well.

Since this year has brought such great declines of public and private fortune, at which it is no wonder if even the most steadfast are disturbed, would that my voice were so eloquent that with that consolation, which is almost the only one left, and which is uniquely suited and, as it were, proper to these most sacred solemnities, I might soothe the sad memory of evils and cheer your minds on this day, the most abundant source of joy for me, for you, and for the whole fatherland!

For if we consider what it is that our fatherland, along with a few lands, has remained at least free from civil disturbances and perfectly peaceful, although some new provinces, and those scattered over the longest distances, are not only near in situation but also joined by natural kinship to those peoples who have either fallen completely into madness, or have been not moderately affected by the desire for new things:
What is offered to us first but the image of Frederick William, which, like the Dioscuri, calmed the storm and the waves with its serenity, and the state?

Indeed, Frederick William held together what could have fallen apart, not so much by the strength of armies, whose help is unsafe in civil unrest, as by those arts which alone you may apply with success even to fervent minds;
He came to the aid of his people in good time, that is, before it was demanded, by lightening burdens of every kind, by removing those things which are hateful to the peoples.
He provided for necessities, so that medicine should not be prepared too late.

He bound and occupied minds with good deeds, so that they were convinced that he wanted nothing except the happiness of citizens, and that he did not look out for himself and his own power, but for the common welfare.

Finally, both by his administration of the state and by his other virtues, by which he also won for himself the admiration and reverence of foreigners, he brought it about that the citizens loved him equally, just as they both felt and knew that they were loved by him.

Indeed it happens even to the best princes that they are not repaid by the people with the gratitude they deserve, either because factious men with various goads render the citizens hostile to the prince, or because different and unsociable peoples have been imprudently united under one master, and one of them spurns him;
Nevertheless, you will find no firmer or more certain pledge of public tranquility than that character of the prince by which the mutual love of the ruler and the parents is fostered.
This the splendid character of Frederick William provides for this kingdom;
this is that consolation with which we are especially delighted, and it is so implanted in your hearts that I bring it forth not more from my own than from your breasts;
This is the public happiness of Prussia, which will be enjoyed as long as these princes rule over us, and the people, most loving of their kings, will preserve their faith whole and uncorrupted.
This, whatever evils press upon it, alone will not perish, and it is not consumed by scarcity or high price of grain, nor by diseases, nor by wars;
Indeed, it will alleviate whatever inconveniences, as long as the prince helps the citizens and the citizens help the prince:
Just as about twenty years ago we overcame the most serious times of the republic and completed the greatest wars through mutual harmony and common steadfastness.
It pleases those skilled in civil affairs and the rulers of empires themselves that peoples and kingdoms are held together by agreements.

Indeed, since many kingdoms have been brought together by force of arms, but arms and force are contrary to law, unless the sanctity of treaties and of an oath has been added, victors and vanquished will not coalesce into any civil bond.
But those treaties, in establishing which only necessity presided, are found to be not void in fact, so that they are firm by law:
And so those things, as you may see daily, are changed and abolished by a new agreement, when another necessity presses again.
But love, true and wise indeed, not feigned and foolish, is everlasting;
by which kingdoms are founded much more securely.
Thus the foundation and bond of the family is love, not a contract:
surely it would have been ill for marriage, ill for parents and children, if they were held together by a contract, not by love:

And just as a state, whose image the family reproduces as if in a very small form, when it has grown from primitive simplicity into a more perfect condition, changes the appearance of the family, nevertheless when the mutual love of prince and citizens has perished, the vital force is extinguished, the light of the state is put out.
By agreements the private affairs, by agreements the public affairs are so ordered that nevertheless without love the condition of both is unpleasant and sad.
Therefore not even the Romans, in so great a mass of empire, were unwilling that the prince be called father of the fatherland and that this honorable surname be earned;
so that he might seem to rule the state not by power alone and skill and strength of forces, but by the natural affection of a father of a family:

nor has that virtue, which is referred to the duties of the fatherland to be performed, obtained a name of whatever sort derived from the condition of a pact, but it is called affection and love of the fatherland.

Now indeed this bond of love most closely unites the nation with that prince especially, whose lineage, imbued with the ancestral institutions and customs, has contracted a familiarity with the people through a long and benign hereditary rule, has not only recently proved beneficent to them, but has inherited from its ancestors a zeal for doing good, and through its deeds has given to the state and the nation a name and glory among foreigners.

Even for this reason, how devoted and bound to Frederick William the greatest part of the Prussian people is, escapes no one who considers what those glorious ancestors accomplished, and what he himself, following in their footsteps, has done.

But if some provinces have been acquired only recently, in which that innate love is not present, besides the distinguished and manifest virtue of the Prince himself, the consensus of very many also draws these provinces, and that virtue of this empire, long since proven by the clearest examples, by which it brings it about that it attracts even foreigners by the usefulness, justice, and fairness of its institutions and makes them its own.
Thus it happens that mutual affection unites the Prince not only with the old, but also with the new Prussians, and that all judge him to be the father of the fatherland and revere him piously.
This story has often been told by many, that the Prussian state is not native, but artificial:
to me that state seems truly native, whose foundation is affection;
which falls most plainly upon our case.
For that one is especially to be regarded as natural which is closest to the family, the natural image of the state;
those which rest on agreements are artificially composed:
and for the most part agreements arise from dissensions, when the natural state has been disturbed.
But the natural state is not perfect, just as the natural man is imperfect.
I hear you:
but not even agreements and constitutions, however much they adorn the state and aid public confidence, are perfect:
And this kingdom also has some instruments of public security:
Finally, if there were only a choice between agreements without love and love without agreements, who would not prefer the latter?
It is added that benefits offered by a willing person are better than those forced:
Gratitude is not felt for things extorted by necessity.

Therefore, although there are things that are desired, the recently subjected people love Frederick William all the more ardently, because he conferred benefits on them willingly, bound by no other law than love, by which a prince is obliged to do good to the people.
It is indeed the mark of this love that nothing too harsh or violent be decreed, and that all things be conducted without deceit.
By this, kingdoms are especially strengthened.
Indeed, the memory of past events tells us that power cannot be retained for long by force.
And those who strive to circumvent their subjects with arts and cunning incur even greater hatred.

Nevertheless, many states are governed by this perverse principle, in which the prince is surrounded by cohorts of prefects, magistrates, and officials, not those who are in harmony with the subjects, but who, like a hostile army, by cunning and fear suppress those whose interests they ought to have provided for:

That our republic rests on mutual love, you may also recognize from this, that the ministers of every public kind conspire excellently in mind and counsel with those whom they govern, and are not compelled to oppose their desires.

These ministers themselves in the universities are not educated according to a prescribed formula from a master, but with liberal learning, and they are not considered mercenaries of the prince, performing servile work and caring for that Thrasymachean advantage of the more powerful, but, obeying the prince with due deference, they have this duty imposed on them: that what they understand to be best in common for the king and the people, they strive to accomplish.
Therefore, Frederick William wants intelligent men to be in charge of the state.
Hence no class of citizens is excluded from access to honors.
This is what is uniquely fitting for mutual affection.
For where a certain order of administering the state enjoys the prerogative, the rest are slaves or close to servitude;
who, even if they obey in some part, certainly do not love those in command:
and very many are offended, if the state is, as it were, the inheritance of a few.
There are, however, those who want the people to serve forever;

They, since they take care of nothing more than that the people should not become intelligent, among the other arts employ this worst art or rather force upon minds, so that they render them, as far as possible, dull, stupid, superstitious, not even refraining from sacred things, so that they may use these too for accomplishing their plans, with a purpose the more wicked the farther they are from the love which they pretend, and moreover equally foolish as if a father should wish his children to be foolish, so that they may be more obedient.
Among us there is nothing of that sort.

Our institutions of schools and churches serve to educate, enlighten, and console minds, and with few exceptions of men who shun the light, we seek a sincere, simple, and vigorous piety, such as the King excels in, not a feigned and cunning one, or one wrapped in clouds, and truly or in appearance sad.

Now I need not explain the administration of justice, in which the paternal authority of Frederick William is not missed insofar as the law, by its nature severe and inexorable, admits of mercy and yields place to the gentleness of a mild prince:
Who does not see that the administration of taxes and public revenues is directed entirely to the advantage of the people?
For neither is silver collected for the use of the royal house and court, nor is effort given to filling the private treasury of the king:
Wealth taken from the people is not used to support a life of extravagance, nor to strengthen unjust power.
But what the subjects pay is spent on public necessities and utilities, and, if anything remains, on honor.
Thus the money returns to where it was sought.
Nor are taxes imposed in such a way that as much as possible is paid, but so that the burdens are very light, and commerce and private profits are hindered as little as possible.

What of the fact that alliances with foreign states were made not without a temporary loss of revenues, as I think, only so that private individuals might have a greater and freer opportunity of acquiring wealth?

Although, however, the state also flourishes more if private citizens are not poor, nevertheless the King does not help them for this reason, that a richer profit might flow back from it to himself, just as masters or shepherds tend their flocks;
But the people, grateful, feel that he is led by fairness and love.
Finally, in no part of the state does the mutual love by which this city is held together seem to me to shine forth more than in military affairs.
For where that bond embraces the prince and the people, there is no need for mercenary soldiers, no bodyguard collected from foreigners;
Citizens will protect the king best.

Indeed, in ancient times, among the most important things by which a king and a tyrant were distinguished, this was held both by the common people and by philosophers: that the former was guarded by his own men, the latter by hired foreigners.
For the former seem to guard the prince against outsiders, the latter against citizens.
But you will also read of guards from among the natives, who are no more civil or popular.

A certain class of soldiers, not very prudently established and not properly restrained, easily becomes hostile to a well-ordered republic, to the multitude of the countryside, and to the very nobles.
This happened to the Romans in the age of the emperors.
Therefore a king who has been forced to entrust himself to such an army is far different from ours.
Among us there are no fierce cohorts of soldiers, often more troublesome to their own side than formidable to the enemy.

From the whole people, with no distinction of place where each person was born, by a most just selection, the legions are equipped, not to guard the king at home, who is most safe among his own, but to defend the fatherland from foreigners.

Nor are soldiers, as in former times, kept under the standards until old age, so that they become thoroughly hardened and inured to obedience that is hateful to themselves and to every kind of cruelty, but after a few years, when they have been properly subdued and trained, they are discharged by a lawful discharge and returned to their own people, always ready to return to the ranks at the king's command.

Whereas in former times nothing was so hateful to the pagans as serving in the army, now no one except the most cowardly refuses this honorable military service, which is not inhuman, not too burdensome.

Is this a slight proof that the Prince is dear to the citizens, that the fatherland is dear, and that private individuals do not separate their own advantage from the interests of the Prince and the fatherland?
Thus far I have considered the public counsels of Frederick William, by which mutual love has been effected, the honor and strength of the Prussian state.
But that the prince may be sufficient for all the duties of the empire:
if he, as a private person, is not equally innocent, and is not only not better, but somewhat worse than an ordinary citizen;
if at home he is either too harsh or excessively patient and indulgent;
Prodigal, and when there is leisure, given to idleness, pleasures, and delights, or on the other hand excessively stingy and gloomy;
If he is not a good father of the family, if he is harsh to his household:
Something will leak out even outside, and either his softness and secret lusts will hand him over to contempt, or his untimely severity will diminish the people's love.

The suspicious minds of the citizens, if anything adverse to the state should happen, will transfer the blame to the ruler, because he who presides badly over his own household does not seem able to preside rightly over the state, and private vices spread into the commonwealth.
Indeed, Frederick William wins the hearts of his subjects by his private virtues no less than by his public ones.
He who judges that no more license in morals should be granted to a king than to any private person.
who combines the duties of a father of a family and a prince with excellent moderation;
courteous and at the same time energetic, splendid and generous without extravagance, moderating himself for the state as much as for himself.

Finally, just as he respects the judgment of men, because he respects those whom each one loves, so the reverence for the divine power perfects the virtue of a private person, as far as is permitted to mortals.

Therefore, whether we consider the public or the private life of Frederick William, we understand that he himself is the source of that love by which I have judged the happiness of Prussia to be contained.

But if nevertheless under this king we have not been and are not free from enormous evils, if wars were waged at first unsuccessfully, then indeed successfully but so much the bloodier, from which a great mass of debt had to be contracted by the state, if in peace now scarcity of profit and sterility of the fields oppress, now fertility itself and abundance of crops and the resulting cheapness of grain press upon the owners of estates and the farmers, indeed to some even the excessive population, which agriculture, manufactures, and commerce can scarcely suffice to feed, seems to bring dangers, if at the very moment fear of war and the general agitation of minds born from so many disturbances and the savagery of a raging disease together with the intemperance of the climate torment us, and demand great expenses for the armies and for guarding the boundaries of the empire even against friends:

What else can you conclude, except that by a hidden law of fate or by the design of divine providence, evils afflict both men and nature, which no human prudence, and not even the kindness of the best prince, can guard against or heal?
This we may illustrate, not now for the first time discovered and approved, by an example, though ancient, yet, I think, not foreign to our affairs.
Certainly no ruler was ever more benevolent in spirit toward the human race, none was so merciful and gentle, as Marcus.

Antoninus the Philosopher, so beloved by all that he was called by some father, by others brother, by others son, as each one's age permitted, and at his funeral all were certain that he, lent by the gods, had returned to the gods, and with one voice the Senate and People called him a propitious god.

Indeed, he who not only had on his lips Plato's opinion that a state would be happy if either philosophers ruled or rulers philosophized, but also tried to demonstrate it by his own example, and who, although wise, did not want what pleased himself but what pleased the wisest to be ratified, declaring that it was more just that he himself should follow the counsels of so many and such friends than that so many and such friends should follow the will of one man alone—he, I say, is not to be thought to have omitted anything by which the happiness of the citizens might be furthered.
But he himself foresaw and, at the time when he was adopted into the kingdom, argued what evils the empire contained in itself:

Among these, I think that it was not the least that the world was afflicted with the greatest calamities under the prince himself, and, as an old writer says, almost nothing can be said or thought by which mortals are wont to be exceedingly tormented, that did not rage during his rule.
Nowhere is there rest from arms:
The East, Illyricum, Italy, Gaul, and Germany were afflicted by wars.
Cities were swallowed up and buried by an earthquake.

Floods of rivers pressed upon them, locusts were hostile to the fields, there was a most severe famine, and finally the greatest evil, a pestilence that rushed in with repeated and increased force over several years.

For after the Roman soldier, under the leadership of Avidius Cassius, plundered and burned Seleucia of Babylonia, a city inhabited by four hundred thousand, or as others have reported, six hundred thousand people, situated between the Tigris and the Euphrates, contrary to all law and right;

In that city, not far from the recess of the Persian Gulf, whence that disease, which has now begun to spread through Europe, entered western Asia, the plague is said to have been born, released from a narrow opening, as superstitious rumor reported, from the inner sanctuary of the temple of Apollo or from a golden chest, with a primordial stain.

Soon the pestilential breath was carried through the soldiers and the trade routes of the rivers into Mesopotamia and especially Nisibis, and from there it filled the Parthians and the whole world, Lucius.

The contagion, spreading through the armies of Verus and Cassius into all the provinces through which they were returning, polluted everything from the borders of Persia all the way to the Rhine and into the Gallic provinces with deaths, and killed nearly all the troops, and having spread throughout all Italy, also consumed at Rome many thousands of men and not a few of the nobles.
And this indeed was the state of the Roman Empire under those delights of the human race, M.
Aurelius:

Concerning this, not a contemporary, upon whom suspicion of flattery might fall, but some later person not undeservedly said that it seemed to have been granted by divine providence that, while the law of the world or of nature or whatever else unknown to men produces those evils, the counsels of the prince, as remedies, should bring relief.
Who would fear to apply the same opinion to Frederick William?

Of course, what happens even to a good prince, that, wearied by frequent experience of adversity and by cares, he relaxes his exertion and diligence, the constancy of Frederick William does not allow:
He has not become hardened to the misfortunes of his citizens;

As soon as any calamity, of whatever kind, has invaded any part of the kingdom, he strives to help each person not only when warned but of his own accord, not only mindful of his royal duty but from human feeling of compassion, bearing another's distress as if it were his own, just as a father helps his children, a brother his brother, a son his parents.
Therefore, as the Senate and People of Rome, M.

Antoninus, so we have long proclaimed that Frederick William was divinely sent to the state, and we proclaim it now especially, and we give thanks to the supreme deity, because, if our age had to endure both the unusual evils of nature and to see those things in which the state could scarcely stand firm, unless that prince reigned who would bind the minds of his people with the bond of mutual love, a king has fallen to our lot who is most just, most merciful, most kind, in whose love the state might find rest.

Finally, we make vows to God, the Best and Greatest, that Frederick William, together with his entire August house, may be preserved safe and most flourishing; that under his leadership our fatherland may be strengthened day by day with firmer and more liberal institutions; that the most sacred bond of love may not be broken by any imprudence or wickedness; that, if possible, an end may be put to the slaughters by which nations are worn away; and that peace, the nurse of arts and letters, the mother of all good things, may be confirmed, and that common fear may cease and security be restored.

div.head: XX. Oratio nataliciis Friderici Guilelmi III. celebrandis d. III. m. Aug. a. MDCCCXXXII. habita.
On propagating morals, letters, and arts through public education

p.s: Just as, when the civil year has ended, it is pleasant even for a prudent man to recall what pleasing and what adverse events the nearest course of the sun has brought, although he knows well that the motion and flux of things is neither held back nor interrupted by these boundaries which we set, but that it runs on continuously with infinite force toward its eternal goal;

Thus we, the audience, we who are bound by piety to count the years from the most auspicious birthday of Frederick William, have been accustomed in this assembly, when conducting our business, to recall especially the memory of each previous year, and to draw fresh material for rejoicing from the events most recently accomplished, which flowed in from all sides with joyful abundance.

A year ago, when I spoke from this place, my task was almost more to dispel the sad expectation of impending calamity by setting forth the virtues of our excellent King, than to speak of our prosperity:
So many evils threatened, so many disturbances took away security.
What shall I say now about this year, listeners?
Shall I judge the fierce spirits composed, or not yet composed?
Shall I speak of the victories and defeats of foreigners and civil wars, in which, whichever side was victorious, it is compelled not to afflict enemies, but its own people?
Or to stop at our own affairs, the fatal disease, which we foresaw approaching the previous year, shall I say was overcome with a small loss or a very great one?
Certainly it exhausted the public resources, certainly it snatched from the kingdom great leaders, and from us a great wise man, just as about four lustra earlier the plague had carried off Fichte.
Certainly, the attendance at our school has diminished somewhat.
But accidental losses are repaired, as long as vigor, virtue, prudence, and industry survive;

but if morals are corrupt, and ignorance and stupidity, and the barbaric injustice and harshness of the empire, have gradually and little by little brought everyone to a state of weakness, the people die with a slow wasting away.
Up to now, indeed, the world, suspended between hope and fear, trembles as to where this state of affairs is about to turn out.

Our republic, amid the general disturbance which seemed likely to bring extreme violence even to the prudent, as if tested by fire, rests in the mutual affection of the King and the people, which perhaps you remember when I explained more fully.
Meanwhile the word liberty resounded everywhere; would that it could be borne more easily than it is procured!
That it should remain moderate, that it should harm when excessive, not a few have forgotten; not a few, slipping under the appearance and pretext of liberty, have fallen into extreme madness.

Indeed, to temper liberty with laws in such a way that a measure is maintained, which liberty itself strives to exceed, not indeed by its own nature, but by a fault joined with it, is a matter of great skill and the highest wisdom:

For since liberty is such that you may do what you ought to will, and are not compelled to do what it is right to be unwilling to do, at no age have peoples not seemed to themselves free, unless it were permitted to do whatever they wished, themselves imitating those whom they least approve, unbridled spirits, to whom not what is fair and just pleases, but what pleases seems fair and just.
But if I consider the nature of this kingdom:

But I often and carefully consider, not because my own pursuits call me here, but because the praises of Frederick William are to be pursued by me, and I am devoted to him and to the Prussian state with my whole heart:
I seem to see that we enjoy a greater liberty than can be displayed, while many who seem to themselves most free are in reality slaves.
For true liberty is placed in morals and in the common consent of all good men;
And, as Tacitus attributes to our ancestors, among us good morals prevail more than good laws do elsewhere.
