These ensure that the limit is not exceeded on either side;
these draw even the unwilling, they restrain violence however great;

if these have been corrupted, if citizens have become unaccustomed to obeying laws and magistrates, to holding dear ancestral institutions, to keeping faith and oath, to being bound by the religion of the supreme deity, what then does the name of liberty profit?
But by what means especially do you think that morals are formed?
I think no one of you will disagree with me, if I say that the life of the prince contributes much to that matter, and also the things that are done publicly by him and his ministers.
I will not sketch for you the image of Frederick William, which you hold as if by daily sight, which is inscribed in your hearts, which has been described by me more than once;
This has often been explained by me before, that he by his example equally corrected morals, just as other princes corrupted them.
And in governing the state, you may find nothing excessive, nothing too unjust, nothing harsh:
By his moderation the King mitigates his rule and lightens whatever burdens.
Concerning these matters, since I have spoken not once before, now I will embrace everything in a few words.
Indeed, violent domination holds its subjects in check through fear, but we are governed by affection and reason:
the people do not fear the prince, but they revere him;
the prince does not fear his own people, but he loves them.
That not everything pleases everyone is human;
and concerning matters which are debated with the greatest intensity at any time, the judgment of the present age is corrupted by partiality and flattery, by hatred and anger:

What is good, what is useful, posterity weighs with a sure balance by weighing wills, causes, and outcomes, and they enjoy the good deeds of their ancestors as much as grandchildren rest in the shade of trees that their parents planted, as they pay for the imprudence and faults of their predecessors, just as future generations pay off the debt contracted in the age of their fathers.
Now indeed, beyond those things that are done publicly, character is shaped by education and training.
In this, divine matters hold the first place.

Concerning these, the more erroneous the opinions of men are, the more superstitious anxiety prevails, or the more prone to impiety is their fickleness, so much the more widely does the corruption of morals spread.
Examples also have great influence here, and it is agreed that Frederick William's mind excels in this matter as well by a remarkable moderation;

At the same time, in no state, I think, have sacred matters been arranged more wisely than in ours, and better directed to that end, that untrained minds may be imbued with those things which it is in everyone's interest to know, that as much knowledge as they acquire, so much may be administered to them by upright teachers, and finally that they may not be bound by ceremonies, but by inner feeling and, as far as possible, by free intellect may be led to God.
But if public education governs morals, schools of every kind, in which boys and adolescents are instructed, also have no small influence on that most important matter;
Among these, since universities are especially conspicuous, according as these have been arranged, morals can be changed somewhat for the better or worse.
What need is there of words?
Rightly, integrity of morals is demanded from both teachers and students;
Rightly are those of either class blamed, if their life, being insufficiently honorable and dissolute, disgraces the order;

Nor is it in any way to be tolerated that it has been said, formerly more often than now, if not openly, at least secretly and in roundabout ways, that the private life of great scholars is not to be examined according to the commonly received moral norms.
For shall we impose this duty on princes, that they unite uprightness with power, and shall we grant to the learned and talented man that he set forth bad examples?
But a burning passion has carried me away in another direction than the one toward which I was heading.
I have said that customs have very great influence in this kingdom, and that education is subservient to customs:

And so rightly among us very much is attributed to public education and to the propagation of the liberal arts, which among the other instruments of empire the most clement King uses both most wisely and most liberally:
Since this argument especially pertains to us, grant me this indulgence, listeners, that I may dwell on it a little.
As truly as wittily, an elegant man, who recently lived among us as a guest, called Prussia the land of schools and camps.
And indeed the excessive crowding of camps undoubtedly oppresses the peoples:
Therefore, with the military system more correctly established, Frederick William reduced the standing armies:
He also increased the number of schools, which cannot easily become greater than is right;

For never under this sky will that happen which we read was done in the Indian Ocean through the fault of imprudent preachers of the divine word, that the common and pagan multitude, having abandoned their trades and agriculture, wholly occupied in reading and reciting sacred formulas and prayers, perishes by the most extreme kind of idleness and misery.

Then indeed, when the state lay prostrate under extreme calamities, we saw, as it were, sanctuaries founded by literature, and with the strength of the fatherland restored and its borders extended, learning grew marvelously.
I am not the sort of person who disparages the good qualities of others and seeks praise for my fatherland by despising them.

I freely confess that many things in Britain are excellently established and invented, and many in Gaul, and the more willingly because the learned men of those most learned peoples now by no means despise our [institutions], and even partly prefer them to their own:

Indeed, in certain arts, and especially in those that require great apparatus, or whose resources must be gathered with the help of almost boundless commerce and distant travels, our poverty cannot enter the contest with wealthier communities;
Nor is it surprising if the princes of greater kingdoms nurtured our cities, which are much more populous and abound in richest resources, and also nurtured most distinguished talents:

Indeed, even some cities of Germany itself, inferior to Prussia, have their own distinctions, of which they may justly boast, and they have contributed and still contribute much to the flourishing of literature and the arts.
Nevertheless, foreigners especially celebrate that care which, under the auspices of Frederick William, is publicly devoted to nurturing studies;
Nor is one or another part fostered while others are neglected, but almost all desires are provided for evenly and consistently.
The splendor of great academies dazzles the eyes in other places, while the rustic multitude, for the most part, has not even learned to distinguish and write the elements of letters.
Who would wish that so great a number of most useful men, on whose strength the state rests, should be utterly uncultivated like cattle, so that, of course, it might obey more readily?
Therefore we take pains that these also may be educated according to their own capacity.
Although this matter is hindered by very great difficulties, nevertheless will accomplishes much when combined with judgment.
What shall I say of the urban games of every kind, by which the age of boys is formed;
the schools, which by a new institution have undertaken to teach those who do not indeed profess literature, but transfer it to the use and enjoyment of common life;
the gymnasia, by which young men are prepared for higher knowledge;
technical exercises of whatever kind;
the academies, as they call them, of architecture, painting, sculpture;
Finally, are our universities equipped and adorned with all resources?
But also teachers, who would be adequate for the duties, had to be procured;
Therefore, seminaries for popular and scholarly teachers were established, and certain other things that would serve the cultivation of certain specific disciplines.
How many training schools have recently been founded for physicians and surgeons, both civil and military, to be more perfectly trained in learning and practice!

And lest anything anywhere should be lacking of the necessary equipment, which in such a great mass of present learning, lest it seem too small, ought to be most abundant and, I might almost say, immense, the King's munificence has supplied the most ample libraries, museums filled with the most precious and most elegant works of art, with natural objects collected from all over the whole world, and gardens, and other things of this kind, and he increases them daily.

Although these benefits are common to the whole kingdom, because no province of it is placed after the others, nevertheless our university has this, as it were, a prerogative, that since it is situated in the very seat of the empire, into which very many resources flow of their own accord, and which it is fitting to be distinguished with all ornaments, we abound in many things, which one would hardly find in smaller cities:
Therefore we owe the greater gratitude to the most kind King.

Now indeed let it be permitted to wander a little more widely, so that from the inner condition of literature itself we may understand what I said above, that liberty is rightly contained within morals.
For since literature cannot be rightly handled unless material of every kind is gathered, for which unwearying industry is required;
since many things must be held in memory, the proper path of each discipline and, as it were, the form of art must be learned by long use and practice;
Much effort and labor must be spent on these matters.
But we must be careful that minds laden with learning and constrained by ever so learned formulas do not lose that which literature ought especially to provide: the light and freedom of the spirit.
It is not enough to be learned.
Wisdom is needed.
With the Stoics, I call the wise man free.
That you may in some way be a perfect grammarian, a perfect physicist or mathematician, that you may have thoroughly learned any other art or science:
If this, which I demand, is lacking, the highest thing will be lacking.

Without doubt, even if minds are held by certain prescribed laws and are bound by formulas of superiors, which it is impious to transgress, one or another art that is less entangled with them can be cultivated with great success;
which the Society of Jesus has shown by outstanding examples:

For by a most prudent arrangement he had also determined that those pursuits should excel in letters, partly because he revered and cherished them, partly because he understood that his glory and power were increased and strengthened thereby:

But the closer each discipline is to wisdom, the more it is engaged in the highest utilities of the human race—not those that pertain to livelihood and profit, but those that are placed in notions that illuminate the mind—the more it is hindered by bonds of that sort, until the mind, by its own force, which you would hardly tame, breaks through the prison.
Thus philosophy, since it especially hammers out those notions which I have mentioned, cannot make progress without freedom;
Nevertheless, in almost every age, men equally ignorant and powerful have opposed this very thing most of all, and yet they have not achieved what they wanted.

Anaxagoras, who was the first to think that the universe was adorned and governed by mind, was accused as if impious by the superstitious, and condemned by the Athenians, although they were the most cultured of all Greeks; and they would have punished him more severely, had he not had Pericles as his patron, a man far superior in his native city and in the age in which he lived:
After the philosopher died, the people of Lampsacus erected altars to him as to a god.
What happened to Socrates, no one does not know;
He seemed to corrupt the youth, he who eminently corrected their morals, who called the mind back from external and visible things to itself, so that it might know itself:
After the citizens killed him with poison, soon they repented of the public atrocity.
And to come closer to our own times, the foolish and bloodthirsty inquisitors burned Giordano Bruno alive, who rightly called himself a lover of wisdom.
Our age concedes that he was free from our impiety; it detests these men.
René Descartes, who was considered an atheist by some religious contemporaries, soon seemed to have supplied the strongest weapons against atheists;

Many have inveighed against Benedict Spinoza, not without fury, because he taught that human freedom consists in the knowledge of God, that the knowledge of God leads to the love of God, and that in the love of God the happiness of mortals is placed.
These are covered by darkness, while his name remains and will remain, and even those wise men confess that he was most holy and most acute, who shrink from his doctrines.

What of the fact that in the previous century turbulent adversaries of the arts expelled Christian Wolf from this kingdom, who professed to be conducting the cause of God and natural religion against him?
But King Frederick honorably recalled him, and no one today doubts that Wolfian philosophy is nothing more innocent.
Finally, in our memory, Fichte was accused of impiety:
This city provided him a refuge, and we who lived with him know that he was a pious man.
The sight of all cannot endure the light of history either.
Nevertheless, this also penetrates whatever darkness is spread before it.
For the curious posterity of earlier ages scrutinizes nothing, not even the most hidden things;
Long time opens nothing, which rewards virtue with the perpetuity of memory and punishes crimes.
Though offenses may lie hidden for a while, though calumny may obscure probity:

Soon there will come a worthy herald of glorious deeds, a keen chastiser of vices, who, like that Tacitus, having attained eternity through the monuments of his genius, may rescue the conscience of the human race from oblivion.
But why do I speak of history?
Not even mathematics did they spare.
Who would believe that a lawsuit was brought against the astronomical discoveries of Copernicus and Galileo on account of superstition, if we had not received it from our ancestors?

What shall we say about Luther and those who, before him and with him, undertook with the boldest enterprise to reform the sacred rites, so that I may not mix the cradle of the most holy religion with human affairs?
Wherever we turn our eyes, we see errors defended by prejudiced opinions, and the knowledge of truth retarded.
Nor is it the question whether the human race advances or stands still, but who advances eagerly, who are left behind weary.
Indeed, when the freedom of the mind is taken away, not only is progress hindered, but ruin is accelerated.

We read in Dionysius of Halicarnassus that Aristodemus, the tyrant of Cumae in Italy, in order that no noble and manly spirit might arise in any citizen, wanted to effeminate the young offspring by abolishing gymnasia and military exercises, and ordered that the boys, like girls, should let their hair grow, adorn it with flowers, curl it into ringlets, and gather it into knots, let variegated robes fall to their ankles, be led by female pedagogues carrying fans and parasols to dancing schools, to flute players, and to baths, where, after being anointed with ointments, they would be adorned before a mirror.
This was gradually accomplished not so much by weakening bodies as by enervating and dulling minds, as the Roman Empire declined in both respects.
Indeed, even that age did not lack brilliant talents;
but to avoid envy, they hid at home, not without public detriment:
virtue and honor and whatever remained of good counsels perished;
but greed grew and base ambition, and the cunning of pretenders and flatterers prevailed;
Finally, with the strength of the empire broken, the vast and flourishing regions of Europe and Asia fell as prey to the barbarians.

And so, although it is understood that license, which is by no means to be tolerated, and pernicious attempts that overturn the foundations of the republic, must be altogether restrained, and that the monstrous passion for revolution must be suppressed;
and to literature of any kind and to talents laboring in any discipline, lest kingdoms perish together with the worn-out strength of minds, just liberty is granted:
especially since what is true and what is false must be demonstrated by reason and arguments, not established by power and decrees.
And in this very serious matter, what influence customs have can now be said in a few words.

For when in former times even among more civilized peoples punishment had been inflicted with the most bitter and capital penalties upon those whom the magistrates had often judged, by the most foolish decisions, to have committed crimes — namely, not only upon heretics and those accused of impiety, whose vengeance was to be committed rather to God as avenger than to mortals, but also upon enchanters and magicians, who never existed at all, condemned to the fire —
Thus, as humanity and a certain simple wisdom were gradually disseminated, and as morals were softened, deeds that were once deemed worthy of impartial judges were now called abominable crimes.

The number of those madmen gradually diminished, who judged that one must attack with chains and iron against established beliefs and opinions, and that whatever of others' opinions on any matter of greater importance displeased them should be dragged to punishment.
Finally, this common moderation of nearly all prevailed over laws and princes, who, according to the ancient arbiters, are living and animated laws.
Thus liberty, which is truly Christian, grew with customs;
For our most holy religion demands no other servitude, any more than civil servitude.
These customs, this moderation among us was confirmed by him who confirmed the kingdom, Frederick the Great;
These Frederick William does not disapprove, commanding himself no less than his own people.
The immortal name of Greek and Latin literature reminds me.

It is well known that Frederick, when advanced in age, ordered that the classical Greek and Latin authors, by whose aid learning and the arts had been restored, and who from the revival of culture had served scholastic instruction, should be treated in the gymnasia with greater diligence and in such a way especially that not only the words of the writers should be committed to memory, but also that minds should be imbued with the matter, the sentiments, and the doctrine contained in them, and with the method and system of discourse which they had set forth for subsequent ages.

For when he wished his people to use free thought, by which alone as a guide inveterate errors and the corrupt institutions of any kind whatsoever can be corrected, he most rightly approved these ancient goods common to the human race, not only because they are especially perfect, but because from them one can learn with an unbiased judgment what is good, what is to be avoided, the virtues and vices, the deeds of peoples and princes by which they have procured for themselves greatness and glory or decline and finally destruction, not with that judgment preoccupied by precepts, opinions, untimely studies, fear, hatreds, and desires, which the state of affairs in the present age and in every state is accustomed to excite.

But if the tender minds of the students cannot derive this benefit from it, certainly a certain form is impressed even upon the unknowing, and men, attracted by the excellence of the best models, will retain what as boys they began to love, and the exercises of youth will prelude the counsels of a more mature age.

Since the wisest men, who preside over public education in this kingdom, perceive this, under the auspices of Frederick William the most ancient institution of scholastic discipline flourishes, although the more inexperienced, who estimate every matter by the weight of silver that redounds to the state and to private individuals, may wish it to be abolished or diminished.
But do you think that the learning of the universities ought to be less liberal?
But these were established for the formation of public ministries, and are maintained for this purpose.
I hear it, but I am not persuaded.
Not yet at that time, when the universities were being born, had a certain order of officials, in a way separated from other men, been established;

And indeed the state can rightly demand that our discipline send forth students who may at some time be able to bear the burdens of the republic, because those will be equal to this task who are intelligent in every kind of literature, and states are governed by reason and understanding:
Moreover, learned and wise men seek and teach the truth, which is at once good and useful, and together with it they inspire love of country, without which nothing in the world is sound.
But the truth, which we seek, is one; error is manifold.

I think that what is true cannot be different in Spain, different in Britain, different in Germany, but only according to the nature of the climate and the character of the peoples is one nation more prone than another to a certain corruption of morals and to other errors at a particular time.
Whose task would it have been to confront these things, if not of the learned?

In order to accomplish this more safely, they must take care not to allow themselves to be swept away by the waves of events or by any other force, but to hold well-fortified elevated temples of learning, from which a view opens in every direction.

Where it is permitted to follow this path under the guidance of teachers, and where, moreover, universities, which derive their very name from the fact that they are associations or bodies that manage their own affairs according to fixed laws, are not deprived of the rights that belong to them, nor are they governed too strictly or more severely than is right, but are governed moderately and benevolently by those whom the prince appoints as curators and, as it were, guardians, there, in my opinion, true academic freedom is preserved.

By this is also included that, since equals are to be judged by equals, and equals are not indeed in skill and age, in which it is fitting that the judge excels, but in rank and order, teachers distinguished in learning are for studious young men, the governance of morals and the judgments which pertain to morals are exercised by the teachers.

For you yourselves know, most beloved fellow soldiers, that that liberty does not consist in the license of feasts and contests, nor in the tyranny of clubs, and your modesty and integrity have brought it about that although the magistrates are attentive, scarcely any punishments have had to be employed for a long time.

If you continue this course vigorously, you will satisfy the wishes of the best king, and you will show that you feel gratitude toward him for such great benefits as he has conferred upon us all, not only in words but in your conduct.

We both express and feel the same gratitude to Frederick William, the founder and nourisher of our school, who not only maintains and protects the inherited zeal for supporting literature from our ancestors, but far surpasses them in generosity and kindness, and throughout all the provinces of the widely extended kingdom has established for the good arts as new and flourishing seats as antiquity furnished more splendidly, and does not confine public education to narrower formulas, but only imposes on teachers the reverence due to sacred laws.
May what Frederick William most desires happen to this republic, lasting peace and tranquility, and may it strengthen, not weaken, this state.

May the gentleness of government, by which Frederick William won for himself veneration and love, while the authority of the laws remains strong and the power of the empire intact, bring to completion the happiness of the people, toward which the most benevolent King has been accustomed to direct his counsels alone, and may virtue and faith, charity and concord, which are more powerful than any power, strengthen this kingdom and defend it from every danger.
Finally, we make the most sacred vows, that Frederick William, together with the entire August house, may be preserved safe, sound, and unharmed by divine providence.

div.head: XXI. Oratio nataliciis Friderici Guilelmi III. celebrandis d. III. m. Aug. a. MDCCCXXXIII. habita.
That human affairs are expanded and nourished by the struggle and reconciliation of opposites.

p.s: You have gathered here with me, listeners, so that, just as today not only throughout this entire city, but through all provinces and all cities, towns, and fields of the empire widely extending, joyful celebrations are conducted by the citizens, so in this place you might be participants and witnesses of that piety with which our literary republic, founded and flourishing under the auspices of Frederick William, would honor its founder and preserver.
For indeed we, if anyone else, ought not only to feel gratitude to our most gracious Prince, but there are also many reasons why we should publicly declare what feelings our hearts are steeped in.

Among these, this is not the least: that for some years now discord has been nourished and spread more and more, which threatens to break the pleasant and useful alliance of princes and peoples, and that this very discord is thought to have taken root especially in the literary universities.
But if I consider how great changes we have seen since that time, when our school was founded by the distinguished institutions of Frederick William;

The span of a few years seems to contain such great floods and outcomes of events, and such headlong successions of most diverse plans and wills, that you would believe the world is moved and runs with an accelerated impetus, and even he who has not been pressed by any Epimenidean sleep cannot find his little sheep.
Hastening time supplies so much experience of things in a short span, that we seem to be born gray like Cycnus and Tarchon.
We who first saw the state afflicted by a disastrous war and, in a manner, sent under the yoke:
but in the greatest calamity, the steadfastness of the most beloved King and the harmony of the Prince and the people consoled every best man, who had together decided either to stand or to perish:
Never was mutual love kindled by sharper goads;
never was the whole republic held together by firmer bonds of faith and love:

Therefore, the more these words of veneration and piety, spoken and acclaimed to the best King, displeased the foreign master full of suspicions, the more willingly and intently they were spoken and acclaimed.
Soon, with spirits and strength strengthened through adversity, the King conquered with his allies, and not only restored the empire, but also increased it;
From the fields stained with blood, a most joyful harvest of good things has come forth;
Glory was followed by security, wealth, public and private prosperity;
And not only our state enjoyed tranquility and harmony, but the Germans as a whole agreed among themselves and with us.
But since the human race is prone to excess, not all endured moderate happiness for long:
From those who pursue vain things, torches of disturbances were kindled and thrown;
Already the present hour does not allow us to enjoy its fruit without cares, while from every side, like a sword over the head, some fear of the future hangs over us.

Yet in this revolution of affairs, which, even if for a time the force of the disease has either spontaneously relaxed or has been repressed, can seem to no one except the improvident to be light or hardly worthy of mention, the Prussian state has remained safe, the loyalty of the people has remained safe, the love of the Prince has remained safe:
the times have changed; we have not changed in them:

And with the same ardor with which, above all, we have venerated the name of that man in the solemnities celebrated in this hall for Frederick William, with that same ardor today we pray to the supreme deity that he may bestow upon that excellent soul all those goods by which mortals can be blessed and the minds of rulers can be refreshed.

These vows I pour forth on behalf of you all, I who, not so much an orator as an interpreter and herald of your feelings, stationed publicly on this platform every year, seem to myself to have looked into the virtues of Frederick William from within and to have embraced them with manifold thought.

Now, after I have already stated at the very threshold of my speech what you, my listeners, most expected from me, it will be permissible to digress a little from the present matters, so that at the end I may return to the point from which I began.
Yet I will not entirely digress from my purpose.
Indeed, the discord by which the world is now troubled has arisen more from an agitation of minds than from any other somewhat greater cause.
And it is an evil, but an evil admitted by providence, which from the very evils brings forth good things:
By which one consolation the grief is soothed, which less favorable events bring.
I shall say nothing new, nothing recondite, nothing more distinguished either in richness of learning or in weight or subtlety of thought:
That whatever mortals have done and performed, has been done and performed for the most part through contests, the memory of almost all things warns.

For just as it pleased Empedocles of Agrigentum that the nature of things is moved by these two principles, discord and friendship, and as Heraclitus of Ephesus attributed to all things the resisting union of bow and lyre and the harmony from dissonant elements, and without opposites there is no composition and generation:
so human affairs are agitated and nourished by contention, lest they fall apart through idleness and sloth, and thus the outcome is prepared, which has been established by divine will.
This is especially what poetry sketches out, which Aristotle rightly judges to be more philosophical and more excellent than history, because the former presents universals, the latter particulars;

Therefore, when in tragedy, which is a mirror of a more severe life, it accomplishes and brings to a conclusion any more serious action, not without discord of the parts, which involves the characters in very many difficulties and dangers, it shows generally, although in individual plays, from what elements human life and fortune are composed.

And, as it is fitting that the learned should attend to this above all, although the powers of the mind, in the highest harmony which nature has formed, nevertheless diverge into different directions, and impel those in whom this or that power prevails to embrace various sects of life and studies;

These very varied studies, although they all proceed from the same source and express in different forms one and the same divine reason of the human mind, are nevertheless separated and dissociated and fight among themselves, so that at last they are reconciled more perfectly.
Indeed, the most ancient cognitions of the human mind, in which truly something divine was inherent, were concerned with the consciousness of the supreme deity, which we call religion;
From this source especially flowed the most ancient civil institutions, from this the arts and sciences, of which philosophy is the chief.
But when religion had formed the names, figures, and characters of the gods, and had taught that they had done and suffered those things which are contained in mythical doctrines and narratives,
Soon after came the philosophers, who, imbued with those very primitive notions and spurred on to discover higher things,

These men, using a purer reason, condemned mythology as a whole, and just as Jupiter deprived his father of his rule and bound him, they conquered the ancient discipline, while this, like Saturn devouring his offspring, in turn defeats those ethnic heretics with their own weapons.
This discord is as old as the cradle of philosophy.
Thus Heraclitus and Xenophanes judged Homer and Hesiod, the authors of divine fables, worthy of the greatest disgrace because of the things they had said badly about the gods.
And they say that Pythagoras reported that he had seen Homer and Hesiod paying the penalties in the underworld for those stories which they had handed down.
Thus Plato expels Homer from his most perfect republic, and rejects all those little stories about the gods, whether changed into human form or affected with mortal habits.

Finally, this division recurs in almost every age, because priestly discipline wishes to stand on what has been handed down and rejects novelty by its own right, while science dares to know beyond what has been handed down and to trust common judgment:

until after the troublesome controversies of many centuries both sides have reached the point that the teachings of neither are understood to be entirely contrary to the other, but theology recalls its doctrines to the principles of science, and philosophy not only concedes but demonstrates that the forms in which the consciousness of the divine power has been comprehended in religions are necessary and derived from the divinity of the mind itself:
which agreement seems to be gradually brought about from our age onward.
But what about the arts?
Were not the sculptors and painters, by divine inspiration, impelled to express, through visible images, that one and hidden thing which our ancestors beheld only with reverence?
Was not the whole chorus of the arts, from the beginning, devoted to the ceremonies and worship of the gods?
Did not music also, and all poetry, filled with divine spirit, celebrate and adorn the sacred rites from their very origins?

But what formerly conspired uniquely, religion and the arts, were afterwards more than once so divided that images were broken, and nothing seemed more wicked than statues and scenic performances, finally so that actors, as if impious, were excluded from participation in sacred rites and burial.

Now, although these and similar matters were once debated with the utmost effort, how few are the priests or theologians who are hostile to painted panels, or who think that theaters, even in this decline of scenic poetry, are the abodes and workshops of evil demons?
Even greater quarrels arose quite early between the priests of the sacred rites and the rulers of the states.

For already in the heroic age of the Greeks, in which nevertheless the minds of men were wholly bound by the bonds of religion, such as it was, and scarcely any somewhat more brilliant civil wisdom had yet emerged, the king accuses the augur of ambition, falsehood, and fraud, and the augur accuses the king of contempt of the gods, pride, and tyranny:

And although the Christian faith may seem to have set the boundaries of both parties with more inward and certain limits, the more sacred that faith was and the greater the papal power, the more fiercely the conflict blazed up, which was not even extinguished by wars waged to the point of extermination, but is even now nourished openly or secretly in many lands of Europe:
Although the reform of the sacred rites, begun in the fourth century before and accomplished not without bloodshed, was a prelude to the firm peace which posterity will enjoy.

Moreover, civil discipline, just as it comes into conflict with priests, so also with those who devote themselves to the knowledge of a more recondite and abstruse philosophy, although that same reason, which the students of wisdom seek, seems to permeate the state in a somewhat more perfect way, since, as a man not moderately skilled in public affairs declares on the authority of the philosophers themselves, M.

The law, that law by which states are governed, is the highest reason implanted in nature and established and perfected in the human mind, which commands the things that ought to be done and forbids the contrary.
And yet, to say nothing of the desires and party interests by which the powerful are sometimes driven off course, whether they are princes or leaders of factions:

As all human affairs are corrupted, law is not infrequently enacted for the advantage of the powerful, and that pernicious opinion of some sophist, that the just is what is useful to the stronger, is confirmed by long experience of things.
And although Machiavelli, by no means the last of the prudent, may have proved this, yet it is impious for a wise man to approve it.

And those who conduct public affairs necessarily plunge themselves into the immense floods of individual matters, and being tossed about by them, they generally become dull for the contemplation of universal notions, just as those scholars who are especially engaged in investigating individual things are accustomed to be drawn away from the understanding of those same notions.
On the contrary, philosophers in any matter pursue that general thing which they call the idea, being sometimes less skilled in individual things than they ought to be.
And likewise those people easily acquiesce in the present state of affairs, which is present at every time, and they strive to preserve it as much as possible, or to correct it by slow progress:

These people, often neglecting what is placed before their eyes (which is reproached to that Thales), seize with their thought projected further the future more perfect condition of the human race, and as if by divining they anticipate it.
Now there is enough of reasons why the one party resists the other.

Therefore, the one example we know of perfect harmony between philosophy and politics, namely the power of the Pythagorean society in Italy, we see passed away quickly, because turbulent men had stirred up the common people against those most holy and most wise men and had burned down the meeting-houses of the Pythagoreans.

Indeed at Athens, when the teaching of morality first began to be treated more carefully by the philosophers, the wise men censured the rule of the people as imprudent, fickle, and tyrannical; and again, men hostile to them who were conducting public affairs, such as that Anytus was, kept shouting that the youth were being corrupted by the philosophers, because they were calling them away from respect for popular government:

Nor was there any other cause so intimate for which the leader and founder of Attic philosophy was condemned, than that he had had Critias and Alcibiades, most eager for revolutionary changes, as disciples and followers.

Soon Plato exaggerated the incompatibility of public affairs and knowledge to such an extent that he said that those who from adolescence had been occupied in the courts and around the forum were compared, as it were, to slaves in relation to free men, when compared with those who had been educated in philosophy and studies of this kind.
so that he thought that these, from their earliest age, did not even know the way to the forum, nor where a court or an assembly or any other public meeting of the state was held.

But they say that they have neither heard nor seen the laws and decrees, whether spoken or written, and that they do not even in their dreams think about bribery and conspiracies for creating magistrates and about forming clubs, but that in reality only their bodies dwell in the state, while their minds, deeming all those things trivial or worthless, are occupied with higher thoughts:

But those civil lawyers and fierce advocates, who would laugh at a philosopher's inexperience, if someone tried to raise them to higher things, would either themselves withdraw from such a question as, "What wrong have I done to you, or you to me?" in order to inquire what justice and injustice themselves are, and how these differ from each other and from all other concepts, or if they passed from this opinion, "Happy is the king who possesses much gold," to questions about the nature of kingship and about human happiness and misery in general;

Therefore, when they ought to give an account of these matters, they were seized with dizziness as if placed on a high watchtower, from which they were not accustomed to look out, and being at a loss for counsel and distressed, they uttered barbarous words.
Afterwards, because the philosophers approved above all a kingly rule, tempered indeed and liberal, they were afflicted with many dangers.
After the death of Alexander the Great, Aristotle himself, accused of impiety, left the city.

Theophrastus, when he was accused by Hagnonides, pleaded the same cause, indeed, more successfully, but afterwards he too was forced to withdraw for a short time, when Sophocles, son of Amphiclides, had carried a law that no one should preside over a school of philosophers unless it had pleased the Senate and the People;
whoever did otherwise, it was a capital offense:
by which decree all philosophers seem to have been driven from Athens, until a year later, when the law was repealed and Sophocles was fined, the return was granted.

At Rome too we have learned that, in the sixth century of the city drawing to a close, after words had been spoken about philosophers and rhetoricians, the Senate had so decreed that the Praetor should take notice and take care, as seemed to him to be in the interest of the state and consistent with his good faith, that they should not be at Rome.

Why should I mention Domitian, who banished the teachers of wisdom and all philosophers from the city and Italy, as Tiberius once did the actors, and, as Tacitus says, drove every noble art into exile, and that because of the praises alone paid to Paetus Thrasea and Priscus Helvidius by Arulenus Rusticus and Herennius Senecio?
What of the fact that under the Emperor Justinian the pagan philosophers had to seek refuge in Persia?

And so we see that philosophers were hated by those in power for the most diverse reasons, sometimes because they favored the rule of the best, sometimes because they favored royal power, sometimes because they favored ancient institutions and ceremonies.
But in our age this discord has almost become obsolete:
gradually many things that the wise have taught have been received into the laws themselves:
it is agreed that the state ought to be illuminated by the lights of knowledge;

And the learned understand that their own discipline ought not to be opposed to the public one, but that by both, morals are to be corrected, the misery of mortals is to be alleviated, the darkness of error is to be dispelled, and finally a more perfect state of the human race is to be brought about.

But if men have not yet attained that which, in Plato's judgment, is the highest good, namely that either philosophers should rule or rulers should philosophize, nevertheless the two are not even now separated by as great an interval as then, when it was difficult for him not to write a satire against the state.
But you would wonder more at the fact that knowledge did not even maintain a lasting harmony with the arts, than at what I have set forth up to this point.

Indeed, that does not seem to have been accidental, that he who was almost the first to turn the mind from the contemplation of natural things to the mind itself, was a sculptor, indeed like Silenus himself, but not displeasing to the Graces, whom he is said to have fashioned with exceptional beauty.
But he regretted his art and the Graces expressed in marble, because he preferred to contemplate the inner Graces of the human mind.
And his student, by far the most outstanding in talent, had nearly the same fortune.

He, who was born in a certain sense for poetry, and while still quite young had practiced almost all the genres of this art, and had composed an epic poem, emulating Homer, as well as lyric poems and tragedies, is said soon to have burned the whole heap of his verses in fire, so that he might practice only the music of philosophy.

We see, then, that these men, for reasons not unlike those for which later certain Christian sects rejected poetry and all imitative arts (and there is none that is not imitative), despised them, as those which would render and represent images of images, shadows of shadows, not pure and absolute notions of things and, if one may use a Ciceronian term, their essence;

And if Aristotle was not too hostile to the arts, whose nature he tried to investigate like that of all other things, philosophy certainly afterwards, if not in express words, yet by its neglect, for a long time despised them, until, when they were flourishing, it embraced them in the previous century when they were aging and for the most part lying prostrate, and with a new name, although inconvenient, formed a new part of its discipline, which would be entirely concerned with establishing the principles of the arts.

Thus this separation also was endured by the age, and it was understood that both art and science tend toward the same end, so that in these fleeting and fragile forms of things, which fall under the senses, the traces of the divine mind may be recognized.
But truly, just as the reason of the whole world is seen expressed in its individual parts, as if in some smaller image of the world;

Thus we see that the division which has existed among the most important kinds of studies to which the human mind applies itself, and which to some extent still exists, is repeated within the very boundaries of those studies.

Therefore in no discipline have countless sects not arisen, of which some attribute more to history, others to philosophy, others again to reason, others to faith or to some obscure sense of truth, and others to experience;
From all of which, amid manifest discord, a certain hidden harmony is brought about.
From all things one, and from one all things.

Finally, if the mind itself is compelled by its own nature to descend into these conflicts, why should not the necessities and desires be urged on, by which the wars of peoples are inflamed, both foreign and domestic?
So much for these matters.
Now I will briefly finish what seems to remain to be said.
For God is free from error, evil, and discord.

Mortals must endure evils and grieve, because something good is always opposed to what is necessary, be moved by disturbances, experience joys and sorrows and human weakness, so that they may come forth more approved and more purified from trials, err, so that error may be corrected, disagree, so that they may be seized by a desire for concord all the more vehement.
And these dissonant things must be brought together into a harmony:
And the more men have accomplished this, the more they will be assimilated to God.
But harmony is not achieved by removing and uprooting opposing forces, but by combining and tempering them.
Nor does the climate become temperate by removing the cold or the heat, and again neither by removing the moist nor the dry.
Music itself, which especially strives for consonance, mixes contraries, the high and the low, the fast and the slow, and sometimes even admits dissonances, which it resolves.
Remove the dissimilar elements, and you will destroy harmony itself.

But in the state, the one who is at the head of all affairs is the most suitable of all for reconciling opposites, and he will be able to accomplish this more certainly, the greater the power with which he has been endowed.
If he is also entirely free from desire, he will even calm the desires of his subjects, not kindle them;
if he is provident and kind, he will consult the needs of the same people, so that not even a pretext is left for the instigators of revolution.
Who, therefore, could be a more longed-for governor of the state in this age than Frederick William?
He shaped the people into harmony, in which the highest virtue of the state is placed;
he, abhorring most greatly from all pride, by his own example also accustomed the citizens to moderation;
he provided for the comforts and fortunes of his subjects;

Here, in our common fatherland, as Pliny says of Pompey and Trajan, by his authority, counsel, and loyalty he opened up roads, restored routes to the lands, and united kindred peoples through commerce that had been forbidden for too long.

He, giving to each his own, also keeps those diverse spheres in which the pursuits of the human mind are engaged so harmoniously arranged in this kingdom that none stands out to the detriment of the others.
Civil power does not oppress the church, nor does the church invade the duties of the state;
Neither the arts nor the sciences are neglected by the state, nor is a formula prescribed to those who teach, nor do the masters of knowledge cross their own boundaries;
In short, all arts and disciplines dwell together in harmony.
Let those states divide these, in which the church is separated from the republic, and literature is separated from both:
among us they have grown together firmly;
we do not fear contamination.
But this moderation, spread throughout the whole state, is a pledge of lasting happiness;
pride perishes by its own blows, and whatever raises itself too high is cast down, sooner or later, from the order divinely established in nature and human affairs, with a ruin the more fatal.
Seized by this pride, certain ambitious men have drawn away a part of the youth, which is wont to admire forbidden things and to lend an ear to corruptors;

She has forgotten that even in the freest states it was anciently established that young men, however liberally educated and treated, were not nevertheless allowed to mix freely in the conduct of public affairs, but were under the superintendents, gymnasiarchs, and sophronists.

She does not know that, as the writer most devoted to freedom has taught, obedience and modesty, if industry and vigor are present, reach that point of praise which others have attained through precipitous paths, but with no benefit to the state, having become famous through ambitious ruin.
Since he said this about that age which had endured the most unjust masters, how much more truly will it be said about kingdoms that are most equitable and most just?
But who would defend and repel that disease with better counsels and a more favorable success than Frederick William's serene and temperate mind?
To whom, without any suspicion of flattery, one may exclaim with the poet:
You indeed are the most opportune physician, and Paean favors your fortune!
Therefore, in Frederick William's kindness, virtue, and wisdom, this republic finds rest.
From him and from his excellent counsels it obtains and expects whatever good things are possible in this state of affairs and according to the resources and strength of this kingdom.

For him, with that love with which he himself embraces his own, with that piety which you all know to be in him, we again pray from the divine power for a most prosperous course of his undertakings, and a long, vigorous, and unclouded old age, free from any evil or sickness.

We, bound also by his benefits, are obliged to him with the highest religious duty, and we, reverently, desire and pray again and again that in his grace and favor a perpetual and most firm protection may be placed for this school founded by him.

div.head: XXII. Oratio nataliciis Friderici Guilelmi III. celebrandis d. III. m. Aug. a. MDCCCXXXIV. habita.
A demonstration of the plans by which Frederick William III founded, preserved, and enlarged the University of Berlin

p.s: It was the sixteenth day of August in the year 1809, most illustrious minister of the King, most respected listeners of all ranks, when Frederick William, at Königsberg, where he then had the seat of his kingdom, wrote back to several of his ministers and councilors that what they had reported to him about founding a general institution of learning at Berlin, as our ancestors called it, was pleasing to him and ratified, and that this matter seemed to him so weighty and destined to be of such great moment for the higher cultivation of minds, not only in the Prussian state but also to be disseminated and propagated more widely beyond its borders, for attracting men preeminent in every kind of learning and winning them over to this realm, and finally for bringing about, with profit, the union, as it were into one body, of the Berlin academies and the various apparatuses and institutions serving learning which this city contained, that he was unwilling to postpone the establishment of such a school, which, called by the ancient name of a literary university and furnished and adorned with the right of conferring academic honors, should be placed in this city and in these buildings where we now are assembled.
I pass over the other additions, whether they were soon carried out or postponed to later times and entrusted to favorable circumstances.
That day, colleagues, created this leisure for us; it provided for your studies, fellow soldiers;
The very title, which the most kind king ordered to be inscribed on this house, refers that donation, plainly royal, to that year.

Therefore, although our duties were only begun a year later, and indeed this school was to be dedicated with solemn rites only in the eighth year, we shall trace and count the beginnings of the university from that year and that truly natal day:

Since, according to this most just calculation, in the few days in which we are celebrating this assembly for the birthday of Frederick William, the Frederick William University will complete five lustra, and has, I think, not without honor traversed the first and perhaps most laborious stage of the contest;
Why should we not, on the most auspicious birthday of the founder, also commemorate the memory of our own, as it were, birth?
For this memory is to be recalled solely to the praise of Frederick William;

Thus it will be at the same time less ambitious, less foreign to the spirit of this time, which now especially does not allow universities to boast about their affairs and to congratulate themselves greatly, and finally more suitable to that modesty, by which modesty we who were present know that the dedication of the university, celebrated seventeen years ago, was also admirably performed.

But as it has always been a pleasure to me to give thanks in the name of Frederick William and in your name, my hearers, and in my own person, for the great benefits with which he has blessed us and the whole state;
so this duty ought to seem the more acceptable every year, the longer we experience that we have remained in the King's favor by the addition of each year.
Yet there is something by which this joy of mine is disturbed.

If I compare myself with my own heart, I do not doubt that there will be no one who can proclaim the King more earnestly and sincerely than I, and who may seem more worthy to undertake this office, which I today sustain on behalf of you all.
But the strength must suffice for the mind;

Although these things are thought to be strengthened by frequent practice, yet who does not understand that moderate abilities are exhausted by more frequent use, and that the edge of the mind is blunted by much fighting, and that a style of speaking already too well known by much hearing easily brings disgust to learned ears, unless, whenever you speak, you vary it with the greatest art and distinguish it with new ornaments?

Therefore I seem to myself to be able to be charged with the fault of rashness, I who dare to illustrate the same subject, although it is noble and magnificent, now for the twenty-first time in an oration.
Should I then yield my place?
Not yet, not even now, as long as your indulgence, listeners, remains, which I know has never failed me before and will not fail me today.

For you yourselves, my dearest colleagues, will rather impute that rashness of mine to yourselves than to me, since you would prefer that I be kept under the standard after so many campaigns than be presented with the discharge staff.

And the concern that arises, lest my speech should no longer be worthy of the King, I dispel with those words with which the great interpreter of nature, Pliny, uses in a similar case, offering his work to Titus, son of Vespasian:

"But truly," he says, "rustics and many peoples supplicate the gods with milk, and they only offer salted meal, because they do not have frankincense." And why would you desire frankincense, where the work praises the craftsman?

For the King's wisdom and kindness will have been abundantly praised, when I shall have sketched with what counsels, how generous and magnanimous, by what novel and never-before-attempted path he founded this seat of the arts;
His prudence has been abundantly shown, when I have shown that success responded to his counsels.

His constancy has been abundantly shown, when I have demonstrated that nothing was relaxed through the changes of times, but that our affairs were preserved and increased by Frederick William through constant zeal and munificence.

For if we except that age in which literary universities were born in great cities, because into these flowed all the learning that then existed outside the monasteries, and if we rightly deny that certain universities, which even in this century seem to survive in some leading cities, are universities except in name;
This was a new undertaking, listeners, that Frederick William wanted these schools to be established especially in the more important cities.

These were then distributed in such a way that of the three parts of the kingdom, Prussia proper had its seat of the liberal arts at Königsberg, Silesia at Breslau, and the remaining German provinces, which indeed survived from the great shipwreck, at Berlin.
Thus it seemed possible that, since larger cities and seats of government provide a more splendid apparatus, from this side at least more could be accomplished with less expense;
so that, because a small band could not dominate the youths, however numerous, in a large town, the manners of the academic citizens might become more modest;

Moreover, so that those very capitals of provinces might be reconciled to a higher and more subtle science, and that those things which held the first place in position and rank should not be secondary in literature, and so that the learned might be less separated from the administrators of the highest government, but that learning might in a way penetrate into the state, and that the learned, in turn, might become less alien to the management of public affairs, and less, as they say, bookish.
But novelty then brought it about that this matter seemed full of risk:
The corruption of youth was feared, the snares of pleasures and luxury, by which great cities were infected.
That academic freedom, which lovers of the old discipline hold in the highest regard, was also feared.
Indeed, most people forgot that even the less frequented towns, and especially those in which universities were established, have their own secret lusts;
that there, not infrequently, more licentious drinking parties and Bacchanalia are celebrated than in the very foremost cities;
And that the crowdedness of the city does not harm just liberty, provided that arrogance and insolence are absent, since it allows each person to live in his own way.
Nor is that liberty such that it is permitted to insult citizens with impunity and to hold every most innocent person up to ridicule.
In short:

The outcome has so confirmed Frederick William's judgment that, since neither the charm of the place, nor the abundance of wine, nor the indulgence of insolence enticed anyone to come here, no part of the youth has spent its time more innocently than this our band, none has been more distinguished for eagerness in study, industry, and strictness—indeed, as many now admit, and especially the governors of states—nothing is more useful than this most tranquil residence of universities in capital cities.
Indeed, I would explain this topic even more fully, were it not that, while I am engaged in it, I recall that it has already been deliberately explained by me long ago:
For who would not have it happen that, in treating the same subject, the same thought or sentiment should repeatedly recur?

And indeed I fear that, although I strive to avoid all display of our affairs, I may seem unwittingly to disparage the allied universities, which are most closely connected with us in common interests, and to compare our advantages with the disadvantages of others.
This would have been more unjust at no time than now.
Indeed, almost all of them deserve very well of literature.
Nor indeed did Frederick William think that all things should be reduced to one form.

It retained even those universities with which other towns are adorned and enriched, and it furnished these very ones far more splendidly, and moreover founded in the most ancient town on the bank of the Rhine a new school of the finest arts, the eye of the fatherland's river, the bright jewel of the Prussian crown.

But how truly the wisest king prophesied that the great power of our university would also lie in this, that the literary equipment of every kind, which was scattered throughout this city, would be properly arranged, enlarged, and offered for common use.
For these treasures have become especially famous from that very time when they were liberally turned to the benefit of the university.

Nor would they ever have attained such great abundance, usefulness, and dignity, nor would they themselves have brought such great adornment to the city, had not the Friedrich Wilhelm University more keenly stimulated the studies of Berlin.

For this is the condition of studies in Germany, that neither the so-called special schools, whose meagerness and languor please some people, nor the academies of learning, however learned and splendid, nor any other scholastic institutions add such great stimuli to minds, nor inflame youthful souls with such great ardor for cultivating the good arts with the utmost exertion, as this discipline of universities, without which, as the culture of the European peoples is now indeed constituted, letters do not seem able to thrive and flourish.

But that the best Prince had persuaded himself that the establishment of this university would greatly avail for forming minds, not only in the lands subject to him but also beyond the borders of the empire, how greatly do you think it has been approved by the outcome?
For since from its very beginnings the number of citizens has been such that it has equaled moderate universities, our [university] ...

Then, after the most fortunate calamity happened, that we dismissed the noble youth, called to the camp, not unwillingly, who at that time had devoted themselves of their own accord for the safety of the King and the fatherland, since with the whole people they were about to redeem and recover our liberty and the Prussian glory and the integrity of the empire and other goods with their blood, not only was the damage given to this school immediately repaired, but with continuous increases the number of citizens soon grew so much that in a short time we surpassed all other universities.
Indeed, the plague, which three years ago carried off very many of our fellow students, did not greatly diminish our numbers.
Thus from all the provinces and from the rest of Germany and even from foreign lands the flower of youth has flowed in anew.
For how excellent a training ground for studies Frederick William has opened here for young men, both the natives and foreigners see.

Nor do I fear so much that I will greatly incur the censure of the learned, when perhaps I say somewhat more ambitiously in passing, that by this celebrated gathering of our school it is brought about that the virtue of the Prussian kingdom is better understood, while young men of good character, flocking here from all sides, come to know more closely the goods and advantages of this commonwealth, and, as I have often experienced myself, are gradually imbued with and drawn by the esteem of the Prussian name, even unwilling and in a way unknowing.

But if Frederick the Great, by generously equipping the academy of sciences, sought to promote the growth of learning in his own and foreign lands, which under that king flourished especially with men preeminent in their kind, particularly famous mathematicians and philosophers, Frederick William, in order to attain the same end, preferred that institution which almost all declare to be truly German, and which is far more effective for that purpose;

And by summoning professors who would teach in the university, he not only wonderfully nourished the learning of this city, but also provided the most abundant opportunity for increasing, from the common people at the same time, that society which Frederick the Great had uniquely loved.

This is an ancient glory of the Prussian kingdom, listeners, and it has not been boasted by its own natives with empty grandiloquence, but celebrated by the mouth of every most learned nation, because its power has rested no more on arms than on the cultivation of minds.
This indeed was more keenly perceived during those years in which the state lay prostrate, struck by a most disastrous calamity:
How much more does it delight to recall the memory of that time, in which the wisdom of Frederick William was so employed that from the very adversities it drew forth the greatest prosperities.

Then nothing was left undone by which the powers hidden in hearts and minds, which you could not exhaust by imposing taxes, nor by placing garrisons, nor by any other injustice, might be nourished and fostered with the most diligent care.
To this care we owe our life, colleagues and fellow soldiers, not the life that nature gave in common with the animals, but the life by which our minds thrive:
This care any schools of the good arts in this kingdom have experienced.
But oh, the pain!

We have degenerated so much in these five lustra that there are already those who say that when the schools were re-established, this ruin was sown, which now creeps through all Germany, so that the most audacious youth attempts new things.

By a wonderful inclination of minds, that character of the German schools which was once hateful to enemies is now approved by foreigners, but displeases some of our countrymen, who seem to themselves to be led by love of fatherland;
Formerly, the most talented men defended them against external slander, among whom were also the teachers of this school, especially distinguished;
Now a war, as it were civil, has blazed up concerning them.

And what you may especially grieve, lest they seem to have utterly brazen-faced, like informers, they commit crimes and outrages, which may be imputed with some appearance of truth both to the universities and to the other schools.

Indeed, most of those who judge in journals and in certain assemblies of the civil orders what schools and universities are or ought to be, do not know their nature and character better than adolescents know public affairs, whose thoughtless judgments about these matters those very critics of public education rightly take offense at.

At one moment we are envied and reproached for this shadow of form and of the right of associations, because we are said to have retained something from the Middle Ages, being too tenacious of ancient institutions;
at another time, quite the contrary, we are thought to despise the old, to grasp at the new, and to be eager for liberty, or rather license.
But to those who judge rightly, the one will seem most justly tempered with the other:
for those bonds of associations have been so loosened that nothing has been left more illiberal;
license, as far as lies in our power, we restrain:
But when one cannot tear it out by the roots, why should it be surprising that we have not succeeded in doing what not even the bravest and most powerful leaders were able to accomplish?
And we claim freedom for ourselves to this extent, that we think no one ought to teach anything that he himself does not approve:
that it cannot be commanded what must be taught or how, but that whatever one has understood to be true by careful inquiry, from that one is not allowed to deviate a finger's breadth:

Nor is it to be taught for this reason, that the listener may take down in writing or in memory what is handed down, but that the students themselves may become accustomed to penetrate the inner sanctuaries of literature by free thought.

Nor should these young men be trained and instructed like slaves, according to certain fixed doctrines, from a prescribed rule, for specific services, which they would then perform and execute without feeling; but rather the inner reason of things divine and human, as far as we are able, should be explained, and youthful minds should be filled with the most burning love of the true, the good, and the beautiful.
Since the King wished this, he did not say that he was founding a university in order that young men might be trained for the ministries and public offices:
although it is not doubtful that they are also formed for these things by the right instruction of arts and sciences:
but so that he might provide for the cultivation of minds both in his own lands and beyond the borders of the empire.
But that these crimes of a few have not flowed from the teaching of universities is clearer than light;
And if one may judge other schools by our own, it was not even the gentleness of academic discipline, which is not so great as is supposed, that brought it about that such things could be committed.
Truly other forces drove Gaul, Italy, Belgium, Poland, Spain, and Portugal;
By the same movements and the common flaw of the age, whose origins it is not ours to investigate, some German youths were drawn to attempt new things, not incited by the discipline of the schools.

But as in barbarous ages, when pestilence was raging, the superstitious common people, ignorant of how to investigate the natural causes of things, used to accuse the Jews, as those who had poisoned wells and springs:
so in more cultivated ages, certain ingenious men took delight in this, that they demonstrated to the credulous that the seeds of all the greatest disturbances had been scattered by the learned.

Who does not know, I ask, how often that oft-repeated story has been told, that philosophy, as they called it, and the philosophers and the authors of encyclopedias brought about that great revolution in France, by which the whole world was shaken more violently than by an earthquake?
Indeed, if those philosophers were able to accomplish so much, we will not despair that German philosophy from pure concepts will one day create some new world:
This is a capability that, up to now, only comedy has dared to grant them.

What about the fact that some have even been pleased by this, and it has been received with applause from certain quarters, since the notions that we seem to hold about the condition of the ancient states are so imperfect and false that we do not hold even the first elements of the civil discipline of the Greeks and Romans except as confused and corrupted by the most shameful errors?

It can now be understood how correct and true the explanation of the ancient writers is rendered in the schools, on how firm foundations rests the knowledge of the ancient civil liberty, with which the teachers of the schools imbue their pupils:

Indeed, both teachers and learners, instead of clear and distinct notions and opinions, hunt after certain obscure and confused feelings, by which they stir their minds even to the point of disturbance, and, instead of a modest and honest confession of ignorance, they arrogate to themselves judgment concerning civil institutions, which not even men most experienced in public affairs have been able to fully understand up to this time.

Therefore, it must be asked whether it is consistent with reason that young offspring, from childhood, should be accustomed, trained, and educated at public expense to a superficial and cursory estimation of public affairs, and to the forming of false, perverse, and pernicious notions about them.

Since this has been the case for several centuries already, but in our century it is pursued more eagerly than ever, it should not be surprising if now with incredible haste the abolition of any public rights is demanded and granted with equanimity, and the peoples of Europe, corrupted in their morals by this vice of public education, rush unwittingly and fall back into barbarism.
Those who toss about these and similar claims most confidently, do they not portray for us the teachers of the schools as some kind of Gracchi?
Do they not affirm and prophesy that civil disturbances of any kind and even barbarism itself are brought on by the study of Greek and Latin literature?
But others complain rather that boys are over-exercised by the subtlety of grammarians;
and certainly much is attributed to grammatical precepts in our schools, and never has not been attributed:

Finally, those schoolmasters, in whom so much distrust is placed, are partly so occupied with the most serious and abstruse studies that they scarcely have time to examine public affairs, and the pupils are so trained by learning every kind of liberal education that scarcely any leisure is left for attending to the affairs of others.
Indeed, I will not deny that the love of just liberty and the hatred of unjust tyranny are nourished by the study of ancient literature;
And our ancestors judged that this too should be counted among the most important benefits of these studies, together with every best prince.

Moreover, from our scholastic discipline, properly tempered by laws, and from the study of antiquity, you would not more justly derive a blemish on account of the age than if someone, just as the Greeks had persuaded themselves that by learning softer and more licentious harmonies the minds of boys were rendered idle and intemperate, should in like manner derive this, as it were, intemperance of the age from our musicians, or from the theaters, in which indeed we not infrequently hear most distinguished poets, the glories of Germany, proclaiming civil liberty.
Finally, in the Prussian schools, to whom, I ask, are those pernicious precepts taught?
And if anything of this kind has been taught by one or another, are the whole schools therefore to be slandered?
Away, then, with those accusations:

let us rather congratulate Frederick William, because, as the old proverb has it, he did not hesitate to sow, and he did not sow dragon's teeth, from which a deadly and bloody crop might spring up, but he brought back a joyful and innocent harvest of the best studies;
And let us be confident in the clemency of the most excellent Prince and in the character of the Prussian state, which do not allow that anything be decreed against literature more unjustly.

For what can be applied to a state with better right than that which the most upright man Isocrates used in the Athenian republic, when he was accused of the same crime as formerly the son of Sophroniscus, namely that he corrupted the youth by his instruction?
For he used to say that the Athenians excelled all other states in literature.

Therefore, if they wished to be hostile to those who strove to surpass their contemporaries in the same things by which the Athenians surpassed all others, and who used that education of which Athens had been the leader and parent, the city would condemn itself by its own judgment, and would do the same as if the Lacedaemonians punished the teachers of the military art, or the Thessalians those who taught the methods of horsemanship.

Now, to return to the point from which I may perhaps seem to have digressed a little, since often the princes, in the first fervor of promoting literature, promised much, but soon failed, either through negligence, or from weariness, or because they thought that the studies and characters of teachers and students did not meet expectations;
Frederick William, having by natural goodness attained a union of constancy with munificence, preserved and enlarged the university with no less benevolence than he had founded it.
I will not speak of the very extensive increases in equipment, nor will I pursue the individual details that pertain to this matter:
For although these things are necessary and precious, just as they are devoid of life, so they lack force and vigor, unless the keen, ready, and energetic talents of teachers have been added.

In this matter there is need of constant diligence and kindness, so that, since the life of man is short, the succession may be worthy and illustrious, and lest, however great the names that have celebrated the school, it should gradually decline to lesser things, as often the titles and goods, not the virtue, of excellent men are transferred to their heirs.
And how great do you think the number of colleagues is, to whom successors have had to be given within this short space of a few lustra?
Twenty-five full professors, together with seven extraordinary professors, opened this school.
Of those twenty-five, no more than ten survive.
Even of those who later joined as full professors, eight have died, and only six have departed elsewhere.
Of the extraordinary professors, three have met their fate.
Twenty-two, mostly the younger ones, have changed their position.
And how great they were—indeed, by the fame and memory of men they still are—whose sweetest friendship fortune has begrudged us!
Today we celebrate a birthday, listeners, not a funeral.
Therefore let all mourning and lamentation be absent.
But it was nevertheless permitted to indicate in a word how great losses had to be repaired for the most merciful King.
Of these, two, and among them the most recent, were almost irreparable.
Those that could be repaired have been repaired in such a way that at the same time the number of teachers has increased as much as in no other literary university in Germany.
This is the King's disposition toward us.
But the royal house favors us no less, and especially you, fellow soldiers.
For although this university was never not well-equipped with those things that pertained to letters,
Nevertheless, another kind of support was lacking, intended for relieving the need and poverty of the citizens:
Only older schools are accustomed to enjoy an abundance of such supports, because the earlier age was more inclined to pious generosity.
Gradually, indeed, this necessity has been moderately provided for by private individuals, especially by providing food supplies.

But nothing more distinguished, nothing more desirable for us could have happened, than that the heir to the throne and the other most serene princes of the August house and their most serene consorts have recently contributed such large sums, so that they alone equaled the benefits of all others.
Nor was the gift gratifying only because of its magnitude.
Indeed, the courtesy of the donors and the confidence with which they entrusted this matter to the Senate to be administered, themselves plead on behalf of this seat of the arts.
We indeed, colleagues and fellow soldiers, cannot return thanks to Frederick William and the royal line, nor even offer thanks worthy of such great gifts;
but we can take care that our plans, institutions, studies, and life do not displease the Father of the fatherland:
