I promise this to all of you in your name, that we will diligently do it for you.

But may God, the Best and Greatest, reward the King with the highest goods and prosperity, and keep him safe and unharmed, together with his son, the noble heir to the kingdom, and his entire most flourishing house!

div.head: XXIII. Oratio nataliciis Friderici Guilelmi III. celebrandis d. III. m. Aug. a. MDCCCXXXV. habita.
On providence governing human affairs

p.s: Among most peoples, as among us, listeners, the parents, relatives, and all who wish well to the parents and the newborn child consider each person's birthday happy and auspicious, and they celebrate it every year with great joy and solemn festivity.
Good hope receives the new offspring with a joyful omen;
We give thanks to God, we pour out prayers and make vows for the tender infant, whom we bring to the altar to be purified;
We congratulate the birth of a new star, an immortal soul, which, like a spark, has flashed forth from the divine fire and has penetrated into this mortal little body:
Finally, although anxious about his safety, with God's favor we expect that he will reach a more robust age, will excel in uprightness, honor, and virtue, and will someday be a comfort to his own.
There were few nations, and those rather uncultivated, to whom it seemed otherwise:
This is what Herodotus has handed down about the Trausi.

For among these people, who followed a custom that was, I know not whether more severe or more soft and effeminate, but certainly more gloomy, they used to surround the newly born child with relatives lamenting and bewailing his fortune;
but the one who had died they buried with rejoicing and jesting, and they proclaimed blessed the one who had escaped so many and such great evils.
Nor are these entirely without reason.
For we enter upon a path of life that is steep, rough, and dangerous;
we are tossed about by the roughest waves and storms:
In short, no one is happy before death.
How many are there who, from these calamities by which we are surrounded on all sides, emerge safe and unharmed?
Most indeed fall short of their undertakings and prayers;
there are those who seem born neither for their own advantage nor for that of other men:
and not a few are stained with crimes and disgraceful acts, and become famous for the magnitude of their vices rather than their virtues:
Who would not think that for such men death is more to be desired than life?

And although these things apply to all men of any rank, even to those who are born in a humble station, yet they are especially suited to those who are born to the throne, because these are born not for themselves and for their father and mother alone, but for the state and all the citizens, and they are called by their very birth not to manage their own private fortune, but to conduct the great affairs of the empire.
And so they are received not only by their parents and relatives, but by the whole people with congratulatory greetings and immense exultation of spirit.
For the people feels and understands how great a pledge of tranquility and public security is placed in the perpetual succession of legitimate princes.

It understands that the fortune of the empire depends on the heir of the kingdom, and that according as the lots of birth have fallen, either the happiness of the republic or most disastrous losses are portended.
But the omens are obscure.
It is not clear by evident signs whether the Graces, courtesy, gentleness, or cruelty and the Furies stood by at his birth:
The outcome proves each one.
Certainly this outcome is not in our power alone;
Human affairs obey the more powerful laws of providence and fate, divinely established;

Yet the counsel of the divine power uses human beings as instruments, and indeed especially kings in public affairs, but in those matters which pertain to the cultivation and advancement of the mind and spirit, then both those same kings and others, whom you might call kings in their own kind, as living and acting with their own free will;
Whatever instrument resists that plan is thrown away as useless before the work is finished, and what had been accomplished by it becomes void.

I call him fortunate, for whom that part of the common work has succeeded, which he has received as assigned by the supreme maker of all things, that is, the one who knows how to direct his plans so that they harmonize with the hidden plan of the supreme divinity.
The outcome approved him;
From the birth of this man, that foul and inhuman mourning of the Trausi was deservedly absent.

I call the King blessed, who, after a long reign, after various vicissitudes, to which the human race is subject, constantly endured, as often as these most holy birthdays return, may repeatedly acclaim:
God favors your cares, God, who destined you, that you might be the dispenser of those good things, of those prosperities which he wishes to confer upon this people;

You, who seem to adapt your actions to the counsels of providence, as far as we can judge with human understanding, and not to resist the course of events established by divine will, and to handle with ready and sure hand what has been entrusted to you!
You increase the happiness of the empire every year;
You understand that human affairs are governed not by anger but by the love of the supreme deity, and are accomplished through the endless courses of ages:
You, comparing and composing yourself to his example, as far as mortal nature permits, prefer freedom to servitude, obedience tempered by reason to necessity, gentleness to savage severity.
We venerate you as king, we love you as father!

I have said that kings and those who in every kind of human culture excel in wisdom, and rule as if with royal power and write laws for the less gifted, less clear-sighted multitude, are instruments which providence uses to carry out its plans.
But what are these plans?

Who, I ask, even if he seems by far the wisest, would dare to define what are the reasons and ways of providence, whence it proceeds and whither it tends, what ends it has set for the human race, and, once you have known the end, by what means it impels mortals so that they may at last reach the goal?
Indeed, it would be the part of a prophet to know and to discuss these things:

Yet if one who is skilled in past events is rightly considered a prophet turned backward, this man, from those traces which have been impressed on earlier ages, may have divined a little about the ends of human affairs;

And although I seem to perceive, after a long interval and as if through a mist, what he has divined, and it happens that what is itself small and obscure is represented to me by my blunter vision as even smaller and duller, yet it pleases me, even with an unpolished voice, as far as can be done within the narrowness of time, to sketch out what sort of thing appears before my eyes.

For if this visible nature of things, which nevertheless seems to many to be devoid of mind, is not moved by a random impulse, nor are the stars whirled about by some blind rotation, but the masses, intervals, spaces, and times are balanced and arranged in a lawful order:

Shall we think that the mind, which alone was able to arrange and adorn rude matter into the form of the world, alone to establish a law for the whole mass, when it was first implanted in the human race, was driven without law, wandered, was carried recklessly wherever chance might hurl it headlong?

Or shall we say that human affairs indeed have their prescribed changes, but just as the sky and the stars, moving in a circle perpetually, after completing their course also return to the same place from which they set out, so human affairs too, imitating the heavenly order, are driven around in a circle as if by certain whirlwinds, and after completing the circle, after so many ages, after so many and such great labors of mortals, have not advanced a step, but have been cast back to the beginning of the course, and that the human race, pierced through, performs the leaky jars of the Danaids, continually pouring in water that continually flows out?
Indeed, it is a common saying that what once existed returns again and again, and that nothing new happens under the sun.
But it is equally true that the same things never return, and that one cannot step into the same river twice.
Indeed, while in human affairs earlier ages seem in a certain way to be repeated, nevertheless these things, which you might think to be the same, have greatly changed their character.
By this change, although with a slow motion, the human race progresses and advances, striving of its own accord toward perfection.

For such is the nature of the mind, that, while the body, which we share with the beasts, only reproduces bodies no better than those from which they were born, the reason implanted in the mind grows with the succession of ages, because each later person, taught by the earlier, increases the riches of the mind, and purges, corrects, and amplifies what was previously known and discovered;
But although the body is enslaved, let the mind be free and command itself, and while the powers of the mind grow, freedom grows, which no one will think I confuse with license:
For license uses only the appearance of freedom, in order to exercise the most atrocious tyranny:

Now, with freedom increased gradually and step by step, we shall be less constrained by the bonds of necessity, because we govern ourselves, and with a gentler rule day by day love and clemency will reign in place of severity and vengeance.
This is that law which history, unless I am mistaken, proclaims as prescribed for human affairs by providence.

But when I dare to set this forth, although I would not deny that, just as in nature cities are shaken by earthquakes and swallowed up by the opening of the earth, and the most fertile regions are devastated by floods, and great families are destroyed by pestilence;

Thus you might think that whole nations and ages are attacked by diseases of the mind, and that many things happen otherwise than is consistent with that law, which I have mentioned, and with the wisdom and goodness of the divine will.
that obstacles are placed in the way of the human mind's course;
that barbarism sometimes breaks in;
that some states grow, others are diminished;

that peoples, once most adorned with every kind of civilization, are lulled into torpor and grow old in indolence, and that the whole human race does not rejoice at the same time in equal flourishing, but that the seats of more perfect culture and learning change in turn:

Nevertheless, I am not more disturbed by these things than anyone a little more intelligent will doubt about providence, if he has seen not a few of the best men oppressed by diseases and poverty, shut up in prison, tortured by torments, and afflicted with disgrace, while meanwhile others, to use the words of a certain most eloquent man, covered with all sorts of crimes, live in the greatest pleasures and enjoy the most favorable fortune in all their affairs.
But I think that the human race takes growth from the very obstacles, because in the struggle strength is nourished and sinews are stretched.

And those who resist reason already on the verge of victory, we see them generally carried away as if by a river and overcome, whom I said a little while ago are cast aside as now useless instruments, remnants of a past age, not supports for the present.
Finally, a more refined culture, although it changes its abode, nevertheless gradually spreads wider and wider, and strikes its roots deeper, and is established more firmly.
Now let it be permitted to illustrate with a few examples what I have said.
It is agreed that the beginnings of culture are to be sought in the East.

There in ancient times, what each person had to handle was not determined by his own will, not by his character and talent, but with the tasks assigned by family lines, the origin of each person cast the die for his entire life:
which now, in this culture of states, is restricted to the princes alone.
Therefore the human mind obeyed the necessity of nature;
this necessity had subjected the greatest part of men to the harshest slavery;
nor was there any place left for flight, nor did anyone seek better things:
so much did slavery itself please.
Marriages were uncertain, almost like those of brute beasts:
they were maidservants rather than mothers of families:
there were almost no states, but for the most part the most unjust domination.
The arts were not neglected;

But the unformed shapes, which had been born and fashioned by a certain natural impulse, have been consecrated forever and have remained unmoved, because the mind, not yet mature, preferred to acquiesce in what had been handed down, and was not yet equal to undertaking new inventions and attempting more perfect works:

In the same way, the priests among the Egyptians most diligently sanctioned those figures and songs that seemed to them to be proper, and they took care that no sculptor or painter or any other craftsman should fashion or invent anything else besides those.

From this it came about that things that had been sketched or carved many thousands of years before did not differ from the most recent ones, nor were they more beautiful or more deformed, but were made with exactly the same skill.
But literature and learning were generally confined within the bounds of religions, not differing much from mythology.
But the poetry and wisdom of the Indians, as if by divination, opened up a more sublime understanding of things.
And the nation of the Jews, although not even it was freed from superstitious fear, occupied a more sacred opinion concerning the supreme deity.
Now the Greeks, with a freer movement of their intellects, broke those bonds by which the East was constrained, and escaped from custody.
Liberty shone forth in the state, if not tempered in the most just manner, at least as the mother and leader of the greatest deeds and most beautiful achievements.
Private affairs, even marriages, which they say Cecrops instituted, were arranged according to the law of a more correct reason;
Arts and letters advance, as he says, with winged step;
The form of beauty, immortal and eternal, a visible image of the eternal mind, is expressed in the most perfect and, as it were, living and walking images:
Philosophy begins to penetrate the inner sanctuaries of nature and the mind with deep thought.
Nevertheless, traces of ancient inhumanity and harshness remain:
Some are free, others are slaves;
and not yet does the female sex have its own honor;
and not yet is the common people freed from immense superstition, although the wise see the truth.
And Greece was also infected with other vices;
These things rather brought destruction upon it than the Macedonians and Romans.
I will not speak of the kingdom of the Persians, overthrown by Alexander the Great.

Although even through this man the light of the mind was propagated, as is shown by the Egyptian kingdom and the strength and force of Alexandrian learning, which was greater and more useful than it has seemed to most people.
Soon Rome imposed laws on the whole world;

Although it was inferior to Greece in learning, yet it not only adorned the institutions of life and the public and domestic affairs better, but that very part of humanity which it owed to the Greeks, it spread widely among the barbarian peoples of old, and civilized the wild nations, to whom amid arms it gave at once laws, and prepared the soil for a new sowing.
This greatest sowing, as from the smallest seeds huge things are born, the beginnings of the Christian religion made.

For just as Aeschylus established that after the ancient gods, that stern and harsh offspring of eternal night, there succeeded milder and more intelligent gods and gods more favorable to men, he, the first, as it seems to me, augured with a lofty mind that the progress of the human mind gradually grew stronger:

Thus the Christian religion, after the old ceremonies were abolished, tamed the world, and not only reconciled the mortal race to God, but also strove to reconcile man to man, people to people, and all to grace and freedom, and to bring it about that, as that excellent poet famously declared, you may be just without necessity and hence not without a share of the blessed life, but never perish utterly.
Indeed, the divine providence had long since prepared the beginnings for that better understanding of divine and human affairs;
nor do I fear to affirm that there were long since not a few who judged and discoursed most worthily about these things;

already Plato, as it were, proclaimed the sovereignty of purer reason, and Socrates and the Stoics, although they did not deny that the duties of a good citizen also must be performed, exalted humanity above the state:
Those who profess this opinion are so far from causing harm to the state that they are even likely to improve civil affairs according to the laws of humanity.
Indeed, there were those who, with a truly Christian sense, valued humanity itself solely by its likeness to divinity.
But nevertheless both the priests and those who administered the state resisted, until the Christian cause prevailed.

However, I would not want us to be too angry with men of lofty intellect, who, fixed in the excellence of earlier learning and dazzled by its splendor, followed with no ignoble grief the ruin of the old discipline:
for these too seemed to themselves to be filled with God, and they did not yet understand those good things which the new superstition, as they called it, was about to bring;

And it excuses them the greater frenzy of the Christian fanatics, who raged against dissenters with such cruelty as might perhaps befit the furious priestesses of Bellona among the Comans, not those who were instructed by the divine teacher in the precepts of charity.

Indeed, after the Christian religion brought such great light and improvement to the human race, and subdued so many barbarous nations under its gentle yoke, nations which, roused from their ancient seats, had invaded and reduced to subjection the most cultivated lands of Europe;
soon that very religion itself, no less than the affairs of the Greeks and Romans once, as if worn out by old age, decayed, and was corrupted in various ways.

For although it had freed bodies to a great extent, it had especially freed minds, and led them into a new servitude, from which not even philosophy, which is by its nature most free, could sufficiently vindicate itself:
the pontifical power even attempted to subject kingdoms and princes to a not very equitable rule:

The unlearned clergy, for the most part devoid of good literature, dissolved in softness and luxury, were polluted by lust, avarice, treachery, and any evil arts more than the priests of the pagan gods were of old.

These and other evils, not without providence, I think, were remedied by the great things which, from the fifteenth century onward and shortly after, the human mind accomplished, using not arms but the strength of intellect:
Although afterwards even arms were taken up, because power sought to use force against intellect.
For first, by the most fierce contentions of the most excellent men, literature was restored:

Whatever survived from antiquity was brought out of the darkness and turned with the greatest zeal to this end, that the fog by which minds had been covered might be dispelled, that a sound judgment about divine and human matters might be established, that preconceived opinions by which the freedom of minds is hindered might be cast aside, and that a more refined cultivation of talents might be restored:

And to this lively movement, the recently invented printing press brought enormous weight, which not only disseminates whatever is entrusted to it so quickly and over such immense spaces that this Daedalian contrivance seems at last to have given words truly winged and flying, but at the same time also provides an airy firmness and permanence to these flying sayings, and brings it about that common understanding can now scarcely be suppressed by anyone's force.

A new flower of the arts, especially of painting, has arisen, which arts themselves, if you except a few genres of poetry and a certain not-to-be-despised form of architecture, had lain prostrate after the destruction of Greek and Roman antiquity.

Now what was more desired than a more correct and more holy constitution of sacred things and a salutary restoration of the church, attempted indeed earlier by one and another, but suppressed by fire through the barbarous cruelty of priestly tyrants?
Luther therefore undertook this reformation of sacred rites with a bold enterprise and accomplished it:
which, without doubt, would have brought forth more joyful fruits sooner, had not most atrocious wars intercepted the harvest.
But when the world was somewhat pacified, in many lands of Europe letters and disciplines grew with continuous success:
the most important peoples so cultivated their languages and especially poetry, that they could emulate antiquity;
the studies of history, nature, and mathematics were advanced very far by the constant labors of innumerable scholars;

Philosophy, however, through many successive steps, which it seems superfluous to enumerate before this assembly of most learned men and studious young men, especially since some of those who excelled in philosophy lived in the very Prussian kingdom, partly in this very city and among ourselves, ascended to the highest and broadest knowledge.
I am not the sort of person who would marvel at the greatness of this age and think that our learning is perfect and complete in every respect.

But he would be unfair and no less ungrateful to our ancestors, whose good deeds we enjoy, than to the present generation, if he denied that the human race has made great progress, and that culture is growing day by day better, more liberal, and more gentle; which, after a new world besides emerged, as it were, from the Ocean more than three hundred years ago, now surrounds and occupies this whole earthly globe, whereas in the most flourishing times of Greece it was confined to the narrow circuit of the Mediterranean Sea.

Already now even barbarians are beginning to taste and to love the arts of more civilized Europe, and peoples who had languished in idleness and long torpor are beginning to rise again and recover their strength.

Therefore, both princes and peoples ought to serve the common interests of the human race by increasing them, and each one ought to strive according to his ability to satisfy the position in which he has been placed.
No man returns to his cradle, no one offers himself to be bound in swaddling clothes;
Nor shall we fall back more into the condition of the East or of Greek antiquity, or of the so-called Middle Ages.

However, since not all peoples, as we indicated above, move at the same pace, nor do human affairs advance with equal effort, some through sloth and stupidity retain a worse condition for a longer time;
others certainly follow the foreign impulse promptly and allow themselves to be dragged along;
Some are leaders beyond others in undertaking better things, especially when they have been stirred and driven by the genius of some excellent man.

And sometimes provinces have even been divided among these, with one people deserving well by cultivating literature or arts exceptionally, another by ordering public affairs or other institutions of life more correctly.
But those peoples who are leaders toward better things and in every age, and who follow not too late, even if they are small, almost alone come into the census of humanity;
The rest, like proletarians, are counted almost only by number of heads.
Thus those small Athens, placed especially by Pericles on the highest summit, were the eye of the world and the delight of every most learned person;

The Persian kingdom, extending most widely through the vast regions of Asia, is placed in a much lower position by just estimators of things, who compare nations by the virtue of the mind, not by the multitude of slaves:
But the Scythians, Sarmatians, and Huns, however strong and powerful they may have been at some time, you would count among the last of mortals.

But I will say in very few words how much this kingdom, which is now called by the name of Prussia, has contributed and contributes to the progress of mind and reason among the more civilized states of the modern age.
The line of our princes, together with the peoples who then obeyed them, was among the first to join in the reformation of sacred things;

And today Frederick William is regarded as the leader and, in a way, the defender of the evangelical confession, the same man who was the wisest reconciler of parties once in disagreement, thinking that all good men ought to be united by mutual charity, not to be separated by hatreds on account of certain doctrines scarcely, and not even scarcely, understood.
Frederick the Great taught by example and by law to tolerate those who held a different persuasion about divine matters, and he granted [the freedom] to think what you wish and to say what you think.
The barbarous and cruel institutions, once sanctioned by the laws themselves, have been abolished.
The Prussian kings greatly fostered letters and arts, but no one more brilliantly than Frederick William.
By this merit, just as he consulted for all Germany, so he also holds forth the torch to the same and to all Europe for extending the community of commerce more widely every year:
which itself also may be counted among the progress of the human race.

Now if no one who is even a little more prudent fails to understand that many things are still lacking for the perfection of culture, and that in not a few matters the present state is so far surpassed by earlier centuries, and that any human society, as soon as it has begun to take shape, is carried backward, and that for minds as for bodies there is need of frequent motion to preserve health, lest the juices stagnate and become corrupted, and lest, as Tacitus says, even the sweetness of idleness itself creep in, and laziness, at first hated, afterwards be loved;

if moreover it must be conceded that the whole affairs of the human race are governed by one mind and reason, and accordingly that from the knowledge and science alone, as it were, of divine and human things, institutions both public and private proceed, depend, and improve somewhat better:

This is what seems to have moved Cicero, a man far wiser than most of those who despise him, to say that philosophy gave birth to cities, called scattered men together into a community of life, joined them to one another first by dwellings, then by marriages, then by the sharing of letters and speech, and was the inventor of laws, the teacher of morals and discipline:

Therefore, if what I have said is true, whoever devotes themselves to learning has this glorious task imposed upon their most honorable leisure: to provide those things by which public and private welfare may be increased.
This is first accomplished by preserving the memory of the best things, which a previous age has produced.
Whoever destroys or neglects that memory, which removes that knowledge to which our life owes itself, seems to me to be, as it were, a parricide.
Then that only field, which our parents left to us as heirs, must be cultivated and worked with new labor, lest it become barren, and from it new things must be generated.
Of these things, one belongs to historical learning in each kind of erudition, the other to rational meditation.
But both of these have been entrusted to us, the teachers of universities, so that we may hand over the knowledge of our age to the young men who will be the doctors of a future age.
We sow the seeds;
we scarcely see the ripe fruits.
But if we are rightly minded, we will shape our students so that they may advance further than we ourselves have progressed.

And to use an old saying, when we are weary with years, just as in the gymnasium games among the Greeks, we will hand the burning torches to a fresh runner — what wonder if he, entering upon a new course, will run more swiftly than we, exhausted?
The Spartans ordered their boys to promise in a public ceremony, in song, that they would one day be much braver than those who then excelled in courage.
So why should we not willingly allow ourselves to be surpassed by those who come after us?
By this path the mind and reason emerge victorious, virtue grows, and the human race is formed toward the end divinely appointed for it.
This path is approved by Frederick William, who, if he had not wished to be walked on in this way, would not have so greatly supported literature and the arts:
for these do not lead to any other path than this one:
he would not have founded this our wrestling-school of the best studies.
Therefore, what was for me today the beginning of speaking, let the same be the end.

So often, when I have been discoursing at these solemn ceremonies, such a great light of royal wisdom, liberality, humanity, and gentleness has arisen for me, that, since I judge that man to be perfected by these virtues who offers himself as the most suitable instrument for carrying out the counsels of providence, I think that Frederick William fulfills the office entrusted to him so greatly that he serves not only the growth of the republic but of human affairs with the most favorable success.
Therefore we venerate him as king, we love him as father.
I have spoken.

div.head: XXIV. Oratio nataliciis Friderici Guilelmi III. celebrandis d. III. m. Aug. a. MDCCCXXXVI. habita.
On the temperance of the prince

p.s: There are two things, listeners, from which anyone who has decided to praise either a state or a prince or a private citizen can seek material for praise: fortune and virtue.
And fortune indeed, although it is not in our power, nevertheless has its own admirers:

Partly by right and rightly, because, as proverbial wisdom teaches, each person contributes something to shaping his own fortune, and the highest prosperity comes by the benefit of nature and of the divine will, whose favor no one doubts to place in the category of praise;
Partly by a more imprudent estimation, which the common people generally follow, marveling at the splendor of birth, wealth, and power.
But who is ignorant of the fragility of fortune?
Who has not seen that a man who was just now regarded as most fortunate has been struck down by sudden ruin and overwhelmed by the waves of calamity?
Therefore virtue alone is what, in the judgment of the wise, is worthy of praise.

I, now about to speak of the prince, will not boast of the title of good fortune, with which Rome did not disdain to adorn her Augusti, more through foolish flattery than from the truth of the matter:
I will take my stand on virtue.
This is indeed a great subject, and one that demands a great orator:
for one may declaim about happiness, but not likewise about virtue:
But you, such is your indulgence, will judge my speech not by what I have accomplished, but by what I have intended.
But if you ask by what means the virtue of a prince is completed and perfected, although the answer may seem difficult, I have one that is both ready and very simple.

I maintain that the prince, because he must fulfill all the duties of a private master in his own household, and because in public he is not occupied with one or another single business, but presides over the whole of affairs and embraces all parts of the state, cannot be considered perfect unless he is equipped with all the virtues that human nature can attain.
Since no single mortal seems adequate for this task, one might say that the perfect virtue of a prince can indeed be conceived in the mind, but not realized in practice.

Therefore, both the lot of a prince is miserable, since he, although he may be the best, nevertheless cannot attain the highest good, and a hard necessity is imposed on men of obeying those who, even with the most intense exertion, cannot reach universal princely virtue, but must be content with certain small parts or fragments of virtue.
And indeed such is the weakness of the human race that it cannot accomplish anything perfect without divine aid.
Nevertheless, I deny that anyone is equal to attaining all the virtues.
Therefore I do not even grant that a prince can be sufficient in some part for all his duties.

For if the virtues were so constituted that they dwelt in separate abodes, as it were, and did not remain harmonious in one seat, and wherever one had entered, the other would rush out and withdraw from there, or would resist outside the doors and threshold;
You would rightly doubt whether anyone could satisfy all his duties, whether private or public.
But I see that the greatest philosophers decide otherwise, and it is by far the safest to follow them in a matter that cannot be rightly judged except by philosophers.

For it is not the case that, just as the mouth, nostrils, eyes, and ears are distinct and different parts of the face, so the individual virtues are parts of the whole of virtue, divided and separated from one another; nor is it the case that, just as one who has been deprived of eyes nevertheless retains the ears and the other parts of the face, so one who lacks wisdom or courage can nonetheless be adorned with the remaining virtues:
But there is one virtue which embraces each of the individual virtues, and each individual virtue contains both the rest and the whole.
There is no virtue that excludes any other, and there is no virtue contrary to any other.
To discuss especially the cardinal virtues, as they are called: justice contains in itself wisdom, temperance, and fortitude.
And courage—I mean true courage, not what is commonly regarded as courage, boldness carried by blind impulse—courage, I say, belongs to no one unless he is both just and wise and temperate.
And similarly the rest in turn.

To add sanctity, can anyone be considered holy who is not also intelligent, just and fair, with temperate and moderate character in any part of life, and finally, when circumstances demand it, even courageous?
Therefore, in whatever position each person is placed, he must share in the whole of virtue, so that he may rightly perform his duty.
And so far is it from being the case that anyone can be possessed of it, that whoever has fully attained one virtue holds the whole.
Therefore it is less fitting to ask anxiously whether anyone can attain the whole royal virtue.

How these things are present in our most merciful King, both all of you who have come together here for reverence of him know well, and I have often either sketched in passing or explained with deliberate effort.
Today I will confine myself to considering a single virtue.
For although all virtues dwell together in the greatest harmony, yet different matters, different times, and different outcomes demand that one virtue be brought forward especially.
Frederick William indeed fell into that age which commanded one virtue to be shown after another.

His steadfastness of mind and courage in the great calamity, both his own and that of the state, and in waging the most savage wars; his wisdom and justice in restoring and ordering the commonwealth, which we saw shaken and prostrate; his moderation in calming and soothing the minds that had been stirred or exasperated by various goads.
Indeed, Frederick William is most temperate; he is born for the reconciliation of citizens, nations, and peoples:
which is especially needed now.

Indeed, whether in the very bosom of the state or beyond it somewhat greater disturbances have arisen, before it has come to arms, nothing will be more effective than moderation combined with constancy, which makes leading men fair to all parties and does not allow them to be carried away by passions:
Thus it happens that, like gods from on high and serene, they look down securely upon the turbulent crowd and the fickle multitude's passions, which are for the most part transient and vain.
By this moderation, as far as possible, both seditions and wars are guarded against, which greed and pride provoke and nourish.
What then?
Does not empire itself seem by its very nature to be impatient of limit?
Is it not difficult for those who, from their very birth, have been placed at the highest pinnacle not to be proud?
Whom almost no one contradicts, whom no one dares to correct?
Who see everything placed in their own hand, everything done at their nod, destined by divine will to hold the place of gods on earth?
Indeed, a good natural disposition is needed, lest the leading men fall into that vice to which the very position in which they are placed easily gives them a headlong tendency.

But a self-controlled prince never forgets that he shares the common human weakness with even the humblest person, and that although the prince is indeed a living and animate law, yet because the prince's will stands for law, his own will must be established according to the norm of reason, which alone ought to govern all things, not according to arbitrary desire and lust, and that although he has been placed by divine will over the highest affairs, he is a man commanding men.

Finally, so that no sane person may dare to compare himself with him, and so that the dignity and majesty of the prince may be separated from all other mortals by a greater interval, the more moderately can one deal with those who depend entirely on him.
But someone may say that these things are trite and common;
more recondite things are desired.

I indeed, although I think that commonplaces are not to be avoided, provided they are true, and I judge them to be safer for me, because one who wishes to bring forth more recondite matters about the principate ought to have been much engaged in public affairs, from which no one is more remote than I am, since I lurk in the shadow of the school, not unwillingly:
Nevertheless, I will try to discuss briefly those matters in which the prince's moderation, if not solely, certainly to a great extent and especially, may seem to shine forth.
I will arrange this argument into three topics, of which two pertain to domestic matters, the third to foreign affairs.
First, I say that the prince should not, with excessive zeal, exalt any one way of life in the state above the rest, and neglect these:

But if any part is nourished too much, while the rest truly wither, it is clear that this part becomes burdensome to them, and the state is sick, since the harmony, concord, and just proportion of the individual limbs have been removed, just as the body does not enjoy full health when some one organ swells excessively and drains the juices from the others.
The second point is that the prince should not involve himself in the partisan zeal and anger of the factions that arise in most states;
Third, that he be fair to foreign nations as well and be far removed from envy and hatreds, with which one people is accustomed to attack another.

For first, although we grant this indulgence not only to a private individual, that he should apply his mind especially to some one thing, but we also think this very thing useful and necessary, for the reason that individuals are both by their own nature more suited to certain particular things or arts to be practiced, and by practice become even more skillful, while those who do not dwell and persevere in any art, but flitting about here and there, like bees from flowers, are accustomed to draw some nourishment and gather fruits from various disciplines, attempt many things and are imbued with some rough learning, but neither are they perfected themselves nor do they accomplish anything at all.

Nevertheless, a leader, who is not engaged in handling individual matters and performing some particular duty, but holds the reins of government, ought not to hold any art or business so dear as to think that the rest are to be neglected or despised, but, just as the divine power that governs the universe provides for all parts of this world, he should embrace all things with equal care, judge all kinds of life according to their own dignity and importance with keen judgment, and show himself kind to all of them.
In this matter no one will deny that mistakes are sometimes made.
For some rulers care only for military matters, others for civil affairs:
or they favor profitable arts, crafts, and commerce, thinking that liberal education is unprofitable and not worthy of public care;
or they neglect too much those things that are altogether necessary for acquiring wealth:
indeed, from these very things, sometimes agriculture, sometimes commerce has seemed more excellent to rulers.
There are those who favor the arts but care little for literature.

And from literature we have just seen that mathematics and the natural sciences were neglected by them, or that these alone pleased them, while whatever pertains to the cultivation of the human race and the memory of deeds done displeased them greatly, and philosophy was especially hateful.
Again, others, devoted and enslaved to sacred rites and ceremonies, careless of profane matters, even the most serious ones;
Others, alienated from sacred rites, or even hostile to them.
What moderation, how wise, how just, Frederick William has maintained and maintains in all these matters, there is none of us who does not understand:
He presents a prince almost perfect, as far as human nature allows, burdensome to no kind of life or business, favorable to all, giving to each his due honor.

Now, to come to the second point, where great danger threatens the state from a great agitation of minds, the temperate prince is indeed on watch and keeps guard for the safety of all, lest the republic suffer any harm;
He goes to meet destructive and wicked attempts in good time, so that medicine may not be prepared too late:

And yet he does not serve the interests and plans of any party, whether these have arisen from the teachings of some civil doctrine, which we see happening frequently in our age, or are adapted to the advantages of some order or class of citizens.
He does not court the popular breeze, nor the favor of the aristocrats.
He does what Solon, the wisest and most just of legislators and the most excellent example of moderation and self-restraint, proclaims that he did:
"I granted the plebs only as much power as is sufficient," he says, "neither taking away anything from their honor nor adding too much;"
But those who were endowed with power and strong in resources, for these too I provided, lest they suffer anything unworthy:

I stood firm for both sides, surrounding them with a shield, and I did not allow either to win unjustly." By this means it cannot happen but that the prince wins the hearts of all for himself, even of those who, perhaps because they have recently joined his kingdom, have not yet grown together with the new lord in that mutual bond of affection by which the other subjects are united.

Moreover, because he knows that no one contends with him for the highest place, he will not unwillingly descend from his height, so that he may hear the wishes of the citizens and listen to the advice of the experienced.

He alone is truly above all who understands that he can obey the admonitions of each one while preserving his authority; he is truly free from the laws who has bound himself to the law willingly, and does not think that by observing the law any violence is done to his own will.

Even if some have offended, although their audacity and impious deeds deserve punishment, he will prefer leniency and clemency to the most severe punishment and will incline to the more humane side, as far as the guardianship of morals and the security of the empire permit:
For temperance is the mother of clemency, while pride gives birth to cruelty.

Who would deny that this must be counted among the most important blessings of this age, that we have ceased to take pleasure in cruelty when punishing offenses, and that most of us understand that the most severe punishments, which our ancestors employed very frequently, are not suited except to rude ages and to uncultivated morals and minds, which have persuaded themselves that the savagery of a crime must be either equaled or surpassed by the savagery of the punishment, so that fierce and savage men might be deterred by the cruelty of retribution?
There have long been those who think that it is not even lawful to condemn anyone to death.

However this matter may be judged (for I do not interpose my own opinion, since it makes no difference), all the more humane agree on this: that it is unworthy of a state to teach cruelty by its own example, and that too with no public advantage.

For it is so far from being the case that crimes are prevented by this means, that while a person commits them, hardly anyone is mindful of the laws and punishments, but is driven by anger and hatred and mad desires, or hopes that he can escape punishment and hide from the avenger, that even wrongdoings seem to be provoked by cruel punishment, because wicked and bold men are trained to cruelty by the example of the state.
The law itself has not rarely pointed out and has given birth to crime:

As Seneca, who lived in that age in which the frequency of punishments could teach attentive people what fruit the most severe punishments could bear, saying about parricide, "The highest prudence," he says, "of the most profound men and most skilled in the nature of things preferred to pass over an incredible crime and one placed beyond audacity, rather than, while they punish it, show that it can be done:"

And so they began with the law of parricide, and the punishment showed them the crime. But when the state itself uses milder laws, the minds of all citizens are gradually imbued with a sense of gentleness, which our Christian religion also demands, and morals are softened;

And not to speak only of laws and institutions, whether written or unwritten, the prince especially, who as we said above is a living and breathing law, according as he has been gentle or fierce, by his example will shape the multitude of the more ignorant, which is ruled more by examples than by precepts, either to humanity or to barbarous cruelty.
But when a common movement adds sharper goads to minds and disturbs tranquility, you may see that most people sin more from error than from a bad disposition:

If these are not to be forgiven, certainly a lighter punishment should be inflicted, and only those dispositions that are desperate and incurable should be restrained with harsher penalties, lest they be able to harm again.
Indeed, the more people are punished, the more enemies rise up again, just as the Hydra regenerated two heads for each one cut off.

And if fear is needed (and it is certainly needed in the state of affairs I have mentioned, lest impunity increase audacity), certainly a moderate amount must be employed, because excessive fear makes people more stubborn.

"For moderate fear," as that same wise writer whom I just brought forward says, "restrains the mind, but constant and sharp fear, driving to extremes, rouses those lying in idleness to boldness and urges them to try everything." Now, lest I linger too long on these matters, to which the sequence of events and the course of my speech have brought me, [I turn to] not the character and nature of this kingdom:

For these things, even if Frederick William were not by nature most gentle and most mild, and rather bore the character of a father of his subjects than a master, nevertheless could scarcely invite anyone to propose these things, because almost all cruelty has long been banished from our state:
I pass to the third of the arguments which I have proposed.

For just as in one and the same state, both the interests of different orders, as they themselves think, are different and accordingly their pursuits are different, and moreover each one according to his own feeling or the principles with which he is imbued, and according to the opinions either his own or those of his patrons, thinks that one form of the republic and other institutions are advantageous:
so peoples differ in customs and natural dispositions;
Different things seem fair, just, and useful to different states.
Different peoples use different laws, which confirm that discrepancy which nature itself has established.
Thus it happens that one nation is alienated from another:
Neighboring peoples especially are wont to exercise offenses, because one seems to stand in the way of another's advantages:
And especially great states, from an innate desire of acquiring, strive to extend the boundaries of their empire and to take possession of neighboring fields.

But if envy has been increased by frequent wars and many mutual disasters, hatreds are kindled more fiercely, so that they seem scarcely ever able to be extinguished, and, hidden in the inmost hearts, they are easily brought forth at every opportunity.

I think there is no one among our elders who has not burned with this hatred himself, at the time when the proud enemy, after he had continually provoked the most just and most self-controlled king and finally forced him to wage war, with the army defeated in battles, also tore apart this kingdom and most unjustly harassed the Prussian lands;

And I freely confess that in these very orations, in which I was celebrating the praises of Frederick William, I not infrequently indulged a rather irritated mind and yielded to the hatreds which the reason of the times demanded.
But with the causes removed, the effects must be moderated;

As it is the mark of a man too prone to anger to extend hatreds to the end of life, so a state, which it befits to be more temperate than individuals, ought to lay aside enmities as soon as an opportunity for reconciliation has been made.

Therefore, since in no age and among no people are there lacking those who please themselves in this, that they nourish discords and incite to the exercise of enmities, that prince is especially to be praised who surpasses private individuals in moderation, and feels that a duty has been entrusted to him by God, not to afflict his own people and foreigners with the slaughter of contests, which those do who undertake wars for no other reason than to satisfy ambition and greed, but to aid the human race with peace, to which it has deservedly been reproached that most evils come to man from man, since not even beasts rage except against different species, and not even the ferocity of lions fights among themselves.

Certainly it is understood more and more day by day that the human race tends toward that end, that peoples may securely enjoy common goods, not only those who are of the same stock, as the Germans are now almost all most closely united with us, but also those of a different stock, and that all nations may come together into a great society of the whole race.

And so it has been shown by earlier times, and now by these most recent ones, that the most serene mind of Frederick William is so disposed that no one is more suitable than he for bringing about this better state of affairs.
And so the swords that were just now threatening battles have been drawn and sheathed, and the fears by which we were held in suspense for several years have been dispelled.
Finally, Frederick William is not only the most certain founder and preserver of the republic, but also of peace.
From that moderation of his, both the people and the learned can take an example for themselves, so that, by attributing too much to domestic matters, they may not be more unfair to foreigners.
For although it is proper and pious to hold one's fatherland dearer than all things and to prefer it and its institutions to foreign ones, unless these are manifestly better;
From this source, how much strength accrues to the state, the Lacedaemonians and Romans excellently teach:

Yet just as parents, out of a foolish love for their offspring or rather for themselves, love and approve even the faults of their children, so often peoples rejoice in their own blemishes and even boast of them, and do not wish to be corrected, but spurn and hate the physician who announces a hidden disease and judges a cure necessary, while they applaud flatterers who keep saying that not only is the body sound, but that it is most perfect, and that this nation surpasses all other mortals.
Therefore it cannot happen that the people are gradually given over to sloth and languor.

At the same time, this people, because it alone pleases itself, just as the Chinese please themselves, is lifted up with pride above the other nations, and despises and scorns them before itself, and disparages their virtues:
And since the Jews once seemed to do this notably, hatred of the human race was reproached against them, and they themselves incurred the hatred of all.
What of the fact that this popular envy, with the most perverse rivalry, rages even in literature?

Since these things are common to all nations, that injustice should be considered more remote from nothing than from them, which looks not so much at what is provided, as at from what nation, and is distressed by the good arts of foreigners and disparages their merits.

Perhaps, listeners, I will seem to have departed too far from the praises of Frederick William, and to have spoken more generally about the moderation of a prince, with other opinions mixed in besides, which did not even pertain to the princely virtue:

But I did not want to repeat what has been set forth by me more than once about Frederick William's generous mind, and yet I have brought back the most important parts of the argument to the person of the most beloved King.
Now if I wanted, I could add more:

For also in private life, especially in marriage, and in the whole domestic and family economy, in choosing and cultivating friends, in the just measure of liberality and frugality, and in other almost countless matters, the self-control and moderation of the Prince is so clearly seen that it is all too easy to demonstrate from these things as well, as from those which he does publicly, the most temperate character of Frederick William.

But I altogether confine myself to narrower limits, because it is not fitting even for a moderate prince to be pleased with a more detailed eulogy, and I consider it enough to have indicated one or two things and to have pointed a finger at his famous institutions and plans.

But if it seems that praise should be tempered, nevertheless the feelings of affection, devotion, and gratitude should not be tempered, with which all citizens of this literary university ought to and do accompany the most kind Prince.
However, not many words are needed:
A genuine feeling of gratitude completes the action with a more concise speech.

Therefore, since I have often deliberately discussed what Frederick William had done for literature and the arts throughout so many years of his reign, although they were troubled by the tumults of wars, with what care and at what great expense he had provided for every kind of school, not only, as ambitious princes are wont to do, for those from whose dignity some splendor might seem to accrue to the empire, but especially with what zeal, with what liberality, with what equitable laws he had founded, adorned, and cherished this our seat of learning, I have often discoursed at length.
Now I shall give thanks in your name to the most gracious King for two things, one of which pertains to moderation, the other to munificence.

For after that nearly incurable plague of secret societies, which we saw growing worse up to conspiracy and arms, extorted from the German Confederation a common decree, by which the academic discipline might be established on a more prudent basis;

Because among us almost everything had been arranged correctly and according to the standard, in accordance with a strict and just norm, nothing was taken away from our dignity and authority, and very few new institutions were added, which we accepted with the most willing mind.

This ought also to be an incentive to you, fellow soldiers, so that you may satisfy the will of the most beloved Prince by preserving for the future the same honesty and innocence of character that you have almost all approved up to now.

He who very recently gratified the university he founded with a most welcome gift, in that, although the buildings which he most generously gave us more than twenty-five years ago together with the establishment of this school, although they are very spacious and magnificent, are no longer in good repair, that eminent man, who as minister of royal wisdom and kindness governs the affairs of universities and schools excellently, yielding to our prayers has granted sufficient money, from which they might not only be restored, but might be better adapted to the needs that have arisen in the meantime, especially with the increased number of both teachers and students.
This work will be completed in the course of a few years in such a way that no hindrance arises from it for holding lectures.
And indeed, after so many other benefits, Frederick William has heaped us with these favors;
but to no part of the state is he equally gracious.

Therefore, however much the earlier kings deserved well of this empire, just as the king excels in power, so the people seems to flourish more joyfully than ever, especially since with lasting peace and with wise and salutary institutions both public and private resources are more and more restored, and tranquility has succeeded the disturbances;

And there is hope that it will come to pass that Frederick William, rejoicing in vigorous old age, just as he has not been wearied by years, so may he not be wearied in doing good, and at the same time, along with his life, most dear to his citizens, may he prolong the happiness of his citizens.

May God, the Best and Greatest, therefore assent to those prayers, which indeed always, but on this his birthday with more sacred ceremonies, all the provinces, cities, and colleges of the kingdom offer for the health of Frederick William.
But if those vows shall not have been in vain, the common safety of the Prussians will be ratified.

div.head: XXV. Oratio nataliciis Friderici Guilelmi III. celebrandis d. III. m. Aug. a. MDCCCXXXVII. habita.
On the benevolence of the prince

p.s: The task entrusted to me, listeners, on this most auspicious day, which the piety of the citizens has publicly dedicated and consecrated to the honoring of the name of Frederick William, from this most distinguished place of speaking, although I understand with most people that it is as honorable to every most distinguished man and pleasant to me, so on account of the dignity of the matter it is especially serious, and that an oration would better correspond to the gravity of the subject, where not I alone am adorned with this splendid prerogative, but in turns another orator succeeds another each year:

Yet so far am I from confessing myself exhausted by frequent repetition and from thinking that the praises of Frederick William have already been exhausted by me, that I even deny that in any year an orator need fear that he may repeat, unknowingly and unwillingly, what he has said before, and thus affect with some weariness those who happen to remember his earlier words.

When I say this, I would not have it understood in such a way that you think that each latest year brings entirely new material to the speaker, by which alone, if it were more richly set forth, you could sufficiently celebrate the most beloved Prince.
Rather, I would count this among the chief blessings of this kingdom, that not so many new things happen every year.

An orator could almost every year congratulate the Roman Republic and the Roman emperors, who waged wars almost without interruption and rarely kept the temple of Janus closed, on some notable success.

And even in a peace that is not well established, when affairs fluctuate this way and that, and there is need day by day of new devices and counsels, so that an empire threatening ruin is held together from time to time, new laws and institutions are founded every year, which you might refer to the praise of the prince:

But the auspices of this kingdom of Frederick William have not only kept it peaceful from foreign wars for a long time, but have also led it to a certain even state of affairs, indeed not lacking motion, but rejoicing in quiet motion, in which, unless something extraordinary happens, nothing single stands out so much that in these greatest and most sacred solemnities it seems right that the speech be directed uniquely to that one thing, and that all material for praise be sought from it.
Nor does he himself seem to wish that the things which are being done by our Prince in a distinguished manner should be extolled individually and too lavishly.
And the things that were done in secret, although they are extraordinary and not entirely unknown, ought not to be discussed publicly.
But I do not lack new arguments:

The human mind is so constituted that scarcely anyone, in illustrating those matters which are set forth by a free course of thought and words, would fall upon exactly the same opinions, connected with one another in the same series, and the same words, after any long interval.

This is the difference between a free mind and the necessity of nature: that nature, at the same season every year, regenerates the same plants, flowers, and fruits, while the human mind, at different times, is driven by different impulses, and hammers out and brings forth different thoughts and ideas.
Yet the mind is not moved by a random impulse:
Different times remind us of different things.

But this most peaceful and most fortunate state of the Prussian empire has brought me down to no other thought more than to contemplating the benevolence of Frederick William, which he shows to all in common.
For we are well off, because he does good to us:
but he does good, because he wishes well from the heart.
I affirm that to the benevolent spirit of Frederick William is chiefly owed this happiness of the republic, this flourishing of letters in the republic:
For nothing is more salutary to states than the benevolent mind of the prince.

As I am about to illustrate this opinion, I wish that the breeze of your goodwill may also be present to me, listeners, and I ask pardon from you in advance, so that, since I am not speaking in the forum, not in the senate-house, not before the people, but before an assembly of learned and of those eager for learning, it may be permitted to mix in here and there something that may seem to smell rather of the shade of the school than to be suited to the light of a public assembly.
But if we ask what benevolence is:

Just as it is established that some are by nature inclined to sadness, severity, and cruelty, so the feeling of benevolence, although it is cultivated by reason and practice, is not acquired by art, but comes as a gift of nature, and it is a certain innate habit and disposition of the mind, by which you wish that as many good things as possible may be for all those with whom you associate, and you pursue them with love.
But since the prince alone among all men is born to make citizens happy, and ought to provide for their safety and all their prosperity;
This disposition of mind is truly princely, and is the mother and nurse of almost all civic virtues.
By this virtue the Emperor Titus, whom an ancient writer says was by nature most benevolent, earned that most beautiful praise, that he was called the love and delight of the human race;

By this virtue, the prince, as far as it can be done through human weakness, emulates the highest divinity, to which, in order that they may be assimilated according to their strength, it befits both the rest of mortals to strive with utmost effort and indeed princes, who from ancient times have seemed to hold the place of gods on earth.
For God, as our religion especially teaches, embraces the whole human race with immense love, and is the most benevolent author and dispenser of all good things:
It is not moved by envy or hatred, which two vices are contrary to goodwill.

For envy pursues those who seem to be happy, because they have been increased and adorned with goods and virtues; it attacks and casts down the splendid, raising up obscure names, and it is distressed by the prosperity of others, even if the envious man perceives no harm to himself from it;

And hatred is that disposition of the mind which watches for and eagerly seeks the opportunity to do harm with pleasure, because those who hate think that the one they hate is either evil or stands in the way of their own interests.
From these things nothing falls to God.

For indeed, what you know pleased Herodotus most, that divine envy casts down whatever exalts itself too much, and does not allow anything to be magnificent, but that the wrath of God spares humble conditions, that cannot be reconciled with the purity and sincerity of the divine mind:
although that opinion has some truth in it to this extent, that if any are more proud, they are accustomed to fall with a heavier ruin by their own fault:

But Plato long ago decided much more correctly that the maker of the world, for this very reason, because he is good, was free from the feeling of envy, and therefore wished to make all things as similar to himself as possible;

Nor does it seem right to attribute hatred to the divine nature, and the anger and vengeance that flow from hatred, since not even a good man indulges in revenge, and even a wrongdoer should not be punished so that he suffers evil and becomes worse, but so that he may be corrected by the appearance of evil and the offense may be expiated.
Now I would not fear to apply these same things to a prince.

A good prince, just as no one envies him, because he is placed so far above all that no private person can be compared with him, neither envies anyone, nor again pursues anyone with hatred, not even a guilty person:
And if any punishment is needed, so that public safety may be provided for, he does not satisfy his mind with punishment, but punishes unwillingly and pities the necessity of punishing.
Indeed, because good princes are not disturbed by those emotions of the mind, but are led by kindness and goodwill, they are deservedly called serene and most serene:
And that state which is governed by these arts seems to come closest to perfection, not the one that is held together by force of arms and cunning, however firmly.
But who is more serene than our King, who more kind to all?

Finally, who is there that does not understand that it is especially through this noble character of Frederick William, which all citizens feel in their inmost hearts, that it has been brought about that the Prussian kingdom, after so many changes of fortune, has flourished most happily, and amid various and most violent disturbances has rejoiced and rejoices in complete tranquility?

These things indeed I have discussed to this end, listeners, that since kings rightly seem to command by divine authority, I might demonstrate that benevolence has been enjoined upon princes from the very nature of the divine mind, as far as we mortals can attain to it.
But he cannot do good who does not act according to reason:
therefore this is the chief point of princely benevolence, that he who reigns should follow reason as his guide.
But the reason by which a provident deity governs the whole nature of things established in the fellowship of human life a law, which, as the old poet says, is the queen of mortals and immortals:
Therefore, from reason and from the law that reason brings, a benevolent prince will administer the state, not from caprice and lust.

He alone will truly be said to rule with divine authority, who, as our most temperate King does perpetually, guards himself by reason, which dwells in him, and takes care that nothing more thoughtless or unjust escapes him, and employs it in governing the state.

Unless perhaps someone, not fearing to utter an insult against God, will affirm that even Nero, Commodus, Caracalla, and similar monsters, who were called to empire by birth or inheritance, have by divine authority harassed and afflicted the human race, and that whatever was done by the most cruel princes was rightly done:

Just as once Anaxarchus of Abdera, who had entered upon a certain peculiar way of philosophizing and scorned the common judgment of men, when he saw Alexander the Great afflicted with the deepest grief because of the murder of Clitus, reproved the king, whom the whole world might admire, because, cast down like a slave, he wept, respecting the institutions of men and fearing reproaches:
He should not serve vain opinion;
He himself was the law and the standard of what is right and just;
For this reason, Justice and Themis are represented as sitting beside Jupiter, so that whatever has been done and performed by the ruler should be considered just and lawful.
Rather, that which is divine in a prince is extinguished as soon as he has thoroughly deviated from what is right, just, and pious, and is defiled by crimes.

Moreover, a prince who derives all his plans from reason, not from caprice, will also desire that reason and understanding be diffused and disseminated throughout the whole state; and since those goods which are in the power of men, namely knowledge and virtue, surpass all others, he can be more beneficent to the whole state in no way than by so aiding and directing the studies of letters that letters may both flourish and be turned to the common use.

They will, however, be turned especially to the common good, when men are placed at the head of the individual parts of the state who, besides the probity and skill altogether necessary for conducting affairs, have been cultivated with accurate learning, the fruit of which they may each in his own place spread abroad.
Since they are formed especially in the universities, Frederick William has with good reason devoted the greatest care to founding, partly correcting, and partly restoring them.

And indeed, while he adorns these, he has not neglected the other schools, but with equal kindness he aids all, and he also looks out for the common and rural multitude, so that it may be able to become a participant in those rudiments, without which it can scarcely attain to culture.
Nevertheless, the most wise King did not provide subsidies to literature only to the extent that they are of benefit to the state and repay the favor by use:
If this were to happen, it would be a bad decision for literature, which cannot return the same measure of gifts as it received.
For his own sake and for the sake of ministers worthy of this king, literature seems to need support.
In this you may discern the genuine affection of princely benevolence.
For it is not kindness that, as in a purchase, calculates what it will receive, and it is by no means kingly but characteristic of servile baseness to look to the profit of one's benefits.

Finally, Frederick William, not only in literature but in fostering any parts of the state whatsoever, does not look to his own advantages, but seeks the good of his citizens, and directs all his plans to this end, as the greatest philosopher long ago taught that a good prince should do, and as Frederick the Great approved by his own judgment.

By this very fact it is brought about that the royal house and the people are united by a mutual bond of love, and so this kingdom has grown together with this republic that they cannot be separated without damage and ruin to the people themselves.
There is not one way, listeners, by which the benevolent mind of a prince may aid the affairs of citizens.
First, by the mere feeling of affection, by mere courtesy and popularity, by mere judgment and approval, he nourishes, excites, and inflames the zeal of men.

If the prince holds no class of parents in low esteem, if he shows that the farmer, the artisan, the merchant, and the scholar are dear to him, if he deigns to address them, approves them, praises them, by this very token of goodwill he is generous without a gift.

Pericles, not indeed a king, but equal to kings in his authority, because he was on familiar terms with Anaxagoras, Damon, and Phidias; Scipio Aemilianus, because he had Polybius and Panaetius in his company; that same Scipio and Laelius, because they cultivated Terence—these, by their judgment, nourished literature and the arts.
Frederick the Great was reproached because, by despising native poets and writers and by preferring foreigners, he hindered the education of the Germans.
Although he has a valid excuse, which it is unnecessary to mention, nevertheless you may understand from this how harmful the judgment of so great a prince was thought to be.
But the prince gives a greater and more effective proof of goodwill, who grants to each class of men in the state as much liberty in conducting their own affairs as is allowed for the safety of all.
Rightly indeed we call a good prince the father of his country:
In this there is this, that he rules over subjects not as slaves but as free men:
For the father of a family is the parent of free children, not of slaves;
For him to whom the prince is similar in this matter, that seems to be the true power of paternal authority, from which some wish that royal power was born.

Indeed, that state cannot be considered free in which, whatever business you undertake, whatever art you practice, whatever work the citizens undertake, laws, decrees, taxes, monopolies surround and hinder you on all sides, established either for the sake of the treasury or from a perverse desire to draw everything to the state and from excessive anxiety.
This is what in some states, which seem very free, is not rarely found to happen.

In this matter, how wise a moderation Frederick William maintained, and how much he supported agriculture, manufactures, and commerce with wiser laws and by granting due liberty, without detriment to anyone, I need not explain to those who know.
But indeed, what is more necessary for literature than liberty?

Since some of these are engaged in investigating natural things, others in the memory of past deeds, others in mathematics, others in philosophy, whether natural or moral, and in politics, which are included in moral philosophy, and finally others are mixed from the philosophical and historical or physical kind, to which I refer theology, legal expertise, and medicine;
Although some of these seem able to flourish even without freedom, because even the most suspicious person does not regard them as suspect:

For who will fear from arithmetic and geometry, from the history of plants, from grammar and metrical theory, or from the archaeology of the arts and similar literature, that the state will suffer any harm?

Nevertheless, none of the most important parts of literature, not even poetry, which I have not mentioned earlier only because it is more remote from university studies, can reach its full flower, if other laws must be followed for them than those which are founded in the very nature and character of the art itself:
And with those most important ones corrupted, the rest will contribute little to the cultivation of the mind.

For to mention but a few examples, if a philosopher is not allowed to direct the course of his mind wherever his deepest meditation may carry him, but a certain fixed limit of philosophizing is prescribed, which the opinion of others has established as a rule;

If the historian and the politician are not allowed to report events as they happened, but are forced to conceal some things, to gloss over others, and to approve what right reason does not approve, or not to approve what reason does approve;
if the theologian and the jurist are forbidden to inquire further into the causes of divine and human affairs and of what is just and right than seems expedient to those in power;

If a natural philosopher must fear that what he has discovered by investigating the nature of things, because it seems contrary to certain doctrines which men have set up as divine, may be publicly condemned as impious:

Science, which by its nature strives toward perfection, will halt its progress as far as the state is concerned, and with science, the human race, whose progress science and intellect move and measure.
Students who swear by the words of their teacher are criticized.
Should we want teachers to swear allegiance to the opinions of others, who cannot even be considered as masters?
Thus it will happen that the voice sticks in the throat of the teacher:
sensible men will become silent:
truth will yield to pretense.
Science itself teaches what is right, good, and beautiful, and to that extent it is impatient of authority, insofar as what is commanded is not consistent with reason.
And often science anticipates by many centuries the truth not perceived by the multitude.

What of the fact that the teachings of the learned, which a few centuries ago seemed impious to the multitude, now the common people themselves approve, and laugh at the superstition of their ancestors, who condemned them?
And do we understand that what the earlier age held pious is impious, cruel, and wicked?
For such is the power of knowledge, that it overcomes whatever obstacles are thrown in its way, even iron and fire.
There is indeed, there is a course for the human mind destined by providence and preordained by divine will, which it pursues with unimpaired strength, even if it sometimes pauses for a little while.
The very intervals, the very obstacles add new strength, and the very windings and bypaths of errors are wont to lead the runner back to the straight course.
And so nothing from literature seems to be feared for the republic;

And the errors of learned men, by which I do not deny that even states have sometimes been disturbed, although I deny that those who disturb human affairs are truly learned — those errors, I say, are refuted by arguments:
But immodesty and impudence, unless contempt is preferable, must be chastised, and fierce spirits must be restrained.
Indeed, the kindness and wisdom of Frederick William has not separated us, who are strangers to these vices, by a harsher guard:
We enjoy perfect freedom of teaching and learning;
This is not the least reason why we should be bound to Frederick William with all our heart.
And we all feel this and are most grateful.

But besides fear, envy also can assail literature, if at times it is fostered more eagerly and equipped with more ample and more splendid resources, and learned men are increased with honors and wealth, although to those envious ones they seem to be useless and undeservedly preferred to more useful men;
