Just as we have often heard that a dancer or a singer or a mime actress is envied for her rather generous salaries, not even this is right, because even to the refined arts, which move and delight the minds of the more elegant with eyes and ears and form a sense of beauty, something is owed among more cultivated peoples, and because those things which no one else can perform, since the graces of voice and gesture fall to one by a gift of nature, if indeed it is worth the effort to hear and see them, are to be remunerated so much more generously, the more people you will have found who are equal to performing common tasks for a cheaper wage.
Among us, I think, this whole kind of envy has become obsolete, which attacked the learned on this side and that:
indeed, since that is a matter of private individuals, it now ought not to have been mentioned at all.
But princes also can envy the learned:
to this pertains the fact that they bear with difficulty the disagreement of the more learned and wiser and do not wish to be defeated by them.

A rare example of this matter, and so much the more illustrious, is the Emperor Hadrian, a prince of ambiguous reputation, but of immense intellectual ability, and who seems to have surpassed the not inconsiderable vices of his nature by his virtues and by doing good, and not often to have forgotten what he had promised, that he would so conduct the state as to know that it was the people's affair, not his own:

He, therefore, since from boyhood he had been excellently imbued with Greek and Latin letters, and had devoted not contemptible effort to music, painting, and kindred arts, indeed held grammarians, rhetoricians, philosophers, geometers, musicians, painters, and architects in the closest intimacy, and honored and enriched professors of every kind, but with excessive ambition, because he wished to appear more learned than all, he mocked, ridiculed, and oppressed with envy every most learned man; and Apollodorus the architect, who had criticized his diagrams rather freely, he not only drove into exile, but finally, with his characteristic cruelty, even killed.
Even under such a prince, however fond of literature, literature can hardly retain its freedom;

And wittily Favorinus of Arles, when he had been rebuked by Hadrian and had come off badly with the Emperor, and was therefore criticized by his friends, replied that he had to put up with it that the one who had thirty legions should seem more learned.
I have lingered longer, listeners, in illustrating those matters in which, although no small part of princely goodwill is discerned, nevertheless it may seem less manifest.
Now I will dispatch in a few words those things which are set before us.
It is a sign of goodwill to bestow rewards, which are chiefly honorary.
Indeed, by ambition, which is the desire for honors, men are driven almost equally to base and to right actions;

And a state that excessively cultivates the ambition of its citizens seems to corrupt them rather than to raise them to virtue, and moreover brings it about that the honors, which it had wished to use for rousing their spirits, gradually lose their value and no longer serve their purpose:

This you may clearly perceive in the ancient states, from the time when, as the severity of morals simultaneously declined and love of country diminished, they were accustomed to lavish rather than to bestow honors and distinctions.
Yet a good prince will show his goodwill, which is common to all orders, when he excludes no order from those honors which it is customary to bestow on the well-deserving.
I come to those things by which alone most people think benefits are to be measured, to monetary subsidies.

Most people need these at all times, and since private resources are not sufficient, so that by their contribution the needs of the needy may be provided for, recourse is had to the state and to the head of the state, the prince.
Help must be given to the sick, the weak, widows, and orphans:
at one time the barrenness of crops, scarcity of food, lack of livelihood presses;
at another time the cheapness of provisions afflicts the farmers, a plague breaks out, estates and fields are overwhelmed by sudden flood, men and cattle are carried off;
As soon as the money supply fails, with gold and silver coinage as it were absorbed and drained away for various uses, the people are oppressed by debt.
Our age has experienced every one of these calamities;

and in all of them, in his kingdom, Frederick William brought the most provident and most benign remedy, whether by remitting or lightening burdens, or by lending and giving money, or by any good plans and institutions.
But even in the greatest integrity of all things, many and most excellent things cannot be accomplished unless the expenses are provided from the public treasury.

But indeed the condition of the liberal arts and letters is now such that they must for the most part be publicly supported, because the work they provide is greater than the profit from the fee that would be paid by a private individual, and because our present state of learning demands manifold and most ample apparatus, and finally because both artists and scholars need leisure in order to produce good works, which seem scarcely able to be completed when a taskmaster daily presses and urges on.
Behold, a most beautiful material for royal munificence is set before us; shall we say that any king has more perfectly embraced it than Frederick William?
So much for his generosity:
I see that one thing remains for me, in which the king's benevolent spirit is especially to be observed.
For I said that a good prince is unwilling to exact punishment and pities the necessity of punishing:
and so, as far as public safety allows, he is uniquely inclined to forgive.

Titus not only did not punish two patrician men, who had been convicted of actually aspiring to the empire, but, after warning them not to dare anything further, he admitted them to his private dinner, and promised them that if they wanted anything, he would give it to them:
The next day, when he was watching the gladiators, he placed the same men around himself, and when weapons of the fighters were offered to him, he handed them to them to inspect.
Similarly, once Octavian Augustus, after he realized that he had scarcely accomplished anything by severity, with L.
He had acted with Cinna, the grandson of Gnaeus Pompeius, as his own would-be assassin.
But in Octavian's case, either his own prudence or, as has been handed down to memory, the prudence of his wife Livia managed this.
In Titus's case, certainly it was not prudence that persuaded him to do that, but greatness of soul and innate clemency.

Although even the most severe will not deny that pardons are useful to human and public affairs, even that most harsh Cato the Censor did not deny it, but even in the speech which he delivered in the Senate on behalf of the Rhodians, he publicly professed it.
I do not praise impunity for crimes, nor would I have promised that by pardoning crimes are entirely prevented:
But still, fierce spirits seem to be disarmed more by clemency than by harsh punishment.

I have sketched, as far as I could in a brief speech, the image of a benevolent prince, my hearers, and in many places at the same time I have indicated how much Frederick William corresponds to this image.

And yet I do not think that anyone has missed this indication either in those places or in the remaining parts, since the whole life of Frederick William testifies to all that for which I have chosen this subject: the serenity and benevolence of the King, ignorant of hatred and envy.

From this most noble disposition of mind, whatever good deeds are born, we, who are engaged in teaching and learning literature, have not only experienced and experience daily, but the whole republic and very many of the subjects individually, whom it has aided and blessed either with rewards or with wealth or by pardoning and with every kind of favor;

And not only the state and the citizens, but also foreigners, because he was moderate, gentle, and forgetful of anger and offense, did not want feuds to be prolonged and perpetuated, but he stood forth as the establisher of peace, the leader and author of sincere reconciliation.
In few words I have said a very great matter.
But what the most merciful King has conferred and confers upon us will never fade from our minds:

Keep these things diligently in mind, my dearest fellow soldiers, who are being prepared in this school of arts founded by Frederick William for the pursuit of literature and the discharge of the duties of the state, and take care that by the uprightness of your character, by the eagerness of your studies, by embracing now all the best counsels, and finally by the love of the excellent Prince, who alone is the parent of liberal obedience, you show yourselves worthy of that kindness with which you have been judged worthy by the Father of the fatherland.

Finally, I pray to God, the Best and Greatest, that, as under the auspices of that prince through whose leadership Prussia, having been led through the greatest dangers of old, has remained whole, and now flourishes renewed and enlarged, so it will stand firm and unmoved hereafter; that He may further provide for the welfare of Frederick William, and may favor and add perpetuity to the benefits conferred through his hands upon the state; and together with the most beloved King, may He keep the Augustan house safe and unharmed.

div.head: XXVI. Oratio nataliciis Friderici Guilelmi III. celebrandis d. III. m. Aug. a. MDCCCXXXIX. habita.
An inquiry into what a prince can contribute to the flourishing of letters at any given time and in any state condition, and what he cannot achieve even with the greatest effort applied

p.s: Since, in these most holy annual solemnities, which the piety of the citizens has dedicated to the best king, I have been accustomed to speak almost from the very cradle of our school, and since I had reluctantly omitted the previous year, being occupied with public duties, and my dearest colleague had succeeded in my place, whom we then heard with the greatest pleasure discoursing elegantly, copiously, and gravely on the praises of Frederick William:

I was hoping that it would happen that, if by chance my strength, whether weakened or fatigued by frequent repetition, should fail without my knowledge, I would be refreshed by this rest, and that the example of an excellent orator would kindle not my will, of which I have so often given proof, but the emulation and ardor of my talent.
But contrary to expectation, the matter turned out.
Up to this point I had compared myself with myself;
it was permitted me to yield to a pleasing hope, that I would not descend below myself:

Now, in the most blessed and most abundant abundance of resources, that very thing breaks and afflicts me, by which I had seemed to myself to be able to be raised up, since, with old age already approaching and the weapons of eloquence exhausted, I am not so strong either in weight of thoughts or in richness of speech or in lungs, that I could contend with stronger and unimpaired men, to whom I would rather yield than be compared.

But if weariness should creep upon me, and I should not equal the vigor of previous years, I ask that you transfer to this time some of that zeal with which you once seem to have pursued me as I spoke, and that you allow my mind, which has not been restored by resting, to be refreshed by the memory of your former indulgence.

What of the fact that I think I have the right not only to beg but to demand your indulgence, because the more prudent you are, listeners, the more you understand into what a critical situation he is placed who, having often and in every part fulfilled the praises of the King, is forced either, by repeating what he said before, not to satisfy himself, or, by departing further from his purpose, to respond less to the dignity of this day and to your great expectation?

Therefore, relying on you, I proceed to speak, intending to use this moderation, that neither my reverence in honoring the King may be lacking, nor may I fear to depart somewhat from the praise of the most beloved Prince.

For to dwell on literature today, we Prussians do not merely boast—though we might be regarded as vendors of our own affairs—but all foreigners also declare with remarkable unanimity that literature has been aided by none of the present princes, by none of those who previously held this kingdom, not even by Frederick the Great, who nevertheless was imbued with the best arts and was himself learned, both a poet and a philosopher, with such great care and munificence as by Frederick William.
He founded, preserves, enlarges, and adorns our seat of the fine arts, which is especially flourishing.
He spares no expense to provide for our needs.
He does not cease to repair losses, to add new distinctions, to summon distinguished professors here, and to increase the equipment and apparatus of learning.

The very fact that we have been compelled to assemble here today in an unusual place testifies that the Prince's generosity is not exhausted, since he is magnificently restoring our almost royal buildings, which he gave us about thirty years ago, with equally royal expenditure.
Nor has he done and does he do less for other universities;
finally, throughout the whole kingdom he protects schools of every kind and the literary republic with admirable kindness.

Thus Frederick William earned this praise, than which nothing can more adorn a prince, that he is considered in his kingdom the most ready and most fortunate establisher, nourisher, and preserver of letters.

But when I consider how much literature owes to Frederick William, this thought has occurred to me: what it is that a prince can contribute to the flourishing of literature at any time and in any state of the republic, and what he cannot contribute even with the greatest diligence.
I shall therefore now undertake the role of a just examination of the state of affairs rather than of vague praise that wanders here and there.
By this I hope to achieve that it becomes clear that Frederick William has accomplished everything that lies within the power of a prince.
Therefore, to begin with those things that a prince cannot accomplish, these are of two kinds:
For some things cannot be accomplished at all by helping and assisting, while others cannot be accomplished under certain conditions.
For what about the fact that it has been doubted whether literature can be advanced by any rewards, by any subsidies and aids to be supplied from outside?
What about the fact that the Medici seemed to have accomplished too little with the greatest zeal and munificence, while Louis XIV, king of the French, even seemed to have done some harm?
Lest anyone think this judgment too inexperienced, it helps to cite Lessing as its author, or at least as its supporter, the far most prudent judge of all things pertaining to literature.
Of course, great minds are born spontaneously, not cultivated by training:

But those men open up paths of literature that no one's feet have trodden before; they are the leaders and standard-bearers for the rest of the crowd of scholars, and they are moved by their own strength rather than by the supports of others, and they move others.
For talent is spurred on by the very obstacles, and the greater the difficulties to be overcome, the more it is strengthened and stands out.

This you may observe especially in poets, but in none more clearly than in Shakespeare, the prince of British poets, who, born in a humble station and equipped with very scanty means of learning and attracted by rewards either none or very slight, by his inborn excellence attained to the highest rank.
I would indeed proclaim the felicity of that age, which not only produced a prince who fostered literature and the arts, but also those talents which could satisfy the desires of such a prince.
so that both the kingdom of that one may be illuminated by the splendor of these, and the harbor and refuge of minds worthy of the highest favors may be foremost.

But certain kinds of literature, and those the most noble, especially poetry and those things most closely related to poetry, when they have been brought to perfection by the efforts of the most distinguished men, are accustomed generally to halt their step and, as it were, to rest upon the laurels of their fathers.

Just as among the Greeks after Aeschylus, Sophocles, and Euripides no one arose who could be compared with them in tragedy, so among the Germans no one has yet surpassed or equaled Schiller and Goethe.
You would do an injustice to your contemporaries if you said that the excellence of the race has died out throughout the whole nation.

But those who succeed are pressed by the examples of their predecessors, and, as it seems, by a natural law, each nation cannot attain the highest point in any kind except once, until by a singular gift of providence a wholly new age is born and, as it were, a great year of nations returns, in which another generative spring is brought, a new crop of talents springs up, and finally the human race, having recovered and even increased its strength, hastens to complete a new course;
Just as a tree produces flowers and fruits only once in the same year, but, as the year turns, regenerates them most joyfully.
But what we have said about poetry, the same may be seen in philosophy, whose history contains almost all the vicissitudes of the human mind.

Indeed, among the Greeks, from Thales onward all the way to Aristotle, it poured forth in a certain continuous stream of the most weighty thoughts, soon divided into rivulets, one or another of which watered the Stoa and the gardens of Epicurus;
then, the longer it survived, the more it grew old, unless you except certain divine minds;
the same was brought back in the Middle Ages and again flowed away;

Finally, after many efforts of great men had been interposed, it was strengthened by Kant on new foundations, and then by Fichte, Schelling, and Hegel, of which triumvirate two were ours and among the foremost of our men, it was increased with such great increments and carried to such a point that this succession also seems to have been exhausted, and now one must pause for a while.

And when this point has been reached, the nation is accustomed to reap no small fruit of its studies, so that not only are there some few and distinguished men as guardians and stewards of literature, but with the resources for acquiring learning increased, with easy access to it provided, and with the method and system of treating every art with some success spread abroad, which those who led the way had discovered and taught, learning has been more widely scattered and disseminated, and has many authors not to be despised, none of whom so stands out as to surpass the rest by a long interval.

Thus it happens that, with the resources of learning, which were once possessed by a few rich men, being divided among many, the literary republic, which the aristocrats had previously held in a certain way, is changed into a kind of popular state.
The sum of all these things, if I see anything, does not depend on the will of the prince:
but the fatal course of the human mind, obeying its own laws and the eternal order, draws them on, dragging mortals unwilling and resisting toward the destined end;

A divine power presides over them, which sends forth and recalls talents, and, as with the whole human race, so also for individual peoples, it has appointed and marked out for each its own ages, distinguished by certain definite signs.
I have said that the prince, moreover, cannot accomplish certain things that pertain to the flourishing of literature under certain conditions.
Thus it is, to use these examples, that there are some kinds of literature that cannot be brought to completion except in a certain state of the republic.

Among these, eloquence holds the first place—I mean civil eloquence, not sacred, not the shadowy eloquence of the schools, which, even if it retains the color and appearance of a polished speech, would nevertheless have lost its sap and blood.
Indeed, no one denies that this eloquence was not the last part of the ancient learning of the Greeks and Romans:
But for this to flourish, two civic virtues are needed.

For citizens ought to be so inclined to the cultivation of the finer arts and of all humanity, that they not only cultivate their native language with the greatest zeal, but also eagerly inquire into all those matters which pertain to the protection of human society, to the establishment, preservation, and correction of laws and rights, and to enjoy that liberty which affords speakers the opportunity of showing how much eloquence avails in the commonwealth:

Since these two things had come together exceptionally in the Athenian state, while in other states, although by no means unacquainted with the arts, they had come together less, among the Greeks that art of speaking stood out as almost peculiar to them, and one Attic city flourished with more orators than all the rest of Greece together.

Although it can scarcely be said how great an influence this art has in public affairs, because it gives back to liberty, its parent, its nurse, because it exposes the hidden decay of states and their public pretense, because it warns of impending dangers, because it provides, exhorts, reproaches, drives out idleness, depresses the inactive and those unequal to the conduct of affairs, and brings to the helm of the republic the most prudent, the bravest, the most ready:
Nevertheless, it also exercises great power in literature.

For orators together with philosophers and poets form and shape diction, and they lift up the minds by the weight of their thoughts, and they sharpen the sense of elegance, and they educate the ears, and what I judge to be most important, they increase the force and strength of the language wonderfully.
Take away the orators:
you will have cut off much of the sinews of the language, you will have snatched away from the poets themselves, the philosopher, the writer of history much nourishment full of healthy juice;
How much all of them are nourished by eloquence can be conjectured from Greek literature.
But eloquence has no place in every republic:
and so not even the Ptolemies, although they were very fond of literature, were able to restore eloquence.
I do not contend that that supreme liberty, which gave birth to and nourished the oratorical art, should be preferred to this stable condition of affairs and public security:
nay, if the old wisdom rightly taught that the half is more than the whole, it might perhaps be better to be half-free:

I affirm this, led by the inner causes of things, that this kind of literature cannot be cultivated in those forms of government in which the state of affairs is not otherwise established than if it is rendered to one person.

Nor do I fear to transfer the same thing in some measure to history, which cannot be well written except by an eloquent and fluent speaker, which moreover demands nearly the same freedom of speech as eloquence, because this is the first law of history, that you dare not only to say nothing false, but to say whatever is true, and finally which brilliant minds will flee from and shrink to approach, when they have first perceived that things must be concealed and suppressed not those which displease themselves, but those which displease any other judges whatsoever, and that he who is unwilling either to pretend or to dissemble would bring upon himself envy and offenses with no public benefit.

Although the indulgence of a good prince will alleviate these disadvantages as much as the condition of the empire will allow, yet how much they may suffer, especially in more serious times for the republic and in great upheaval, is neither clear to all nor easy to understand.

Whatever may be decided about this, whoever weighs the matter fairly, since I have freely professed what I have established, will understand, in treating the subject we are discussing, that both times must be considered and the state of the republic and its condition, whatever it may be at any time.
I now turn to a more cheerful and pleasant explanation of those matters which, whatever the state of the city, depend on the prince.
And although he is not the sower of talents, nevertheless he can seek them out, recognize them, foster them, bring them to light, and finally use them in various ways.

But the correct use will be this: that he does not wish to direct their studies himself and give them laws, but that he yields to their course, which is spontaneously borne toward that which is most excellent.

And since in the ruder age of any people a prince can most especially lay the foundations of a more cultivated life and of all learning by founding and equipping schools, which we know Charles the Great once did, and now see in Greece, where, in order that inveterate barbarism may be driven out, it must be done and is being done:

Then he who has received a culture already spread throughout his kingdom, as Frederick William received it, because each new age demands new aids for itself, and the things that seemed sufficient for the needs of the previous age do not suffice for the present, has an immense field for benefiting literature, which consists in this: that he supply what his ancestors left unfinished; that, especially if the boundaries of the empire have been extended, he add new seats of the liberal arts; that he adapt all schools and other institutions of learning to that better state of culture and knowledge which has been attained, and to the common good; finally, that he omit nothing by which both what has been acquired may be preserved, and present things may be turned to good account, and new advances of the arts may be prepared, and new lights may be drawn forth and spread more widely.
For the human mind never rests.
But if, as we have said, certain studies sometimes relax, others are kindled all the more fiercely.

Indeed, let him demand that we waste our labor, whoever should desire that I demonstrate that, in all these desires of literature, none of those princes who are now and who were formerly have satisfied and do satisfy Frederick William more prudently, more effectively, more munificently; that no one, led by such great and so sincere benevolence of mind, by his own sole will of doing good, with no stimulus of ambition, has been so far from ostentation and extravagance as from unseasonable parsimony and tenacity.

But let me be allowed to look a little more closely at those arts by which the prince and the prince's ministers seem to deserve best of the whole republic of letters, especially in the condition of the literary republic which now exists.

For since learning has now grown to such an extent that in almost every field there is an abundant supply of those who are imbued with a plausible appearance of knowledge, and not only imbued with this appearance, but also equipped with those aids of learning which seem to make them fit for instructing the young;
the greater the number of competitors, the easier is the choice, and again the more difficult:
easier, if it is considered sufficient to have placed a not unworthy person in the chair;
It is more difficult, if one asks who is most worthy.
But indeed the most worthy must be sought:
This matter, difficult in itself, is often additionally disturbed by ambition and favor, sometimes even by envy, which attacks the highest, heedless of lesser men.
I praise the golden mean, provided it is not placed at the summit:
Rewards, honors, magistracies, offices, any services whatsoever become worthless, unless they are conferred upon the most worthy.
But among such great cares of empire, how few are the princes who can descend to this, that they themselves choose the professors and teachers of every kind?

And so, to whatever perfection literature will be able to attain by its own virtue without a skilled moderator, it is of the greatest interest to literature what sort of men the king entrusts with the care and governance of public instruction.

For this province, if any other, demands a man who is equipped with the other virtues, but especially endowed with a liberal mind, and a lover of all literature and of the learned and the studious, and so instructed in a certain circle of all disciplines that he knows each and every part of these, and discerns with keen judgment what is excellent in each kind;
a man of no ordinary but of exceptional talent, lest, since equals generally delight in equals, he should favor mediocre rather than excellent scholars;
a shrewd judge of talents and most attentive to opportunities, so that he may win over those whom he has approved;

finally, one capable of great designs, lest he be content with acquiring slight and most necessary supplies of learning, or rest satisfied with defending present circumstances, but rather that he may undertake something more magnificent, something worthy of so great an empire, so great a prince.

It would not be beside the point, nor, I think, unpleasant to you, my hearers, if, just as the Greek lyric and tragic poets used the masks of ancient heroes in such a way that, by describing their characters, deeds, and fortune, whether prosperous or adverse, they expressed the virtues of the famous men who then flourished or indicated the condition of present affairs—not declaring what thing or what men they were to whom they wished these things to be referred, because sometimes the nature of poetry did not permit it, sometimes another reason dissuaded them, but leaving the interpretation to the audience, who, as if looking into a mirror, would have offered to them spontaneously the image of the man described or the thing signified—

You will not regret it, I assure you, if I now, in almost the same manner, summon to mind the memory of an immortal man, who in the last century, not in our own particular fatherland, but in the common fatherland of Germany, rendered distinguished service to literature.

I mean Münchhausen, who under the auspices of George II, King of the Britons, founded the Georgia Augusta University and for more than thirty years governed it with tireless diligence and embraced it with fatherly love:
Whom, when he was dead, the Göttingen people mourned, as children mourn a father, because they understood that they owed him all their goods and as much as each one owes to his own parents;

Whom, to use the words of Heynius, a most trustworthy authority, they did not fear as a master, although gentle and well deserving, but they all addressed and loved as a patron, helper, best friend, most devoted to their interests;
To whom they freely brought their cares, wishes, and longings;

He who by his counsel, authority, and action would resolve or alleviate their difficulties, or if what was sought had to be refused, he would refuse with a calm brow, gentle words, and kind address, like an indulgent father refusing his children.
And when I now recall these things before you, dearest colleagues, who have experienced the same and experience it daily, do you, I ask, need an interpreter?
And there were in Münchhausen nearly all things which would make him most suitable even for governing letters in a larger realm:
He had formed in his mind an outline of all the disciplines, and he knew the dignity, necessity, usefulness, growth, and decline of each, and the connection of all with one another.
He understood the character of the age.
Nor was his mind unequal to a new undertaking, however arduous.
Indeed, he was deficient in no kind of literature, except that he was somewhat more estranged from philosophy, whose face at that time was not very cheerful.

And he was almost the first to bring together nearly all kinds of studies, a great part of which had previously been cultivated outside the boundaries of the university, into this most ample body of academic discipline.
In this matter, however, how much greater the interval left to our age and to our republic under the auspices of Frederick William, there is no need for me to explain.

But in the selection of learned men, which Heynius most rightly calls the second anchor of the academic republic, it is wonderful how happy a discoverer of talents he showed himself, and he shrank from no trouble of care:
I pass over how great apparatus he collected, how much labor and assiduity he himself expended on equipping the university library, especially that most copious and most select one.

But Heynius, especially that one skilled in academic governance, in which he himself afterwards held great authority, does not dwell at length on any part of his praises in that speech, by which nearly seventy years ago he paid his due respects to Münchhusius, nor does he insist more earnestly on any point, than that Münchhusius, when he led literature as it were out of the cells of monasteries into the field and dust of civil life, at the same time knew the freedom of thinking, feeling, and writing.
This is the aegis, this is the Palladium of the university.
And if any wicked fraud of a man should snatch it away, then at last he thinks he will have something on account of which he might fear for the fortune of the university.

For this reason he proclaims that Münchhausen brought new light into almost all disciplines, especially into the historical and the public law discipline, which it greatly matters to the princes and states to be handed down whole and undefiled, and that he illuminated everything far and wide.
Such, therefore, was that Münchhausen.

When I look at him, I am moved in my mind both for his own sake and because of the admirable judgment of our most wise, most kind, most just King in choosing his administrator of magnificent plans, a judgment most useful to our affairs.
While I am setting these things forth, listeners, I have taken up a great subject implicitly, by unfolding and explaining which I could pursue the praises of Frederick William more eloquently.
But why should I set forth what everyone sees, feels, and understands from the daily experience of royal beneficence?
However, let no one take in a bad sense what I have discussed about those studies which a leading citizen cannot support in any state of the republic:
although I know that all ill-will is absent from you, and the consciousness of my devotion, most devoted to the best King, reassures me:
I freely affirm that that liberty, without which the life of universities is not vital, and by which the highest glory and ornament of letters is contained, remains safe and sound among us.

Recall, you older men, as many of you as have been present here with me from the beginning of this school, having been summoned here at that time in large part from other seats of learning by Frederick William, recall the condition which then existed in other universities and especially in our own, of which none of us was then ashamed, and compare with it this condition which we now enjoy.
What, by your faith, have we lost?
How little has changed among us in these six lustra, in these most serious times for universities?
For Frederick William does not approve those who try to obstruct the lights of the mind:
this citadel, this bulwark of our freedom, as long as we ourselves do not fail ourselves.
That we ourselves may not fail ourselves, both the dignity of knowledge and a certain continuity of discipline and of purposes long since established make provision.

For our ancestors most wisely established this, that they founded these colleges of learned men, which are called by the name of universities, not because they embrace the whole circle of letters, but because they are bodies endowed with their own rights and constituted in the likeness of a commonwealth.
In these, unless they are corrupted by the evil arts of ambitious men, excellent plans are handed down from ancestors to descendants by a constant succession.

Will it seem surprising that this very thing is counted among the benefits conferred upon us by Frederick William, namely that our school too was at that age reduced to the form of a college, when, of course, very many thought that these ruinous remnants of the barbarous age should be entirely removed?
There is indeed, there is very great power in this communion and fellowship of studies, institutions, necessities, and utilities.
Those who individually had been weak, to them union adds strength.
Disagreements of opinions, accidental quarrels, and private enmities yield to the public good, and we are like children of one family under a king as patron.
That grief and mourning, equally domestic and public, is evidence, if any of us has been taken from us by death and from literature.

Oh, if only our colleague, endowed with the most excellent gifts of mind and character, had not recently been lamented! No one more than he considered all the advantages and disadvantages of the university as pertaining to himself; no one was a more certain and sincere friend; no one was more benevolent to his fellow students.
I consider it a religious duty not to mention him in these solemn ceremonies, at which he was never absent from venerating the King.

Whom the very logic of this speech of mine demands that I mention not more for his own sake than for the sake of praising the state, because in him it was made clear how much of liberty this empire can bear.
As we despair that an equal can succeed this man, so we pray that one wholly unlike him may not follow.

As I now profess these things in three words, I was moved by piety, which is the mother of all virtues, not that piety consisting of formulas and ceremonies, but dwelling in the hearts of men, not that foul nurse of hatreds and discords, by which the priestly sedition and the obstinacy of the Roman curia disturbed the security of this most tranquil city, but the teacher of charity and love, with which Frederick William embraces his people.
But what is piety without a grateful remembrance of benefits?
Who would not call those who repay with evil deeds those who have deserved well of them not only inhuman but savage and wild, since not even the tamer beasts lack all sense of gratitude?

But if the remaining virtue of Frederick William, beneficent to all, and the sanctity of the oath did not bind us to devote ourselves to him, nevertheless the remembrance of the benefits with which he has heaped this university ought to bring it about that whatever he expects from us (for he expects nothing that cannot be performed without violating religion), that we should strive to perform diligently and strenuously.
At this point, fellow soldiers, you must be encouraged by me to repay with gratitude, in the ways you can, the most merciful King, who takes exceptional care of your prosperity, with those arts.
I mean love for the Prince and affection for the fatherland, diligence in studies, reverence for the laws, and modesty and strictness of morals.
Although I advise that thanks should be given to the best Prince, I do not do this because this admonition seems necessary to me now, but to indulge my own feelings.

For the more ungrateful we have seen those men toward the King, whose power, dignity, and resources he alone restored, the more earnestly do all good men love Frederick William, and congratulate him on the constancy of his purposes, and hope that he will be the avenger and preserver of the highest goods of the soul for his people, and that he will not yield to the superstition which everywhere grows strong, and is nourished secretly and openly by deceits and authority, and threatens a most sad slavery.
I pray you, God, Best and Greatest, that you would defend and avert this evil from our state;

I pray that you may grant to Frederick William a vigorous old age, free from all hardship; that you may direct his counsels to the strengthening of the safety of his people; that you may preserve harmony and mutual affection between the ruling family and the people; and finally, that you may keep safe the magnanimous Prince, heir to the kingdom, in whom the nearest hope of the fatherland is placed, together with his august consort restored to us by your favor, and the entire royal house.

div.head: XXVII. Friderici Guilelmi III. laudatio d. XXVII. m. Iunii a. MDCCCXL. dicta.
Funeral eulogy of Frederick William III

p.s: I, who from my youth, with the continuous success of many years, have celebrated in my speech the most joyful solemnity of that day on which Frederick William was born for the happiness of the fatherland, most distinguished men, most learned men, most honored fellow soldiers, now about to pay the last rites to the ashes of the Father of the Fatherland, with what feeling do you think I am affected, with what confidence instructed, to approach so great a matter, so grave and arduous, so sad and mournful?

Indeed, each of you, as many as are present, can gauge the feeling of my mind from your own heart, from the common grief and longing of all, since we mourn the death of a king so beloved that every best man, if it had been possible, would have been willing to redeem his life with his own death.
I fear that few sufficiently realize how much confidence fails me, and rightly fails me.
For although there are many things that make the praise of a living master difficult and uncertain, nevertheless in performing that duty the mind is lifted up and strengthened by not a few things:
the serene image of a flourishing prince presents itself to the speaker, which may fill the orator with joy;
the mind of the speaker is moved by the most pleasing and sweetest emotions, when he congratulates the good king on his successes and makes vows for his safety;
The joyful faces of the listeners add strength to my weak powers and even spurs to the slow.

But in these most mournful solemnities everything is arranged to disturb and confound the mind: the sad appearance of the place, your sorrow, the grief of the republic, and finally my own grief and distress, which would break even a stronger man and close the mouth of the eloquent.
To be brief:
If your kindness has conceived any good opinion of me from my frequent praises of the surviving King, that opinion seems to me to have been extinguished by the death of that excellent King.

Indeed, I who had wished rather to hide myself in solitude and silently ponder with myself the virtues of the deceased Prince, silently to grieve the bitter misfortune, am dragged into the light, though some time has been granted for collecting my mind, which I cannot bear, as if one were to expose a sick man, to whom darkness brings relief, to the endurance of the sun's glare.
Therefore the spirit is cast down;
I despair of fulfilling so great a task as has been entrusted to me today by you, dearest colleagues, who trust me too much not so much because of my skill as because of your goodwill.
Nevertheless I will speak as best I can, since I cannot speak as I wish.

Finally, to strengthen myself as much as possible, I will not indulge in tears, but I will restrain my lamentation and tearful cries, which do not even seem fitting for the funeral rites of a brave man:

I shall try to recall both myself and you somewhat from the bitterness of grief, and to lift up our minds by contemplating the life of our most beloved King, not so much his death, by which we have been struck down, as his life, which has been and is salutary for the citizens, for the Prussian kingdom, and for all Europe, as far as my strength suffices.
When I say life, I mean something great, and perhaps something greater than I seem to mean.
For this is not the only life that our bodies live, and the soul in the body, but a future life follows this one lived on earth, that one constant and everlasting, this one fleeting and fragile.

Indeed, if there is anything that offers us a better hope of dying, that can console those who are left mourning for the death of a dear one, what consolation is more effective, what is more worthy of a philosopher and a Christian man, than that we not only hope and believe, but know that, when the bonds of the body are loosened and the prison broken, the soul, a particle of the divine breath, freed, returns to the kindred gods from whom it came forth?
That the life we now lead is a pilgrimage, pleasant by the sight and survey of various things, delightful by the abundance of favorable circumstances, sweet by pleasures;

The same life is troublesome with cares and tumults, obstructed with rough places and dangers, filled with miseries and evils, which not even he can escape who is placed on the highest pinnacle, being liable to so much the more severe misfortunes and greater losses, as his goods are more ample and his position more elevated.

When this earthly journey has been traversed, the death that follows is the beginning of a higher life, and the ancient sages, anticipating the divine precepts of our faith, rightly conjectured that what we call life is that death, and what we call death is life.
And so, since death seems to begin the true life, this life which we now lead is a meditation on death:

We divine and believe that for those who have lived justly and piously, who in the greatest fortune have never forgotten that they are mortal, and have so lived as to know that human souls, stripped and bared of all pomp and splendor at some time, will render an account to the supreme judge of all those things which they have administered in this earthly province, that life will be more blessed, when they are led back to the supreme divinity.

So that you cannot tell whether death is rather to be congratulated for the good, who indeed, besides the common weakness of mankind, conscious of no fault of their own, meet it with good hope, while the same death terrifies the wicked and the criminal.
Therefore the Father of his country has not died, but has been carried up to a more blessed abode, which is firmer and more sublime than the very royal throne he had obtained;
Therefore he is not to be lamented:
But we who are left behind, measuring our grief by our own longing, not by the most blessed condition of that heavenly soul, nevertheless stand here sorrowfully at the funeral, and rightly so.
This immortality, which truly belongs to the divine part of man, I think I am not mistaken if I call it divine;
But there is also another human immortality, which must not be counted last, and that is not simple but divided into two parts.

For indeed, next to that divine immortality is the second one, the immortality of a name, which is preserved by the memory of deeds and by the monuments of talent, virtue, and kindness, which each person has left behind after himself.
In this, a great prerogative has been given to princes.
For we are all born and die indiscriminately, and with equal foot death, to use a common word, strikes the towers of kings and the huts of the poor.
Nor is the richest man, at his last breath, different from a beggar, nor a king from a private citizen or a slave.
But they differ in the comforts and discomforts of life, in the resources and outcomes of their affairs.

For a prince, by his very birth, obtains an immense abundance and opportunity for great deeds and for benefiting the human race, and again license for idleness, luxury, cruelty, and any evil arts whatsoever, which we generally see go unpunished.
Indeed, the memory of a conspicuous vice is propagated to posterity just as much as that of virtue.
But we do not attribute the immortality of a name except to virtue.
This is the second immortality of Frederick William, that his virtue not only we have admired and do admire, but future ages will proclaim it;

Because the things he accomplished brilliantly at home and in war will live no less in the memory of men than the mighty deeds of Frederick the Great, and will be handed down forever by historians with the highest praise, as long as the good arts, which he fostered with such great zeal, do not become obsolete.

Because he left to his people, to Germany, to all of Europe, lasting examples of the best counsels and, even amid the pressing necessities of the present time, benefits of such a kind that they would benefit not only his contemporaries but also posterity, who will rest under the shade of the trees that he planted and will gather the harvest that he sowed.
Thirdly, in the degree of immortality, why should we not value the eternity of the stock and the race, by which even that which is mortal is propagated?
The most flourishing offspring of Frederick William lives and thrives, sons and grandsons, those already now supports of the empire, these in time to come to follow the footsteps of their fathers;
The son has taken up the kingdom equal to his father, whom we now venerate as our most serene lord with no less piety than his most blessed father:

He will protect the republic with innate virtue, he has already won the hearts of all to himself by his courtesy before his principate, and with prudence and kindness he will diligently provide for all the prosperity of his people.

Truly, how great a consolation for such a loss and relief of grief is this, that a King has succeeded to the Prince who was uniquely beloved, a King of most robust age, distinguished by the most beautiful gifts of mind and talent, equipped with the best arts, whose public and private virtues we have come to know through use and experience and through benefits conferred upon us, whose excellent disposition I would not hesitate even now to celebrate more fully, were it not that an untimely eulogy of a Prince just beginning seemed to be in this common and deepest sorrow.

But since leading men can attain that other immortality of name, which I have mentioned, not by one single path, and especially either by military glory or by the arts of peace, it has been for a long time the good fortune of Prussia that its kings excel in both kinds of glory.
But different men have entered upon different paths of performing glorious deeds;

Most blessed Father of the Fatherland, with what character, with what deeds, with what institutions, with what changes of fortune, and finally with what success he earned this eternity of his name, there is none of you, listeners, who does not understand that I must discuss this uniquely, avoiding any digressions of speech, and who does not uniquely desire to hear it.

Since I have set forth these matters individually and separately, almost throughout the whole course of my life, with the greatest zeal and admiration for royal virtue, now I will make, as it were, a very brief summary of them.
I will speak simple words;
true feeling does not run out into a luxuriant and exultant speech.
What of the fact that even one who should open up the most abundant flow of eloquence could not but fall far short of the dignity and greatness of the subject?

Considering the character of Frederick William, I do not hesitate to trace the series of his many virtues, both because I myself know that all these virtues were in him, and because I would judge your piety poorly if I thought that any of you thought otherwise.
For why was he so dear to all, why did he pass away mourned by all, why was he so missed, if not because of the very many virtues that stood out in him?
There was indeed an admirable union and harmony of the liberal arts in that man.

But this harmony, just as sharp and deep tones are blended into a concord, is produced in the human soul by moderation and temperance, which seems to me to have been that virtue of the most blessed Father of his country from which nearly all the others flowed, and by which they were held together as by a very strong bond.
This he never failed to maintain both in public and in private.
For Frederick William was not indeed a good prince, but he was of ambiguous reputation in private life;
not good at home, but unequal to the conduct of the state:
which in so great fortune seem able neither easily to be united nor separated, private and public virtues were equally conspicuous in him.

A most faithful and loving husband, an excellent head of a household, gentle and courteous toward domestic servants, so averse to the luxury of the court that in his daily food and dress he scarcely equaled the splendor of a somewhat wealthier private citizen, he restored the ancient simplicity and strictness of morals, a most useful example to the citizens.

Now, since a perfect prince ought to excel both in courage and in clemency and wisdom, Frederick William proved himself brave not only by leading an army and by military glory and by enduring hardships, but also by steadfastness of mind in bearing any calamities whatsoever:

He, no less than Frederick the Great, combined with that strength of mind wisdom and gentleness, I mean the genuine wisdom of the mind, which would not aim at the praise of manifold learning, and would differ greatly from the cunning and deceits by which, as many think that peoples are to be ruled, so Frederick William, a most upright and honest man, thought that nothing should be done through those arts, but through faith and sincerity;

And being stern where the situation demanded it, whenever it could be done without public harm, he never failed to give way to more lenient measures, like a prudent and humane physician preferring milder remedies to fire and the knife.
Fair and just to all, he not only took the greatest care that no one should suffer injury, but he also strove to repair any injury whatsoever.

With what feelings he had been toward those by whom he had been wronged, who did not read in that will of his, drawn up thirteen years ago, by the promulgation of which Frederick William IV auspiciously began his reign, with the greatest emotion and with tears that welled up unbidden?
Indeed, that man's heart must have been imbued with not even the slightest sense of humanity and harder than flint and adamant, whose heart that royal will did not touch!

What shall I say of the piety and holiness of the most blessed King, with which he worshipped and revered the divine power, which never allowed him to depart a finger's breadth from a right conscience?

But with what excellent moderation did he combine liberality and munificence with frugality, being neither tenacious of wealth nor prodigal, having spent much on the flourishing of literature and the arts and on the necessities of the church, having spent much to aid provinces afflicted by famine, pestilence, low grain prices, or floods, and having also bestowed no small sums from his private treasury to relieve the poverty and straitened circumstances of individuals who had fled to him!
He never hardened himself against anyone's misfortune, but amid the very cares of empire, which would bid a heart to be hardened with triple bronze, he retained human compassion.
And the most modest of all princes we know did nothing for display and ostentation, and if not careless of fame, at least not eagerly or ambitiously desirous of it.
On the contrary, the virtues which I said were conspicuous in him, he himself did not want to be conspicuous.

He, drawn by no party zeal, favoring no order of citizens above others, subject to no voices, whispers, and goads of servants—as the Roman emperors of old were to freedmen—nor of household members, if indeed a prince has household members, nor of informers or spies, like that famous Marcus Antoninus, always maintained his own character most steadfastly.
Antoninus always maintained his own character most steadfastly.
These things, for the most part, are all very closely connected with continence and moderation, which I have indicated was, as it were, peculiar to the most blessed King.

He who held the supreme command of so great a state had nothing more important or more ancient than to command himself with a composed mind, keeping far away hatreds, angers, desires, and any emotions of the mind that disturb too much.
What wonder, then, if the same moderation which he himself employed in his whole life he also shared with the state?

For through all parts of the state, through the minds of the King's friends and ministers, magistrates, soldiers, and citizens, this moderation has spread from the highest place, which alone promises lasting happiness to the people;
From this was born public tranquility, a certain even state of the kingdom, a quiet course and progress of affairs, neither headlong nor without sluggishness.

When, in addition, that singular goodwill toward all subjects, that intimate feeling of benevolence and courtesy, and that popularity combined with majesty, came to him; when in administering the empire he sought not his own advantage but the safety of the people, which he believed had been entrusted to him by divine providence; and when, moreover, he wished to do everything not by his own judgment alone, but willingly listened to those who were distinguished in any field, and yielded to their wishes:
That which a prince, in such great power, obtains from himself with difficulty, unless he has firmly resolved within himself to obey reason alone.

He brought it about that not only was his rule easily borne, being circumscribed by almost no agreements, by no laws except those which the King alone had given, but also that the greatest harmony of the whole republic arose, never disturbed except by chance and, as it were, playful gatherings of the city crowd, and mutual love between King and people, by which the kingdom is held much more firmly than by the strength of armies.
so that the people might feel and understand that their own safety could not be separated from the safety of the King;

that the King might live as secure among a people enjoying just liberty as a father of a family among good children, and finally that he might draw those very provinces, which had recently been added by the outcome of wars, into that same consensus of goodwill and love of royal virtue, reverence, and admiration.
By these arts was accomplished whatever the most glorious Father of his Country did during the forty-three years of his reign.
In what condition Frederick William the Third received his father's kingdom is known to no one, neither among the older nor the younger generation.

After the King, whose distinguished character is known to have been prophesied as that of Frederick the Great, had gained control of the highest affairs, he corrected morals, restored the resources of the treasury, which had been exhausted by the war of which he himself had been a witness in his youth and by lavish expenditures, and he either restored or confirmed the force of the laws and the freedom of thought and speech that had been sanctioned by Frederick the Great, and he earnestly strove to maintain peace.
The first years of his reign flowed by in a calm course;
Although there were those to whom the peace, which was then at hand, seemed to have been a little too sluggish and remiss.
Meanwhile, by the Treaty of Lunéville, the borders of the kingdom were advanced without bloodshed, with more territory received than had been lost.
Soon a sad reversal of all things followed.
For mortals must experience both prosperity and adversity, rejoice and grieve;
And although kings hold the place of gods on earth, they are nevertheless not exempt from the lot of men, so that they are overtaken by the vicissitude and injustice of fortune.
Indeed, the best king has fallen, together with us, into that age in which the immense power of one man shook the world with continuous disturbances.
In this common disaster of the human race, Frederick William, being drawn along, endured such great evils as no one could bear unless he were a most steadfast and most brave man.
God had willed that his pious worshipper should be tested like gold by fire, so that he might shine forth all the more brightly.
And relying on God's help, he overcame all the evils, however great they were.

A most just and most religious prince, I will not say in what difficulties he was then entangled, by what snares he was assailed, by what wrongs and insults he was provoked and challenged to a war which he had uniquely striven to avoid:
It is hardly pleasing to revive old grievances and to perpetuate feuds that have scarcely been extinguished to some extent.
Why say more?

One most fatal day destroyed a most powerful and best-equipped army, overthrew a whole kingdom, and afflicted the Prussian people with extreme calamities that had to be endured for more than six years.
The King was conquered, but conquered by whom?
Indeed, by that man who conquered all, until he was conquered by the combined forces of all, not without God as his helper.
The war was ended by a peace, which was more ruinous than the war itself:
the kingdom was punished by the loss of the greater part of its territories;
Against the King's will, so many most faithful peoples were dismissed unwillingly.
On the lands that Frederick William retained, very harsh conditions were imposed.

To the King came the most bitter addition of grief: his dearest wife, snatched away by untimely death, the mother of so many children, the companion of such great misfortunes, was taken from him, and she was the darling of the people both while she flourished and after she died.
Yet Frederick William was not overwhelmed by the waves of such a storm, but emerged more noble and stronger and greater than himself.
For the greater the loss of territory was, with so much more zealous care did he nourish the strength of the kingdom that was left.

To pass over everything else at this point, although Frederick William, even when the Prussian state was flourishing, had favored literature exceptionally and had conferred many benefits especially upon the universities, particularly Halle and Erlangen, nevertheless, after the strength of arms was broken, he understood more keenly that the forces of the mind, which are stronger than arms themselves, must be aroused and strengthened.
But he saw this most wisely, that it should be accomplished especially by aiding literature.
And so, for nurturing these, greater expenditures were made then, even in the greatest straits of the treasury, than ever before.
But I recall myself from this most abundant material for praise, to which I see I must return hereafter.

For we must hasten to the most joyful memory of that time, when Frederick William, by his magnanimous counsels and greatest deeds, together with his allies, vindicated his Prussia and all Germany into liberty, testifying by immortal documents to all Europe then and to future ages how great a burden he was capable of, and to what great undertakings he was equal.

Then how much that mutual love and concord could accomplish was demonstrated by a most clear example, when Frederick William called his people to the supreme contest, in which the King with the people, the people with the King, would either conquer together or perish together;

when, roused by his voice, they flocked through the midst of the enemy into his camp, not only those who were strong in bodily strength, but even the weaker ones and those scarcely yet equal to enduring military service;

When they contributed money, weapons, and any military equipment whatsoever, not only those who were powerful in resources, but even the poor, brought whatever little each had, to the King and the fatherland.
I am moved in my soul when I recall those times;
But indeed the brevity of the hour, which has been granted to me for speaking, compels me to cut short not only my words but even my very thoughts.
Nor will I proclaim so many most noble victories:
I do not pass over the victory of Culm, a great part of which is acknowledged to be due to the counsel and courage of the King himself.
His valor in Gaul was equal, and the moderation of the victor was no less.
This is the reward of the victories won in both wars, that now Frederick William the Fourth, our most gracious Lord, has left a greater empire than he had received.

But that he left not only more, but also more firmly and more flourishingly, we owe to that wisdom of his, by which, after overcoming dangers and enduring labors, he restored the republic through the arts of peace, which was not even then disturbed, when all Europe trembled with a new commotion.

For when, ten years ago, so many new disturbances, discords, seditions, and civil wars were harassing the neighboring nations, the Prussian state stood peaceful and unmoved, not so much because it was held together by skill and arms, as because the minds of the people were bound and obligated by the benefits of Frederick William; and although there were things that were desired, the mutual affection of the ruler and the subjects compensated for those agreements and rights which the people then longed to extort.

What of the fact that the most blessed King, both in that fear and danger and afterwards, by his moderation settled feuds and hatreds, and brought it about that threatening swords were sheathed, that princes were reconciled among themselves, and nations together with the princes?

The day would fail me, listeners, if I wished to enumerate all those things, or even a great part of them, however briefly, which the most blessed Father of the Fatherland instituted excellently in the ordering of the state during the forty-three years of his reign.
Nevertheless, piety demands that I run through briefly those parts of the state which he especially brought to a better condition.
I have said that he was fair to all orders;
The same care embraced almost all parts of the republic with equal attention.
The division of the whole empire was changed, the entire system and form of administering the provinces;
Cities and towns were enlarged by new constitutions, so that citizens could manage their own affairs more conveniently, more usefully, more freely through their own magistrates and decurions;
The workshops were loosened from the bonds of the guilds, not only released, but so tempered that access to making work might not be too much closed off;
The farmers were freed from slavery, and the fields themselves became more fertile after the division was established.
Where once there were vast sands, now there are excellently paved roads.
The taxes were established in a new way, not so that as much as possible should be exacted, but so that they should be most equitable.
The towns, once closed by the guards of the tax collectors, are now open day and night.

Trade, once hindered in many ways, is now most ready and most free, since a most beneficial treaty has been concluded with very many states of Germany, not for the sake of profit but so that the resources of the citizens might increase and the opportunity of seeking might be more ample and easier, concerning the commonality of revenues, and it is equally most acceptable to foreigners as to our own people.

Now as for military affairs, which nevertheless seemed to have been excellently organized under the earlier kings, Frederick William so arranged them by a new institution that, whereas previously soldiers were for the most part mercenaries, those men were barely restrained by the most savage punishments and tortures, while the rest were conscripted from the lower classes of subjects and kept in the ranks for many continuous years, now all citizens earn the most honorable service with easy compliance, whether they take up arms voluntarily or by lawful levy, and the former are discharged after a year, the latter after a period of three years, with a temporary militia thereafter, not overly burdensome, to be exercised every year, and citizens and soldiers are not, as before, estranged from one another, but have coalesced, as it were, into one body.
There was a time when it was attributed to Prussia as a fault that it was too military:
But the last years of the most blessed King, in a very different part of the state, were subject to various judgments.
For long before, it had been close to his heart to establish a certain order of sacred rites, not because he was devoted to ceremonies or wanted to strengthen his rule by fostering superstition:
For no one doubts that he was imbued with true piety and that he propagated it into the minds of the citizens by his example.
But, unless I am mistaken, he thought that in these matters not too much should be left to the judgment of individuals.

For my part, although I think that everyone should have his own judgment about divine matters (and Frederick William thought no differently), the most blessed King seems to me to have done this excellently, that he strove to reconcile both Protestant confessions and did reconcile them.
But if they cry out that something in this matter was done too sharply, whose fault this was, let the judgment rest with others.
The Germans, indeed, with one voice have long proclaimed Frederick William as the leader and defender of the evangelical faith.

And he deserved that reward of his zeal which befell him, namely, that he was permitted to celebrate two secular festivals of the Reformation, one for the church restored by Luther, the other for the evangelical doctrine received from his ancestors in the land of Brandenburg.
Yet he, with his characteristic fairness, vigorously protected the Catholic Church in his kingdom.
Who does not know how much the Roman Pontiff himself owed to him, when he was restored to his dominion?
Who does not know that by royal munificence the dignity and splendor of the Catholic Church were restored in this kingdom?

For this reason it is the more to be lamented, that since the royal mind could not endure priestly obstinacy, the old age of the most pious King, if not afflicted, was at least saddened by the difficulties and disturbances which arose from that source.
I pass on to the other pursuits of Frederick William, for which greater gratitude was felt toward him and is still felt.
For he was so generous toward literature and the arts that he surpassed both all the greater kings and very many kings in the number and magnitude of his benefactions.

And he did not only support literature by his generosity, but also, although at this age a certain part of the studies both of the learned and of those eager for learning was greatly suspected, nevertheless he treated us most liberally and gently.
We have retained the freedom of speaking and teaching;

As for the freedom of writing, or rather the license, if you prefer to call it that, which seemed to be diminished, it should be attributed not so much to the royal will as to the common failing of this age.
It is not unpleasant to recall at this point with what courtesy that great-hearted man treated the learned, to whom at last the most wise King had entrusted the supreme care of public education;

from which it can be understood with what sort of men, with what talent, with what skill in literature, with what sincerity of mind endowed, and finally how courteous and indulgent the most blessed King judged this province should be entrusted.
But we recently conducted the funeral of this most excellent man too, not without tears.
Under the auspices of Frederick William, moreover, both academies, that of the sciences and that of the arts, were better established.
Equipment of every kind, necessary for the pursuit of the disciplines, was procured in the choicest and most abundant manner.
The universities, both the old ones restored and better equipped, and new and most celebrated ones founded at great expense.

By a new and most salutary arrangement, the King has placed our university in the very seat of the kingdom, and not in a less conspicuous place, but in the most frequented and most adorned street of the city, and in the immediate vicinity of his own house and within his own view, and in these royal buildings, which he began to splendidly restore in the last few years:
And so that there might be proofs of the greatest affection with which he embraced learning, he wished both our university and the beloved Rhenish one to bear his name.

Therefore, just as the Greek states of old honored their founders with heroic honors, what religion, what piety, what veneration of ours can be so great that it does not fall short of the thanks that must be paid to the most blessed soul of Frederick William, our hero?

He also supported the gymnasia and the schools below them with no small subsidies, and ordered that many popular and rural games be founded, in which the common and rustic multitude might be instructed in the precepts of the Christian faith and the first rudiments of letters, not thinking that men would be the more ignorant, but the more civilized, and therefore easier to rule.
Moreover, how much the cultivation of the arts grew and advanced under this King is evident.

With truly Periclean zeal he roused sculptors, painters, architects, musicians, actors, and choral performers, thinking it a civic duty, following the example of Augustus, to share in the pleasures of the people.

He founded that magnificent treasury for the arts, filled it with the most elegant works, and opened it to all with the freest access, so that artists might have models to follow, and the minds and eyes of all might be delighted and educated.
He so changed the face of the city that almost wherever we cast our eyes, we see monuments of royal magnificence.
The one thing that seemed to be missing, the monument to Frederick the Great, he ordered to be founded when he was already on the point of death.

O that joyful and at the same time sad spectacle, when the heir to the kingdom, by his father's command and with the greatest enthusiasm of the people, inaugurated that work with his own hand, while in these most favorable auspices nothing was lacking, with the nobles and magistrates and the immense multitude that was present, except the presence of the Father of his country, about whom we were already then anxiously worried!
O happy Prussia, whose honor and glory Frederick William held in his heart even to his last breath!

I declare the rule of the most blessed king fortunate, a rule which, although it was not free from the gravest evils, drew prosperity from those very evils, bringing so salutary a remedy to them that Frederick William seemed to have been sent by divine providence, who, relying on the love of his people, would emerge as the restorer and renewer of the Prussian state in war and peace.
He also died fortunate.
For although with him ruling almost the whole world was changed, the mutual love between King and people among us has not changed:
witness is this universal grief, that mournful sight as of a captured city:

For indeed, although a change of ruler is wont to hold minds in suspense between hope and fear, there is no place for any fear among us, since Frederick William IV has taken possession of affairs with the highest hope and confidence of the people, but the tears that burst forth were elicited by nothing other than that love.
The King departed from the palace, surrounded not by guards but by sorrowful crowds of citizens, with the entire imperial family standing beside him.
The Empress, his most beloved daughter, had flown from the throne of the East;
As he was dying, the King bade farewell to his son-in-law, the Emperor.
He left the kingdom to his most august son, whom he knew would follow in his footsteps.

We therefore give thanks to you, God, Best and Greatest, that after you did not wish the Father of the Fatherland to live longer among us, but received into your bosom a most holy man on the most holy day on which we celebrate the outpouring of your Spirit, you gave Frederick William IV, our most merciful Lord, as successor to the kingdom, whom we trust will hold as ratified whatever the best of everyone expects of him, and will add a crowning glory to the greatest benefits that the most blessed father conferred upon the fatherland, he excellently perceiving what the new principate, the new times demand.

Preserve, I pray, and keep safe the most august King with his consort the most august Queen and the whole august royal house, and fill his most noble mind with the best counsels, by which he may confirm the harmony of the commonwealth handed down by his father, procure for the most loyal people every advantage and utility, and protect and increase the honor and glory of the Prussian name and the safety, security, and majesty of the kingdom.
So may God help us, as these vows have been solemnly made by us.
I have spoken.

div.head: XXVIII. Oratio nataliciis Friderici Guilelmi IV. celebrandis d. XV. m. Octobris a. MDCCCXLI. habita.
The character of Frederick William IV is compared with royal virtue

p.s: In this most joyful assembly, which we are holding for the first time today, listeners, in order to duly and piously celebrate the birthday of our most beloved King, it does not seem right to me to take any other beginning of speaking except from giving thanks to God, the Best and Greatest, in my own name and in yours and that of the whole commonwealth, because, since it is not permitted to cherish in person that prince to whose veneration the common rejoicing and, as it were, a father's love had so often summoned us into this hall, He has willed that by the most sacred right of legitimate succession the rule be transferred to this most merciful Lord, whom it would be more difficult not to love, not to praise, than to love with deepest affection and to praise with truest speech.

For since everything human is fragile and subject to many changes, and since a change of ruler brings anxiety to kingdoms, especially after a long reign, whose citizens have experienced such great kindness that better things can scarcely be hoped for, but because nothing is wont to remain long in the same state, losses may be feared:

What can be received from God by more devoted minds as a gift, than that which was most earnestly sought by the prayers of all, namely that the most excellent blessings should remain, which the most blessed Father of the fatherland had bestowed upon the republic, so that the heir of the empire might nourish the seeds sown by him and scatter new ones, about to yield a most abundant and most joyful harvest?

Still resound and will resound forever, not so much in our ears as in our minds, those most weighty words of the King, poured forth from a moved heart and witnesses of excellent intentions; those acclamations of the envoys and the people, marked by no suspicion of pretense or flattery, by which that mutual affection, which had joined the most blessed father with his people, was confirmed between the successor and all the provinces of the kingdom and all orders of the state, and was so declared by the most certain proofs that the fame of this illustrious and almost unprecedented harmony spread throughout the world, that at the rising of a new star all nations turned their eyes, and even the incredulous recognized the faith, happiness, and strength of Prussia, and even the bolder ones feared them.

And if that sudden heat, or rather ardor and impulse of love, could not be publicly continued, love itself relaxed nothing, but like a river that had overflowed, once returned to its channel and enclosed and restrained by its banks, it holds a moderate course and promises perpetuity with even temper.
The King follows in his father's footsteps, his father's admonitions, neither too desirous of new things, nor too tenacious of the previous state:
