And so the state is led to better things by a gentle and not precipitate step, and although not yet two years have passed since Frederick William IV took possession of the supreme power, we have seen and heard many things which before were unheard of;
The minds of the citizens have been roused, raised, and inflamed, not by a turbulent movement, but by an inner impulse and instinct, which proceeds from the King, and which the King moderates.

But as for what I said, that the praises of this king are most ready at hand, I do not want it to be taken as said in such a way that one might think that I consider the king can be worthily praised by me.

To speak the truth, what I said in the funeral oration, in which I venerated the shades of the most blessed king, that together with his death it seemed to me that whatever eloquence there was in me had died out — and I well understand how slight it was — that I now feel has plainly come to pass.

Indeed, having for nearly thirty years accustomed myself, as it were, to the life, character, institutions, and deeds of Frederick William III, by repeatedly contemplating and explaining them, I had conformed my own mind to his nature and my own disposition to his genius.
For unless you have thoroughly immersed yourself in the character of the one you wish to praise, success will not answer to your undertaking.

Now I see that, although our most merciful Lord has recently regenerated the father, yet he himself is endowed with a special and peculiar character, wonderfully excellent, and that a different talent must be assumed for speaking of him, and, as it were, a different role; nor do I trust that this loftiness of mind can be equaled by my words, nor that my speech, already fading and growing old, can be compared with the force, vigor, and ardor of this new empire.

There are, moreover, those who think that this empire should not be proclaimed as truly German and popular in this learned or dead and foreign language, which they even disdain, but in the native language, open to the common understanding, which I myself confess I gladly use on other occasions.

Nevertheless, though I am weak in strength, this thought raises and strengthens me: that just as on the birthday of our most blessed Father of the Fatherland, it was customary to allow and grant me, regarding the greatness of my task, to digress a little from the praises of the King to other matters which were connected with our affairs, so also today I shall seem to have done enough to some extent, or at least I shall obtain pardon, if I speak so much about our most beloved King that no one misses our devotion, and everyone understands how greatly we are bound and devoted to our most merciful Lord; but at the same time I shall take it upon myself, while I set forth the royal virtue, not to fear to mix in something about the study of literature, concerning which, when I am speaking before you, who are engaged in these pursuits, and on a day dedicated to the Prince who is most fond of literature, who is there of any refinement who would think that I am dealing with a matter foreign to the occasion or far-fetched?

The royal power over all human affairs is the greatest and most serious, surrounded by very many cares and requiring immense keenness of mind, goodness, industry, and diligence, so that the interests of the state may be provided for and the safety of the people may be looked after, who are destined to reach the highest prosperity, when the king, on whose nod everything depends, will manage affairs wisely, kindly, vigorously, and promptly; but they are destined to perish or certainly to suffer great calamities, if they obey an imprudent, cruel, lazy, and negligent master.
What has been said in general terms, I hardly dare indeed to apply and explain at length to the praise of our King;
yet those things which are both most true and evident do not seem to be entirely passed over in silence in this place.

Therefore I will not be silent, that no easy prince can be found, who is more skilled in all things that pertain to the administration of the republic, of ancestral and foreign institutions, of the necessities of the people and of the counsels by which the state is to be governed, and more instructed in letters and good arts, and more ready in speaking, and endowed with a keener sense of the beautiful and the good and the true, and more reverent of sacred things without superstition:
by which things I think the greatest part of wisdom is contained:
Again, there is no one who is of a milder and more merciful disposition, who is more inclined to bring help and to confer benefits:
But how tolerant of business he is, and almost beyond his strength energetic and industrious, we who love him deeply learn not without some anxiety.

Now in royal life this is the most difficult thing: since most of those whom the king uses as ministers and counselors ought not to excel and be practiced except in individual fields, the king, who wishes to be fully adequate to the burden placed on his shoulders, ought to embrace all parts of the state with a great mind, to grasp at least the sum of the most diverse matters, if not every smallest detail, and finally to join and mix these diverse things with his own mind in such a way that, as from variations of sounds, one harmony is produced.
And peace and war are very different things:
The king must excel in the arts of both, at least in this form and condition of the republic in which we Prussians live.
Therefore, so that these may be tempered with just measure not only in the republic but in the very soul of the king, extraordinary greatness of soul is needed, which rarely falls to a mortal:
It had fallen to the lot of one man in the previous century, to the light and leader of Prussia and Germany, indeed of all Europe, Frederick the Great.
Frederick William IV, at the very beginning of his reign, declared in a most solemn voice what path he would follow:
He declared that he would keep peace in his own lifetime, unless he were provoked to war;
but that he would wage war, trusting in the love and valor of his people and in that common ardor of all by which his father had conquered.
He did not threaten war in order to keep peace;
He kept peace, because he declared that he preferred it, yet he did not fear war, for which Prussia in peace itself is never unprepared.
Thus, by acting neither arrogantly nor timidly, the dangers that were feared a year ago were overcome, and security was restored.

Meanwhile, although he may not wish all the forces of the state to be turned to military service, he provides excellently for the military, and if anything seems to require correction in this outstanding and almost completely perfect military establishment, which his father instituted, he diligently strives to correct it.
But in the domestic affairs of the republic, what things are to be done in our age and indeed in this kingdom, it is both difficult to perceive, and not within my duty or ability to set forth;

except that some things, which are not derived from the inner and business-like knowledge of civil affairs but are of common and popular judgment, it will be permissible to pour forth as it were in a medley.

For since almost all nations have been raised to that height, that they are not led like herds of beings destitute of reason, as in the age of Saturn according to Plato's opinion they were led by the gods, but the people with those who hold the helm of government, through their ambassadors, either deliberate or decide about the most important matters:

It was understood in this republic as well, which increases the strength of arms by the powers of the mind and the vigor of spirits, that citizens must be roused, so that they may apply their minds to public affairs, lest this kingdom be conquered by others in the excellence of its institutions and the vigor of its people and civic skill, and lest the minds of the citizens grow weak and be dulled, and, oppressed by sleep and inactivity, they should abandon the state in times of danger.
At the same time, however, the full and undivided force of imperial power must be retained, and tranquility must be retained, which more agitated minds easily disturb.
How difficult it is to reconcile these with each other, there is no need to explain.
Whoever reconciles them will rightly deserve that splendid praise which Tacitus attributes to the Emperor Nerva, because he united things formerly incompatible: imperial power and liberty.
But that this very purpose belongs to the wisest King, it will be enough to have indicated in a word.

In this very difficult matter, the prince will make the most progress if nature has so formed him that he attracts the interests of men by his kindness and affability, and does not fear to humble himself and to mingle with the people;
which he can do without any loss of dignity, he who is placed so far above all that no one dares to compare himself with him:
Charm and wit will also please, provided that he does not hurt with witty remarks, which are easily forgiven in a private person, but never in a prince.
He will remove fear from the good, having removed spies and informers;

He will not even inflict punishments on the wicked himself, but he will leave any charges whatsoever to be judged by whole and undaunted judges according to the laws, which should be common and fair to all;

By his uprightness and prudence he will bring it about that everyone is convinced that he both wishes to consult the interests and safety of the citizens, and that he understands very well what is beneficial, what is harmful, and by what means the former are obtained and the latter avoided.
He will not wish to favor any one order, to summon this one alone to counsel, and to disregard the rest.

When this happens, envy will be stirred up against that order to which the prerogative has been given, even if this very thing imposes no burden on those who are placed after, and the harmony of the republic will be dissolved.
To the people, to use Solon's words, it will give as much as suffices, and it will take care that the powerful and wealthy have nothing unjust.

He will no more provide for the treasury and the public purse than for the private property of his subjects, because he who rules over the poor is not himself rich, and a good prince has only as much as everyone has;
He will foster the cultivation of fields, crafts, and commerce;
He will reduce taxes and tributes as far as the necessities of the state allow, and will so arrange them that they themselves and their collection are as little burdensome as possible.
He will show generosity not in things that quickly perish, but in those that may be a lasting ornament to the state and bring enduring benefits.

He will not think that only those are faithful to him who praise whatever he himself has said and done, but he will add confidence to those who, with an upright and constant mind and relying on the consciousness of a best intention and duty, profess candidly and modestly what has seemed right to them.

He will restrain prosecutions for treason as much as can be done without public harm, being more a despiser than an avenger of slander and slight injury, not delighting in punishments but in the love of citizens.
He will command himself as well as the citizens, and while he does not want them to be ruled by passions, he himself will not be ruled by them.
Thus he will be true and sincere, so that his word will be more certain than the oath of others.
With all these things set before you, will any of you demand, my hearers, that I explain at length how the character of our most merciful King responds to them?
Of course, if I were speaking before those who did not know him, someone might say that I must enumerate and describe each of his virtues;

But you, just as you recognize the king's face in a painted picture, even if his name is not written underneath, so in the things I have set forth, you will recognize, not indeed all the excellent gifts of Frederick William, which it would be long to pursue, nor his perfect image, but nevertheless certain features as if sketched in outline.
I have not yet touched upon the things, colleagues and fellow soldiers, which pertain especially to us.

For since from the character of Frederick William IV a most beautiful omen had long since been taken of the future most flourishing flower of arts and letters, which nevertheless had been so nourished by Frederick William III that it seemed that one should be satisfied if they suffered no loss;
The most merciful king now already seems to have surpassed even the highest hope:

He showed how favorable he was to good studies not only at the very beginning of his reign, when he received most graciously the embassies sent by the first colleges of letters and arts, and, what is far most pleasing to those who receive benefits, even without waiting until he was asked, he most lavishly increased the revenues of this very university, but he also summoned here the most distinguished ornaments of Germany, with annual salaries liberally established, not only so that each one might practice and teach his own art among us, but also so that he himself might enjoy their presence.

For he loves learned men for the sake of learning, but he loves literature and the arts not because they offer some advantage or utility, whatever it may be, to a ruler, but so that, as their most skilled and most refined judge, he may honor them for the excellence inherent in them, that is, for the true and the beautiful.
But the good is not separated from these, since it flows from the same divine source as the true and the beautiful, which together contain these three best things, inseparable.

But in human affairs, however, not entirely indeed but to some extent, they are seen as separated in such a way that science seeks the true, art strives to produce the beautiful, and the good is set as the goal for the state and for the institutions of public and private life founded by divine will.

But science, on which alone I will now dwell, is concerned partly with the knowledge of pure concepts, which we call philosophy, partly with mathematics demonstrating quantity, partly with the observation and description of natural things and laws, and partly with the history of the human race and of all those things which human reason has devised and established—of states, customs, and institutions both sacred and profane, of languages, literatures, and arts—which must be set forth.

And from these parts of knowledge, those disciplines also either depend on or are mixed with them, which are found joined together in three particular bodies of the universities according to ancient custom.

And since knowledge, which indeed is true knowledge, cannot be contrary to knowledge, because truth cannot be contrary to truth, that is, to itself, and false, all those parts of cognition necessarily agree among themselves.
They are indeed different:
but just as in the natural universe each star occupies its own place, and the world is held together and moved by the harmony of all;
so all disciplines, as it were so many lights and stars of the human mind, in this rational and literary universe of men, are joined together and harmonious with one another.
The common end of all is truth, because all are occupied in knowledge, not utility, not pleasure;
Nevertheless, they also have utility, just as they have pleasure.
But in our age many people so basely and servilely distort the force and purpose of knowledge that they think it should be directed solely to that which is connected with it as useful.

If we obey these, we must fear that the highest usefulness of knowledge and literature may perish, because those who judge the dignity of all things by usefulness are not wont to perceive what the greatest and purest uses are, placing, with dull judgment, usefulness chiefly in bread and money and the comforts and pleasures of life, just as those who are pleasure-loving do not pursue the purest pleasures of the mind, but luxurious and lustful ones.
But I call that the greatest utility which is most closely connected with the end that is set before the human race.
But since the end of each thing is placed in its notion, I think that humanity is the end of the human race:
not because I deny that mortals ought to take pains to become like God, nor because I deny that each one was born for his country and state, not for himself alone and his parents;

But I think that both are comprehended by humanity itself, since it is true that man was created in the image of God and that man's reason proceeded from the divine, and by his nature, as Aristotle teaches, man is a civil animal.
Therefore, for humanity, men are to be educated and instructed;
which alone is liberal and perfect education.

But if men are shaped for anything else whatsoever, education is either restricted to the necessities of life, that is, of the body, or, neglecting the highest end, is directed toward something fortuitous.
Suppose, as someone used to say, that men should be educated in such a way that each one corresponds as much as possible to the form of the state in which he was born;

The standard will be unstable and harmful to humanity, because among the same nations different forms of government prevail, and the human race cannot be brought to a better condition unless public institutions are corrected under the guidance of reason, in proportion as the minds of citizens have become more cultivated.
But education cultivates the minds and reason.

Would not indeed one wonder who would want knowledge (for in this is contained almost the whole instruction, and for this reason I have begun this discussion), who would want knowledge, I say, and what follows from it, the truth, to be one thing in a popular government, another in the rule of the best, another among peoples who are ruled by kings?
On the contrary, to the state, whatever its form may be, he will rightly adapt and accommodate himself whose mind has been properly cultivated to humanity.
What shall I say about the education that must be arranged differently for the different orders of citizens?

For the rustic and urban common people are imbued only with the first elements of letters and the precepts of morals and the rudiments of sacred doctrine, so that they become partakers of humanity only insofar as it is permitted to those whom poverty and labor do not leave leisure:
From this it is understood that these too are educated, although imperfectly, with the same end as the rest:

Indeed, so far is it from being the case that an education separated from the rest of mankind and from humanity suits the nobles, that if they are trained with a special discipline, they seem to be educated more for pride and a certain empty elegance and for perpetuating certain fictions of opinions, than for virtue and wisdom.
It is rather fitting for them to exercise and shape body and mind most diligently of all with any good arts, lest they be noble only in name.
Finally, according as each person is destined for the handling of a certain business, different things are certainly to be learned by different people;

but all are to be formed, as far as possible, in common for humanity, and the higher the rank in which each one was born and the higher things he aims at, the more intense effort he ought to give, so that he may unite humane learning with the business skill and cleverness, which is altogether necessary.

There are certainly, there are excellent goods of the mind, removed from all business affairs, which if partly retained and partly increased, the human race progresses, if they are abolished or diminished, it rushes into worse:
Among these, besides piety and good morals, I count poetry and the other elegant arts, and the liberal cultivation of the mind joined with freedom of spirit.
This one is not enslaved to any part of science, but is common to all letters;
But some disciplines are more than others referred to common use.

Therefore those who judge the dignity of knowledge from this alone slander one or another discipline, of which, like that Strepsiades of Aristophanes, a truly rustic man and unskilled in the fine arts, they see no use for the public or for procuring a livelihood.
And indeed in our age, two disciplines especially, which seem to contribute much to culture, have the most bitter detractors and adversaries: philosophy and the study of antiquity.
Certain revived Anytuses and Meletuses cry out against the mother of all learning, shouting that she is hostile to religion and hostile to the state;

To me, the reason of the human mind, which philosophy explains, does not seem able to conflict either with religion or with the state, but rather to purify the former from superstition and the latter from the perversity of its institutions.
Let philosophers err a little:
Have the lawgivers and the teachers of sacred discipline erred in nothing?
I know that what we have recently heard, not as it seemed to Plato, a pagan and impious man, that these our states can be instructed from the precepts of philosophy:

But philosophy gradually educates and enlightens minds, and while it enlightens them, it gradually corrects laws and institutions, not those that pertain to fields and rivers and forests, but those by which the highest principles of the human race are contained.
We would still be burning innocent little old women, if the most savage and stupid laws had not been repealed at philosophy's urging.

How much more humane, then, is Cicero, formed by experience of affairs much more than by the subtlety of the schools, and trained in the dust and wrestling-ground of the greatest of all states, who calls that philosophy innate in the human race, which those devoted to wisdom strive to perfect, the guide of life, the seeker-out and expeller of vices, and says that it gave birth to cities and was the inventor of laws, the teacher of morals and of discipline.
And so our Prussia rightly attracted and cherished the greatest philosophers from Leibniz down to those whom the present age has produced.
Now I do not wish to discuss the literature of antiquity at greater length, lest I seem to be boasting about my own studies.

I would have them remember this above all, those who desire that the tender minds of boys and young men be nourished in schools chiefly by other subjects and technical ones: that it is not only a matter of future theologians and jurists sipping just so much from Greek and Latin literature as is most necessary for a moderate acquaintance with the sources of their discipline; nor that future physicians should learn the vocabulary of their art; but that all who are about to approach any branch of learning should enjoy to the full that most abundant inheritance which the most cultivated earlier generations left to succeeding ages, and that they should be moulded by the best models, by which almost all who have become famous in letters were formed, by which Frederick the Great himself, though he had been trained chiefly in French literature, wished the pupils of the gymnasia to be instructed, not thinking that those studies could be compensated by other arts or by the use of modern languages and books.

I would wish that those who fear harm to the Christian faith from ancient literature remember that the Emperor Julian forbade Christians to open schools of rhetoric and letters, in order that they might become more uncultivated, and that he was reproached for this by Gregory, a most holy man, because he had begrudged Christians those goods which were common to all men.

But if literature will seem to be held in high regard only insofar as it appears to serve the common utilities and conveniences of life, and not to the nourishment of the mind's lights, then certainly philosophy and the study of antiquity are to be despised, and along with these a great part of the rest of history, and I know not whether also some part of the physical and mathematical disciplines will be.
Thus indeed the usefulness of knowledge, which I have mentioned, will perish, and at the same time the freedom of the mind, which those cannot retain who refer everything to gain and profit.
Indeed, it is to be feared that the freedom of the republic also may be endangered, if citizens exclusively seek and pursue that which I have called useful.
For then, the more richly one will feed them, the more willingly they will accept each as master, and they will rest in a peaceful servitude.

But noble citizens, taught to look at something greater than profit and the pleasures of life, devote not only all their goods but life itself for the fatherland, for liberty, and for the legitimate prince.
By this art Prussia grew;
these counsels pleased the earlier kings.
But what of Frederick William the Fourth?
He provides for the resources of the citizens;
With the most wholesome institutions, having called the envoys of the people into counsel, it strives to bring about whatever seems to conduce to the prosperity not of individuals but of all.

But it perceives with deep mind that the safety of the republic is placed not in the mere comforts of life, but that those are to be blessed with those highest goods of the soul whom providence has entrusted to its care.

Indeed, to return at last to the point from which I seem to have digressed, our most gracious Lord is so constituted by his own nature that he is filled, as it were, with a divine inspiration by the love of truth and beauty, and he loves literature and the arts not for the sake of some base advantage but for their own sake; and if he seeks any utility from them, he regards especially that liberal and most excellent one which I have tried to explain.
I have finished what I had proposed to say, listeners, about to describe the most generous character of Frederick William.

And since the minds of subjects are wont to be assimilated to the mind of the prince, I do not fear that in this most flourishing kingdom those counsels and wills which are unworthy of free men will ever prevail.

And you will give your effort especially, dearest fellow soldiers, whom, while the most blessed Father of the Fatherland is still alive, your parents raised in the most pleasant hope of liberty and security, which Frederick William IV makes firm; you, I say, will give effort, so that you may zealously emulate the liberal character of the wisest king, as much as a private person can emulate a prince.
This also includes that you should show to the King, who governs his people with a liberal rule, both now and in the future, a liberal obedience in your duties.
For he does not demand servile obedience.
The time has passed when you were to be warned and dissuaded, lest you be drawn into that audacity, for which the clemency of Frederick William the Fourth recently granted pardon to the condemned;
You must be urged to that which I said at the beginning of my speech is very easy, namely, to love him by whom we are loved.
Although there is no need for this exhortation, nevertheless I have added it, to indulge my mind and my love.
We all understand our blessings;
we must strive that we may seem worthy of their use.

Let us, the elders, joyfully enter this new age of Prussia that is rising, because it has fallen to our lot to see an age than which none could have been founded more happily for ripening the fruits that an earlier generation sowed.
You younger ones, strong with fresher powers, gird yourselves so that you may follow the ardor of Frederick William IV and respond to his expectation.

Finally, whatever great and excellent thing is being undertaken here, may God, without whom nothing can be brought to lasting completion, support it, and may He preserve for him the spirit which He gave, and may He, to whose safety the prayers of all are directed, keep him safe and unharmed for the public welfare, together with his most august Queen, through the longest span of time.
I have spoken.

div.head: XXIX. Oratio nataliciis Friderici Guilelmi IV. celebrandis d. XV. m. Octobris a. MDCCCXXXXII. habita.
On love of fatherland and prince

p.s: Although I perceive that this duty, which I undertake every year on behalf of all of you, listeners, of speaking at the most sacred solemnities dedicated to the far best Prince, is most difficult, nevertheless it is to me both honorable and also pleasant and delightful.

For although it may seem tedious to dwell on the same subject on the same day every year, and it may seem flattering to praise the same prince, however worthy, with lavish praise, whether with the same repeated encomiums or with newly devised ones, on a fixed day as if by command:

This consideration removes these scruples, because hardly anyone expects or demands that today we should discuss nothing but the praises of the King, but rather, provided the orator tries to satisfy both his own and your devotion, something is remitted from the burden's magnitude, and it is permitted to treat some particular subject, certainly such that it is not so alien to the sanctity and celebration of this day, so that it can neither be referred to the Prince's person, to the Prince's love and praise, nor be considered in some measure adapted to your minds, who have come together to revere the King.

And so, when I reflected with myself that, after I had spoken at greater length last year about the virtues of the most beloved king, with deliberate effort, no one would hold this against me as a fault, if, as I have often done in the birthday celebrations of the blessed father of the fatherland, not unwillingly on your part, I should choose for the sake of variety a subject of that kind, not one which I would explain and complete and perfect with philosophical subtlety, but one in which I might rather wander somewhat more freely in an oratorical manner:
I have proposed to myself to undertake an inquiry concerning the very love of country and of the prince, which you will grant is more fitting and suitable to these solemnities than any other.
For, to begin with this point on which all agree, we all love the most kind King, and for the sake of publicly testifying this love we have gathered in this place.
We also greatly esteem the King for his virtues, and we revere him for his majesty, but love and affection are stronger than judgment and reverence.
And indeed not only those whom he has benefited pursue the King with this love, but he is dear to all citizens, even those who have not seen him, who have only heard of him by report:
Finally, the love of a prince, as of a fatherland, is something greater, which far exceeds the measure of private advantage and the feeling of a grateful mind.
There is a certain piety, which, if it were permissible for Christians to compare any mortal with God Almighty, you would say should be compared with the piety that is owed to His divinity.

But the loyalty with which the king is loved, as it seems to me, does not flow from the divine authority of the kingdom; for although any rule can be regarded as having come from God, yet God and a prince differ by an immense interval:
so I do not hesitate to call it most closely related to that loyalty with which each person honors his own parents.

When the Romans understood this, they publicly and by decree honored good emperors, and sometimes even bad ones through vile flattery, with the title of Father of the Fatherland, which has a greater feeling of affection than the word parent;
The Germans do not confer this name on their princes as a formal title, but they grant it spontaneously from the feeling and will of their hearts:
And again, those who obey a king are considered to be free citizens of the state and consequently of the prince.

Therefore Frederick the Great, whom I do not hesitate to name as the principal authority for the public and domestic discipline of our kings, says that a well-governed kingdom ought to be like a family, whose father is the prince, and the citizens truly free:
For he says citizens, not subjects, as many kings prefer to hear:
and that good and bad things are common among them;
for neither can the prince rejoice in happiness, where the people labors in misery.
And from this, in my judgment at least, it is concluded that the love of a prince cannot be separated from love of one's country:
For because he is the father of his country, therefore those who love rightly love him.
But what can be more delightful than to speak at once about one's country and about the prince, and about the most intimate union of the love with which we cherish both the one and the other?
Since this subject is especially suited to the celebration of this day, it can now be understood that I have not without reason called this office, which I have undertaken today, a pleasant one.

Yet it will not be possible for me to enjoy this pleasure completely, unless the breeze of your kindness fills the sails of my speech, and the indulgence of my audience responds to the weakness of my powers, of which I am fully aware, which I would beg from you more earnestly, had I not often experienced it before.
Therefore, relying on this, even now, whatever I am about to say, I will say with confidence.

But it seems to me, who am about to say something about the fatherland, hardly necessary to warn, although everyone is especially accustomed to the place where he was born and brought up, and most gladly rests in the memory of those things which there surrounded his infancy and boyhood, yet that the fatherland cannot be contained within the narrow boundaries of that place;

Indeed, although each person's fatherland is connected with a certain region, nevertheless it is not constituted by this surface, these fields, these mountains and forests, rivers and lakes, these houses and beams, and this heap of stones, those mute and inanimate things, which, as Tacitus says, are liable to fall and be rebuilt indiscriminately, but rather by this society of men, in which we were born, individual and in a way eternal, whether one prefers to call it a nation or a republic.

That this fellowship is not, as it were, bound to the soil, but can be transferred from one place to another and extended and enlarged, the Greeks especially, burning with the greatest love of their fatherland, both determined and proved by examples:

And in our age too, who would deny that true Germany is not a certain definite land, which geographers call by this name, but that it is that [land] in which the society of the German nation has been established and flourishes, [namely] Prussia and the fatherland of the Prussians, not these provinces alone, which are either upper...
They may have been included under this name even earlier, but this entire community of nations, which through the virtue and auspices of our kings has coalesced into one very strong body;

Finally, who would not say that if any people, driven from their own seats, has established its republic in a foreign land, only the soil has been changed, but the fatherland has been transferred rather than lost?
Therefore we measure the boundaries of the fatherland by the boundaries of the people.

The language of the people and its literature, customs and habits, common institutions both private and public, which are strengthened by education and laws, finally the memory of ancestors and the glory of distinguished deeds, which is propagated from them to posterity—these seem to me to be, as it were, the strongest bonds of the fatherland.
And indeed we rejoice that very many lands of Prussia are certainly included in all these things;
But no kingdom of the whole world, nor any state, has more famous examples of ancestors:

And although indeed the royal stock itself has exhibited these things, I cannot but mention in a word that this, which is placed in the memory of former times, would by no means have been enjoyed by Prussia as a most effective bond, unless the greatness of our princes had stood out so much.
One happiness did not fall to this state, which is placed in the communion of religions:

For religion, especially the Christian religion, by which mortals ought to be joined in brotherly love, the greater and more destructive divisions it once stirred up and may also stir up in our age, if fanatical fury, to which some are inclined, is nourished zealously and skillfully;

So much happier does that state seem to me, in which either nearly all profess the same faith, or if any diversity of sects prevails, the one party bears with the other with gentle minds, and no sect is subject to a foreign master.

But if the boundaries of the fatherland, as I said, are to be determined by the boundaries of the people, and the fatherland consists not so much in the soil as in the fellowship of men and in the state, it must be conceded that many have a double fatherland, one narrower, the other wider, because that one people is divided into several nations, and, what seems to be greater, into several states, whether they are completely separate or joined by treaty, and either different in their form of government or, what is far better, equipped with the same institutions and laws.

For states that use very different laws will never coalesce well, but they will be suspicious of one another, both because the citizens of the one that is more freely constituted will distrust those to which the less free one is subject, and will judge, not without reason, that danger to their liberty threatens from them, and because the masters of this less free republic will fear that from that more free one the love of liberty may be disseminated and propagated among their own subjects and may make them more impatient of rule.
But for us Prussians, to whom, as to the other Germans, a twofold fatherland has been given, as it were, by divine providence, he would be peevish who should think that we ought to grieve;

Rather must the magnanimity of our kings, and especially of Frederick William IV, be proclaimed, who, although the institutions of our republic differ somewhat from those of most Germans and seem to be less popular, nevertheless did not wish that they themselves should not be Germans, nor that their Prussians should not be Germans.

Therefore Frederick William III, not content that he had joined the federation by which the whole German name is held together, useful indeed as it seems especially against foreigners, established this more useful union of commerce and customs, by which certainly the greatest part of the Germans is now united.
But Frederick William the Fourth, our most beloved King, both in sad and in joyful circumstances declares, and in this very year has declared, that our common fatherland is Germany:

who, when the Hamburgers were afflicted by that pitiable calamity, was the first of all princes to declare that this common misfortune had befallen the Germans, which had to be repaired by us to the best of our ability;

And a little later, when he wished to honor with letters, by which the Germans are especially united among themselves, and with arts, he did not want the rest of Germany to be distinguished from Prussia in this matter.
And very recently, when he celebrated those truly magnificent Cologne festivities, he clearly indicated with his usual eloquence how much he valued the harmony of the Germans.
Finally, there is no land of Germany that receives Germans as its own, not as foreigners, more readily and more willingly than our Prussia.
Now indeed, we are not bound by a pact, as some used to say, to love this fatherland, both the broader and the narrower one.
For no one loves from a pact.
But just as the source of any love is the inner harmony of souls, so we love our fatherland because our character agrees with the nature of the whole people and state;

Moreover, this love is increased by the recollection of benefits owed to the fatherland, which has both educated us and protected us and has furnished us with all goods of mind and body, and daily furnishes us:

Hence it happens that the fatherland is loved more easily and more ardently, which has set before itself that which the princes of Prussia have set before themselves, namely, to enrich their citizens with any good things, both external and internal, as much as possible.
But by what things do we show that we are held by love of the fatherland?
By civic virtue, I think.
But in what does civic virtue consist?
In this, I think, that you be a good citizen.
But what is a good citizen?
Frederick the Great answers:

"A good citizen," he says, "is he who follows this immutable law, that he be as useful as possible to that society to which he is assigned." Therefore, he by whom we wish the fatherland to be loved must be a citizen and consequently free.
For he who is above the citizen will be a lover of domination, not of the fatherland;
he who is below the citizen does not have a fatherland.
Thus among the ancient nations in the eastern kingdoms ruled tyrannically, you would find no love of country, because in them there were no citizens, but only masters and slaves;

and in the middle age, as they call it, if you except free cities, it was not love of country that drove men to great deeds, but the impulse of religions and that fidelity toward masters which seems to have taken the place of love of country.
But what shall I say about liberty?
For whoever is not free is not even a part of the people, nor even a person, but a possessed thing;
And wittily an ancient author said:

“Fifteen free men are a people, as many slaves a household, as many prisoners a prison.” What wonder, therefore, that those who are imbued with genuine love of country are most devoted to liberty, and that civic virtue and love of liberty are considered almost the same thing?
This is proved by what Demosthenes says about the Athenians.

"For who among Greeks or barbarians," he says, "does not know that the Athenians could most easily and with much gratitude have obtained from the Thebans and from those who previously had power, the Lacedaemonians and the Persian king, that, having received whatever they wanted and with their own affairs retained, they would do what was ordered and allow another to rule over the Greeks?"
Indeed, that was not their ancestral custom, not tolerable, not implanted by nature:
For they were not then seeking an orator or a praetor, by whose service they might happily be slaves, but they thought that they should not even live, unless it were permitted to live with liberty:
For each one of them thought that he was born not only for his father and mother, but also for his fatherland:
But he who thinks that he was born only for his parents will await death that is destined by fate and comes of its own accord;
But he who also belongs to his country will want to die, lest he see it enslaved, and he will fear disgrace and insults more than death, which must be endured in an oppressed country." Thus he spoke.
Therefore, by the best use of liberty, not by serving best, is love of country maintained:

But since flattery and obsequiousness are no small part of servitude, that worst plague of the human race, the one who approves, praises, and extols whatever is done in his state is not to be considered a lover of his country, but rather the one who exposes the hidden evils of the state, chastises those that are open, attacks imprudence and perverse counsels, if it suffices, modestly and humbly, but if there is need, even sharply and severely.
By this art Demosthenes and Cicero earned the gratitude of their country.
By this art, among the ancients, comedy itself was useful to the state, which, because many in our age cannot bear it, told the truth by laughing most freely.

Indeed, some bitterness, although it is troublesome to those who have not yet become accustomed to freedom of speech, is preferable to indolent patience; and he who is content with that patience differs not much from the man whom that Solon, the wisest lawgiver, judged worthy of severe punishment—I mean the man who, in the discord and sedition of the people, was unwilling to take the side of either party, but withdrew alone and apart from the common evil of the state.

For here it cannot happen that he is held by love of country, since he lives for himself, not for the state, and is not moved by its advantages or disadvantages, but led by private advantage and, almost according to Epicurus' teaching, indulging in sluggish leisure and careless of the public safety, and if not a traitor to his country, certainly next to a traitor.

While I speak of the fatherland, not of the prince, hearers, nevertheless both the matter itself and this occasion and my own piety have impelled me, at the same time, to make mention both of the earlier kings of Prussia and of the magnanimous counsels of Frederick William IV:

Now I come to the point to which you perhaps expected even earlier that I would turn, namely to consider what relation exists between fatherland and prince, between love of fatherland and love of prince.
This matter, before these two years, shortly after Frederick William IV had assumed the government, I remember that I touched upon in another solemn assembly.

But just as the Theban poet, most copious in the songs with which he celebrated the victors of the games, did not avoid treating the deeds of Hercules and Achilles and the Aeacidae at different times, yet in such a way that he would set forth differently about them in different places, so I hope that I will not now say exactly the same thing about the same subject.
We see that it has been asked whether love of one's country was peculiar to free states, in which, at least among the ancients, it especially stood out, or whether it also had a place in kingdoms.

Indeed, what we said a little earlier, that he who is above the citizen is a lover of domination, not of the fatherland, someone might twist this to mean that the fatherland cannot be dear to the prince himself, but that he alone is dear to himself, since, like Louis XIV, king of the Gauls, he himself alone seems to himself to be the state.

Therefore it is more valuable to mention, Athenians, that those who nevertheless were uniquely devoted to liberty and popular government established the most brilliant examples of love of country set forth by their ancient kings, from Erechtheus, who had sacrificed his daughter for his country, from Codrus, who, lest Athens should yield to the enemy, had offered himself to certain death.

And indeed, as long as the prince does not fail to know—what is certain that Frederick the Great did not fail to know, and that our most merciful lord does not fail to know—that he too is a citizen, who could be more inflamed with love of country than the head of the state, on whom especially the safety of the country depends?
But what shall we say about those who are subject to kings?
It is pleasing to recall what that same Frederick the Great decided about this matter.

When he discusses the love of one's country, after he has denied that there are no citizens in kingdoms, he says that well-constituted kingdoms, since their administration is wise and full of kindness, in his age come closer to the rule of a few than to tyranny, and that only laws rule in them:

Since the Greeks say that these [laws] rule even in a popular government, it can be understood, if indeed both statements are true, that well-constituted states, whatever their form may be, are equally just and fair.

But descending to particulars, Frederick says that all who are admitted into the councils, who are occupied in the administration of justice, who manage the revenues, taxes, and commerce, who undertake embassies, who command the armies, who provide for public security at home, and moreover who cast their votes in the affairs of individual provinces—all these, as many as they are, are participants in the supreme power in the kingdoms.

Therefore, the prince should not be a tyrant, who has no law except his own will (not to mention his lust), but he should be like the center of a circle, in which all lines from the circumference converge.

If there is any kingdom in Europe into which these things do not fit aptly, that is the Turkish empire, and one or another that has not yet learned to perfectly combine the interests of private individuals with the interests of those in power, being ignorant of its true advantage.
He adds, what I mentioned a little before from that source, that a well-governed kingdom is like a family, and that goods are common to rulers and parents alike.

That this community and concord, when it has been well cemented, produces a feeling of gratitude, so that good citizens come to be so united with the state that they cannot separate themselves from it;
For if they are separated, they will lose everything and gain nothing.
After these points have been excellently discussed by that great man, what I said in general about love of country fits in well:
namely, in kingdoms too love of country will have a place, if the kingdom is at the same time a state, and in this state there is liberty.

But nevertheless, the love of country is one thing in a popular and aristocratic government, another in a monarchy, inasmuch as the safety of the monarchy and of the governed nation can hardly be separated from the safety of the prince, and when the princely house is overthrown, the state of the republic rarely remains untouched, and in a monarchy the love of country itself is transferred entirely to the person of the prince as the father of his children.

For it is so far from being the case that liberty diminishes and breaks the love of the prince, that a prince cannot be loved except by free men, while by slaves he may rather be feared; and that the more freely a kingdom has been established, the more sincerely and vehemently the prince is wont to be loved, especially where, as in our age in Britain, power has been confirmed by long duration of time, and has not been acquired only recently, nor against the will of a great multitude of citizens; and especially where the prince himself has established liberty of his own accord, and has not waited until it was extorted by force or by the untimely opportunity of adverse circumstances.

Therefore, since love of country and love of the prince admirably conspire, the latter will be approved by almost the same means as the former, that is, not by illiberal servitude, but by the virtue of a good citizen, such as we have indicated above, and by the proper use of liberty, which Frederick William IV does not begrudge us, but rather promotes and increases.
But it would be a long story to speak about this matter;
Now I will set forth another thing, which I deliberately omitted above, where I spoke about the fatherland and love of the fatherland.

For since there are not a few kingdoms composed of several nations, and these differing in language and customs, and since moreover the provinces of the same kingdom, even if the characters of their inhabitants do not differ so much that they seem to be of different stocks, nevertheless because they had been completely separated for a long time, are accustomed to be more or less estranged from one another, and their inhabitants to indulge in a certain degenerate love of country, which is love of one's province;
Those who preside over such states, or who devote their efforts to the end that that diversity of nations and provinces may be removed:

that which will then especially be brought about, when the whole force of the empire shall be placed in the city, the seat of the kingdom, just as the ancients comprehended the whole state in one city, Attica in Athens, Laconia in Sparta, Arcadia in Megalopolis, and Rome, mistress of the world, that immense Roman state:

Or they tear those nations, which are subject to one ruler, into different kingdoms, and, wonderfully delighted with these distinctions of provinces, they strive to preserve and increase these very things.
With what difficulties each of the two methods is hindered, with what disadvantages it labors, it is not my task now to explain:

That is clear: different nations, and even provinces that are too much alienated from one another, cannot be firmly united into one republic, unless they understand that their common interests are contained in this union, and that as soon as this alliance is dissolved, the safety of each individual will be endangered, and the parts, now weak, will fall as prey to a more powerful enemy.

But this fellowship, which rests solely on utility, will be greatly strengthened by the love of the prince, who, as it were, from these elements of the whole kingdom, will have bound and united all parts to himself by the magnitude of his benefits.
What man among you, listeners, is there who does not see, even without being warned, why these things are now mentioned by me?

Who does not see that, as formerly by the kindness and clemency of Frederick William III, so now by that of Frederick William IV, the nations which obey the Prussian rule, though separated not only by language and customs but also by the chances of fortune and by their desires and expectations, are united, as far as possible, into one body, and that they, if not in all things, yet certainly in love for their excellent King, conspire with one unanimous feeling?
Therefore, by the gift of this harmony, which is placed in the love of the dearest Prince, I judge that Prussia is strong and happy:
strong not only in favorable circumstances, but also in adverse ones, if they should ever happen, and not only against external enemies, but also against internal dissensions;

Let him be called happy not for abundance of wealth and luxury, but for the virtue of his citizens, who, devoted to their fatherland and to the Prince, would sooner suffer anything than violate their faith, and let all recognize the King's excellent will joined with wisdom.
For the King wishes to be the author of evil to no one, but the author of all good things to everyone;
Nor do I fear that anyone may think I am courting favor with flattery, if I have compared his most gentle disposition, leniency, and courtesy with Titus.
And indeed no part of the state is lacking to him, but he embraces all with equal care, as befits one who holds the helm of the whole empire;

yet he so favors literature and the arts and all things that pertain to the cultivation of minds, that unless you knew how much effort he devotes to equipping the military, to establishing and amending law, to agriculture, to aiding trades and commerce, you would have been ready to believe that he spends his whole time in liberal studies.
But indeed, he cannot rightly favor literature who thinks that it should be governed so that it serves to strengthen domination or to defend certain opinions.
Literature cannot flourish unless it is free.
Therefore, a prince who desires that their flower increase will hold nothing more important or more ancient than to grant that you may think what you wish and say what you think:
That our most merciful Lord wishes this in general is established by the most certain documents:
But he will rather despise than love those who twist their face to his nod.
For when all things become worthless through servitude, then nothing is more abject than letters that serve.

But genuine science, which seeks universal, necessary, and immutable notions, which depends on itself alone, not on things, plans, or chance events, which has its end placed in itself, and finally which, being impatient of any authority whatsoever, whether papal, princely, or academic, pursues straight ahead the course that reason demonstrates and prescribes, and does not anxiously look around to see what pleases each of the bystanders.
It is of the greatest interest to us that the rulers of states should be persuaded that this is the nature and character of science.
But Frederick William IV, a king of the most generous disposition, is persuaded of this.

Will anyone therefore think, listeners, that in a state in which literature and especially these literary universities had retained their freedom at that time, when the most unjust tyranny of a very powerful and almost omnipotent man, because it feared danger to itself from the free movement of minds, was most hostile to literature and especially to this discipline of universities?

In that subsequent age, when because of some rash undertakings of young men the German universities had been brought into such suspicion that we seemed to need to be publicly restrained and guarded by new laws and institutions,

In that republic now, with Frederick William IV holding the reins of government, will letters and schools of letters suffer any loss of liberty, as long as they themselves vigorously defend their own affairs?
By Hercules, no one will think this.

Rather let us give thanks to the most kind Father of the Fatherland, because he supports literature not only by paying salaries, by providing equipment, by supplying expense of every kind, and by conferring other benefits, but also grants to those who teach and those who learn that freedom which the wisest men agree is the soul and vital force of literature, and have agreed in every age;
Let us give thanks to the Father of the Fatherland, because he governs the whole commonwealth in the same manner with liberal, good, and wise institutions:

Let us give thanks to God, the Best and Greatest, because He so shaped the mind of Frederick William that there is no one who does not understand that a better king could not have been desired by the citizens nor given by the supreme deity.

Finally, we send most holy prayers to the supreme deity, that he may look after the welfare of Frederick William and aid his counsels, and preserve him together with his most august consort the Queen and the entire august house for the commonwealth, whose flower and happiness cannot be separated from the safety of the royal family, and that he may strengthen and confirm the forces of the empire and the virtue and concord of the citizens.

div.head: XXX. Oratio nataliciis Friderici Guilelmi IV. celebrandis d. XV. m. Octobris a. MDCCCXXXXIII. habita.

An inquiry into how far princes can deserve well of letters and especially what the judgments of a prince regarding individual branches of letters can or cannot contribute to the flourishing of scholarship. This question is illustrated by the example of Frederick the Great's essay on German literature

p.s: I think that none of you, most distinguished and most honored auditors of all ranks, judges that there is nothing more fitting, nothing more proper, than the giving of thanks, which the whole republic, and especially this our literary university, which has appointed me as its speaker, together with the other schools of the liberal arts in this kingdom, owes to the most gracious Prince, for those solemn rites which are consecrated to the observance of the memory of that day on which the supreme deity willed that Frederick William should be born into the hope of succession, so that the safety and dignity of this empire and the welfare and opportunities of the citizens might be provided for.

When I consider that two main paths can be taken to carry out this duty, one being that whatever the King has done excellently, whether from the time he took up the government or in this one year that has flowed from the most recent solemnities, should be enumerated one by one and weighed, and how much good has flowed from this into any parts of the state should be explained with deliberate effort;

The other, so that in some chosen singular argument, which may not be alien from the person of the King or from this most noble royal stock, yet pertains especially to the condition of letters, as if reflected in a mirror, a certain part of that virtue by which the best King excels may be represented:

Indeed, I feel that I am scarcely, and not even scarcely, equal to undertaking this first path, and I do not think that I will seem to you, and especially to my most learned colleagues, who both know my weakness and are themselves much more prudent than I, to be sufficiently suited to undertaking so great a province, I say, who have constantly held to that way of life which has hidden me far away from public affairs and from the contemplation of present things in the shade of the school and the seclusion of letters.

But as for that one, which I mentioned in the second place, although I may not be equal to it, yet perhaps I shall seem to be able to claim it for myself with some right, because it is closer to scholastic learning than to the handling of civil and public affairs.

What about the fact that, if something else and greater were demanded or expected from this orator, you would see neither me nor anyone else from that family of bookworms, in which I am counted, placed on this platform, but rather someone from the jurists, who, as common opinion holds, are usually especially skilled in public affairs, or at least a philosopher or a professor of political doctrine?

There is present a distinguished man, the Rector of this university, who is about to lay down the office he has most successfully administered, and who, having once been eminently active in public life, and being so renowned for his knowledge of events from the remotest antiquity down to the present, for his subtlety and fairness of judgment, for his elegance of mind, and finally for his eloquence and freedom of speech, that no one could sustain that more important and weighty office with greater success than he.

Therefore I think, listeners, that the fact that I have been appointed almost alone from this most distinguished college of professors to speak on behalf of all has this force, that it is permitted to propose here something of such a kind as I indicated a little earlier, yet in such a way that it must be explained so that that whole argument, whatever it is, is brought back to the sense of gratitude owed to our most merciful Lord, and that that sense, like the soul the body, permeates what we say.

In this system, besides eloquent proclamations, there is also a certain silent praise, indeed more modest and more inward and more sincere than that which may boast many bombastic phrases of high-sounding words.

I will speak today, therefore, about literature, yet not about literature in general, but insofar as princes can deserve well of it; and I will not even treat this subject fully, but after first setting forth one or two more general observations, I will confine myself thereafter to the question of what the judgments of a prince concerning the individual branches of learning can or cannot contribute to the flourishing of scholarship, and I will illustrate this by the great example of Frederick the Great, which seems to me to be all the more appropriate to use, inasmuch as Frederick William the Fourth—since, according to the ancient precept, like is not known except by like—recognizes more fully the genius of that hero, and desires it to be recognized also by his contemporaries and posterity, inasmuch as he has undertaken, with illustrious purpose and the utmost zeal, to complete the monuments worthy of both his name and that of his most blessed father, which had scarcely been begun.

But if I doubt that I will achieve this by setting forth these matters, that my speech may please and be approved, certainly I desire that you not miss my goodwill, and I want pardon to be sought and obtained from you both for the things I shall have said and for the things I shall have omitted.
What about the fact that even other things seem to me to need to be excused today?
I speak of the use of the Latin language, which rumor has reported to have already been abolished from our university, and, what is more important, the scarcity of academic citizens.
But him, if indeed there is need of an excuse, the law excuses; if anyone is released from it, this seems to be granted to the person, not to the matter.

But this solitude around us is not because piety has relaxed, but because our cohorts of comrades, which used to celebrate this most sacred assembly elsewhere, are detained far from the city by legitimate but ill-timed holidays.

I take my beginning from that division, which I remember I explained more fully in the last speech, in which I praised Frederick William III, the most blessed Father of the Fatherland, while he was still alive, in an oration delivered before you.
At that time I distinguished what the prince could contribute to the flourishing of literature, and what he could not, even with the utmost care and diligence.
And those things that he could not [do] were of two kinds:
For these were either not at all within the prince's power, or [were] not [within it] under certain conditions.
The prince cannot bring it about that great minds are born, which nature brings forth of its own accord or [which are] a gift of the divine will;

And by a certain fatal order and a course of ages divinely described, just as peoples themselves, so in each people the arts and disciplines take their beginnings, increases, and again grow old with languor.
Indeed Frederick the Great, in that essay from which I shall quote more shortly, auguring future glory for German letters, hopes that when we shall have our Medicis, talents will flourish;
that Augustuses will bring it about that there will be Virgils;

Although Germany produces men equal to the most laborious investigations, both philosophers and other most ingenious men, and everything you might require, nothing is lacking except a Prometheus who would seize the heavenly fire with which to kindle them:

But rather, whenever literature and the arts flourished more joyfully, the same age, by a certain felicity of the times, brought forth both poets, learned men, and distinguished artists, who, since the way had already been prepared beforehand, might advance further, and leading men powerful in wealth and influence, who might favor literature and the arts;
Nor could you easily say which side was provoked by the other.

However it may be, no one will deny that, unless the character of the age itself inclines toward a more perfect state of the arts and sciences, this cannot be brought about even by the munificence of princes or by any rewards that may be proposed; and that, to use this example, in the seventeenth century German poets such as Goethe and Schiller later became would not have emerged, even if some Saxon duke had then cultivated poets as recently the noble house of the princes of Weimar cultivated them.

Now, to touch in a few words upon those letters which cannot be advanced under certain conditions of the state, I have once used the example of eloquence, which cannot be cultivated unless, with fear removed, you have given freedom of speech, and not only freedom, but also places and subjects in which eloquence can be shown;
Nor is the method of writing history different, in which we Germans especially are lacking.

But who does not understand that philosophy and those disciplines that are most closely related to it are not permitted, under priestly or pontifical domination, which they commonly call hierarchy, to know anything beyond the elementary training of boyhood?

As I consider these and similar things, since our most merciful King is an outstanding judge of all elegance and a great lover of arts and letters, and knows how to distinguish whatever is ingenious, beautiful, and magnificent from the commonplace and vulgar, and seeks out, invites, and draws to himself those who provide the best things, it seems to me especially desirable that a rich supply of talents should not fail him, so that he may assist them generously, and that the character of his own age and the condition of the state may give him the opportunity to promote any good arts with success, and that the outcome may correspond to his magnanimous plans and expectations.

For at this age, unless I am mistaken, almost all people are found to be devoted exclusively either to the utilities and conveniences of life, which, under the guidance of science itself, have recently been increased by so many inventions that anyone who had predicted them in earlier centuries would have seemed to be mad;
or they turn to examining the condition of public affairs not without desire and partisanship, toward which goal poetry itself is carried with no small impetus;

Or they begin to stir up controversies about those matters which seem to pertain to religion, and indeed to arouse or nourish certain disturbances connected with this matter, and to mix sacred things with public affairs:

From these inclinations of minds, just as a provident deity can draw forth great benefits, so how much danger threatens the liberal arts from this, or how much growth is about to come, I, who am not a soothsayer, do not care to divine.
But many things, without doubt, and indeed excellent ones, by which the liberal arts may be aided, depend in any state of the commonwealth on the will of the prince:
that he may bring to light the talents which have been born;

that he may preserve and increase the instruments and supports of learning handed down from our ancestors, give the people the opportunity of learning by establishing schools of every kind, and supply expenses not only most necessary but sufficient and generous;
so that he may show that he holds letters in high regard, and that he may honor men of letters with no less distinctions than those who discharge public offices;

that he may order and temper with wholesome and liberal laws and institutions both the whole literary enterprise and the schools, both lower and higher, and the associations destined for either transmitting or cultivating learning.
In order that these things may be brought about, much care, effort, and diligence must be applied.
But whatever was needed to be done for these things, the most blessed Father of the Fatherland provided and administered.

From him, Frederick William IV protects the province of deserving well of literature, received, so that, in accordance with his extraordinary goodness, he continually adds new honors to the former ones.
It is long to pursue these things;
nor does that seem necessary, especially since I have not now for the first time begun to speak about these matters.
Therefore I proceed to that which I have just declared I would especially dwell upon in explaining.

There is no one who does not know that Frederick the Great almost entirely despised the literature of the Germans, such as it appeared in his own age, or at least conceived a very moderate opinion of it;

And he, in a special little commentary, which he entitled 'On German Literature,' not only attempted to disclose the reasons why the Germans, although endowed with the best natural disposition, were hindered from equaling the other more learned nations in the cultivation of letters and the elegant arts, but also sought out remedies and gave advice by which it might be brought about that our fatherland's language and literature and all kinds of learning should be improved and the rough rust of minds should be rubbed off.
I am not the sort of person who would think myself able to judge more wisely than so great a man on matters of the highest importance.

Nevertheless, to confess what I think, as he says that even good Homer sometimes nods, so I think I will not have many adversaries when I have classified that little book, which I believe was poured out by Frederick extemporaneously, not composed with care and diligence, among the lighter works of the philosopher king, not particularly conspicuous for order of material or weight of thought.
When I say this, I by no means deny that excellent things are also contained in this treatise, and indeed prophetic words;
nor would it be of value to me to quote anything from it, if it seemed to be unworthy of our acquaintance.
And first, let me briefly explain what things seemed to Frederick the Great to have retarded the progress of the Germans in more elegant learning and to have been held as if in bonds;

While Italy was refined by the good arts, he says that Germany was agitated by theologians and torn into two factions, distinguished by fanatical impulse and by hatred and envy, each inflamed against the other:

Soon after, when in Gaul the plans once conceived by Francis I for restoring humane studies were renewed, and under King Louis XIV it was brought about that Paris no longer yielded to Rome and Florence, which had been illuminated by the Medici with the lights of arts and learning, Germany was afflicted and exhausted by the most disastrous devastation of the Thirty Years' War, by twenty armies, now victorious, now vanquished, one after another inflicting such depopulation, solitude, and vast desolation that farmers abandoned their fields and villages, inhabitants their towns, and all things lay deserted, uncultivated, and squalid.

And that Germany was not immediately revived by the Peace of Westphalia, but that it had to be defended at that time both against the Turks, who were filling everything with immense terror, and against the arms of the French, who had entered the German provinces in order to extend their own borders.

While Vienna, the capital of the empire, was being besieged, while villages, towns, and fortresses of the Palatinate were being destroyed by sword and fire, along with the very tombs of the princes, it was not possible for them to take pleasure in poetry there.

Therefore, the accidents of fortune and continuous wars, which would exhaust the resources and men of the fatherland, not a scarcity of talents, stood in the way of the Germans, so that they did not achieve what other nations achieved.
Those losses had to be repaired first by cultivating the fields, restoring buildings, propagating offspring, fostering the industry of artisans, and increasing trade.
By these means, wealth later grew, not without luxury.
At the same time, the love of literature was recalled.
Nevertheless, to use a Horatian word, traces of the countryside remain.

In order that these may be extinguished and that literature of every kind may be corrected and perfected, he gives many precepts in detail, both pertaining to the regulation of gymnasia and to the schools of universities.
From this discussion I will cull a few things, though not preserving exactly either the order of topics or the divisions which he himself used.
For the fact that the German style is neither clear nor exact, he attributes to the neglect of good studies.

But this indeed arose from the fact that, since the learned Germans seemed to cling to trifles and to a fastidious and stale erudition, many, in order to wash off the stain of that reputation, abandoned Greek and Latin letters, from whose most abundant springs they had drawn, by whose excellent examples the Italians, French, and British had been formed.
Thucydides and Xenophon must be handled, so that strength and grace may be won for one's words;
the vehemence of Demosthenes must be rendered;
Sallust, Julius Caesar, Tacitus, and M.
Antoninus should be read, so that a brief, sententious, and grave style may be formed;
He adds Aristotle's Poetics and Horace's Epistle to the Pisos, and one or two French books.
The classic authors of the ancients and the moderns should be translated into German, so that both our language may be refined and the knowledge of the best things may be spread more widely:
It is proper for learned men to use the vernacular language;
Since the leading writers among the Italians, Gauls, and English had done this, and their successors, their books were devoured by the people, and studies were spread throughout the whole nation.

But for us, from the controversies and disputes undertaken about religion, there has flowed an abundance of contentious men, who would discuss obscurely things that cannot be understood, defend and attack the same arguments, and mix insults with the sophists' fallacies.

He says that our first learned men, as among all peoples, were men who, by heaping one thing upon another, filled their memory, men of the study, destitute of judgment, Lipsiuses, Freinshemiuses, Gronoviuses, Graeviuses:
Some Gaul, as I think, from the cohort of friends could hardly have supplied their names, scarcely proper to Germany, to a most august patron about to write this little book:

These slow-moving restorers of some obscure phrases, which are found in old manuscripts, have indeed rendered useful service to some extent, yet not all industry and diligence ought to be consumed on such trifling matters and consequently of little importance.

But nevertheless, which is especially to be lamented, they gained the applause of all Europe, since they wrote in Latin, in order to boast of their Latinity and even to carry off the admiration of foreign scholars of the same stripe.
I pass over with what right that great man censured these scholars, whom without doubt he had little known:
but we owe him thanks, because he vindicated the dignity of ancient literature:
Unless perhaps this is rather an accusation than a vindication, because Frederick the Great defended them.
But let them disparage them, both those who disparage Frederick the Great and those who praise him, and try to drive them out;
driven out, they will always return, just as they returned in that age in which literature was reborn, and immortal and eternal they will survive the memory of obscure adversaries.

Now I turn to those matters which the most learned king proposes concerning the individual disciplines, partly criticizing the customary method of teaching them, partly describing the path which seems to him to be the best:
He nevertheless omits mathematics, because these alone are not divided into sects, because nothing can be added to their evidence, and one and the same method of teaching this obtains in all lands;
He omits theology with modest silence for certain reasons, which it is not necessary to mention.
But in the other disciplines, since only one method of teaching and learning can be correct and this must be followed, he wants a definite standard to be prescribed for each professor.
Therefore he directs his speech to the teachers of each discipline in turn, namely to the professors of philosophy, of medicine, of law, and of history.
For example, from the things that he discusses about the teaching of philosophy, I report a few opinions.
He does not expect from the philosopher that he should contribute anything to the forming and polishing of language.
This is the business of the poet and the orator.
The province of the philosopher is the refutation of errors, the exploration and discovery of truth.
He should not, as is commonly done, be wholly devoted and enslaved to some particular system of doctrines, which they call a system.

For students who will set out from the instruction of such a philosopher will be filled everywhere with precepts and opinions, and will have known only a small part of the doctrines devised by men, and not all the errors and absurd fancies.

He says that one must begin, when about to teach philosophy, with an exact definition of this discipline, and then the various systems from the most remote age must be explained in order of time and judged or refuted.
He adds examples taken from the opinions of the Stoics and Epicureans;
For example, if the Stoics say so.
