That the human soul is a particle of the divine breath, that it is the professor's duty to teach this, that this statement contains a contradiction, because if man were a particle of God, it would be necessary that man be endowed with infinite knowledge, and that if God inhabited men, it would come to pass that a British God would fight with a French God or a Spanish God, and that from that doctrine it would follow that any crimes of men whatsoever are committed by God.

Now after he has spoken about certain other ancient philosophers, he demands that the master of philosophy clearly expound the teachings of Galileo, and in explaining them not omit to rebuke the stupidity of the Roman clergy, who refuse to believe that the earth moves and rebel against the antipodes;
He says that one must speak about Copernicus, Tycho, whom he names late, about Descartes, Newton, Leibniz:
He brings forward his monads and pre-established harmony:
This is a story invented by a most ingenious man;
That which is to be demonstrated by the professor.
Spinoza, he says, the professor will refute without any trouble, in the same way as the Stoics;

But if that same man shall seem to deny the supreme deity, nothing will be easier for the teacher than to crush him to ashes, especially when our professor demonstrates the end of each thing, to which it is destined:
For the whole nature of things, from the smallest thing up to man, bears witness to the divinity.

To pass over other things, a professor who is endowed with common sense says that he will not forget the wise Locke, that one among metaphysicians who embraced sound reason, rejected the dreams of imaginations, followed experience as far as it could lead, and prudently stopped where it began to fail as a guide of the journey.
Finally, when it comes to morals, the professor will say a few words about Socrates, and will give due praise to M.
He will speak more fully about Antoninus, and will digress more widely in setting forth Cicero's work On Duties, the best of all works, as many as have been written and can be written on morals.
This is, in brief, the sum of the rules to which that great man wishes the schools of philosophers to be directed.

But if the hour were not pressing, and if I did not fear that, while I myself do not grow weary, I might tire your patience, I would have related these things more fully, and I would have added those things which in like manner he teaches to the remaining teachers.
Indeed, whoever has considered all these things will also admire in these matters the genius of the great prince, equipped and adorned with varied and manifold learning;

He will marvel that the king, amid his very greatest and most serious occupations, not only personally pursued literature, but placed part of his leisure in examining the method and manner by which literature was to be taught.
Yet in that discussion you may detect excellent judgments mixed with lighter ones:
And reverence due to the greatest man brought it about that I willingly passed over certain things which have been sufficiently and more than sufficiently reproached to him by critics.

Of course it could not happen that a man, however richly endowed with all the gifts of the mind, when he was unwilling to confine himself to general notions, but descended to the individual parts of nearly all disciplines, to which he could not devote anything but a rather superficial effort, should be less wise than those who dwell wholly in these individual parts.
And I think that Frederick the Great, in his wisdom, tacitly conceded this.

For although he did not hesitate, as a private citizen, to express his opinion on matters about which even men who excel in no force of talent nor abundance of learning have both been accustomed to judge from of old and are especially accustomed at the present time, nevertheless, as it is especially kingly to distrust oneself in many things and to listen to those who excel in each art, he by no means carried out what seemed to him regarding the teaching of letters.

He himself, indeed, when he advises that something be changed in the formation of German words, so that they become more pleasant and sonorous, says wittily that if the Emperor and the eight Electors were to pass laws on this matter in the solemn assemblies of the Empire, the zealous followers of Teutonic barbarism would receive these decrees with laughter and would shout out this:

"Caesar is not above the grammarians." But if Caesar is not above the grammarians, let him see by what right Caesar is above the philosophers, or above the rhetoricians, or above the authors of history.
The emperor appointed Quintilian as professor of eloquence;
the precepts of eloquence were established not by the emperor, but by Quintilian.

But how little is that which we see literature accomplish in those kingdoms, where certain fixed doctrines are to be taught by masters according to a certain method, and pupils are to be educated according to certain publicly approved compendia, and even the very manuscripts of the teachers' commentaries are subjected to the examination of censors?
What, to use a most brilliant example, would Kant have accomplished, if he had been forced to teach that philosophy according to the precepts of Frederick the Second, his master, however great?

Whence I seem rightly to infer that the judgments of leading men about the individual parts of literature, especially insofar as they pertain to the way and method of transmitting disciplines, can contribute not a little to bringing about the perfection of learning.
I do not deny that a state, which in its bosom cherishes and nourishes science, ought to establish laws by which the public education of youth is regulated;
but these laws, whatever they are:
for concerning these it is not my place to decide:

As long as there is caution that the highest matter not be corrupted by pernicious doctrines, the wise prince will no more force his own judgment about individual disciplines upon the teachers of the good arts.

But if the prince loves literature, if he loves it so much that he favors no part of it, that he is equally kind to all, and is persuaded that all [parts] by their own nature tend to the common prosperity of the human race, what can more favor the course of literature than this judgment of the prince?
Indeed, this has been and is no small good fortune of the Prussian state, that nearly all its princes have conceived this opinion about literature:

Frederick William IV, however, our most gracious Lord, both before he attained the highest power and afterwards, after he had assumed the government, testified his most ardent zeal for the good arts by such manifest proofs that from the very beginning no one doubted that from this king, as far as it lies with a prince, a new and truly golden age of letters was about to come forth.
What then do you think, listeners?
Would anyone wish that this king, rather than Frederick the Great, should impose unjust laws on the professors of universities, and command from his own will what and how they should teach?

Indeed, the most illustrious man, to whom the king entrusted the care of public education, declared most clearly and certainly that he was persuaded of this very thing which has now been set forth by me, when in a speech recently delivered at Bonn he explained that the king did not wish to use his own command and authority to bring about a new and better state of affairs, which he is about to introduce, nor to send mandates to his ministers about this matter, nor to make decrees, but only desired and earnestly wished that many talents and energies might be roused, which would act of their own accord.
This is surely the mark of a prince who values literature and loves it.
But there is an old saying, that no one can love what he does not know;
and that what one does not know is wont to be hateful to him.
Therefore those who are unskilled in the good arts are wont to be hostile to them, and the more cultivated a prince is himself, the more diligently he provides for literature.

God therefore granted this benefit to our fatherland, that He adorned Frederick William IV with such great gifts of intellect that he comprehended in his lofty mind the whole world of the finest arts.
But I would not want what I just said to be taken in such a way that only the one who knows science perfectly loves it;
But just as Plato thinks that no god philosophizes nor desires to become wise, because he is already wise, nor does anyone who is wise philosophize at all;

and again, those who are completely destitute of knowledge are least desirous of becoming wise, because ignorance has this worst feature, that he who is not good and intelligent thinks himself to be sufficiently equipped with virtue and knowledge:

Thus we judge that he loves learning, not the one who thinks himself to be filled with all wisdom, but the one who, like that Platonic Love, is in the middle between knowledge and ignorance and seems to himself to be so, and therefore philosophizes, that is, strives for wisdom.

He likewise understands that, just as no single person has ever been perfectly wise, and the wiser each person is, the more keenly he perceives how much there is that he does not know, so the human race has in no age reached such a summit of knowledge that one could already stop and nothing would need to be added to discoveries, but one must rest content in handing down those things that have been established before.
Indeed, the future is contained in the past, just as the tree is contained in the seed:
But seeds are entrusted to mother earth, so that from them the green growth may be drawn forth, not stored away like the dead.
That Frederick the Great, however, judged no differently than we do is sufficiently established.
He thought that by that path, which he himself had described, not prescribed, it could be brought about that a new order of the ages should be born for German letters.
And it was born of its own accord.

The greatest king had foreseen in his mind that the best times for the literature of the fatherland were approaching, times in which honor was to be established for our learning throughout nearly all of Europe, and, to use his own words, like Moses he was looking from afar at the promised land, yet he was not to enter it:
except that to some extent he had already entered without knowing it.
The diligence and kindness of Frederick William III aided the good fortune of these times, which will never fall from the memory of men;
We pray to the highest deity that this fortune may not fail our fatherland.

Divine providence has given us Frederick William IV, a most merciful, best, and wisest prince, who not only preserves the goods that he received as handed down, but also, with new plans and with inexhaustible new liberality, has excellently aided both the other parts of the state and especially all the best studies.

For these benefits, we all first give thanks and express gratitude to God, the Best and Greatest, King of kings, Lord of lords, from whose nod all things depend, and then to the most august Prince, under whose leadership, command, and auspices the Prussian kingdom is increased and adorned.

Finally, I make a most sacred vow, which alone embraces all our prosperities, that God, the Best and Greatest, may grant perpetual health and safety to Frederick William and to the most august Queen his consort, together with the entire royal house.

div.head: XXXI. Oratio nataliciis Friderici Guilelmi IV. celebrandis d. XV. m. Octobris a. MDCCCXXXXV. habita.
An explanation of the nature of princely kindness and the influence it possesses

p.s: Since it has never seemed to me not especially difficult, most distinguished and most honored auditors of all ranks, on this day from this place before this assembly of yours, to speak not in my own name alone, but in the name of the great university composed of various and most ample bodies of most learned men, about the supreme ruler of so great a republic, about whom, even if you have proclaimed the best and most excellent things, you nevertheless understand that your words fall far short of his magnificence and goodness confirmed by deeds;

When I compare the present times with the earlier ones, which nourished my youth, strengthened and exercised my manhood, it seems to me that the condition in which we now live, whether one should call it happiness or a difficulty mixed with happiness, greatly hinders the orator.

For if there is anything by which an orator can diminish the magnitude of this office to his own advantage, I think it is placed in that license which is usually granted to everyone, namely, that having digressed a little from the main point, he may occupy himself with some other argument not too trivial, to which he feels his powers are either equal or at least less unequal:
I greatly fear, therefore, that this expedient, by which a mediocre talent has been able to help itself to some extent, may have been snatched from our hands.

Of course, since it befits one who is going to speak in the name of the college and by public mandate to take pains and carefully ensure that, like a contractor to the owner, he approves his work to as many as possible and wins common assent;
Indeed, the state of affairs was calm and tranquil, in which you would achieve that with some diligence applied.
Now minds are more agitated:
But in this agitation, though not unfruitful yet inconvenient, in this distraction of parts, how few things are there, dissonant and turbulent, in which most agree?
Wherever you turn, offense is more ready and certain than gratitude:

You would believe that the orator, even one who lives far from anger and partisanship, and removed from that ambition which drives many astray, in literature alone, is rather practicing the military art than exercising the art of peace.
While he desires and strives, if not to please everyone, which is not possible in any matter, at least to avoid offense, what he has said and what he has not said are blamed.

And suspicious envy, which is wont of its own accord to scent out hidden feelings, almost drives the speaker to the point that, just as the Greek comic poets sometimes deformed their actors with masks having a mouth drawn beyond the human nature and monstrous eyebrows, lest if they bore any chance resemblance to some powerful Macedonian, he should seem to have been deliberately mocked by them, so he composes things utterly discordant and abhorrent from any principles of life.

But amid such great dissensions, nevertheless, one thing remains as a resource, the greatest hope and anchor of public safety, in which all agree: I mean the love of our most excellent Prince, whose veneration has today called you here, most distinguished and most honored listeners, so that you might learn, through my interpretation, however I am equipped, with what feeling this school of ours, devoted to the liberal arts, was affected toward the Father of the Fatherland.
This is the sixth year now, listeners, since his most blessed father, who was also the most loving father of the people, was succeeded by Frederick William the Fourth.
Meanwhile many things have happened, joyful, auspicious, excellent, others sad, deadly;
and causes already seem to be building up for future changes, so that you might doubt where they will end;
but through things as sad and adverse as joyful and prosperous, the love of the Prince has remained constant.
But what is the source of this affection?
I answer very briefly:
the Prince's character.
For kindness begets affection:

Since this cannot be feigned nor acquired by art, but is a good implanted by nature, unless the prince is by nature inclined to benevolence, he cannot win for himself the love of his people, by which alone, as it were, nations that are ruled can be firmly held together.

Therefore, what could have happened more happily to the Prussian kingdom than that it obtained a prince who was by nature courteous, gentle, kind, and generous, who by his very character would provoke the love of the people?
But what argument could be more suitable for these solemnities, what more pleasant, finally what more adapted to the person of the most beloved King than princely kindness?
But if by sketching the image of a benevolent prince, it is at the same time established that the character of Frederick William is sketched;

I think I do a favor to myself, who have myself experienced the favor of the most august king and am devoted to him with all my heart, and I think I do a favor to you, who honor him with equal piety, when I describe in outline, both by tacitly citing the opinions of the most approved authors in this field and by explaining my own reasoning, what the nature of princely kindness is and what power it has, and, as far as the narrowness of time permits, the rest, being more constrained than before by the magnificent speeches of my colleagues, which are to be delivered today.
It is indeed, I do not deny it, this kind of speaking which I now undertake, closer to moral philosophy than to a formal oration;

but the more I feel that my eloquence, or any appearance of eloquence, if ever there was any in me, has been worn away by use and extinguished by age and ill health, and that I am kept in this office longer than is fitting for my reputation and especially for the dignity of this most sacred solemnity, the more it seems suited to my condition.
Therefore, to begin with that, what it is that I am about to discuss: I call it kindness, a disposition of the mind to do good to those who are in need of something good.

This cannot exist without gentleness and mildness, and it is joined with mercy and clemency, except that we are so affected by mercy that we are afflicted in mind together with the wretched, while the affection of kindness is purer and more pleasant, and because clemency consists in remitting sins or punishments and penalties of the guilty, but kindness bestows benefits on the innocent.
And kindness surpasses justice and equity:
For the one who is just and fair gives to each person as much as is owed, obeying only the law and reason;

the one who is kind gives even what is not owed, or more than is owed, and although he may call reason and judgment into use, nevertheless he indulges something to his spirit, so that he may satisfy his inclination to do good;
Then indeed justice conforms itself to the laws established by men, and kindness obeys the divine precept of love, which is also truly human, which Christ proclaimed.
Now although this is a virtue common to all men, who nevertheless can be more kind than a prince?

For no one has a greater capacity for doing good than a prince, not only because he is powerful with the greatest resources of all, but also because his mere will alone, even if no advantage should accrue to you from it, is so much a benefit, adding value and dignity to the gift, that he can show his kindness through those things which are usually called by the name of honors:

In these matters, it is not what is given that matters, but with what mind and intention it is given, and you should not value them by silver nor weigh them on a scale, but measure them by the spirit.
And he has such a great abundance of people to whom he can do good, as no one else has.

To say nothing of foreigners, to say nothing of the afflicted, the whole people over whom he rules, and every single one of them, the highest, the middle, the lowest of citizens, have entrusted themselves and all their possessions to his good faith and will, and they can not demand his favor but rather experience it.
A private individual comes to the aid of one or another of the needy;
From the nod of the prince the fortune of cities and peoples hangs; either the prince's grace and serenity cheers all, or his anger strikes all with fear and sadness.
Again, whom does generosity become more than a prince?

For if a king, as some think, reigns by divine authority, and in the kingdom itself there is something divine, which I approve to this extent, that I should judge a good prince to have approached nearer to divinity, by how much a bad one has been depressed below humanity;

The king will be a kind of image and vicar among mortals of the divine power, and by his example he will have to correspond not more in power than in goodness, which is held to be so great in God that he bestows on us all good things by pure grace, without regard to merits.
Or if a prince exercises power entrusted to him by men, this has been entrusted to him so that those who obey may fare well.
It is added that for a Christian king at least nothing can be dearer than the happiness of the people;

and since in a prince not the mediocrity of a private person but the highest and absolute virtue is required, you would hardly miss in him charity, from which kindness flows, that is, that virtue which seems to Christians rightly the most important.

The vice contrary to kindness, indeed, is by no means fitting for the highest ruler of the state, but a courteous, gentle, and mild disposition, conscious of its own human nature, is fitting, lest, placed in the highest position, it rise too high.
But a sharp and excited temperament is more suited to conducting wars than to ruling the state, while a covetous, wrathful, and fierce one is fit for managing affairs neither at home nor abroad.
Now, to place the matter in a clearer light, let it be permitted to explain briefly what benefits a kind king confers, and on whom, and in what manner.
To the first question I answer with an old saying:
The fatherland owes everything to a good prince.
Therefore, as many kinds of goods as there are, so many are the parts of royal kindness:
But there are some goods of the mind and internal, others of fortune and external.

Therefore, although external circumstances may partly be granted by nature and partly be produced by talent, industry, and hard work, yet scarcely any kingdom shows more clearly how much in these matters depends on the goodness and wisdom or the harshness and imprudence of rulers than this Prussian one, which, amid the barrenness of so many lands and amid unusual calamities, has flourished through the zealous and tireless efforts of Frederick William, while other states, blessed with very fertile soil and a most healthful climate, languish through the perversity of their laws and institutions.

For the kindness of a good prince opens paths to every honorable kind of gain for the prudent by right counsels, and frees farmers, artisans, and trade from the most troublesome bonds and unjust laws, by which they can be so constrained that they can scarcely move their limbs:
In the matter of revenues, in their method and collection, a good prince takes care that the resources of the citizens are not diminished nor the poorer classes oppressed;
he does not seek the profit of the treasury, but provides for the necessities of the state:
Finally, he knows that the prince has as much as all the citizens together, and that whenever the situation demands, they will contribute more willingly than can be extorted from the unwilling.

And since generosity is honorable in time, necessary, and sometimes even useful to the state itself, he repairs damages either accidental or sent by heaven, and with his munificence he kindly relieves the want and misery of men.

Now indeed, although we cannot sustain life well without the possession of external goods, yet in my judgment it is so far from being the case that that perverse opinion, which in this age has invaded very many people and is greatly commended for various reasons, should be approved, from which either the first place is assigned to this kind of goods, or they alone, with nearly all others omitted, are to be regarded, and nothing besides the care of external goods is to be expected and desired from the prince, and whoever has satisfied this seems to have satisfied the principal duties;

so that I think, if this error has completely taken hold of the minds of men and has clung to their innermost marrow, states will be corrupted by the worst and most shameful cowardice, and the human race will go to ruin.

Of course, those who measure the dignity of life solely by the enjoyment of those goods cannot fail, being charmed by the daily ease of living and captivated by the allurements of this, their own happiness, to dare nothing any longer for retaining, defending, and recovering the highest goods of the mind, and to be satisfied if they are allowed, secure and safe, even with insult, to do and to feel what is commanded, and to serve a most unworthy servitude.
Therefore a good prince strives to provide for his citizens especially the goods of the mind, as far as it lies within his power:

This is directed to the end that they may be imbued with reverence and piety for the divine, not that they may be infected and bound by superstition, which would nourish discords and tear apart those whom love ought to unite;
that good morals may be propagated;
finally, that reason and intellect, which is the source of true piety and an honorable life, may be cultivated, not merely ostentatiously paraded.

Since the knowledge of the liberal arts, philosophy, history, and natural science, and the whole vast circle of disciplines of every kind, are brought together here, what the benevolent kings could accomplish by undertaking the patronage of science and letters, the Prussian empire, to say nothing of earlier ones, has admirably demonstrated from Frederick the Great down to Frederick William IV, the most generous patron and defender of the fine arts:
For by their favor, literature has been so firmly established in these lands that we yield to no nation in learning, and even surpass very many.
At the same time, by these studies, superstition has been driven away to some extent.

When last year, in the solemn rites for the most beloved King held elsewhere, I had pointed out that this was owed in large part to natural science, and had said by way of example that no one is now frightened by eclipses of the sun and moon, by which in former times unskilled minds had been struck;

A man most highly regarded for his talent, virtue, and authority, who at Leipzig professes the same art that I do in this city, whether provoked by those words, I do not know, conceded indeed that no one today is frightened by the eclipses of the sun, which we perceive with our eyes, but he said that other and most pernicious darknesses are doubled and that the blackness of night and clouds blinds us, which differs from a solar eclipse only in this, that we know when the shadow will leave the sun's disk, but from those darknesses neither when nor whether light, and not rather thick darkness, will emerge is known to anyone.

But those shadows of ours nevertheless seem to me to have less distinction, because they are not so much natural, as once they were, arising from the character of the age, as they are smoke artificially made in certain very well-known kitchens, which the blasts of the winds scatter.

This kingdom will not be overshadowed by those people, nor the serenity of the wisest King, who, being pious and religious, not fanatical, according to the most sacred institution of the Prussian state, will allow to each his own opinion and judgment concerning things which we do not know, but believe.
Finally, the most precious good of the mind is liberty, which is most closely connected with reason, the prerogative of man among the other animals.
Therefore the kind prince, as a man among men, as a free man among free men, commands;
But a Christian prince especially knows that slavery of both body and soul has been abolished by the teachings of Christ, although excessive lust for domination may have retained or brought it back;

And that Frederick William IV, at the very beginning of his reign, declared excellently that he wished to be a Christian king, that the whole administration of the state testifies to have been said in such a way that he wished to rule free men with love and to lead them by reason to obedience to be rendered under just laws, not to coerce slaves by force.
What of the fact that by this truly royal path the dignity of the empire itself is excellently provided for?
This is indeed so much more excellent, as those who obey are more excellent.

Therefore, he who uses citizens as if they were slaves renders his rule worse, in proportion as slaves are worse than free men, although he has more right over slaves than over free men; and rightly was it said long ago that the master of slaves is not much above the possessor of cattle.

Indeed, just liberty, which is not ignorant of obedience to laws, magistrates, and the prince, quickly increases the strength, resources, and fame of the empire, and again together with it the remaining goods perish;
but license must be restrained, and most truly thus far Galba advised Piso:
"You are about to rule men who can endure neither complete slavery nor complete liberty." And these indeed seem to me to be the most important kinds of benefits;
But if we ask for those things which a good prince gives, the answer is ready:
To the worthy and the needy.
For the reward must be paid to virtue, even if he who excels in virtue should be less grateful;
The prince's kindness forgives even those who are more outspoken, whom he sees to be well-disposed, and with him that saying does not hold:
"Compliance wins friends, truth breeds hatred";
But flatterers, who are born for the ruin of princes and states, he keeps far away.

Then, just as the law and statutes, although they ought to be equal for the poor and the rich, for the noble and the commoner, and to ensure that no injustice is done to either side, nevertheless seem to need to be established in such a way that security is provided especially to those who, because of their lowliness, are more exposed and subject to arrogance, or for this reason, that losses and evils inflicted on the more humble and obscure escape notice more easily without an avenger, but if an injustice has been done to someone more distinguished, the whole world cries out:

Thus the imperial kindness does not turn the good of all to this end, that it makes the rich and the nobles and those who have abundant resources in their own and their relatives' and friends' means even richer and feeds them more generously and more sumptuously;

But it comes to the aid of the peasant afflicted by the barrenness of the fields, by the overflowing of the rivers, to the towns devastated by fire, to the orphans, the widows, the disabled, to those whose household means are more limited; it provides for the children and girls supported by the alimentary fund, and for other things of this kind:

In this category, there is no need for me to describe how merciful our King is with his most beloved Queen, who, indeed, not content with having received reports from the governors about the state of the provinces and the condition of the people, leaving behind the splendor and delights of palaces, themselves visit squalid huts and shabby cottages, so that they may learn the misery of mortals and bring aid to the wretched.
And in this matter especially, observe, listeners, how much more excellent and more commendable a kingdom is than the rule of the people or of a few.
For where a turbulent multitude rules the state:
although in this age certainly in Europe it rules almost none:
the goods of the rich are seized and divided, by which the greedy populace may be fed;
but to the rule of the aristocrats nothing is more hostile to the people:
these consult only for themselves at the expense of the lesser ones;
these pass laws useful to themselves, calamitous to the rest;
These people have no concern for the lower classes, no compassion, but they procure their own advantages generally from the inconvenience of those others.
As Aristotle reports, in certain states governed by the will of a few, the magistrates themselves, when about to assume power, were solemnly bound by such a formula:
“I will be hostile to the common people, and as much as I can I will take care that their condition be miserable.” But a wise and kind king grants to each side as much as is fitting:
It provides the wealthy with a secure and certain possession of their goods;
It cherishes and revives the common people as much as possible;
It knows how to bring about peace and harmony among the different parts of the state, the ways of life, and the orders of citizens, and it strives to do so.

For he does not bestow upon the lower classes of inhabitants only that part of beneficence which is placed in external goods, but since, the greater the opportunity the rich have of instructing their children in every kind of learning and of more elegant education, the more neglected is wont to be the education and training of the rustic and, especially in populous cities, of the working multitude, he will take care that this also may become a partaker of that discipline, without which human life does not even seem to be human, and that the common people, while letters and arts flourish most happily, as they flourished in Egypt under the kings of Macedonian stock and in Italy under the Medici and other most munificent princes, may not, as we see happened in the same times, be left miserably and servilely uncultivated.
So much for relieving the needy.
What shall I say about the guilty?

For although a kind prince will have mercy ready at hand for them and will moderate the severity of punishments and executions, yet no one will deny that the laws must be enforced, and that the head of the state must be formidable to the guilty, and indeed to them alone, and that the rights, judgments, and morals of the state must not be corrupted by a perverse indulgence, which differs greatly from kindness.

Finally, so that I do not entirely omit the third of the questions I proposed above, it is so established that a kind and wise prince bestows benefits, first, that he may restrain his kindness by employing judgment, and not so much throw away benefits as give them, nor corrupt favor by the profusion of favor, diminishing the value of rewards;

Moreover, so that, whatever he himself has understood will be beneficial to the citizens, he certainly, if he rules over somewhat more civilized nations, should not thrust it upon the unwilling, but rather should strive to lead the people to a better estimation of good and evil, in which he himself excels, by shaping their minds and uprooting their corrupt opinions.

Since I have been brought to this point, I cannot help but recall a certain opinion of Fichte, which seems to be opposed with a hostile front to this whole discussion that we have undertaken concerning the principal's kindness, and to overturn our [views] from the foundation.

For a great man, a model of wisdom and virtue and freedom, once an outstanding ornament of this university among a few, whom we older men have seen hurling thunderbolts of eloquence from this very platform, in a certain brilliant essay urges all who are equal to so great a task "to declare an internecine war first upon that error, the poisoned source of all our evils and misery, that it is the prince's duty to provide for our happiness, and to pursue that error through all its hiding places, through the entire world of our knowledge, wherever it has hidden, until it has been destroyed from the face of the earth and returned to Tartarus, whence it emerged." "We do not know," he says, "by what things our happiness is aided;

But if the prince knows this and it is his role to lead us to it, then we must follow him with closed eyes, and he does for us whatever he pleases, and to those who ask he answers with pledged faith that this is necessary for our happiness;
He binds the neck of the human race with a noose, and shouts:
Be silent, be silent;
All these things are done for your benefit.
Are you not, prince, our God?
From God we expect happiness, from you the protection of our rights;
We do not want you to be kind to us; we want you to be just." These words he spoke, as he was naturally sharp, somewhat harshly, more bluntly, more stubbornly:
For us speaking today it will be possible to blunt these stings, which the injustice of earlier times had sharpened.
Indeed, with the sharpness removed, we elicit from the words of the immortal colleague this milder sentiment:

A good prince, such as we describe, does not drag the people to happiness by the neck, nor make them blessed by force, but with reason as their guide and with the sweet-speaking goddess Suadela as their helper, he so shapes them that they learn to judge correctly about their own happiness.
After I have set these things forth a little more fully, it is permitted, listeners, to embrace in summary what the power of this royal kindness is.

For first, even if no advantage should accrue from it to the prince, and not even thanks should be returned to him, the very feeling of kindness itself renders him blessed, because the greatest pleasure is in doing good, and the sweetest fruit of right deeds is to have done them:
He who has subdued the whole world with much blood will be considered great by most, yet he cannot delight his mind with his crimes;
He who has deserved well of the state by his innocent virtues, he alone will enjoy the sweetest fame of himself.

And if the judgments of contemporaries are corrupted by anger and passion, by slander and flattery, the memory of future ages, which alone is the most certain witness and judge of truth, can be abolished neither by any interdictions nor by scissors nor by a little hammer nor by fire; it weighs with equal scale the wills, the counsels, the deeds.
"Not dies," says the poet, "the benevolent virtue of Croesus;"
But Phalaris, the merciless burner with the bronze bull, is pursued everywhere by hostile rumor. Then he who by doing good shows that he loves, is loved in return:
But the mutual love of king and citizens is the clearest source of public happiness and the one impregnable bulwark of the empire.
Hence, as it is more pleasant for both the prince and the citizens, so it is more peaceful, more stable, and more lasting the rule of a benevolent prince.

For, as Seneca says, one obeys a commander who is more lenient more readily, because the human mind is by nature stubborn and strives against what is contrary and difficult, and follows more easily than it is led.

Thus it happens that he who knows how to gain the approval of the citizens for his commands exercises power and retains his authority with less effort than one who has resolved to accomplish everything by force.
Finally, since, according to the most sagacious author of political wisdom, Aristotle, there are especially two things by which kingdoms are overthrown, hatred and contempt;
Contempt indeed follows cowardice, fickleness, rashness, inexperience, imprudence; but that those who hold power may not be despised, wisdom and vigor, which win authority, bring it about:
Hatred, moreover, is contracted by injustice, injuries, pride, cruelty, and the other things of this kind; and, on the other hand, kindness makes it so that neither a master nor a prince is hated.

Therefore you may see that half of the empire rightly retained is placed in kindness, which unless the people experience from the prince, it is to be feared that they may be separated from each other.

Indeed, the king differs greatly from the tyrant in these very arts, because the former, such as Isocrates, Seneca, Erasmus of Rotterdam, and Frederick the Great established him, as one governing the state by the consensus of all, rules free men with affection, beneficence, faith, truth, and sincerity;
the tyrant, such as Machiavelli established him, having at hand that saying, "Let them hate, so long as they fear";
With this worst of guardians, fear and violence, and with the snares of informers and spies, he keeps the slaves in check, and leads them by fraud, lies, pretense, and dissimulation:
The king and the people are united by mutual trust and common interest;
The tyrant fears and is feared, and he desires to be feared and fears being feared, and he measures advantages not from what benefits his subjects, but from his own private power.
Will anyone therefore reproach me if I say that the duty is fulfilled especially by the kindness of a Christian king, as I indicated above?

Indeed, Erasmus, in a book most full of good fruit, which he wrote on the education of a Christian prince to Charles, the grandson of Maximilian, who shortly afterward was created Emperor, did not hesitate to go so far as to affirm, disregarding the custom prudently and decorously received, as my opinion holds, in the titles of princes, that dominion, empire, kingship, majesty, and power are words of the pagans, and to declare that the Christian empire is nothing other than an administration, a guardianship, a beneficence.
But I see that I must hasten to the end, lest I cut short the time of the highest officials of the university, who are to speak after me.

Nor does it seem that I should take up the matter, which I have once and again treated in my peroration, so that I may remind you, most honorable fellow soldiers, of your affairs, and what you owe to the dearest King, what it is fitting for you to perform, what to omit, in order that you may respond to the most wise counsels of the Father of the fatherland, I will set forth with deliberate effort:
This province, indeed, they will now claim as their own right, to whom the care of morals has been entrusted.
I will briefly finish what, after I have discussed the royal kindness, seems to remain, and I will turn my step back to where I began.
For Frederick William is without doubt that prince who thinks that a day has been lost for him on which he has not benefited someone.
He is the prince who looks not to his own advantage, but to that of those whom God has entrusted to him to protect;
who wishes his presence to be felt by doing good, not by terrors, and desires above all that all may be well;
who draws the zeal of citizens by gracious address, and not only is called most serene, but with serene brow and calm mind refreshes all who have had the chance to associate with him.

Just as he now thrives and flourishes through the prayers of all, so we pray that his happiness, which cannot be separated from the prosperity of the Prussian state, may remain firm and undisturbed, that his noble spirit may never be saddened by adverse circumstances, and that, with the same candor, faith, and love with which he provides for the interests of his people, the whole people may reward his virtue, insofar as those below can show gratitude to the supreme ruler of the state.

May God, the Best and Greatest, preserve the most august King with his consort, the best Queen, the most faithful partner in whatever matters may bring either pleasure or anxiety to the King's mind, and may He keep them safe, secure, and unharmed forever for the welfare of this kingdom.
I have spoken.

div.head: XXXII. Oratio nataliciis Friderici Guilelmi IV. celebrandis d. XV. m. Octobris a. MDCCCXXXXVI. habita.
On the present condition of letters, especially philosophy and the study of antiquity

p.s: For the due celebration of these most sacred solemnities, which are dedicated to the best Prince, all of you who are present, hearers of every rank, each to be honored in his own place, easily perceive that something greater is being transacted in this assembly than a simple congratulation to be offered on the birthday of one man, however excellent.

For since the prince and the fatherland are joined as if in one body, so that neither can he be safe unless the state is safe, nor can the fatherland enjoy prosperity without the safety and well-being of the prince;

Although the eternity of the state may seem able to remain through any changes of kings, nevertheless I judge that with the birth of a king the state is born again and regenerated, and that with the birth of a prince the fates and fortune of the city are born, which will be either favorable or unfavorable according as the Fates of his nativity have stood propitious or angry.
Thus the birthday of the prince is the birthday of the fatherland.

This opinion, except in those states in which the principate is handed down not by hereditary right but by election, holds and will hold in all the rest, whatever the form of government and the power of the prince may be:

whether this one alone with his ministers holds the reins of empire, or the people and the commons are participants through their representatives in the making of laws, the imposing of taxes, and the commanding of tributes;

And again, whether the minds of the citizens, languid with torpor and intent solely on their own private affairs, care nothing for public matters, or whether they understand that whatever pertains to the republic pertains to themselves, and are carried with the greatest fervor to know, judge, and, as far as is allowed, to handle the affairs of the state.

When the king makes all the duties of the state his own concern, and the people, careless of the republic, follow their leader like a flock follows its shepherd, which some call a paternal and patriarchal form of government;

Whether the prince provides for the necessities of the people and has persuaded himself that his own advantage and the interests of the citizens are not separate, or whether he uses the resources and bodies of his subjects to satisfy his own desires out of lust or ambition, who does not see that the fates of the people are bound up with the fate of the prince, that whatever has turned out well for the prince, some part of those things falls upon the people itself, and that the Achaeans pay the penalty for the imprudent plans of their leader, and that subjects are even more bitterly ensnared and afflicted by the evils of their master?

But if, instead of that brutish and stupid servitude, citizens begin to apply themselves to the care of common affairs, especially townspeople to governing their small republics in the manner of municipalities, and to come into a share of public administration;

How much it matters what the character of a prince is, whether cruel or gentle, sad or cheerful, stern and harsh or mild and kind, suspicious and distrustful of every good man, or full of joyful confidence, too tenacious of his own authority and power, and taking it as a diminution of himself however small a prerogative the citizens have obtained, or inclined to yield something of his power and to grant as much as can be done without public harm to the colleges and civil orders!
As I say these things in general, so they are especially suited to the person, character, plans, and institutions of Frederick William IV, the most gracious king.

For although the Prussian kingdom has not been established in that most free form, in which, after we were victorious, both the conquered and several peoples who had been allies in the wars and victories were organized, nevertheless that inertia and indolence, which in earlier ages had held not only almost all Germans but also these lands, dragging out a slow life, which is like death;
has been driven away:

And although Frederick William III, the most blessed Father of his country, had understood that the state needed to be restored and to be corrected and adorned in a new way and with new counsels, yet with his characteristic self-restraint and moderation, he especially strove that the commonwealth might pass its time in calm tranquility, and that he might rather strengthen it with forces than wish these new forces to be stirred up after so many disturbances, so many revolutions, so many endured labors;

The most joyful vigor of Frederick William IV roused and even impelled minds that had been almost lulled to sleep by long tranquility, and loosened the reins of government, and with magnanimous counsel sent the people forth, as it were, from the starting-gates into a very spacious field, in which they could run to the appointed goal.
Behold the fates of the republic, fitting and innate to the genius of the prince!

He gave to nearly all these things a new and more beautiful face and appearance, so that one who had been oppressed by an Epimenidean sleep before these seven years would today, on returning, scarcely recognize his homeland.
He has been the author of many and great goods for us.
If evils seem to be mixed in with these, these are not new, but they previously lay hidden under scars drawn over, badly covered.
Indeed, nothing is more dangerous than an ulcer that creeps secretly and gnaws away at the most excellent parts of the body;
And he has made great progress who understands how much is lacking, how much remains.
There are those who grieve that we do not yet enjoy perfect freedom of speech and writing;
but by the kindness of the best King it has been granted that we may complain openly that we do not enjoy it:
Now I ask you, is this not itself an excellent freedom, and one to which not much is lacking for full freedom?
Truly happy are mortals who know their own blessings;
but I do not know whether the beginning of happiness is to know one's own evils, which cannot be healed unless they are known.
There was a time when our wisdom was boasted of not without pride;
but we understand that there are also others who are wise.

Indeed, those people consult the fatherland badly, badly interpret the love of the fatherland, who, just as the Spartans of old, certainly very brave men and not unwise in other respects, but too ignorant of foreign affairs, praise nothing except their own and are uniquely pleased with themselves alone;

And most rightly does Sophocles' Haemon advise that those who seem to themselves alone to be wise and to have a tongue or a mind that no one else has, if they are opened up, are found to be empty and vain.

Since this is evident in individual men, so too we see entire peoples, when, because of the excessive opinion they have conceived of their own virtue and prudence, they have preferred to rest content with their present goods rather than seek new ones, soon cast down from the dignity acquired by great men and through great deeds, and lose the very goods they had, and be conquered by lesser men who strive vigorously toward higher things.
We indeed owe to Frederick William IV not only the greatest benefits but also the knowledge of disadvantages.
After these things were brought to light, indeed we live a life somewhat less comfortable, which before seemed easy, and we proceed on a more obstructed path and here and there we stumble;
but we remember the famous watchword:
"Through hardships to the stars." And by this movement indeed all parts of the state are seized:

There are added other moments of affairs flowing from other causes, and not from fortuitous ones, by which these times of the republic are rendered in an unusual manner either more difficult or at least memorable beyond others.
Nor, however, is it my task to explain these things:

I will not speak of the things that happened this year, whether favorable or adverse, not of the Polish tumult that was quickly suppressed, not of the form of the courts changed in some part, not of the manifold movements of the churches and of the two assemblies that were connected with these, convened by the pious King and held in our city, not of the sudden financial calamity that had threatened, the straits of the loan societies, the public bank established on a new plan, not of the matter of establishing the tolls and taxes and the disputes arising from this both domestic and of the allied states:
All these things, and whatever else of this kind there are, I pass over, since they are foreign to my person and to my studies;

except that it must be said, as far as I can see, that in these matters many things were done by the best King with foresight, caution, gentleness, and kindness, nothing too harsh, nothing proud, nothing rash, nothing excessive.
For us, literature is closer and more immediate;
And who among you, listeners, does not understand that these very things have either been seized or can be seized by this, as it were, whirlwind of affairs?
Here let me be allowed to linger a little.
Therefore, I would not deny that the condition of literature has in our memory experienced somewhat the fortune of common vicissitudes.

At the time when this our literary university was founded and most splendidly equipped, the studies of earlier ages were both sufficiently established and were flourishing more joyfully day by day, especially in the Prussian kingdom, however afflicted, and they seemed then to be among the principal supports by which the restoration of the shaken republic could be accomplished;
Letters were highly valued and were cherished by the very restorers of the republic, one or two of whom were by far the most learned;
Trust was placed in the learned, those keen and undaunted champions against the common enemy, and greatly hated by the most cunning foe;
It was judged to be excellently invested, whatever expense had been laid out for establishing any branches of learning:
Finally, there was the greatest harmony between the republic and letters.
Soon that part of them which had been called out for waging war seemed to have turned the arms it had taken up against the enemy against the state.
Nevertheless, the public care for advancing literature then relaxed nothing, nor was anything mixed into the plans for adopting it that was foreign to literature.

Frederick William IV, however, even before he took up the highest affairs of state, revealed an extraordinary love of the fine arts through distinguished proofs, and after he succeeded his father, he surpassed the expectation that he had aroused.
Meanwhile, a long peace had opened up the whole world and had inflamed the studies of the learned;
hence the apparatus of learning was increased, the necessities of literature were increased;

As knowledge grew to an immense extent, the number of learned men increased, who sought an honorable place for themselves and their studies, and it increased to such a degree that we rather suffer from abundance than from scarcity, and those things which in other times would have been most welcome now seem ungrateful and burdensome.

But two things now seem to me, especially at this time, to bring some difficulty to literature, not indeed new ones but repeated with new force: the one, that very many demand that literature be turned to the common use of life; the other, that certain pious men and some clerics think that nothing is true or tolerable unless it agrees with their own opinions or views about the divine word.
Both of these things are especially hindered by those studies which are commonly called liberal, namely antiquity and philosophy.

Indeed, ancient literature is hateful both to those who refer all knowledge and the pursuit of knowledge to common utility, and to those who want learning to be confined within the limits of the Christian faith:
Nevertheless, I judge that neither group prudently consults its own interest by slandering those studies, much less the proper education of the human race.

But because I, although I am not so much burdened by the reproach of recondite learning as by the undeserved suspicion of the opposite vice, will seem, by defending the literature of antiquity, to wish either to defend or to boast of my own, I will discharge this part of my speech with as few words as possible.

For those who demand that literature be brought into common use, and do not want it to lurk in the shadow of the school, but to approach especially those questions which are most agitated in this age;

Because the most serious questions about true freedom of the mind and civil liberty are now being discussed, they seem to be devastating their own altars and hearths, when they want to expel from the education of youth those ancient letters, the most faithful nurses of that true liberty, because they are the nurses of humanity:

Although I concede that those who teach these letters have detracted something from the genuine usefulness of these [studies], because, forgetting the wise admonition of Aristotle, who does not even want boys to be liberally educated in music to the point where one who is being trained for the practice of the art of music [is trained], they have begun to imbue their pupils more with the more subtle precepts of the art, which are necessary for future grammarians, than to shape their minds to humanity by the reading of ancient authors.

Indeed, there is a certain part of this refinement that is cultivated speech, which the leading authors of the new literature, if you except a few who were learned by nature alone, have shaped according to Greek and Roman models:
And the masculine Roman speech especially, which surpasses Greek itself in strength of power, still seems to me to be the best teacher of a clear, elegant, exact, and serious style.
I say this not with the intention of defending this custom of speaking Latin that has been handed down from our ancestors.

For it matters little to me, especially since I am most fond of my native language, in which language it is spoken, provided it is spoken well; and I will gladly rejoice when, freed from this harsh necessity of speaking in Latin, to which most people now give ear with difficulty, I shall be in a condition similar to that of Laberius, who, a Roman knight, was compelled at the age of sixty to act in mimes at the games:

I do not say this, I say, with that intention, but because I disagree with those who think that however much industry young men have devoted to learning the Latin language thoroughly, they would have invested it with greater profit in their native or French speech.

Now those who fear that the Christian faith is endangered by the literature of the Gentiles, although I doubt that they can be convinced or appeased by my arguments, nevertheless I would like to warn them that the Emperor Julian forbade Christians, in order to afflict them, that pagan learning and education, and that those who reformed our sacred rites in the sixteenth century were helped by nothing more than the revival of classical studies, and that the men who most favored and supported the reform of the church were those most thoroughly trained and polished in ancient literature.
By a better example and a more refined judgment, the most wise King benefits us:

He, with the most liberal mind, embraces, loves, and sets before us whatever is beautiful and good, whatever is worthy of being known, whether it was born in ancient Athens, or in Egypt, or in Gaul or Britain, in the most remote times, or in the middle ages, or very recently.

But will the Germans indeed tolerate that the gloomy peevishness of a few brings into neglect literature, which has been cultivated in Germany for a long time with special care, which nourishes youth, strengthens the prime of life, and delights old age?
that the Greek and Latin Muses are forced to seek refuge among the Gauls, where already now Henricus Stephanus, revived, is undertaking greater things in this kind than any German can;

Even among the Italians, whom recently Paris Zaiottus of Trent, a man both experienced in public affairs and equipped with knowledge of the best works that the more recent age has produced among any of the European peoples, in a most elegant book, which rivals many of our pedagogical pamphlets, which he wrote on youthful literature, has excellently recommended the ancient authors;
Finally, among the Roman Fathers of the Society of Jesus themselves, who pursue these studies of antiquity not without success and defend them against adversaries?
Furthermore, I have warned that philosophy, which I judge, together with Plato, to be the greatest good given to mortals by God, is opposed to what is customarily demanded of literature in this age.
When I say philosophy, I mean not only that which bears this name properly, but also that very broad field of learning in which this order, which they call philosophers, is exercised:
And the remaining orders also share in these studies, if, as was once counted as a praise, they pursue their disciplines with a philosophical mind, as they say.

These disciplines, if it is permissible to use the technical terms of art in this assembly of most learned men, are partly empirical, which are occupied with discovering and establishing the forms, elements, forces, and laws of nature by means of the senses and instruments through observation and experiment;

Some are historical, which investigate, arrange, and compose the deeds and whatever has been founded and accomplished by humans, from handed-down sources with interpretation and critical art applied, and trace them back to their causes to be discovered by the same method;
From this kind is also the entire learning of philologists and grammarians, truly quite varied:
Some are mathematical, which measure pure quantity with the mind and scrutinize its laws with subtle investigation;

Some of them are speculative, which embrace in their lofty minds the divine and human principles of things, the purest notions expressed in the nature of things and founded in the human mind, and the entire principles, causes, and ends of civil and moral life.

Although excellent fruits flow from all these disciplines into human affairs, yet there is no need for me to explain to the learned that whoever wishes their measure to be determined by the usage of daily life will both mutilate them disgracefully and sordidly, and will cut off the very fruits he seeks.

These disciplines cannot flourish unless they themselves determine, from their own principles, both where they begin, and where they tend, and how far it is either permissible or advantageous for them to proceed.
He destroys philosophy who limits it by a law that it did not itself impose.
But the office of philosophy, he says, is nothing other than to explain what has been given;
That is, as it seems to some, to give an account of them in such a way that they are proved to be true and right.
I hear.
Of course, if superstition is given, philosophy will explain superstition and will be adorned with magical and theurgic doctrines and arts, as by the divine Iamblichus;

If slavery has been given, it is the task of philosophy, as Aristotle did, to explain slavery, and there are different kinds of philosophy: one for those times and places where a great part of mankind is oppressed by slavery, another where all are free.

On the contrary, this is the adulterous philosophy, which is obscured by the mists of present things and which serves the times, whether unknowingly or deliberately, and does not seek what it ought, but conceals evils with deceit, and does not do what Cicero most beautifully proclaims of philosophy, that it is the investigator of virtue and the expeller of vices, but rather confirms and perpetuates vices.
Nor is philosophy more the handmaid of theology, as was once proposed with sufficient arrogance.

When I have been brought to this point, it occurs to me that in our age some people attribute very much to those things which they are accustomed to call positive, but that the whole circle of disciplines, which philosophers embrace, is not taught as positive:
from which it can happen that, if nothing else, at least the disciplines of philosophers are brought into contempt.
But it also occurs to me that we mortals very often are led not by things but by the images of things, words:
Therefore the province of the grammarian seems the more serious, because he is engaged in defining the meaning of words.
For indeed things cannot be clearly understood unless the words are understood.

Indeed many, who are so greatly moved by that word, are indeed more ignorant, I admit, but nevertheless not few, especially for this reason seem to want to praise nothing but positive things, because whatever is not positive, they think it is negative, confusing affirmation with position.
That contrariety holds in mathematics and in certain parts of physics, as in the doctrine of electricity:
in human affairs, about which we are now dealing, the negative contrary is not the positive;

But from the Greeks, from whom the Latin language has borrowed these technical terms, it is called positive, because it has been set down by men and established or sanctioned by a certain convention of men; and the opposite of the positive is that which flows and holds from the very nature and reason of the thing, and is valid by its own nature.

Therefore, to begin with examples from philologists, which will seem too common and perhaps ridiculous to fastidious ears, grammarians made syllables that are long by nature opposed to syllables that are long by position or by rule:
and those who thought that the words of a language were formed by whim, by choice, by the chance agreement of men, as did Democritus and Aristotle, called these artificial words positive;

But those who judged with Plato that words were joined to notions by a certain natural principle, struck out by the necessity of nature and mind, or rather born spontaneously, denied that language was positive;
Similarly, Strabo says that some things established among peoples come about by nature, others by convention and practice and use:

And just as law, so religion is partly positive, which is accustomed to be handed down in writings, and partly natural, not written down in letters and tablets, but inscribed without letters in the minds and hearts of men.
This positive [religion], therefore, rests on authority:

which authority is altogether necessary for governing men both in domestic and in public affairs, not only in the peaceful state of the commonwealth but also in the disturbed and turbulent one, especially amid arms:

Therefore, even the most free and at the same time most cultivated peoples did not hesitate in times of crisis to take refuge in dictatorship, from whose harsh necessity the most highly approved authority of royal power exempts us.
But the instrument of science is reason and intellect;
Therefore in science there is no place for authority.
Just as philosophers scorn it, so they will approve the positive [sciences], which they have found to be true and correct;
But who would presume to prescribe to anyone that he should praise what is false and wrong?

Although the philosopher will regard these very things with reverence, as long as they bear the consensus of the many, unless they are excessively harmful, just as the ancient wise men, especially Socrates, although they thought more correctly than the common people about divine matters, nevertheless worshipped the publicly accepted gods with supplication, ceremonies, and sacrifices, and openly rejected only those stories that could not be reconciled with the majesty and perfection of the divine deity:
When they denied that these were true, they did not deny divinity, they did not abolish piety, but they established this, and about that they decided more worthily.
Moreover, in matters that pertain to knowledge, only dull, lazy minds, slow and weak in thinking, do not follow authority:
for it is easy to swear by another's words;

The path of understanding, or rather the narrow track, is difficult and rough, and overgrown with the brambles of much doubt, and it was rightly said long ago that the sinews and joints of wisdom are not to believe rashly.

But what about the fact that all literature, even if it does not want to be immersed in the whirlpool of everyday affairs, nevertheless must treat many matters about which positive authority, whether of the state or of the church, must decide?
Would you not say that here already science has been driven to a standstill?
But we have, if I am not mistaken, even in this crisis something to console us.
For although the human race is tenacious of transmitted traditions, and rightly so, lest it rush headlong at the sudden onset of any momentary impulses;

Nevertheless, because those who hold the helm of public and sacred government are themselves cultivated by literature and trained for conducting affairs, the positive commands and decrees gradually take on a color from the precepts of science, and the common consensus of nations, after it has for a long time followed what it had sanctioned as perverse or at least less probable, and after fanatical judges have been stained by many murders committed against the wisest and most innocent men, is turned to a better course, with reason as the victorious guide, which, implanted in us by God, the highest and absolute reason, he who slanders it would impiously and ungratefully deny.
Therefore, whatever is positive has, as it were, its own ages from the Etruscan discipline, its own courses and advances, not without divine providence.

And each nation, which indeed dares to be wise, at whatever age it establishes for itself through its leaders, learned together with the people, positive institutions, which at whatever age correspond most to the understanding of the nation.
Thus, unless the fates of the people hasten to their destruction, it comes about that, with the good things of the ancestors preserved, the iniquities and evils of former times are removed.

Finally, although some nations advance, others are left behind, nevertheless the whole human race seems to tend toward this, that that ancient disagreement of position and nature or reason becomes more and more obsolete.

Indeed, since that law is most fair and most just which, not fashioned according to arbitrary will and caprice, sets before us the very nature and reason of the things contained in the law, expressed in words, a fair and just law cannot conflict with reason; and most truly did the Stoics, with Cicero as interpreter, establish that law is the highest reason implanted in nature, which commands what must be done and forbids the contrary, and that this reason, when confirmed and perfected in the human mind, is law.

If I have argued these points correctly, do you not think, listeners, that literature, even that which lies hidden at home and does not declaim in the forum, has great power and use for correcting the state of affairs?

But why, in almost no part of human affairs, is peace so difficult to establish between those different and, as it were, hostile things that we have mentioned, as in divine matters, which nevertheless ought to be uniquely suited for pacifying the world torn apart by profane hatreds, is not for me to examine, since I am not a theologian:
This one thing may I be allowed to mention, which can be accepted even as spoken by my mouth.
We have recently mourned the loss of several colleagues who were most closely connected to many of us through long association and especially dear, among them two theologians:

Of these, the one who departed first was undoubtedly devoted to the positive doctrines of the most holy faith, but the same man did not hesitate to use philosophical contemplation in theological matters, and with great effort he seems to have had the purpose that, as far as it lay in his power, that sad division between philosophy and theology might be removed.
But what is more destructive and troublesome than discord, what more pleasant and useful than concord?

Therefore, colleagues and fellow students, let us all earnestly strive that the harmony by which our school once grew may remain and be strengthened—both that of all orders, who, because all parts of literature are bound by an inner bond, are united in this one and indivisible body of the university according to the ancient and approved custom, and that of teachers and learners, and that of the civil and literary commonwealth—and that, removed from all ambition and any desire, we may seek, pursue, and express in our discipline and morals the true, the good, and the beautiful!
And when we do this, what else are we doing than imitating the most noble example of Frederick William IV, the most humane king?

This king, whom I have had the opportunity, both in other public assemblies and from this platform, to celebrate and venerate in speeches every year, I have never ceased to praise for his intellect devoted to the best arts and letters, and not only for his love of learning, but also—what is rarer in a prince—for his love of the learned, and finally for his pursuits entirely removed from common pleasures and delights, turned toward everything excellent, honorable, serious, and sublime; and just as he himself excels in these, so he desires that his peoples be raised to such a degree of perfection and praise that the peoples may deservedly be considered worthy of a great-souled king, and the king worthy of the most cultivated and loyal peoples.
We see, therefore, to conclude where I began, that the fortune of our prince, born with him, is our fortune, by a most auspicious nativity.
From kings, to whom a long reign has fallen, the ages of peoples are reckoned and numbered.

But I judge this century of Prussia to be most fortunate, if God in his mercy grants it, even amid the difficulties of the times, and to be so hereafter, under the leadership and auspices of Frederick William IV.

We pray to God, the Best and Greatest, on this day sacred to the rejoicing fatherland, with pious vows and supplications, that the life of the most beloved King may be prolonged for the welfare of the republic and of the good arts as long as possible, and that he may flourish with the august Queen and with the entire royal house in the highest and perpetual prosperity.
I have spoken.

div.head: XXXIII. Oratio nataliciis Friderici Guilelmi IV. celebrandis d. XV. m. Octobris a. MDCCCXXXXVII. habita.
On the political movement

p.s: Since it is difficult for one man, for very many reasons, to celebrate every year, in the same solemn assemblies, in the same place, in the same gathering of most learned men, in the name of the same college, the praises of the same prince, however distinguished, —

Then, because variety, which the most refined audience requires and the orator desires, cannot generally be sought except from the subject matter, lest it afflict both himself and his listeners with boredom, I think that the greatest difficulty lies in the selection of the subject matter.

But if, whenever one must speak about Frederick William IV, a particularly energetic king, the speaker can never lack an extremely abundant supply of material, nevertheless I do not know whether that very abundance rather than scarcity hinders this choice.
What, then, can be more pleasing to one about to speak, what more desirable, than that state, that condition of affairs, which leaves no room for choice?
Indeed, this advantage falls to me today, listeners.

For this year Frederick William performed so many distinguished deeds in the state that anyone who, in these solemnities dedicated to his name, should choose to treat other matters rather than these public affairs, would have to seem foolish; and that not even an educated man, although he may be little versed in public affairs, unless he wishes to seem a complete closet scholar, could avoid those things which have attracted and moved the minds of all, not only citizens but men; and finally that not even this need be feared, that anyone speaking about public affairs before young men should incur reproach.
For that time has passed when only the ministers and officials of the princes seemed able to judge concerning the state.

This was taken badly, if anyone else expressed an opinion about matters of this kind, by which especially learned men were relegated to their own doctrines alone, and were either kept away from or deterred from those things that pertained to the state, and they were compelled, if at any time they had to give advice about public affairs, to conceal many things and to pass over them or to indicate them with great caution and as if from a distance.
It is understood at last that the saying of Sophocles' Creon and of Louis XIV, king of the Gauls, is false, that he sells the king for the state;

It is understood that the republic, as it is called from the people, and the state, as it derives its name from the citizens, is thus the possession of the citizens and the people, that is, a gathering of men united and joined together, if not by a community of origin and stock, which is far more excellent, at least by a community of law, statutes, and utility.

Indeed, Plato rightly advises that it is just for each person to do his own business, and I do not deny that it is for some to command and to manage public affairs, for others to serve as soldiers, for others to do work, for others to attend to sacred rites and to practice and teach the liberal arts and letters:

But because the affairs of the state are common to all, he who thinks that they pertain to himself does not act as a stranger but as his own, and these common concerns are not neglected by any part of the citizens without common harm, and no one who is a little more prudent, wherever he is placed, ought to be entirely free from this care.
But what shall I say about the young men devoted to literature, from whom a great part of this audience is composed?

That they in the earlier age mixed themselves too much in civil affairs, which I recently explained they did not so much by their own fault as by that of the times, so that they are unequal to counsels and deliberation and to acting prudently, and are headlong toward changing the institutions of the state which they have not yet sufficiently known, and accordingly, especially in troubled times, they should rather be held back than urged on;

Nevertheless, they ought to be imbued with love of country and to be the more inflamed by this flame, the more vehemently youthful minds are carried to any studies, and it is fitting that they be by no means careless of those things which are prosperous or adverse for the state, and especially that they take pains to be instructed in civic learning by a method both philosophical and historical, and learn to judge rightly about public affairs.

Therefore I do not hesitate to touch upon that argument which today alone offers itself and presents itself spontaneously to all, and to adapt my speech to the present circumstances of our state, not that I should enumerate any single matters, but that I should endeavor to embrace some more important heads and, what is especially characteristic of science, to refer them to some one principle.
Therefore, to begin from this starting point, I have not undertaken to say anything new to you, listeners, but something already understood by many and by myself in part in the previous year.
It was proposed.
For when in the previous reign, after so many calamities brought upon the state by foreign wars, everything seemed to need to be settled for peace;
Frederick William IV wanted this settled state to be moved:
And he has accomplished and repeatedly accomplishes what he has determined.
Moreover, the state is moved in two principal ways, either by war or in peace.
And you might wonder at the former movement, because that Platonic Socrates recognizes almost only that one.

After he described the best state, he says that in considering it, almost the same thing happened to him as usually happens to a viewer when looking at a beautiful image, whether painted or sculpted, since it is motionless, that a desire comes over him to see it moved and to undergo some contest of those things that suit the body:
