Thus they would gladly listen to someone telling how that perfect republic would wage war against other states and, in waging war, would achieve those things that are fitting for the education and learning received in that illustrious state, both in joining battle and in conducting negotiations through ambassadors with other states.
But that he wished his state to be moved almost solely by war is nothing surprising.
For he speaks of the perfect state, which has never existed anywhere among nations, nor does it exist now, nor, I think, can it ever be founded because of the character of men:

But that state, since from its very birth it has attained the highest degree, enjoys perpetual and almost divine tranquility and stability, and is neither corrupted nor improved, and lacks internal motion.
A different motion from that which Plato discusses, Frederick William excited;
For he did not receive a perfect state handed down to him, and he promised that he would preserve peace in his own age, if it were allowed, when he began his reign.
Nor indeed does he wish the state to become obsolete through peace with sluggish and inactive quiet, but to be moved and advanced the very institutions of the state.
This movement, if it is properly guided, is much more wholesome than war.

Indeed, when in earlier centuries political affairs were referred almost exclusively to external matters, to friendships and enmities among kingdoms, to treaties and peace and war, to the extension of boundaries and to acquiring territories either by arms or by agreements or by marriages, and in this science he seemed best who was most skillful and cunning in devising and deceiving, not using art but arts, while the just notion of politics, which the Greeks had established and the most excellent recent authors had cultivated, was in most states and especially in Germany already almost consigned to oblivion;

In our age at last it has been examined more keenly again, that the primary province of the political man pertains to the domestic affairs of the state, to establishing and ordering the republic, to the rights and duties of empire, magistrates, citizens, and orders:
This art, in this kingdom indeed, Frederick William IV especially recalled as if from exile and restored.
Thus he gave an inner movement to the state, and that a peaceful one, not a warlike one.
Now, how manifold and varied this agitation of states is, there is no one who does not see:
And so, about to speak on it, I enter an immense field of discussion, from which, lest I be carried far and wide, I will only touch upon a few and the nearest points, in a general way.
I will not say that one motion is of those proceeding forward, another of those going backward:

For no politician can bring this man, who makes no progress, to want it deliberately, because he wants the state to be preserved, but by a backward motion it tends to ruin and slides into destruction:

And if ever a good ruler of the state checks its course or turns it back, he does not do this so that the state should not advance, but so that it should not be hurled headlong with too violent a rush;

Just as a cautious general sounds the retreat, so that those who have advanced too far may not perish, and so that, having been recalled, they may advance again more safely at a suitable place and time.

But it is worth the effort to describe in a few words a certain natural and, as it were, lawful motion and revolution of states, which, in the fortunes of ancient republics, the simpler their principles were, the more distinctly one may perceive.
And it seems to me that from the memory of those ancient things, something is gained for judging our own affairs by looking into them as into a mirror.

For although man is by nature a social animal, not a solitary one, and not because individuals seemed to themselves too weak, by agreement, nor because some more powerful one had subdued the rest, by force and arms, men were brought together into a state, but this community of men was born rather in some way by natural instinct than founded, and from spontaneously coming together kindred stocks peoples were formed to some extent self-sufficient, and from villages cities were contracted:

Then, in the likeness of a family, that which they call the patriarchal kingdom arose, in which the king was in the place of a father, and at the same time the leader of the troops, the priest, and the judge.

These kings, in that age in which the credulous multitude easily persuaded itself that gods descended to men and that men were made gods, were regarded as sons of gods, especially of Jupiter, because Jupiter was the king of the gods, not only among the Greeks but also among the barbarians.

What of the fact that the Old Testament itself reports that mighty giants were born from the sons of God, the angels, or, as Greek Christian authors call them, the Watchers, who had intercourse with the daughters of men?

And so kings born from the gods seemed to reign with divine authority, and one or another, of course, with divine counsels, such as that Minos, the companion of great Jove, and Numa, the partner of the bed of the nymph Egeria.
Therefore, something theocratic was mixed with the kingdom:
For where God is said to reign, a priest reigns, or any prince endowed with priestly and augural auspices.
In this natural monarchy the people obeyed not unwillingly, as bees follow their queen, as the flock follows the shepherd;
By the will of the ruler and according to ancestral institutions, the state was administered without laws, if indeed this administration is to be called such:

Except that already in Homer we read that kings deliberate with a senate of nobles or heroes, who are themselves also called kings, and that the common people are called together into an assembly, so that the king may share his plans with them.
Even then the name of tyranny was unknown along with its concept, because king and tyrant were not distinguished by any fixed mark.

But that form of government could not be maintained any longer than the faith that the rulers were of divine origin and divine right, which a more refined political science, such as Aristotle's, does not recognize, lasted.
But soon the crimes of the rulers and the growing intellect of men destroyed that faith.
Hence, as I think, a threefold change of affairs arose:

For either the patriarchal dominion passed into a hereditary tyranny, which managed everything by force and cunning, or into a kingdom established by skill and laws, or into the dominion of the nobles.
Examples of this tyranny are the kingdoms of the East, such as those of the Assyrians, Persians, and Egyptians, although not even these were without some tempering of laws:

Certainly the Persians had their permanent royal judges, who could not be removed except for a crime, those interpreters of laws and institutions, and in this matter superior to the king's own judgment;

And the kings of the Egyptians were not allowed either to judge or to punish anyone according to their whim, but only according to what the laws had prescribed for each crime, and they used to proclaim themselves blessed because by this institution it had been provided that they should not stray from duty through ignorance or desire.
Moreover, it has been handed down that the judges were bound by oath by the kings of Egypt, so that they would not render an unjust verdict even at the king's command.
Among the Greeks, however, those ancestral kings were gradually bound by laws;

And not even thus, if you except the Spartan kingship divided between two and a few colonies of Sparta, did they long endure, and the power of the Laconian kings was so diminished that you would scarcely recognize a royal power.

For in most all states the royal dignity has been abolished, partly because kings had abused their power, partly because the aristocrats, especially since the strength of the common people was not yet established, were reluctant to bear that the republic was ruled by one man:

Therefore, the rule of a few succeeded the kingship, and then that of the nobles, that is, to use the definition of Aristotle and of Frederick II, the great Emperor of the Germans, of those who prevailed by the ancient virtue of their ancestors and by the ancient wealth of their families, especially by the possession of large estates:

This form of government is usually accompanied by public servitude, whether one preferred to call these slaves farmers Helots, or Penestae, or clients, or serfs bound to the soil, or by any other name whatsoever.

Then, after either a large part of the nobles ceased to be wealthy, or virtue deserted the nobles, and many who were born in a middling or obscure position began to prevail by wealth, and partly also by virtue, the empire was transferred to the rich, and the rights of citizens were defined according to census and classes:
This kind of state has the proper name of timocracy, in which the knights generally had the greatest influence:

until, not without the seditions of factions, with almost all the prerogatives of the classes abolished, the supreme power passed into the hands of the people, and all citizens, with no distinction of birth or wealth, were deemed equal in law.

It also happened that, amid the struggles between the aristocrats and the common people, a very powerful man arose who, under the pretense of protecting the people, seized a tyranny that was indeed unjust but not infrequently beneficial.
In Greece, however, few tyrannies, and those very mild, were long-lasting;
At Rome, late, with the state exhausted by civil wars, tyranny was established under the name of principate by military power.

But that absolute liberty, by which citizens of every fortune are considered equal, is not usually brought about except by an increased population, especially of artisans, and through great disturbances, particularly wars, in which the common multitude has deserved excellently of the safety of the state, by which the minds of all are inflamed, the strength of all is increased, and ambition is intensified, demanding a share of honors as a reward for virtue;
just as the Persian wars hastened democracy at Athens:
And if any state has sustained the sign of liberty, others quickly follow;

so that at almost the same time, after the Pisistratids were expelled, Clisthenes established a freer state of the republic in Athens, and the aristocratic councils of the Pythagoreans in Italy were destroyed, and kings were expelled from Rome, and soon the Ionians rebelled against the Persians.

Now this popular government, at which the ancient philosophers were greatly angry, Plato indeed considers to be one, and he says that no one gives it different names, whether the multitude rules over the wealthy violently or moderately, and again whether it carefully observes the laws or neglects them:

Most people, however, call that a popular state in which the laws prevail and in which honor is given to the laws, the magistrates, and good morals; but they call ochlocracy that in which the republic is managed according to the decrees of the people and the people decide whatever they please.
Nor can a moderate rule of the people long endure;
For the people is wont to run riot insolently and, through contempt of the laws, to slide into any kind of wrongs and to exercise tyrannical power:

Just as flatterers attend a tyrant, so leaders of the people, whom they called demagogues, attend the plebs, flattering its desires and serving its iniquity, and drawing everything away from laws and magistrates to the lust of a turbulent multitude.
From this tyranny of the plebs, the transition to the tyranny of individuals is easy.

Thus excessive liberty not only afflicts the people, while it seems free to itself, with unworthy servitude, because it obeys the unbridled license and madness of the mob and its leaders, but it also brings about the destruction of all liberty.

These, speaking with Polybius and Cicero, were nearly the cycles and revolutions among the ancients in the changes and vicissitudes of republics: this is the order of nature, according to which their condition was changed and again revolved to the same point.
There are indeed those who deny that the states of our age can be comprehended in the kinds of republics which the ancients established;

But I think that the constitutions of the more recent states, along with other very wise men, can conveniently be compared to those forms, which, if they are not now usually found pure, were also among the ancients mixed and composed in more than one way:

Therefore I do not think that even the revolutions of more recent states differ greatly from those cycles which I have described, except that the more recent kingdoms have been remarkably strengthened by a nearly new institution, to which I shall soon come.
Now I must explain with what purpose I have set these things forth, my listeners.

For since these movements and revolutions are partly necessary and useful, partly natural indeed but harmful and yet not inevitable, the supreme ruler of the state ought to take care that, as soon as the opportunity for them has come, he may lead the necessary ones by the most tranquil and expeditious way, lest they be extorted by force too late, and that the harmful ones be warded off and repelled.
Then, just as the individual elements of the state, which prevail in those individual forms, are connected with one another, so that each form contains and encloses the other;
Finally, that by the combination of these forms, as far as possible, a perfect and firm state may be established, and that it may not languish in idleness, but thrive with healthy motion.
These plans Frederick William the Fourth, as far as I can see, has set before himself;
He wants this course to be held in that motion which he has excited.

But of those forms which I have mentioned, some cannot be regarded as republics, but are degenerate forms of the just forms, and corrupted by perversity of morals, by lack of self-control, by luxury, avarice, and ambition:
Thus tyranny is a depravation of kingship, exceeding the measure;

Timocracy or plutocracy and any oligarchy are imperfect or vicious imitations of the true aristocracy, that is, the rule of the most approved and wisest men, established by selection, which I deliberately omitted above;
Finally, ochlocracy is the worst departure of popular government.

Moreover, although monarchy, the rule of the best, and popular government seem to many to be just forms of the state, nevertheless among these, to the ancient philosophers themselves, who had been educated and trained in popular states, if the individual kinds are compared with one another and one is to be approved separately by itself, legitimate monarchy has seemed the best.

Finally, both the ancient wise men and the most prudent of the more recent ones, except for a few admirers of the excessive power of either the princes or the people, arrived at the point that they especially approved of a fourth kind, which was formed and tempered from those three.
You may see certain seeds and sprouts of this constitution, quite imperfect, in the Laconian state, and even more imperfect in other ancient states;
Our age has surpassed antiquity, which discovered this kind of thing by thinking, but refined it too little by experience.

This one is the most just and the most firm, and indeed the most firm, because although it may be greatly disturbed, it is not moved by passing over into another, but it has a motion like that of the celestial spheres, returning as it were in a circle upon itself and fixed in one constant center of gravity.
This embraces the advantages of each kind under the auspices of royal authority, avoids the evils, and the fall that is prone to neighboring vices;

Indeed, from these very more corrupt forms, if you except ochlocracy, it can sometimes receive something that, mixed with good, is salutary, just as poisons, with the harmless admixture of a species, moderated, bring the most efficacious medicine.

Frederick William IV, therefore, when he had received the state prudently administered, equipped with a strong army recruited from the citizens themselves, flourishing in the industry of farmers and artisans, in commerce, revenues, literature, and the arts, because he did not want everything to be done for the people, as they say, and nothing by the people, after the slender beginnings of his most blessed father, laid the foundations of truly political institutions:
Judging the people to be of age and adult, he brought them forth into the light and led them into the wrestling school;

But because what is needed is practical experience and trial, and not everything can be foreseen at one time even by the counsel of the wisest men, he decided not to settle the state with unchangeable institutions, but he wants these very things to grow and unfold gradually, like a tree growing from a shoot and, with its root strengthened, spreading its branches.

This first of the kings of Prussia, in order that all parts of the state might act together, held those great assemblies of all provinces and orders in his own city and in his own palace, to which all citizens and foreigners turned their eyes:
We saw and heard the King not concealing his plans, but most sincerely revealing them with the great eloquence in which he excels;
And with the most free faculty of speaking granted, there followed equal zeal of the people's ambassadors, fervor, with temperance and moderation, energy and noble boldness of speech.
By these lawful contentions the state is healthfully moved, as the air by the blowing of winds;
strength is strengthened and concord is rather brought together than discord is nourished, just as different sounds, grave and acute, are mixed into a harmony;
and the difficulty of entering upon a plan is diminished, and the rashness of deciding is guarded against.
Nothing is born except from contraries.
But all agree that the reins of empire must be retained for the security and power of the republic:

and what in a patriarchal kingdom is granted to the prince by some religion, so that he might seem to reign by divine right, that in the best form of state is retained by right reason to such an extent that royal majesty, placed above any partisan struggles and subject to no one, may be sacred and inviolable;

Nor should the fact that in that same homeland, under the rule of a king, the king was regarded in the place of a parent, seem unworthy in the state of the republic which we have entered, but by ancient custom the king is even now to be judged the father of the fatherland, and with the sweetest feeling of affection and piety he is to be loved as a father by his children, and he is loved among us.

Now how much Frederick William conceded to the nobles and the other delegates of the people, so that the republic might approach more closely that which is tempered from those three kinds, is not the place of this occasion to recount and examine individually:

I have enough to have mentioned that something has been remitted from the highest power and conceded to those who are distinguished by the antiquity of their families and who are more furnished with resources:

And to the timocratic element there has been added of its own accord something from the most just aristocracy, because not the very richest are called to the office of embassy on account of their greatest wealth, but the most approved of the wealthy, chosen by the citizens.

But if some think that wealth should be assessed not only from landed property but also from movable money, which now especially are the sinews of affairs, and that in addition access to the supreme council of the state should be given to the leading men of the church and the legates of the learned colleges, since on these matters one can argue on both sides, we leave them to the judgment of future time.

However it may be, the king's wisdom, together with the most prudent men, judges that not all ranks should be removed from the state, nor that equal honor should be given to the highest and the lowest, and that rights indeed should be equalized, but according to dignity and proportion, not according to numbers, lest equality itself be most unjust.
Finally, I do not seem to myself either ridiculous or rash, if I say that there is even something popular in this kingdom.

For is it not characteristic of a popular government to lighten the burdens and misery of the poor, not by plundering the goods of the rich, but by transferring taxes especially to the wealthy and by seeking a remedy for the poverty that is growing worse and spreading more widely day by day, as the King had proposed?
Is it not popular for urban guilds, which are established by the free votes of all citizens, to be entrusted with very many things that were formerly commanded through the officials of the princes?

By this it comes about that a broad field is opened to the citizens, in which, by handling their own and lesser matters, they may make trial of their political prudence, being thereby better prepared to approach public and greater affairs.
What if that is popular, that those who practice a gainful art are admitted to the comitial embassy?
For those who are more hostile to the plebs keep these from conducting public affairs;

Just as at Thebes it was once provided by law that no one should be allowed to hold public office unless he had been free for ten years from the market of goods for sale and from a gainful occupation.
But especially I judge it to be popular that in this kingdom, by the favor of Frederick William, the greatest matters have already begun to be conducted openly.
For a monarchy tempered by no other forms, and an aristocracy's rule, love to cover everything in darkness, because they think that the principle of ruling cannot stand firm if it is rendered to all.
And clandestine judgments have especially been instruments of unjust power.
We have seen the proceedings of the assemblies communicated very quickly, very fully, and very exactly to everyone daily;
we know that it has been granted to the councils of towns to conduct their municipal affairs in the presence of the citizens;

We see that in this city, the seat of a kingdom, all trials, and especially public ones, are held with the greatest seriousness, with open doors, when the case concerns treason and high treason, and at the same time such great freedom of defense is granted to the defendants and their advocates that citizens of states which seem to themselves most free marvel and are astonished, and recognize how far in this kingdom we are from slavery, with which our detractors once used to clamor that we were oppressed.
Indeed, the rule of the most merciful king is so secure, so firmly supported by the affection of his subjects, that it can bear what in other kingdoms would seem to be intolerable.
By this one institution of speaking openly, which is most acceptable, we have undoubtedly made very great progress.
This is the pledge of just liberty;
By this most favorable movement it increases and adorns the republic.
Finally, a place in the state has been given even to eloquence, which formerly was left to the homilies of priests.
And I do not fear to declare that even the freedom of writing and of the very newspapers was greatly increased under this King, although it was not yet exempt from censorship.
For the most wise King knows that after divine providence, human affairs are moved and governed by mind and thought;

But the thought of the mind is carried freely, and its course, once it has been confirmed by the genius of the age, cannot be checked by any force, but it sweeps along those who rashly oppose it, casting them down:
Only the faults, which are accustomed to cling even to good undertakings, must be corrected, and excessive impulses must be moderated and restrained.

By this path Frederick William forms and drives the citizens to aid the common safety and to overcome the allurements of idle leisure and pleasures, and he brings it about that those who previously, as happens especially in kingdoms, were careless of the republic and sought virtue in a life far removed from such cares, now turn virtue to public use and exercise it in their occupations, and that each citizen in his own place strives with his counsels and labors to render the state safer and more excellent.

But now the sails must be furled, listeners, and it is not permitted to range more widely, especially since after the very pleasing veneration of the royal name, which is common to all, both for me and for my successor there remain to be said and done those things which properly pertain to this school of letters.
And I seem to myself to have accomplished what I wanted;

And I especially desire, being fully aware of my own weakness, that what I have said may seem to you to have been discussed plausibly and appropriately to the occasion and to the dignity of the matters.

Certainly ungrateful would he be who does not acknowledge how many and how great are the things that we owe to the wisdom, kindness, industry, and unwearied zeal and care of Frederick William IV for accomplishing everything that is best in the state, and who measures these things rather by his own or anyone else's particular plans and wishes than by those things which the best King has actually accomplished.

Let us therefore take care, listeners most distinguished in every rank, each in his own place, that we both feel and, as far as it can be done by the younger generation, repay to Frederick William IV the gratitude owed for benefits conferred upon the whole state and upon each individual, and that the harmony and safety of the republic and the majesty, splendor, and power of the kingdom may be perpetuated and strengthened.

Finally, pray with me to God, the Best and Greatest, that He may protect and preserve, as long as possible, His most devout and piously devoted worshipper, adorned with so many and such great virtues, and the author to us of so many blessings, the most merciful King, together with the august Queen and the entire royal house.
I have spoken.
